explanation: The title page identifies the author, title, and “v2, November 2026.” This version number belongs to the theory text; it does not replace the software release number, installed skill version, or date on which research materials were produced.

v2 preserves the first edition’s existing subsection numbers and adds §2.4.3, §2.14, §6.10.1, §7.6.1, §14.4.1, and §14.9.1. Readers can continue in the original order or begin with these six entry points to learn the new evidential and choice boundaries.

This reading site’s source text and current section locations come from v2. boundaries: Constructed conditional counterexample: even if a book is titled “A Reliable Prediction Method,” its title does not prove its predictions reliable. Likewise, this book’s title cannot certify its empirical applicability. This is a logical boundary between naming and proof, not a report that this book has actually failed.

This page contains no formulas, experiments, historical events, or numerical results. No real-world case is therefore assigned, and “v2, November 2026” is not interpreted as an independently verified publication date.

Interpretive connection: the thematic terms correspond to the methodological scope specified later, so later sections can explain the reading direction, provided this is identified as interpretation across sections.

questionAnswers.question: If the title and authorship have both been checked, can we write “this method has been proved applicable to every organization”?
questionAnswers.answer: No. The former only confirms how the manuscript identifies itself; the latter claims effectiveness across objects and requires the corresponding scope and comparative evidence.

questionAnswers.question: Does “bounded action” mean that without execution authority one can only list questions and cannot recommend an option?
questionAnswers.answer: No. An analytical recommendation can be completed when its grounds, value premises, and costs are disclosed; actual adoption and execution require separate checks of protection and authorization.

front-scope.title: Scope and Reading Approach
front-scope.lead: A question can first receive a local answer; the corresponding additional responsibilities arise only when the inquiry turns to the future, recommendation, or execution.
explanation: Source location: complete Chinese theory, lines 9–18, headed “Scope and Reading Approach.” Short quotations, translated from Chinese: “Understanding can be an endpoint” (line 13) and “cannot establish one another” (line 15). This unit has no independent webpage anchor; source/FRONT.md, lines 9–18, contains the verbatim Chinese source. The central questions are which objects the framework studies, which outputs it allows, and how to avoid quietly treating one answer as a different qualification. [T-scope]

The first paragraph contains two levels. The objects of study are objects capable of leaving empirical materials, together with their structures, operation, and state changes; a specific judgment must be bound to this object, question, time window, and available material. Allowing the study of natural processes, technology, and the human world does not mean a common empirical law covering them has already been provided. “Broadly conceived” describes which questions may be raised; “the conditions of this case” determines how much can actually be answered. A formally elegant unifying statement may still fail to explain the differences that matter in a particular domain. [T-scope; T-domain]

The second level concerns connections between judgments. Records supporting a fact do not necessarily identify a mechanism; a grounded mechanism explanation does not establish accurate future prediction; an outcome worth pursuing does not give us the right to impose costs on others. The source lists representation, evidence, mechanism, resources, and permissions as different connection conditions because a break may occur at different points: omitted distinctions require a richer representation; unclear causation requires discriminating evidence; insufficient capacity requires changed scheduling or resources; insufficient permission cannot be repaired by another paragraph of explanation that manufactures execution authority. [T-scope; T-connection]

Distinguishing the universal layer from the human specialization prevents human purposes, commitments, and responsibility from being projected onto natural processes. Water flowing through a pipe permits discussion of flow, resistance, and delay; using the same word “effect” does not mean the water consented to bear responsibility. This is a teaching boundary for concept use, not a measured claim about a particular water project. Nor may human action be reduced in the opposite direction to an object without intention: where the question involves meaning, willingness, rights, or decision-making authority, the relevant materials and normative reasons must be retained. [T-scope; T-human]

Joint representations of actors and multiple circles are conditional tools. Their positive value lies in retaining roles, resources, interfaces, and clocks hidden by a single summary; their cost is additional measurement, privacy, explanation, and maintenance burden. The source does not require the largest model for every question. If a local technical model already sufficiently answers the failure question, adding family, cultural, and institutional layers may provide no necessary information. If the question truly concerns conflicts among care, work, and public services, a single work indicator may omit a crucial constraint. The choice depends on distinctions necessary for the task, not the model’s size. [T-scope; T-intro]

The four outputs are not an automatic escalation pipeline. Explanation accounts for observed phenomena and grounded mechanisms; projection presents possible paths under conditions; conditional foresight must specify targets, horizons, baselines, and failure conditions before outcomes; bounded choice additionally discloses normative premises, costs, and affected positions. Real-world adoption or execution has separate requirements for protection, review, and authorization. One may finish with explanation or retain other grounded answers while one branch remains unresolved. Not making a prediction is not a failure of explanation, and completing an explanation is not successful prediction. [T-scope; T-outputs]

The final paragraph supplies a reading arrangement, not additional empirical evidence: the first two parts explain methods and responsibilities; Parts 3–6 develop universal analysis; Parts 7–11 address human experience and dynamic processes; Parts 12–16 address foresight, choice, tools, and governance; the appendices supply interfaces, an index, proofs, and domain entry points. This grouping differs in emphasis from the four-part grouping in §1.2. Both are navigation aids, not conflicting theoretical layers. [T-scope; T-route]

The most important room for criticism here is “who decides which distinctions are necessary.” An analyst’s target may be too narrow, treating already affected people as irrelevant background. Therefore examine whether the question itself omits protection, distribution, or the practical problems of those concerned, while also avoiding endlessly adding variables for every possible question. A reasonable approach states the current task and exclusions and reopens review when the use changes. Later passages support this interpretation, but it does not prove that the book’s tools have already resolved this tradeoff in actual use. [T-connection; T-evaluation]

distinctions.leftText: Already sufficiently grounded within a specified question’s scope.
distinctions.rightText: Other questions of mechanism, distribution, longer-term outcomes, or authorization may remain unanswered.

distinctions.leftText: Develops paths showing what would happen if the conditions held.
distinctions.rightText: A future judgment with a target, horizon, baseline, and evaluation specified before the outcome.

distinctions.leftText: Can be understood and have its reasons openly compared.
distinctions.rightText: Also require specific protection, review, resources, and permissions.

boundaries: Constructed conditional counterexample: if the only question is how much water two buckets contain in total, an accurate total may suffice; if the question becomes which bucket will overflow first, the distribution is also needed. This counters both “more complex is better” and “one summary always suffices.” It does not measure real buckets or estimate accident risk.

Formal proofs and teaching constructions can explain why an inference holds or fails; they cannot establish that a real object meets its premises. Nor can a real case prove a universally quantified mathematical proposition.

Do not present this paragraph’s design commitments as verified effects. Reader-comprehension testing has not been conducted, and the framework has not been compared with specialist methods on actual time, errors, or net benefit.

argumentSteps: Premise: different outputs answer different questions, so their required inputs and evidential conditions may differ.

Explicit reasoning: moving from a narrower conclusion to a wider use without adding the conditions leaves the additional content without independent grounds; representation, mechanism, resources, and permissions especially cannot substitute for one another.
Positive conclusion: a bounded answer can be given when the distinctions required by the current task are retained and evidence covers them; explaining the whole world first is unnecessary.
Limiting condition: when the target, object, time window, operations, or affected positions change, the original answer cannot be silently transferred.

Evidential responsibility: textual interpretation returns to the source; empirical effects to domain materials; formal conclusions to explicit premises and proofs; recommendations disclose values and costs; execution separately checks permissions and protection.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: a task changes from the average to the local
teachingExamples.text: Let the two pairs of numbers be (0,20) and (10,10), both with mean 10. If the question asks only for the mean, the representation 10 answers exactly. If it asks whether any number exceeds 15, the first answer is yes and the second no, which the mean cannot distinguish. Adding only the maximum answers the latter question; no person’s personality or social relations need be added. This artificial construction cannot prove a real system’s accident rate or that the entire framework is more effective than simple arithmetic.
teachingExamples.assumptions: The two pairs are teaching assumptions; the target threshold is fixed at 15; only these two listed states are compared.
teachingExamples.boundary: Whether mean plus maximum remains sufficient after changing the task or admissible operations requires another check; this example establishes no real-world causation.

counterexamples.text: Constructed conditional counterexample: if the only question is how much water two buckets contain in total, an accurate total may suffice; if the question becomes which bucket will overflow first, the distribution is also needed. This counters both “more complex is better” and “one summary always suffices.” It does not measure real buckets or estimate accident risk.
counterexamples.effect: Limits an overstrong reading that infers real-world effectiveness directly from text identity, contents, or reading arrangements; it does not deny the limited uses explicitly proposed by the source.

questionAnswers.question: A documented failure has been accurately explained, but no future judgment was registered. How should this be reported?
questionAnswers.answer: A bounded explanation of the failure may be reported; verified predictive capability cannot be claimed on that basis. Explanation can be complete within its task boundary.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source lines 13–15; §1.1 and §12.1.

questionAnswers.question: If the same total-quantity material answers the total-budget question, can it establish that everyone receives equal resources?
questionAnswers.answer: No. Total quantity and distribution are different targets, unless additional conditions retain the distribution or permit a valid inference about it.
questionAnswers.basis: The connection conditions in Chinese source line 11; §1.11 and F1 task recovery.

questionAnswers.question: If analysis finds higher average benefits for an option, may it immediately implement it on behalf of those affected?
questionAnswers.answer: No. Normative premises and distributional costs must also be disclosed, and protection, review, and authorization matching the specific action must be obtained; average benefit cannot establish those conditions.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source line 15; Part 14.

front-contents.title: Contents by Part
front-contents.lead: The contents map the questions; reaching an actual conclusion still requires meeting its own burden of argument in the corresponding chapter.
explanation: Chinese source location: lines 19—67 of the complete theory, headed “Contents by Part.” A short quotation, translated here from the Chinese explanation, is “does not presuppose that the four empirical question families suffice to deduce all domain knowledge” (line 64). This unit contains 21 entry points for parts, appendices, and references, followed by a methodological commitment; that paragraph must not be dropped as an irrelevant endnote. The part_1 anchor on line 66 continues navigation into the next part. The contents are a checkable text, not a checklist of completed research. [T-contents]

The contents can be read as follows: the first two parts begin with objects and evidential responsibilities; Part 3 supplies a shared descriptive grammar; Part 4 separates empirical questions, the use of results, and mathematical proof; Parts 5 and 6 examine cross-scale conversions and operational processes. The language of “who is being discussed, on what grounds, and how change occurs” is established before more specific human objects are considered. The sequence supports teaching, but reading an earlier chapter does not automatically confer the empirical conclusions of later ones. [T-contents]

Parts 7 through 11 connect human meaning, uptake, actor states, circle relations, and event projection. The human collective prototypes in Part 8 must especially be kept separate from individual states in Part 9: a collective’s S0—S6 are not personality maturity levels, and an individual’s slow variables are not the collective’s stages. Part 10 retains the different relations among circles; Part 11 then develops conditional paths along channels and clocks. This is guidance for reading the map; specific criteria must still be learned section by section. [T-human；T-prototypes；T-actor]

Parts 12 through 16 address judgments about the future, option choice, tool interfaces, norms, intervention, and governance of the framework. They do not certify the explanations in the first half of the book; they add responsibilities: foresight must be capable of failure, recommendations must disclose values, execution needs specific permission, and tools and the framework itself must permit correction, restriction, replacement, and retirement. The governance chapter also applies to the use of these explanations: complete files establish only the corresponding delivery, not that readers understand them or that real tasks have benefited. [T-contents；T-evaluation]

Appendix A contains the complete human-variable interfaces. A support route must be read together with its conditions and ceilings, rather than extracting only favorable fields. Appendix B indexes identifiers to help locate material; it does not replace definitions. Appendix C contains self-contained mathematical arguments for checking formal premises and derivations. Appendix D offers entry points into 32 domains to connect questions with professional methods, not to add up 32 domains as evidence that the theory is correct. The references list original works that can be revisited; locating a bibliographic entry is not the same as checking its contents. [T-contents；T-appendices]

The basic commitment following the contents rejects a tempting reading: treating G1—G4 as a few natural axioms from which all domain conclusions can be deduced layer by layer. The source says it offers a checkable analytical language and conditional argument; formal propositions, instance evidence, and the effects of using a method have different standards. It is therefore reasonable to expect help locating the conditions for connections, rather than a replacement for physics, history, law, or other professional research. Allowing a simpler, sufficient domain method to take over is an explicit boundary of the book, not a failure of reading. [T-contents；T-bone]

A strongest objection is this: if everything must be checked separately, do the contents merely add procedures? Promises cannot answer that question, nor should it lead us to deny the specific formal results or conceptual distinctions already given. Ask separately which distinctions this task needs, whether a streamlined domain method can preserve them, and whether an additional method reduces substantive errors enough to justify its cost. Without a comparison, universal conclusions of “useful” or “useless” should both remain open. [T-evaluation]

boundaries: Self-constructed conditional counterexample: a contents page listing “randomized experiments” does not mean the book has completed an experiment; listing “governance” does not mean actual use is already safe. This limits the unconditional leap from headings to achievements.

This unit explains only the contents and its methodological commitment; it does not develop all 388 subsequent numbered sections here. Subsequent units must each be delivered independently; this reading map cannot stand in for them.
Allowing a simpler method to take over at the end of the contents does not prove the framework useless; whether there is a net gain requires the corresponding comparison.
questions: Does reading only Appendix B’s glossary count as mastering every contract?
If one case supports a G2 channel effect, can we say that all 32 domains listed in the contents have been validated?
If a sufficient professional method already answers the current question, must the full multi-circle model still be applied?
argumentSteps: Direct material: the titles and order of the 21 links can be checked in Chinese source lines 21—61; the methodological commitment after the contents is on line 64.

Structural explanation: the chapter sequence develops objects and evidence, universal analysis, human objects, foresight and action, and governance in turn; the appendices supplement the text and provide paths for checking back.

Prohibited inference: complete chapters do not establish sufficient empirical coverage; the existence of formal proofs does not show that real objects satisfy their premises; support for a case does not establish a benefit to users.

Positive conclusion: the contents can serve as a route for locating material and, together with each chapter’s explicit conditions, help select an entry point. They do not replace the subsequent main text or professional research.

Method evaluation: comparisons among the framework, streamlined methods, and domain methods should keep the task and necessary protection commensurate. Without actual comparisons, do not certify overall effects as successful or failed.

counterexamples.text: Self-constructed conditional counterexample: a contents page listing “randomized experiments” does not mean the book has completed an experiment; listing “governance” does not mean actual use is already safe. This limits the unconditional leap from headings to achievements.
counterexamples.effect: Limits an overstrong reading that infers real-world effectiveness directly from text identity, contents, or reading arrangements; it does not deny the limited uses explicitly proposed by the source.

questionAnswers.question: Does reading only Appendix B’s glossary count as mastering every contract?
questionAnswers.answer: No. Appendix B is for navigation; definitions, permitted conclusions, and boundaries remain in the corresponding main text. For example, G3’s narrow historical increment cannot be understood from the word “history” alone.
questionAnswers.basis: The contents entry and the opening of Appendix B.

questionAnswers.question: If one case supports a G2 channel effect, can we say that all 32 domains listed in the contents have been validated?
questionAnswers.answer: No. Support for one instance’s object and window does not expand to every domain merely by following the contents. The number 32 is a navigational scope, not a count of independent validations.
questionAnswers.basis: The methodological commitment after the contents and §1.12.

questionAnswers.question: If a sufficient professional method already answers the current question, must the full multi-circle model still be applied?
questionAnswers.answer: No. A sufficient, simpler method may take over while retaining necessary distinctions, sources, and boundaries of use. This does not rule out a joint model when there is a genuine need for one.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source line 64; §1.11 and §16.24.

intro-01-part.title: Part 1: Reading Guide
intro-01-part.lead: First ask what needs explaining, then decide how much structure is needed; a complex model’s value lies in preserving necessary distinctions.
explanation: Chinese source location: lines 68—73 of the complete original, headed “Part 1: Reading Guide,” with the in-source entry #part_1. A short quotation, translated here from the Chinese explanation, is “complexity cannot substitute for explanatory capability” (line 72). The issue is the framework’s use and modeling choices: how to make explanations mutually checkable without expanding every question into the largest possible joint model. [T-intro]

“Working language” can be understood as a set of conventions for expression that enable shared questioning: which object, what state, which conditions, relations and events are being discussed, what materials support a judgment, and where inquiry should stop. It can help different explanations reveal their actual disagreements, but merely rewriting a story in technical terms adds no evidence. Whether a mechanism holds still depends on observations that distinguish competing explanations; here the source states a methodological aim, not an experiment showing that the aim has been achieved. [T-intro; T-domain]

Connecting objects, conditions, actors, events and consequences does not require every object to have intentions. Analysis of natural or technical systems can discuss components and changes; experience, meaning and decision-making positions need to enter when people are involved. A shared grammar can distinguish “different surrounding conditions” from “conflicting explanations.” Its risk is excessive abstraction that loses domain-specific variables or distinctions important to the people concerned. Thus “checking against one another” requires retaining sources and domains of applicability, not erasing differences with uniform vocabulary. [T-intro; T-human]

A joint state places the actors and multiple circles actually involved in the present question within one representation. It does not merge everyone into an average person or arrange every circle as nested dolls from small to large. Parallel relations place distinct positions alongside one another; nesting places one object within another object's boundary; overlap involves shared members or partial states; bridging establishes connections through interfaces; competition must specify the resource or decision-making position being contested; a temporary circle may form around a particular event alone. The source only lists possible relations here; whether they hold must still be checked against the object and relation criteria in Parts 5 and 10. [T-intro; T-circles]

The technical failure and care conflict in the source illustrate two starting points. They must not be expanded into “every technical problem needs only a local model” or “every family problem requires a multilayer model.” The key is whether the current task omits necessary distinctions. For example, a failure's causes may also involve maintenance schedules and responsibility interfaces, whereas a question about the exact time of one appointment may not require modeling the person's entire life. The question's boundary can change which variables are necessary; a domain label alone must not determine complexity. [T-intro]

The justification for added complexity is to explain which answer becomes distinguishable through the additional information. If two actual situations collapse into the same representation in a simple model but require different judgments, there is a specific reason to add information. If additional variables do not change whether the current question is answerable but increase privacy and maintenance costs, consider omitting them. No universal algorithm for a “minimal model” is given here, and analysts must not decide alone that distinctions important to affected people are unimportant. The task being asked and its exclusions must themselves be open to challenge. [T-intro; T-connection; T-cost]

In actual practice, complex models and simple baselines can serve different roles; see the NHC case in this section. It supports only a limited observation: a model's role depends on the task, and retaining simple tools does not mean research is backward. It does not show that Xikari has improved weather forecasting, nor require every variable in a professional model to be translated into the book's terminology. [R-NHC; T-domain]

The strongest objection is whether requiring proof of each variable's usefulness would remove unknown mechanisms too early. A reasonable response is not to retain known factors alone, but to mark exploratory variables as candidates, state what they would distinguish, the cost of obtaining them and when to reconsider them. Exploration awaiting use must remain distinct from explanations already supported. Retain local answers that are currently sufficient while allowing changes of purpose or counterevidence to trigger expansion of the model. [T-intro; T-connection]
argumentSteps: Textual premise: line 70 of the Chinese source states the purpose of the working language; line 72 explicitly makes joint representation an optional tool rather than a universal obligation.

Inferential connection: if the current task requires different answers for two states but the representation merges them completely, that representation alone cannot guarantee a distinction; add information relevant to the difference or narrow the task.

Positive conclusion: a local model that preserves the necessary distinctions for the current question can complete a local explanation; a joint model acquires a specific justification only when cross-circle relations actually need to be addressed.

Limiting conditions: necessary distinctions are relative to the question, window, admissible operations and affected positions; today's sufficiency must not be used to establish sufficiency for every future purpose.

Evidential responsibility: the source supports its stated textual purpose; domain materials are needed to establish whether variables and channels are real and alternative models are better; a mathematical construction verifies logic only within its explicit assumptions.

distinctions.leftText: Makes objects, evidence and stopping points open to questioning.
distinctions.rightText: Putting materials into technical terms does not automatically identify causation.

distinctions.leftText: Preserves multiple relevant positions and relations for the question.
distinctions.rightText: May eliminate differences between members, interfaces and clocks.

distinctions.leftText: The number of variables, layers or model expressions.
distinctions.rightText: The ability to preserve differences relevant to the current question and be tested against evidence.

distinctions.leftText: Has an explicit question to distinguish but has not yet gained support.
distinctions.rightText: Has relevant identification materials while remaining subject to boundaries.

boundaries: Boundary in the source: line 72 of the Chinese source already gives a situation in which a local technical explanation may suffice, directly limiting the strong reading that “every question must be made multi-circle.”

Constructed conditional counterexample: a model that knows only the sum of two quantities can answer a question about the total but cannot say which quantity is larger; requiring everyone's psychological profile to answer the total may also be unnecessary. Representational sufficiency changes with the task asked.

“Retain the simple method first” is not an excuse to reject complex objects. If rights, distribution or different time windows are hidden by a simple representation, they must not be treated as nonexistent merely because they are difficult to measure.
This section does not measure the framework's net benefit relative to domain methods; describing its practical effectiveness as established would exceed the materials.
questions: A model lists 20 more variables but does not explain which judgments they change. Can their greater number alone establish that it is better?
The local evidence for a technical failure is sufficient, but maintenance permissions remain disputed. Should the supported explanation of the failure be revoked?
In the mathematical example, can the total 10 answer whether the first quantity exceeds 4?

caseLinks.title: Actual practice: why NHC retains simple forecast models

caseNotes.title: Actual practice: why NHC retains simple forecast models
caseNotes.text: DeMaria et al.'s 2022 paper explains that NHC's 2021 tropical cyclone model suite includes simple statistical models and uses some models as baselines for comparing forecast skill. This shows that simple models may have explicit responsibilities; it does not establish that simple models are always better than complex models. [R-NHC]
caseNotes.sourceLabel: DeMaria et al. (2022), The National Hurricane Center Tropical Cyclone Model Guidance Suite
caseNotes.sourceLocator: Printed p. 2141 (PDF p. 1), abstract and the first two paragraphs of §1; p. 2143 (PDF p. 3), first paragraph of §2 on CLIPER5's use as a baseline.
caseNotes.boundary: The observation concerns how professional practice assigns roles to tools of different complexity. It is not designated as a validated Xikari instance and does not establish which models are better across all domains.

teachingExamples.title: Mathematical teaching construction: the same summary can be sufficient or insufficient
teachingExamples.text: Let states x=(2,8) and y=(5,5). If only s=a+b is retained, both become 10. If question q₁ asks for the sum, g₁(s)=s recovers the answer exactly. If q₂ asks whether the first quantity exceeds 4, the answer is no for x and yes for y; no deterministic function receiving only the same s=10 can give both different correct answers. Adding the first quantity a suffices to answer q₂ without recovering other information irrelevant to that question. This is a logical example involving two artificial states, not measured error or evidence of social causation.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Only the two stated numerical quantities are considered; the questions and threshold 4 are fixed; the summary retains only the sum and implies no additional information.
teachingExamples.boundary: Adding noise, changing the question or permitting intervention requires a separate check; this does not establish that a particular real-world simplified model must fail.

counterexamples.text: Boundary in the source: line 72 of the Chinese source already gives a situation in which a local technical explanation may suffice, directly limiting the strong reading that “every question must be made multi-circle.”
counterexamples.effect: Excludes the interpretation that the largest possible joint model is unconditionally required.

counterexamples.text: Constructed conditional counterexample: a model that knows only the sum of two quantities can answer a question about the total but cannot say which quantity is larger; requiring everyone's psychological profile to answer the total may also be unnecessary. Representational sufficiency changes with the task asked.
counterexamples.effect: Shows that representational sufficiency depends on the task, not on abstract complexity.

questionAnswers.question: A model lists 20 more variables but does not explain which judgments they change. Can their greater number alone establish that it is better?
questionAnswers.answer: No. The necessary distinctions retained and the corresponding evidence must be specified, with information and procedural costs considered; the number of variables does not certify explanatory capability.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source, line 72.

questionAnswers.question: The local evidence for a technical failure is sufficient, but maintenance permissions remain disputed. Should the supported explanation of the failure be revoked?
questionAnswers.answer: Not necessarily. Retain the supported local explanation and handle the permission issue separately; revise the explanation actually affected if the dispute supplies new material about the failure mechanism.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source, lines 70–72; §1.1's distinction between outputs and permissions.

questionAnswers.question: In the mathematical example, can the total 10 answer whether the first quantity exceeds 4?
questionAnswers.answer: No. x and y have the same summary but different answers; additional distinctions or a restricted question domain are needed.
questionAnswers.basis: The two-state counterexample in this section's mathematical construction.

figures.alt: The current question branches into a local model and a multi-circle joint model. Both must state the necessary distinctions retained, the evidence and the costs; check again when the target changes.
figures.caption: A responsibility diagram created by the explanatory author. The two branches are comparable representations, not real-world observations, mandatory stages or a ranking of merit.

intro-01-part.diagramBrief: Figure 1 starts from the same “current question” and places local and joint representations in parallel. Necessary distinctions and costs are checked below both; higher complexity is not ranked as superior.

applicability.reason: This unit concerns methodological judgment. Actual sources support only the listed facts; the diagram and teaching construction each retain their own status.

openQuestions: Comparing the actual net benefits of two representations requires a concrete task, a common evaluation target and evidence of actual use; this task has not performed that evaluation.

1.1.title: 1.1 Four Types of Output and Eight Layers of Responsibility
1.1.lead: Separate “has been explained,” “may happen,” “judged in advance” and “what should be done” to identify which responsibility is still missing.
explanation: Source location: Chinese source lines 74–90, titled “1.1 Four Types of Output and Eight Layers of Responsibility”; this task's assembly entry is /theory/part-01#section-1-1 (an established internal route name, not a claim that the website has been published). Short quotation, translated from the Chinese: “Predictive capability and decision-making power are established separately” (line 89). This section does two different things: distinguishes four outputs by the question asked and eight layers of responsibility by the work required. [T-11]

Explanation addresses phenomena that have already occurred. It must clarify objects, relations, conditions and possible mechanisms, retaining competing accounts that cannot currently be distinguished. Explanation is neither finding a unique root cause nor merely recounting sequence: one event following another requires examination of channels and comparison with other explanations before it can become a causal account. An explanation may be complete at a supported boundary without continuing to prediction or action. [T-11; T-explain]

Projection starts from explicit states and conditions and develops possible paths after an event. Its direct product is conditional branching such as “if A and B persist, C may follow; if B fails, the path turns toward D.” Without supporting materials, drawing a path must not be taken to mean its probability is known. Branches, unknowns, residuals and stopping conditions are part of the content, not defects waiting to be hidden. The original table lists Parts 9–11 as the main entry points but does not prohibit mechanism material from other chapters. [T-11]

Conditional foresight goes further by making fallible judgments about outcomes that have not yet occurred. The target clarifies what is being measured, the horizon specifies when to evaluate it, a simple baseline supplies the comparator, registration makes visible what was known at the time, and checking and write-back after the outcome permit correction. “More reasonable to expect” here does not select a preferred future by wish; it judges future outcomes under given conditions. Completed registration does not make a prediction correct, and one correct prediction does not automatically establish stable predictive capability. [T-11; T-forecast]

Bounded choice asks whether to act, wait, probe, exit or do nothing. It needs facts, but also value premises, rights claims, the price to be paid and affected positions. Waiting and inaction can have consequences and must not be treated as zero-risk references. A recommendation for deliberation can be formed when its reasons are adequately disclosed without waiting for the analyst to hold execution authority; actual adoption and execution separately require checks of protections, review, lawful authorization and action ceilings. If something called advice actually enters sanctions or eligibility decisions, it must bear responsibilities appropriate to its foreseeable use. [T-11; T-choice]

The original table's four rows connect as follows. Explanation mainly enters through Parts 2–8 and must not independently acquire predictive eligibility or authority to act. Projection mainly enters through Parts 9–11 and must retain branches, unknowns, residuals and stopping conditions. Conditional foresight enters Part 12, registering before outcomes and evaluating and writing back afterward. Bounded choice enters Parts 12–15, constrained by norms, protections, evidence, authorization and action ceilings. “Main entry points” aid navigation; they do not restrict each output to citing only those chapters. [T-11]

Within the eight layers, U is the universal structural core: it helps clarify general questions about objects, states, relations and effects. It does not first certify all reality as an established structure, still less require every U primitive to be used. S handles cross-scale and cross-circle transformations, checking what is retained and lost when representations, boundaries or relations change. U answers which basic grammar describes the object; S asks whether the current question remains preserved when the mode of description or circle relations change. Neither substitutes for the other. [T-11; T-US]

H is the human structured world, adding human distinctions involving experience, meaning, intention, commitment and responsibility; these must not be projected back onto water flows or machines as their own moral will. A concerns actor states, examining slow, intermediate-timescale and fast variables and distinguishing personality candidates from situations; one behavior does not suffice to fix personality directly. MC is the multi-circle joint state, retaining multiple members, roles, interfaces, resources and asynchronous clocks without treating collective prototypes as personal ranks. H, A and MC handle human adaptation, individual states and joint objects respectively; they are not three kinds of people of higher value. [T-11; T-human; T-AMC]

P concerns path projection and conditional foresight, handling conditional paths, branching, clocks and the registration and evaluation of future judgments. One responsibility layer contains two outputs without erasing their distinction. I is the interface between inference and reality, checking eligibility and ceilings when connecting signals, evidence, judgments and action; having data does not mean the data support the current conclusion. N concerns normative choice and authorization, making values, protections, decision-making positions, stopping and remedies explicit. N is not a license calculated from prediction accuracy, and I is not a procedure automatically completed by possessing tools. [T-11; T-PIN]

The four kinds of output specify what kind of answer is to be delivered; the eight layers of responsibility specify which parts of the work must be undertaken. They are not a compulsory 4-by-8 form, still less a ladder of development from U to N. A local explanation of a natural process need not use personality or multi-circle interfaces; a recommendation concerning resource allocation must nevertheless address affected people and normative responsibilities even if it comes from a technical model. One layer of responsibility may support several kinds of output, and one output may depend on work in several layers. [T-11]

This section and §1.4's distinction between explanation, diagnosis, normative choice, and intervention are not two mutually exclusive four-part classifications. §1.1 distinguishes explanation, projection, conditional foresight, and bounded choice by the question each output answers; §1.4 distinguishes understanding, locating risks, normative reasons, and actual action more explicitly. Diagnosis may use explanation and projection, whereas intervention involves real-world actions. The items must not be forced into one-to-one correspondence merely because both lists contain four. [T-11；T-explain]

The additional observation in the case concerns when information becomes available: the same meteorological information is not equally available for retrospective explanation and advance forecasting. Retrospective analysis may reasonably use the best information obtained afterward, provided its status is clear. Presenting that result as something that could already have been predicted at the time crosses the output boundary. This does not mean all historical testing is invalid; it requires preserving the distinction between what information was available at which time. [R-NHC]

One criticism is that actual work often combines explanation, prediction, and choice: might classification fragment the task? Its value lies in preventing evidential responsibilities from being conflated, not in requiring four separate documents. The work may proceed within one paragraph or model, provided the additional conditions are identified. Conversely, requiring every ordinary conversation to complete all eight layers would turn the method into a burden. The source expressly allows different stopping points, and later sections require the intensity of review to vary with use and risk. [T-11；T-cost]
argumentSteps: Premise: the four questions require different content. Past facts, future branches, evaluable foresight, and normative choice do not share all the same conditions for establishment.

Inferential connection: possessing evidence for an explanation does not thereby provide future information, normative premises, or real-world permissions. Adding a conclusion requires supplying its dependencies, rather than borrowing the credibility of an existing conclusion.

Formal non-entailment: cases can be constructed in which an explanation holds but a forecast is unregistered, a forecast is accurate but an action exceeds authority, or a recommendation is grounded but not yet authorized. None of these three automatic transitions therefore holds. This does not deny transitions made under the requisite conditions.

Positive conclusion: choose an output according to the task and complete it within its boundary. The eight layers help locate omissions by dividing responsibilities; they are not a hierarchy of value or a common measure of maturity.

Evidential responsibility: explanation checks materials and competing mechanisms; projection checks states, channels, and branching conditions; foresight additionally checks advance registration and subsequent evaluation; choice additionally checks normative reasons and distribution; real-world action then checks protection, review, and authorization.

Limits of applicability: this section classifies methods and argues for their responsibilities. It does not prove that any specific object is necessarily predictable, or that adopting these classifications has already improved decision quality.

distinctions.leftText: Explains past phenomena and possible mechanisms, while allowing competing accounts to remain.
distinctions.rightText: Addresses a future target and evaluation fixed before the outcome; it is not obtained automatically from explanation.

distinctions.leftText: Unfolds possible branches under assumed conditions.
distinctions.rightText: Requires appropriate statistical models, information, and calibration; it must not be inferred from the number of arrows.

distinctions.leftText: Material for deliberation that discloses facts, values, and the price to be paid.
distinctions.rightText: Must be established separately for the specific action, affected positions, and scope.

distinctions.leftText: Specify what kind of answer the task seeks.
distinctions.rightText: Identify the work to be undertaken; they are not levels of maturity on a single dimension.

distinctions.leftText: May study the past using explicitly identified information obtained afterward.
distinctions.rightText: Its genuine eligibility as foresight can be evaluated only against the information available at the time.

boundaries: Constructed conditional counterexample: suppose a teaching device can operate only on the stated power supply, has no backup supply, and the interruption has been verified to have reached its power input. Together with the power-cut and shutdown records, these mechanism conditions support the explanation of this shutdown, but still do not establish when the next power cut will occur. An established explanation alongside unresolved foresight is not a logical contradiction.

Constructed conditional counterexample: accurately knowing another person's travel schedule does not give someone the power to restrict that person's movement. The non-equivalence of predictive content and permission to execute an action does not depend on the prediction being wrong.

Constructed conditional counterexample: a grounded comparison of options may be submitted for deliberation even when its author has no authority to execute them. If it is actually used to deny another person's eligibility, however, calling it merely a recommendation must not be used to evade review and authorization.

The eight layers concern responsibilities. Natural objects that do not involve people should not be forcibly assigned personality, consent, or normative responsibility. The normative responsibilities of the human users concerned may be analyzed separately.

A single accurate prediction, complete registration documents, or a complete diagram cannot independently certify a method's effectiveness. The actual case here supports only a specific distinction between information sources; it does not establish the effectiveness of the book's theory as a whole.
questions: Does drawing three future paths alone mean that conditional foresight has been completed?
If predictions are repeatedly accurate, does that permit making decisions for the people concerned?
For a question confined to a local technical fault, must A and MC in the eight layers be filled out completely?

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: four answers concerning the same event
teachingExamples.text: Suppose a simulated server room shut down last night, with these explicit teaching assumptions: the equipment can run only while the stated circuit continuously supplies power, no backup power exists, and the interruption has traveled through that circuit to the equipment's input. Together with the shutdown record for the same period, these mechanism conditions support the explanation of this shutdown; two merely simultaneous records would not suffice. Why the power cut itself occurred remains unknown. A projection could state, “If power is interrupted again and backup power is insufficient, service may be interrupted again”; this supplies no probability of occurrence. Foresight additionally requires the target, conditions, and baseline for the next 24 hours to be specified beforehand. The present setup does not provide enough information, so a probability must not be invented. Bounded choice may compare the price of maintenance, waiting, and a reversible probe, but whether another person's service may be cut off requires the corresponding permissions and protections. The whole scenario is a teaching construction, not an actual incident report.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Dependence on the power supply, the circuit channel, and the absence of backup power are explicit teaching assumptions, and the records are also stipulated. Future fault frequencies, actual rights, and authorization are not provided.
teachingExamples.boundary: The example cannot establish the risk of power loss or the best operation in a real server room. The missing information precisely limits how far each kind of output can go.

questionAnswers.question: Does drawing three future paths alone mean that conditional foresight has been completed?
questionAnswers.answer: Not necessarily. A target, horizon, baseline, and evaluation rules must also be specified before the outcome. A path diagram by itself may amount only to conditional projection.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source, lines 78, 83–84.

questionAnswers.question: If predictions are repeatedly accurate, does that permit making decisions for the people concerned?
questionAnswers.answer: That does not follow. Predictive capability and authority to decide must be established separately. Norms, protections, authorization, and the scope of the specific action must also be checked.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source, line 89.

questionAnswers.question: For a question confined to a local technical fault, must A and MC in the eight layers be filled out completely?
questionAnswers.answer: They need not be used mechanically. Explain which responsibilities are relevant to the question. If the actual use involves action concerning an individual or resources across teams, the relevant analysis must expand accordingly, rather than filling boxes because layer numbers exist.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source, line 87 and line 72 of the Part's introduction.

questionAnswers.question: Is evaluating a model using the best information obtained after a storm always illegitimate?
questionAnswers.answer: No. An explicitly identified historical analysis may be completed. Results incorporating information obtained afterward must not silently be presented as foresight performance achievable at the time.
questionAnswers.basis: The final paragraph of §3a on page 2144 of the NHC paper, and this section's output boundaries.

figures.alt: Four parallel boxes: explaining the past, projecting branches, conditional foresight that can be evaluated from an advance record, and bounded choice that discloses norms and the price to be paid. Real-world execution additionally requires protection, review, and authorization.
figures.caption: A methodological diagram made by the author. The parallel layout represents different tasks; it does not mean that completing one box automatically confers eligibility for the next.

figures.alt: Eight equally sized responsibility boxes: U universal core, S transformations, H humans, A actors, MC joint states, P projection and foresight, I interfaces, and N norms and authorization. No hierarchical arrows.
figures.caption: A map of responsibilities made by the author; it is not a ranking of value, a ladder of development, or an eight-column form that must always be filled out.

1.1.diagramBrief: Figure 2 places the four kinds of output side by side, specifying the question and boundary for each. Figure 3 divides the eight layers into equally sized responsibility boxes. Neither figure establishes sequential advancement or connects predictive accuracy directly to authorization to execute.

applicability.reason: This unit concerns methodological judgment. Actual sources support only the listed facts; the diagram and teaching construction each retain their own status.

openQuestions: How to retain the four responsibilities within one actual workflow without creating excessive procedure needs testing in relation to use and risk. No actual workflow experiment has been conducted for this question.

1.2.title: 1.2 Reading Paths through the Book
1.2.lead: Reading in the book's order helps establish the language. When handling an event, proceed as far as the current task requires while retaining an exit at which the work can stop.
explanation: Source location: Chinese source, lines 91–98, headed “1.2 Reading Paths through the Book.” The assembled route /theory/part-01#section-1-2 is the designated internal entry point; the website is not currently deployed. Short quotation, translated from the Chinese: “The appendices help readers return to the contracts they need” (line 97). This section contains three different routes: the book's four-stage reading arrangement, the continuation of analysis for a specific event, and the reference functions of the four appendices. Explaining only the first paragraph must not leave out the event method and the appendices' boundaries. [T-12]

Parts 1–4 first explain where this language applies, what its terms mean, and which evidence supports which claims, distinguishing empirical question families, outcome and mechanism contracts, and conditional formal propositions. This stage helps readers recognize what kind of question they are asking. Support from empirical instances cannot replace mathematical proof, and formal proof cannot replace real-world identification. Appearing together in one book does not eliminate their separate evidential responsibilities. [T-12；T-bone]

Parts 5–8 address scale transformations, operation, human adaptation, and collective state prototypes. The focus shifts from how to describe something to which distinctions survive transformation, how a system operates, and how human meaning enters the account. The collective prototypes in Part 8 are not levels of personal maturity. Readers must not interpret objects as advancing through stages merely because the relevant material appears later in the reading sequence. The chapter arrangement organizes understanding; it is not a necessary evolutionary path for the world. [T-12；T-prototype]

Parts 9–12 connect actor states, multi-circle joint objects, event projection, foresight, and choice. Preserving people's different states, circle relations, and time scales makes it possible to unfold event paths. Even when explanation and projection are adequate, publishing an evaluable judgment about the future brings additional responsibilities, while recommendation and execution each have their own normative and permission conditions. The adjacency of these four Parts therefore does not mean that finishing a model permits prediction, or that finishing a prediction permits action. [T-12；T-11]

Parts 13–16 connect the preceding judgments to tools, norms, intervention, and governance. Tool interfaces must check how signals support conclusions and the action ceiling; normative choice discloses values and affected positions; intervention defines the actual actions; governance allows the framework itself to be corrected, narrowed, replaced, or withdrawn. Governance is not only for evaluating others. The additional costs readers incur when using this language also require scrutiny. [T-12；T-governance]

The second paragraph shifts the perspective to a specific event. Freezing first specifies what this inquiry asks, what the event includes, and the information cutoff, so later readers can distinguish information available beforehand from later additions. Freezing does not mean rejecting new material, nor does it require bringing a changing world to a halt. New material may establish a new version; it must not silently be fed back as if it had already been known when the earlier judgment was made. Nor may the event's scope be narrowed after the outcome to retain only its successful parts. [T-12；T-event；T-forecast]

When identifying actors and candidate circles, first state the roles, boundaries, and relations relevant to the present question. Do not treat everyone on the same list as a collective with an established mechanism. Candidate retains the status of something still requiring examination. Material conditions address how resources, transport, equipment, load, and similar factors constrain feasibility; experience–meaning conditions address how arrangements are understood, how commitments are established, and which feelings enter action. The two may influence each other, but neither can substitute for the other. If the object studied does not involve people, experience or consent must not be imposed on natural processes merely to fill out a form. [T-12；T-human；T-joint]

Update clocks are registered because different states do not change at the same pace. A notification may change available information immediately, service arrangements may change only at the next shift, and long-term trust or eligibility rules may change more slowly still. These are possible conceptual distinctions, not universal time constants observed in this section. Projection along channels must specify what happens first, which conditions transmit the effect to the next position, and whether intervening resource or permission constraints remain. A table describing a single moment must not be treated as a complete process. [T-12；T-event]

Early signals and counter-signals serve to distinguish paths, rather than to let analysts seek confirmation of a favorite story. If a signal occurs under both competing paths, it may have no discriminating power. If an expected signal does not appear, missing information, a clock that has not yet reached its relevant point, or observation failure must also be checked; absence must not always be treated as counterevidence. The direction and magnitude of a signal's effect on the strength of support require appropriate grounds. They must not be assigned by a diagram's colors or arrows. [T-12；T-event]

The two qualifications “only when needed” limit the responsibilities for continuing the work. If the task only seeks to understand an existing event, it may end with a grounded explanation. Publishing a judgment about the future entails registration and evaluation; real-world action or high-impact adoption must enter the relevant normative, protection, and authorization procedures. This does not mean honesty, privacy, and basic protection are unnecessary when no action is taken, or that lacking authority to execute prevents an analytical recommendation. Outputs foreseeably used for high-impact decisions such as sanctions or resource allocation must not have their responsibilities reduced simply by being named reading material. [T-12；T-11；T-use]

The third paragraph identifies each appendix's purpose. A provides full interfaces for human variables, which must be understood together with dependencies, conditions for establishment, and output ceilings. B helps locate numbers and terms; entries must not substitute for the main text. C explains the common method kernel and cross-disciplinary bridging, including formal arguments that must be read under their assumptions. D provides entry points to domain questions and applications, without replacing professional research. The appendices' contracts are the book's arrangements governing conditions for judgments and permitted conclusions; they should not automatically be equated with real-world legal contracts. [T-12；T-appendices]

A reasonable criticism of this route is whether registering so much before examining a simple event might exhaust already limited time. The source's permissive wording and its two task-dependent branches, together with the cost constraint in §1.5.2, support a proportionate reading: prioritize gaps that would change the current judgment or protective arrangements, while retaining established local conclusions. High-risk uses must not omit necessary protections because time is short. Whether this navigation actually saves readers time is not established by effectiveness evidence here; design reasons are not presented as demonstrated results. [T-12；T-cost]
argumentSteps: Material premise: Chinese source line 93 groups the reading in book order, line 95 describes continuation of event work, and line 97 describes the appendices' purposes. These serve different locating functions.

Inferential connection: uncertainty about the question, object scope, information timing, or variable clocks can make the meaning of later paths drift. Fix the boundary of the present judgment first, so supporting and contrary materials have a comparable object.

Positive conclusion: readers may use the four-stage book sequence to establish concepts, then use the event route to select responsibilities relevant to the present task. Appendices supply missing details and enable checking; they do not replace the main text or domain evidence.

Non-equivalence limits: appearing later in the book does not mean greater value; drawing a path does not mean knowing the future; having a recommendation does not confer authority to execute it; complete appendix fields do not mean that real-world materials are complete.

Conditions for challenge: if this path fails to preserve a distinction essential to the current task, or its procedural cost exceeds its gain, identify the gap and revise the representation. Following the navigation must not itself be treated as a successful outcome.

Evidential responsibility: this task explains textual navigation and working conditions. Factual, mechanistic, or foresight conclusions about external events require specific additional materials; the teaching constructions in this section do not discharge that responsibility.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: stopping at the appropriate point in a scheduling conflict
teachingExamples.text: Suppose the fictional A receives a shift-change notice on Tuesday that overlaps with a previously agreed time to accompany someone to a medical appointment. If the question is only where the conflict came from, first fix the times of the notice and agreement, the scope of work and care, and the information cutoff, then compare two explanations: a scheduling change and late-arriving information. Material conditions include transport and alternative time slots; experience–meaning conditions include how A understands the existing commitment. A timetable must not be used to invent A's feelings. Weekly scheduling changes and immediate delivery of notices are assumptions of this example only. Asking whether the conflict will recur next week requires a separate foresight target, window, and baseline. Cancelling the appointment on A's behalf also requires valid authorization from A and the relevant procedures. No actual person or medical arrangement is involved here.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Entirely fictional; supplies no actual medical condition, institutional rule, probability, or authorization. The clocks are illustrative only.
teachingExamples.boundary: Can show only what additional responsibilities arise when the task changes. It cannot establish the real-world causes of care-related scheduling conflicts, the best action, or anyone's wishes.

questionAnswers.question: If important new evidence appears after the information cutoff, does freezing require ignoring it?
questionAnswers.answer: No. Preserve the informational status of the old judgment at the time it was made, create a version identifying the new evidence and cutoff, and revise the conclusions that actually depend on them.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source line 95; Part 12 on registration before outcomes and preventing outcomes from being fed back into earlier records.

questionAnswers.question: After explaining a past event, must one also provide probabilities about the future?
questionAnswers.answer: No. Foresight registration and evaluation become obligations only when a future judgment is to be published. Probabilities also require an appropriate basis; without one, retain the unknown.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source line 95; §1.1.

questionAnswers.question: If Appendix D lists a domain, does that permit skipping experiments or professional assessment in that domain?
questionAnswers.answer: No. It provides an entry point for questions, not a substitute for evidence. Return to the particular domain's variables, units, identification conditions, and professional materials.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source line 97; §1.3.

questionAnswers.question: If a contrary signal has not appeared, does that establish the main path?
questionAnswers.answer: Not automatically. Check whether the signal genuinely discriminates between paths, whether its clock has reached the relevant point, whether observation is reliable, and what other competing paths remain.
questionAnswers.basis: The responsibility for channels and distinguishing signals in Chinese source line 95.

1.3.title: 1.3 The Framework and Domain Knowledge
1.3.lead: A common language should allow different bodies of knowledge to correct one another, without taking over their evidence, professional judgment, or the affected person's position in decision-making.
explanation: Source location: Chinese source lines 99–106, headed ‘1.3 The Framework and Domain Knowledge’. The assembly route /theory/part-01#section-1-3 is a planned internal entry point; the website was not published at the time of this record. Short quotation, translated from Chinese: ‘must not be expanded into a unified admission system for all knowledge’ (line 105). This section both limits the framework's power and states positively what it can do: bring different materials back to a common question so that their grounds and limits become clear. [T-13]

The first paragraph lists four things the framework cannot replace. Disciplinary evidence addresses whether particular facts and mechanisms are supported. Legal procedures concern eligibility, rights, and ways of handling matters within particular institutions. Professional assessment judges the relevant objects using appropriate methods. The affected person's decision-making authority identifies who may choose, and within what scope. A book presenting a framework cannot produce experimental data through terminology, make valid decisions in place of real procedures, replace professional competence merely by taking a comprehensive perspective, or turn ‘my explanation is more complete’ into permission to decide for others. [T-13]

This does not mean that the four are isolated from one another. Professional materials can reveal the consequences of institutional arrangements; people's experiences can identify living costs omitted by a model; institutional research can show technical proposals their actual scope for adoption. Mutual correction means making conflicts specific: is the dispute about inaccurate measurement, insufficient feasibility conditions, differing permissions, or goals that were never aligned? It does not require all materials ultimately to collapse into one language or a single total score. [T-13; T-connection]

The three roles in Chinese source line 103 must be understood separately. Technical research can establish whether something is achievable with the given equipment, resources, and conditions. Institutional research can establish who occupies the decision-making position under the relevant rules. Actors' experiences can show how an arrangement is felt, understood, and taken up in everyday practice. ‘Can’ here identifies responsibilities these materials are capable of bearing; it does not guarantee that any particular technical report, institutional account, or personal account is already correct and complete. Accounts of experience have important evidential standing regarding a person's feelings, but cannot thereby directly establish every external mechanism. Conversely, external measurement does not automatically overturn someone's account of the burdens in their life. [T-13; T-human]

‘One being established does not automatically provide evidence for the others’ is a rule about connections, translated here from Chinese. Equipment being capable of an operation does not establish that an institution has authority to perform it. Rules permitting an arrangement do not guarantee that the equipment can actually operate. Technical feasibility and procedural permission being jointly established do not mean that affected people are willing or will suffer no additional harm. What must be supplied is the missing kind of material and reason, not more of the same material that is already abundant. Where actual interdependence exists, its bridge must also be specified; ‘independent responsibilities’ must not be misread as an absence of real-world connections. [T-13]

Preserving a domain model's variables means preserving what it actually measures. Preserving its units means preserving dimensions, denominators, and the time basis. Preserving its object means preserving the boundaries of the population, equipment, or phenomenon. Preserving its identification conditions means preserving the premises needed to establish the relationship being investigated from the data. For example, ‘capacity’ may mean hourly throughput, simultaneous occupancy, or cumulative storage. Replacing all of these with a structural label loses distinctions that determine the current question. The teaching calculation in this section demonstrates that loss; it does not report the performance of an actual facility. [T-13]

More abstract vocabulary is useful when it helps locate checkable relationships across different materials while still allowing a return to professional units, objects, and reasoning. Abstraction is not prohibited, nor does specialization require every detail to be preserved absolutely. What must be preserved are the distinctions necessary for the present question. If abstraction describes waiting in a queue, inadequate authorization, and harm to experience alike as ‘obstructed flow’, but cannot distinguish adding resources, changing procedures, or seriously considering objections, it may make the explanation worse. [T-13; T-connection]

The third paragraph protects methods' independent epistemic standing. Historical understanding can use materials to explain events' meaning and causal context. Textual interpretation can offer readings that better fit wording and context. Empirical description can faithfully record phenomena. Formal derivation can prove results under assumptions. Normative argument can publicly explain reasons for how to act. These need not first be rewritten completely as object–relation–variable tables to count as knowledge. This does not abolish their respective standards for sources, inference, and challenge, and certainly does not mean all statements are equally reliable. [T-13; T-method]

Formal eligibility within this framework has its own scope: a strong claim made in its name must meet the conditions for that claim. For example, claiming that an instance supports a G-family question, or that a future judgment has received foresight evaluation, entails the book's corresponding requirements. But a well-supported historical study does not lose its original value because these forms were not filled in. Otherwise the reasoning becomes circular: first require all knowledge to enter the framework, then use its coverage of all knowledge to prove that the framework is universally correct. [T-13; T-bone]

The historical judgment provides a concrete example of how professional knowledge and the position of decision-making can be discussed separately within one event. The 2015 judgment is used here to illustrate the boundary that ‘professional risk judgment cannot encompass the patient's understanding and choice’—a translation of the Chinese lesson's formulation. The framework is not used in reverse to certify the court's conclusion, and the judgment's historical medical materials are not presented as current clinical advice. [R-Montgomery]

The strongest objection is this: if the framework does not govern other methods, what additional value can it provide? One defensible answer is that it makes gaps in cross-method connections visible—for example, technical predictions without authorization, institutional documents without demonstrated execution, or aggregate indicators that conceal burdens in people's lives. This value is a testable working claim, not something guaranteed by the phrase ‘common language’. When an existing professional method already handles these distinctions adequately, it should be permitted to be used directly. Without an actual comparison, declare neither that this framework must be superior nor that it must be useless. [T-13; T-evaluation]
argumentSteps: Premise: technical feasibility, institutional decision-making positions, and actors' experiences answer different questions, so their truth values, evidence, and limits can differ.

Public reasoning: if fact A holds but the necessary materials or normative premises connecting A to conclusion B are absent, A alone must not be used to infer B. Adding more instances of A does not supply B's missing grounds.
Positive conclusion: preserving the tasks each method actually performs and allowing the methods to correct one another on a shared question can produce multiple bounded, complementary answers.

Condition for abstraction: structural vocabulary helps make connections only if it preserves the variables, units, objects, and identification conditions necessary for the present question. Renaming that loses these distinctions is not an explanatory gain.

Eligibility boundary: strong claims within the framework are subject to its corresponding requirements. Independent disciplinary or interpretive work continues to stand under its own publicly testable standards; complete rewriting is not a universal prerequisite.

Evidential responsibility: textual meaning rests on the source; a historical judgment on that version of the judgment; a mathematical example on its assumptions and calculations. Whether the framework adds value in actual use requires a separate, proportionate comparison.

boundaries: Constructed conditional counterexample: an equipment experiment establishes that an operation is feasible under the experimental conditions, but the experimental documents contain no consent from affected people. The technical conclusion can still stand; permission to execute must not be inferred from it.

Constructed conditional counterexample: a textual interpretation has sentence-by-sentence sources and contextual arguments, but has not encoded every sentence as a structural variable. That alone is no reason to overturn the interpretation. Specific objections to the text or reasoning are needed.

Constructed conditional counterexample: two capacities both have a numerical value of 6, but one is 6 items per hour and the other is storage for 6 items at once. Writing both as ‘capacity 6’ loses the distinction essential to whether the work can be completed within the current time window.

Arguments about professional expertise and choice in a historical judgment are not the current law of every country and every situation. Without checking the currently applicable rules, this case must not be used for an individual's legal or medical decisions.

Methodological pluralism does not remove responsibilities for accuracy, sources, and ethics. Nor does this section guarantee that any first-person experience directly has final authority over all external facts.

caseNotes.title: Historical judgment: professional knowledge and personal choice in Montgomery
caseNotes.text: The UK Supreme Court's Montgomery judgment of 2015-03-11 addresses disclosure of treatment risks and patient choice. Paragraphs 87–90 distinguish medical knowledge of risks, the risks that matter to the patient, and comprehensible dialogue; materiality must not be determined by percentages alone. Paragraphs 88 and 91 also specify exceptions, which must not be omitted to turn the principle into an unconditional rule. [R-Montgomery]
caseNotes.sourceLabel: UK Supreme Court, Montgomery v Lanarkshire Health Board [2015] UKSC 11
caseNotes.sourceLocator: Date on the judgment's cover; paragraphs 87–91, printed pages 28–29 (PDF pages 29–30). For the issues in the case, see paragraphs 1–4, printed page 2.
caseNotes.boundary: Used only as historical material from the 2015 judgment, without advice on current law in different jurisdictions or personal medical advice; clinical risks are not recalculated, and the judgment is not treated as empirical validation of Xikari.

teachingExamples.title: Mathematical teaching construction: abstraction must not eliminate units
teachingExamples.text: Suppose a fictional device processes tasks at a constant 6 items/hour, with no initial backlog, failures, changeovers, or other bottlenecks. In half an hour it can complete 6×0.5=3 items. If the task requires completing 4 items within half an hour, it falls short by 1 item under these assumptions. Retaining only ‘capacity 6’ while removing ‘per hour’ no longer supports this conclusion; if 6 denotes storage slots, multiplying by time is even less meaningful. The arithmetic illustrates the loss caused by removing necessary units; it does not establish any real device's capability.
teachingExamples.assumptions: 6 items/hour is a constant rate assumed for teaching; continuous operation for half an hour; no initial backlog or additional bottleneck; a task of 4 items.
teachingExamples.boundary: Actual throughput may be affected by queues, changeovers, resources, and random interruptions; domain materials must be obtained anew, and these numbers must not be extrapolated by analogy.

questionAnswers.question: Does a historical study cease to count as knowledge because it has not adopted the book's contracts?
