1.4.title: 1.4 Explanation, Diagnosis, Normative Choice, and Intervention
1.4.lead: First distinguish whether you are seeking understanding, locating risk, comparing reasons, or already changing someone else's circumstances.
explanation: Chinese source location: lines 107–108 of the complete Chinese source, heading ‘1.4 Explanation, Diagnosis, Normative Choice, and Intervention’; this parent unit contains only a heading, with no independent argumentative paragraph. The assembly entry /theory/part-01#section-1-4 is a planned route, not a claim of publication. The short quotation is the heading's ‘Explanation, Diagnosis, Normative Choice, and Intervention’ (translated from Chinese). The four H3 subsections below carry the actual discussion; this task retains an independent output for each, and must not present an explanation of the heading as completion of all four subsections. [T-14]

These headings distinguish four kinds of work: explanation describes how a phenomenon occurs; diagnosis locates constraints or gaps; normative choice explains why an option merits adoption; intervention specifies the scope and responsibilities of actual action. They may connect within one task, but answer different questions. Understanding why someone is in difficulty does not mean that the specific component to change has been identified; identifying risk does not confer authority to act; comparing options does not mean an option has been implemented. [T-141；T-142；T-143；T-144]

These are not item-by-item synonyms for the four output types in §1.1. Section 1.1 distinguishes explanation, projection, conditional foresight, and bounded choice as types of answer; this group emphasizes the responsibilities of diagnosis, norms, and real-world action. Diagnosis may draw on explanation and projection, and intervention may use foresight and comparisons of options, but the fact that both lists contain four items must not be used to equate ‘diagnosis’ with ‘projection’ or ‘intervention’ with ‘bounded choice’. [T-11；T-14]

The parent heading's positive function is navigation: when readers find themselves using statements such as ‘therefore ought to’ or ‘must take action’, they can return to the relevant subsection and check whether they have crossed a boundary of responsibility. It does not impose a mandatory four-step package on all research; a well-grounded explanation may be a stopping point. Nor should urgent harm trigger a mechanical wait until every mechanistic detail is established, although action must still remain within the corresponding evidence, protections, and permissions. [T-141；T-144]
argumentSteps: Textual premise: this parent unit contains only a heading; the actual conditions appear in its four subsections.
Inferential connection: different tasks have different questions and conditions for validity; juxtaposed headings do not constitute an automatic chain of inference.
Conclusion: use four separate entry points to locate responsibilities for explanation, risk, values, and action, then read each subsection; a parent-section overview must not replace the subsections.
Qualification: the parent heading does not independently establish any real-world mechanism or effect of action, nor require every question to end in intervention.

1.4.1.title: 1.4.1 Explanation
1.4.1.lead: A coherent story establishes only that it merits examination; a valid explanation must also withstand competing accounts of the same materials.
explanation: Chinese source location: lines 109–112, heading ‘1.4.1 Explanation’; assembly entry /theory/part-01#section-1-4-1. Short quotation: ‘coherence alone cannot establish causation’ (translated from Chinese, line 111). This section limits not narrative itself but the direct leap from ‘it sounds coherent’ to ‘the cause has been established’. [T-141]

Explanation first specifies the phenomenon and then describes possible mechanisms. Structural explanation pays particular attention to objects, relations, flows, feedback, and conditions: who is connected to whom, what is transmitted along a channel, how a change returns to subsequent states, and which conditions initiate or obstruct the process. These questions can break a vague story into examinable links, but the presence of concepts does not establish that the links actually exist. In particular, the ordinary-language word ‘feedback’ must not substitute for actual materials showing that an output changes subsequent inputs, states, or rules through a return channel; effective feedback does not invariably require durable historical traces. If learning or institutional write-back is also claimed, their respective conditions of retention, change, and classification must be added. [T-141；T-feedback]

Comparing competing accounts is intended to exclude explanations that select only favorable details. The same delay might arise from inadequate capacity, late information, blocked permissions, or recording errors; ‘everyone is busy’ does not distinguish these possibilities. Ask which materials would be expected to differ across these accounts, and which records can test channels, temporal ordering, and alternative causes. Comparing explanations need not always produce one winner; when materials are insufficient, retain both the parts jointly established and the specific unresolved questions. [T-141；T-cause]

Temporal order is a necessary clue for some causal judgments, but not a universally sufficient condition. Two phenomena may share an earlier cause, or their correlation may result from observation or selection; reverse causation and two-way feedback sometimes also need consideration. Counterfactuals and models can propose distinguishing conditions, but actual causal effects still require suitable identification materials. An infeasible experiment does not leave arbitrary storytelling as the only option: historical records, process evidence, and other domain-specific designs can support explanations within their limits. [T-cause；T-independent]

A real investigation report can provide both a strong explanation of an accident and unresolved details, as in the Apollo 13 case. The observation here is that the investigation used materials and tests to identify the most probable failure mode, without withdrawing the whole explanation because some details remained unclear, or turning ‘most probable’ into certainty at every point. This example does not require all explanations to reproduce a spaceflight investigation process. [R-A13]

One objection asks whether every possible explanation in the world must be exhausted before anything may be said. It need not. Priority should go to accounts that can likewise explain the key materials and are genuinely competitive within the current scope, while omissions and counterevidence are disclosed. Arbitrary imaginings with no substantive grounds for competition must not indefinitely block well-grounded conclusions; equally, reasonable alternatives disliked by the analyst must not be omitted. [T-141；T-cause]
argumentSteps: Premise: the same observation may be compatible with multiple mechanisms; narrative coherence indicates only that the statements do not obviously conflict.

Inferential connection: because the materials could arise under alternative mechanisms, presenting a single story cannot exclude them; evidence that distinguishes mechanisms or explicit identification conditions is needed.
Conclusion: present the mechanism as a grounded, bounded explanation and compare the main competing accounts; unresolved parts do not erase local relations already supported.
Conditions: the object, scale, time window, and consequences being asked about remain explicit; use in another setting requires renewed checking.
Evidential responsibility: measurements and archives support what they actually record; teaching counterfactuals show only logical possibilities and do not generate real-world causal effects.

teachingExamples.title: Mathematical teaching construction: one observation, two mechanisms
teachingExamples.text: Let X, Y, and Z be binary variables. Model A specifies Y=X; model B specifies X=Z and Y=Z. If the available materials contain only (X,Y)=(0,0) and (1,1), both models fit. Only if X can be set to 1 while Z=0 in a setup preserving the other conditions does a distinction appear: model A gives Y=1 and model B gives Y=0. This is an artificial construction with explicit equations, not proof that X can be manipulated in reality or that either mechanism is real.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Variables take the value 0 or 1; rules are as stated; the hypothetical intervention changes only X, holding Z and the other mechanisms fixed.
teachingExamples.boundary: Whether an isolated change is feasible in reality, and whether unmeasured variables or selection bias exist, require separate investigation.

1.4.2.title: 1.4.2 Diagnosis
1.4.2.lead: Diagnosis should locate a specific gap while preserving the analyzed party’s standing to dissent; risk is not a license to act.
explanation: Source location: Chinese source lines 113–116, headed “1.4.2 Diagnosis”; page entry /theory/part-01#section-1-4-2. Short quotation translated from Chinese: “within the scope supported by evidence” (line 115). Diagnosis concerns constraints, points of instability, and gaps in carrying capacity; the professional connotations of “diagnosis” must not expand it into a fixed label for a whole person or organization. [T-142]

A constraint limits the attainability of the current target; a point of instability is a location where a change can move the state outside a maintainable range; a gap in carrying capacity is a shortfall between the capabilities, resources, and interfaces required by current tasks, needs, or rights and the actual conditions. They can be related, but are not one overall badness score. Increased demand, reduced resources, conflicting rules, and unavailable interfaces suggest different directions for repair, so diagnosis should identify which problem is involved. [T-142; T-load]

Specifying the object prevents performance in one window from being attached to the whole person; specifying scale prevents an average bottleneck from implying equal shortages everywhere; specifying the window prevents a short peak from being confused with long-term imbalance; specifying risk level makes expression and scrutiny proportionate. Numerical diagnosis must also state units, denominators, and available capacity; nominal resources cannot simply be treated as effective service capacity. [T-142; T-load]

Finding risk does not automatically authorize action: this is the central boundary between diagnosis and intervention. Evidence that an interface may fail can support a bounded risk judgment or a recommendation for review. Who may pause, repair, sanction, or change others’ arrangements requires separate permissions and protection. Judgments about people especially must preserve dissent and appeal; being diagnosed as “risky” does not remove their standing to explain materials, correct errors, and challenge uses. [T-142; T-144]

The additional angle on Apollo 13 here is specific localization: the report identified inadequate protective thermostatic switches in the heater assembly and recommended rigorous requalification after modifying the equipment. This supports separating “locating a specific gap” from “proving the new design reliable,” not extending a technical accident into a diagnosis of someone’s entire capability or personality. [R-A13]

A reasonable criticism asks whether the protection window will close before complete diagnosis is reached. The source does not require zero uncertainty before raising risk, but requires risk judgments to retain their grounds and level. A high-consequence candidate risk, missing discriminating material, and proportionate protective recommendations can be reported together. Whether emergency action is permissible still depends on the specific institution and authorization; neither “diagnosis unresolved” nor “high risk” licenses blanket inaction or arbitrary action. [T-142; T-144]
argumentSteps: Premise: there may be a locatable gap between a target’s required conditions and the object’s current conditions, but observation is limited.
Inferential connection: without a clear object, scale, and window for the gap, a judgment based on local material may be expanded unconditionally into a general label or lasting conclusion.
Conclusion: locate constraints, instability, and gaps in carrying capacity within the material’s support, identifying supported, candidate, and unresolved findings separately.
Non-equivalence: diagnostic support identifies risk locations; it does not independently generate authority for real-world action or remove dissent and appeal.
Evidential responsibility: capacity, load, and interfaces require comparable data; using risk in a high-impact decision requires separate checks of professional and procedural conditions.

distinctions.rightText: Limited observation must not become an eternal attribute of a person or organization.

A numerical threshold is part of the task and evidential agreement; a precise table does not confer natural diagnostic authority. Uncertainty is not absence of risk, and risk is not proof that an event has occurred.

teachingExamples.title: Mathematical teaching construction: a deterministic queue shortfall
teachingExamples.text: Suppose 3 tasks arrive in each of three consecutive hours and hourly processing capacity is 2. Whenever tasks exist, exactly 2 are processed without idle time; the initial queue is 0, with no exits, outside assistance, or other changes. Under Q_next hour=max(0,Q_current+3−2), the queue becomes 1, 2, and 3 tasks. This locates a shortfall of 1 task per hour under the given arrival and service arrangement. It cannot establish that workers are lazy or that adding any type of resource would remove the real bottleneck.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Arrivals, processing capacity, and the rule of processing 2 whenever tasks exist are teaching assumptions, updated hourly at the hour; all tasks are homogeneous.
teachingExamples.boundary: Real task heterogeneity, scheduling, service duration, and interface permissions may change the model; this calculation is not an observed queue.

1.4.3.title: 1.4.3 Normative Choice
1.4.3.lead: Facts tell us what will happen; saying which option is better also requires disclosing why it is worth pursuing and who bears the costs.
explanation: Source location: Chinese source lines 117–120, headed “1.4.3 Normative Choice”; page entry /theory/part-01#section-1-4-3. Short quotation translated from Chinese: “Value choices must not be rewritten as factual necessities to produce a unified conclusion” (line 119). This section does not say facts are useless to choice; it says that normative premises connecting facts to conclusions about what ought to be done must be disclosed. [T-143]

Value premises state what matters, such as reducing losses, protecting basic rights, or distributing fairly. Rights claims identify positions that must not merely be treated as instruments for an aggregate goal. Option consequences identify who may benefit or suffer. Conflicting reasons explain why an attractive slogan cannot settle the argument. Together these form contestable grounds for a recommendation, not moral decoration appended to a predetermined conclusion. [T-143; T-norm]

Moving from facts to evaluation requires at least one connecting premise. “Option A has greater aggregate benefits” describes consequences; “prioritize aggregate benefits when these conditions and protection floors hold” is a choice principle. Omitting the latter hides the basis for moving from totals to an ought. If the principle itself is challenged, repeating the total cannot answer; its applicability, rights boundaries, and shifted costs must be discussed. [T-143; T-bridge]

The same facts can support different normative rankings. Prioritizing totals, the worst-off position, or non-tradable rights can yield different choices. Disclosing disagreement does not mean everything is relative or recommendations are impossible. Analysts can state which principle they adopt, why it is defensible, what would change the judgment, and which reasons cannot all be satisfied. They must not disguise value differences as the other party’s failure to understand facts merely to provide a unique answer. [T-143]

The Belmont Report is a historical example of a text disclosing normative premises. It presents respect for persons, beneficence, and justice as research-ethics principles and acknowledges that they cannot always resolve individual cases without controversy. Here it illustrates that normative argument can explicitly acknowledge principles and tensions; these principles are not described as natural laws directly discovered by an experiment, nor does this example authorize human-subjects research. [R-Belmont]

The strongest objection is that disclosing values can still merely relabel the powerful party’s preferences. That criticism has some force, so one must also examine whether affected positions can offer reasons, which alternatives were excluded, and whether cost distribution is transparent. Writing “fairness” does not make an arrangement fair. Normative reasons require actual argument; adoption and execution still require corresponding review and authorization. [T-143; T-norm]
argumentSteps: Premise: facts describe consequences and constraints but do not by themselves specify every acceptable target or ranking of rights.
Inferential connection: the same consequence vector can have different rankings under different explicit normative principles; facts alone therefore do not uniquely entail an ought.
Conclusion: recommendations must state values, rights, option consequences, and conflicting reasons, and allow criticism of the connecting principle.
Qualification: acknowledging value disagreement neither cancels factual testing nor prevents a clear conditional recommendation.
Evidential responsibility: consequence judgments rely on their empirical or model grounds; normative premises rely on public reasons; actual adoption separately checks protection and authorization.

teachingExamples.title: Mathematical teaching construction: the same consequences, different criteria
teachingExamples.text: Let benefits to two positions be A=(9,0) and B=(4,4); these numbers are artificial benefits of the same dimension. Maximizing the sum selects A because its 9 exceeds B’s 8. Maximizing the minimum benefit among these feasible options selects B because A’s minimum of 0 is below B’s 4. There is no computational conflict; the difference comes from the disclosed normative criteria. This example does not claim that real welfare can be measured this way or prove either criterion universally justified.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Only two options, with known, dimensionally comparable consequences; other rights, risks, and execution constraints are temporarily omitted.
teachingExamples.boundary: Real welfare cannot be arbitrarily converted into numbers; rights floors, different units, or uncertainty may make this ranking inapplicable.

1.4.4.title: 1.4.4 Intervention
1.4.4.lead: An actual action must specify who has authority, its extent, when it stops, and how harm is remedied; small probes and waiting must both be compared through their real costs.
explanation: Source location: Chinese source lines 121–128, headed “1.4.4 Intervention”; page entry /theory/part-01#section-1-4-4. Short quotation translated from Chinese: “The ability to roll back a technical configuration does not mean that losses already borne by others disappear with it” (line 123). The section has three paragraphs: action conditions and reversibility, recommendations’ actual uses, and separate evaluation of outcomes. They cannot be compressed into “act cautiously.” [T-144]

The action level specifies whether the impact occurs through information, probing, configuration changes, or constraints on others. The authorization source states who permits the action through which valid procedure. Scope limits the object, time, resources, and impact boundary. Stopping conditions specify observations triggering suspension or exit. Remedy paths address losses already caused and consequences that cannot be reversed. Stating these makes action constrainable; a table with every field filled does not automatically prove valid authorization. [T-144; T-bridge]

The source gives three linked conditions for small reversible steps: the window permits them, new information can change later choices, and the probe’s benefits sufficiently offset its costs. If the window does not permit waiting, small steps may miss the opportunity; even abundant information has limited probing value if it changes no choice; if others bear the learning costs, the operator’s low cost alone cannot establish that the probe is worthwhile. Meeting these conditions merely makes the approach eligible for priority consideration; actual adoption still needs protection and authorization. [T-144; T-options]

Waiting also has dynamic consequences. Urgent harm, continuing exposure, or a crucial window can mean that inaction accumulates further loss. Compare the actual paths of action, delay, probing, exit, and no action rather than treating waiting as impact-free. Conversely, “emergency” alone does not exempt permissions or protections; lawful, necessary, proportionate responses and stopping limits depend on the specific context. [T-144; T-options]

Reversibility must be checked from affected positions. Restoring a software version may reverse a configuration but cannot automatically return wasted travel time, disclosed information, or missed opportunities. Irrecoverable losses require an account of remedy and remaining responsibility. “Small” is not measured only by the amount of code changed or the budget percentage; a local action may have a high impact on a few positions. [T-144]

The second paragraph protects the legitimate space for analytical recommendations while preventing a mismatch between labels and actual use. Opinions, comparisons of options, and drafts for deliberation do not themselves confer power to bind others. If they actually enter high-impact decisions concerning sanctions, eligibility, or resource allocation, however, they require review and authorization appropriate to their foreseeable use. Labels such as “a human makes the final confirmation” or “only a suggestion” cannot by themselves establish that the actual impact has been eliminated. Whether a boundary is actually crossed requires examining the real chain of use, rather than just the document's title. [T-144；T-interface]

The third paragraph assesses outcomes separately. Industrial capability, workers' lives, political participation, and cross-border connections need not change together. In addressing conflict, the cessation of violence, dispute resolution, political arrangements, accountability, restoration of everyday life, and reconciliation can also change separately. These are distinct outcome questions; the original text has not already asserted how a particular country or war changed. Retain a supported local improvement rather than erasing it because the overall objective remains incomplete. Conversely, one favorable indicator cannot substantiate the other outcomes. [T-144]

The new observation concerning Apollo 13 in this section concerns emergency measures and separate outcomes: the report records measures including reducing power consumption and adapting available purification supplies, while the mission did not achieve its original lunar-surface objective. The material illustrates “separating particular recovery actions from completion of the original mission.” It does not turn a successful return into success on every objective, nor certify from this summary that every decision procedure met this book's normative requirements. [R-A13]

An objection might ask whether so many protections make action impossible in an emergency. The appropriate response distinguishes the minimum action requiring an immediate decision from analysis that can be completed afterward, while retaining necessary authority, boundaries of effect, and responsibility records. Neither miss a protection window in pursuit of a complete narrative nor treat emergency as unlimited authorization. Another objection is that “anything reversible by rollback is safe”; the irrecoverable losses discussed above directly limit that claim. [T-144；T-cost]
argumentSteps: Premise: action and waiting can both have consequences; an action's reversibility may differ across affected positions.

Inferential connection: model benefits, the scale of an action, or technical rollback capability alone cannot establish that an action may be implemented. The window, information value, costs, protection, and valid authority must also be checked.

Conclusion: compare actual actions within an explicit scope and with stopping and remedial conditions. Reversible small steps deserve priority only when their conditions hold; urgent, continuing harm may change the ranking of waiting.

Use limitation: analytical recommendations for discussion do not themselves confer binding authority. Actual use in high-impact decisions carries review and authorization responsibilities appropriate to that use.

Outcome limitation: retain supported improvements separately and check unsupported components separately. Local success is not overall success; an incomplete overall objective does not erase local improvement either.

Evidential responsibility: real consequences require sources and corresponding time windows; norms and authorization require independent grounds. Teaching counterfactuals and historical records cannot themselves authorize any actual action.

caseNotes.text: The Apollo 13 report records that, after the accident, reducing lunar-module power consumption helped preserve electricity and water, and ground personnel devised a way to adapt purification supplies using onboard materials. The report's preface also states that the original lunar-surface mission was aborted. Recovery measures do not mean that all original objectives were achieved. [R-A13]

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: losses remaining after rollback
teachingExamples.text: Suppose a fictional appointment system tries new scheduling for one hour and then restores the old configuration, but one user has consequently wasted two hours on an unnecessary trip. For teaching purposes only, assume an opportunity cost of 15 units per hour: the opportunity cost already incurred is 2×15=30 units. Restoring the configuration does not bring back the past two hours, and compensation of 30 units does not necessarily restore the particular opportunity missed. All people, actions, and values are teaching assumptions, not statistics on actual harm or a compensation standard.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Assumes only one user, two hours already lost, and an artificially assigned hourly value of 15; it stipulates no actual rights dispute, institutional responsibility, or compensation rule.
teachingExamples.boundary: Actual losses need not be monetizable. Remedies must be judged according to the facts, rights, and authorization; this number cannot be applied mechanically.

questionAnswers.question: Is the ability to restore the old configuration sufficient to launch a high-impact pilot directly?
questionAnswers.answer: No. Actual consequences for affected positions, authority, stopping conditions, and remedies must be checked. Technical rollback is only one consideration.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source line 123.

questionAnswers.question: If a “recommendation” is actually used to revoke eligibility, may it still be treated as ordinary discussion?
questionAnswers.answer: No. The appropriate review and authorization must be completed according to the foreseeable high-impact use.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source line 125.

questionAnswers.question: If an intervention reduces immediate conflict but does not improve the restoration of everyday life, should it be called a success or a failure?
questionAnswers.answer: Report the outcomes separately. Retain the evidenced improvement in immediate conflict and obtain separate evidence about restoration of everyday life. If an overall objective was specified beforehand, assess it separately under its evaluation rules as well, rather than merging everything into a general impression.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source line 127.

questionAnswers.question: When should small probes not receive mechanical priority?
questionAnswers.answer: Comparison must be reopened when the window does not allow a probe, its information would not change the choice, its value does not justify its cost, or continuing harm makes waiting more dangerous. Actual actions still require an authorization check.

1.5.title: 1.5 Choosing an entry point by task and risk
1.5.lead: The task to be completed determines the entry point; use and actual risk determine the depth of review.
explanation: Source location: Chinese source lines 129–130, heading “1.5 Choosing an entry point by task and risk.” This parent unit contains only a heading; its short quotation translates as “Choosing an entry point by task and risk” [T-15]. Specific conditions concerning task and risk appear in §1.5.1 and §1.5.2 respectively; reading scope and use of the method are discussed in §1.5.3.

The heading's two dimensions cannot be merged into a ranking in which “more complex means more advanced.” Task specifies whether the aim is to understand a concept, compare scales, explain an event, or take real action. Risk concerns how the conclusion will affect people, how serious error would be, whether recovery is possible, and how power is distributed. Explaining terminology and using it for high-impact classification require different review. Tasks with equally high risk may also require different domain methods. [T-151；T-152]

Entering by task means avoiding irrelevant work; escalating by risk means retaining essential protections. Together they reject two extremes: running every contract for everyday reading, or treating a high-impact use as low risk because it is called “just a simple question.” Selecting an entry point does not confer eligibility on the result, and certainly does not remove the need to check changes in use afterward. [T-151；T-152]
argumentSteps: Premise: task type and risk intensity are different dimensions; model complexity cannot substitute for them.

Connection: first state the answer sought to identify the kinds of material needed, then check actual use and consequences to determine the required degree of review and protection. The scope of the judgment also determines how much of the original text must be read.

Conclusion: use §1.5.1 and §1.5.2 together to choose a proportionate entry point, and use §1.5.3 to match reading scope to the judgment made. Neither maximum procedural coverage nor minimum procedure is itself a criterion of success.
Boundary: this heading provides navigation, not a universal numerical risk measure, and does not independently authorize real action.

questionAnswers.question: If a task is described in one sentence, is that enough to classify it as low risk?
questionAnswers.answer: No. Use, affected people, consequences, and power conditions must also be considered.

questionAnswers.question: After choosing the right entry point, may one declare the conclusion established?
questionAnswers.answer: No. The entry point only identifies the work required; the actual material and reasoning must still be completed.

1.5.1.title: 1.5.1 Entering by task
1.5.1.lead: Formal analysis first states the question in a checkable form, then selects the work relevant to it.
explanation: Source location: Chinese source lines 131–134, heading “1.5.1 Entering by task”; assembled route /theory/part-01#section-1-5-1. A short quotation translated from Chinese reads, “First state the object, question, time window, scale, and required output” (Chinese source line 133). The starting condition here is the need to produce formal analysis; this does not require a complete registration form for every ordinary reading. [T-151]

The object identifies who or what is being analyzed and which neighboring objects are excluded; the question determines the outcome to explain or the comparison to make; the time window bounds the material and the range of change. Besides aggregation level and observational resolution, scale requires the task-relevant spatial, temporal, organizational, causal, impact, network-topological, and jurisdictional/authorization axes; see §5.2. Required output distinguishes conceptual clarification, explanation, projection, foresight, analytical recommendation, and so on. These five items are not decoration: omitting the object risks conflating members with the whole; omitting the question invites collecting material for its own sake; omitting the window can turn short-term fluctuation into a long-term mechanism; omitting scale can turn group averages into individual facts; omitting the output makes it easy to slide from explanation into disposition. [T-151；T-11]

The original text lists four entry points. Understanding concepts may begin with the general grammar in Part III, focusing on how the author defines terms, what is excluded, and how they differ from other concepts. Comparing scales requires examining transformations and checking which necessary distinctions are preserved or lost when representation changes. Analyzing real events requires distinguishing evidence and mechanisms, rather than merely supplying a glossary. Real action also requires proceeding to option selection and intervention procedures, rather than rewriting a description as a command. [T-151；T-map]

“May begin with” identifies useful entry points; it does not turn chapter order into a universal gate for knowledge. Existing domain evidence can support conclusions according to its design. Particular strong claims made in the name of this framework require the corresponding additional requirements. Nor does “by task” mean consulting only chapters that support a predetermined answer: competing explanations, contrary material, and affected positions remain part of what the current task actually requires. [T-151；T-domain；T-evidence]

Understanding, comparison, event analysis, and action may coexist in one project. Their subquestions and actual dependencies should then be stated explicitly, rather than requiring every subquestion to repeat every procedure. Checking a term, for example, can be completed in its own right. A lack of authority for a separate real action does not erase that conceptual explanation, but completion of the explanation does not lift the action's restrictions either. [T-151；T-11]

An example from an actual methodological text is the registration of use and context in NIST's 2023 AI RMF. Its MAP items require descriptions of intended purposes, use contexts, and specific tasks, providing a public design relevant to this section. Comparing the two texts helps reveal different details in task declarations. Their resemblance alone does not show equivalence, mutual validation, or an already achieved reduction in risk. [R-NIST]

An objection might ask whether research may begin while the real question remains vague. It may begin exploratorily, with uncertainties identified and the object and question progressively revised, without pretending that a formal strong conclusion is already established. Clarifying the question is iterative work, not a reason to refuse to understand the user by saying “define it clearly first.” What cannot be retained is silently replacing the original question after reaching a conclusion while continuing to claim success on the original task. [T-151；T-domain]
argumentSteps: Premise: different tasks require different material, representations, and conditions for establishment.
Connection: explicitly stating the object, question, time window, scale, and output provides a shared reference for assigning material, making comparisons, and identifying stopping points.

Conclusion: choose entry points according to needs concerning concepts, transformations, events, real action, and so forth; discharge the relevant responsibilities without mechanically traversing irrelevant contracts.
Condition: reopen affected work when use or scope changes. Exploratory questions may be clarified progressively, while retaining their exploratory status.

Evidential responsibility: the entry-point declaration only defines the task. Actual explanations and eligibility for action still require separate support from domain evidence, norms, and valid authority.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: the same materials, four different starting points
teachingExamples.text: Suppose the fictional material is a service log for one week. Asking “What does interface mean in this book?” mainly returns to the definition. Asking “Can a daily average preserve each period's peak?” enters representational transformation. Asking “Why did waiting increase on Wednesday?” enters evidence and competing mechanisms. Asking “Should next week's allocation change?” enters option comparison, while actual implementation also requires authorization. The log's existence is a teaching assumption; no actual peaks, causes or ranking of options are provided.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Used only to distinguish questions; the contents, units and quality of the records and the permission to execute are unspecified.
teachingExamples.boundary: This must not be used to declare that any real service is congested or needs adjustment.

counterexamples.text: Constructed conditional counterexample: if the question concerns waiting times for a service during one week, treating the annual average as every person's experience that week may simultaneously substitute a different time window, scale and object.
counterexamples.effect: Constrains mechanical checklist use, silent migration of use, and substitution of procedure or linguistic form for substantive judgment.

counterexamples.text: Constructed conditional counterexample: if advice moves from internal discussion to automatic resource allocation, the original low-risk explanation cannot directly transfer into eligibility for execution.

questionAnswers.question: When the same data are used for different questions, can the same analysis always be retained?
questionAnswers.answer: No. Changes to the target, time window, scale or output may require additional distinctions and evidential responsibilities.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source, line 133.

questionAnswers.question: If a question is not yet clear, should a formal conclusion simply be invented?
questionAnswers.answer: No. First formulate a comprehensible exploratory question and continue clarifying it, preserving unresolved issues and scope.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source line 133 and the candidate status in §2.1.

questionAnswers.question: Once the five items including the object are written down, can a G-type instance be considered supported?
questionAnswers.answer: No. A task declaration and empirical instance testing are established separately; complete fields do not imply positive support.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source line 133; §2.1.

1.5.2.title: 1.5.2 Escalate According to Risk
1.5.2.lead: Use review where it can change judgments and protections, while accounting for the burden procedures impose on people.
explanation: Source location: Chinese source lines 135–140, titled “1.5.2 Escalate According to Risk”; assembly route /theory/part-01#section-1-5-2. Short quotation, translated from the Chinese: “Procedures themselves have costs in time, care, privacy and expression” (line 139). This section constrains both careless use with inadequate attention to risk and formal burdens from excessive procedure; it does not simply demand ever more formalities. [T-152]

Increasing review intensity with purpose and actual risk means that the same sentence can carry different responsibilities when used to understand a book and when used to sanction someone. Risk assessment should examine affected objects, severity, recoverability, scope of effects and who can refuse or correct errors. It must not depend solely on how confident the analyst sounds, whether the document is called “advice,” or how large the model is. [T-152; T-use]

Insufficient evidence requires greater caution because the grounds of a potentially mistaken judgment remain insecure: obtain genuinely discriminating materials or narrow the conclusion, rather than increasing confidence by repeating the same source. Power asymmetry requires greater caution because affected people may find it difficult to refuse, exit or express disagreement; apparent cooperation must not automatically count as free consent. Irreversible consequences require greater caution because later correction may not restore the original situation. High-pressure contexts require greater caution because time, dependence and pressure may obstruct understanding and expression; this does not mean that valid judgments are always impossible under pressure. [T-152; T-protection]

These are different sources of risk, not a scoring table whose entries may be added arbitrarily. When an outcome is extremely serious but its probability unknown, one must not invent a low probability to pass the check; fully recorded procedures cannot offset invalid authorization. Grounded descriptions of risk, restricted action scopes and conditions for reopening can be given; numbers lacking support should remain unknown. [T-152; T-ten]

Ordinary reading, local understanding and everyday communication need not run every contract: this is one side of proportionality. It does not lower requirements for honesty, respect for sources or basic privacy, nor let speakers make risk disappear merely by saying so. If an output actually enters a high-impact use, return to its real purpose. Allowing lightweight understanding lets method support knowledge and communication instead of making them the preserve of expert forms. [T-152; T-use]

The four types of procedural cost require concrete examination. Time costs include delayed services or missed windows. Care costs include care burdens transferred to family members or others so someone can participate in review. Privacy costs arise from collecting, retaining and circulating additional materials. Expression costs include repeatedly recounting difficult experiences, learning terminology or describing oneself in unfamiliar formats. Not all additional information is worth obtaining; materials that cannot change the current judgment or protection arrangements particularly require a necessity review. [T-152]

“Prioritize gaps that would change the current judgment or protection arrangements” does not mean looking only for information that reverses the preferred option. A gap may leave the overall recommendation unchanged yet alter who needs protection, the action ceiling, stopping conditions or a local conclusion, which also has substantive value. Conversely, more correctly completed forms and more pages of materials should not by themselves count as procedural success when no relevant judgment changes. [T-152; T-evaluation]

Retaining local conclusions supported by existing materials avoids an all-or-nothing approach. For example, if the available information sufficiently shows that an arrangement creates an additional commuting burden, that supported part should be recognized even while its full causes or long-term consequences remain unclear, rather than requiring the entire theory to be completed first. Recognizing experience is not the same as taking high-impact action without verification; the two can be handled separately. [T-152; T-domain]

The final sentence places fairness at the point of communication: people need not learn technical terms before having experiences and needs. Analysts should bear the responsibility for translation and clarification, enabling people to describe their situations in their own language and retaining their objections. Terminological fluency must not substitute for credibility, eligibility or willingness to cooperate. Listening does not exempt every external causal assertion from verification; it rejects disqualifying materials in advance because of their expressive form. [T-152; T-domain]

The NIST 2023 methodological-text example examines risk prioritization and resources here: it calls for more extensive risk-management effort on higher risks in a particular context while acknowledging that unrealistic expectations of zero risk can waste scarce resources. It provides a comparison for proportionality in methodological design, not evidence that those designs have been realized in practice or grounds for merging all the standards of the two frameworks. [R-NIST]

The strongest objection is who defines risk and “irrelevant costs.” If only those holding power decide, proportionality can become an excuse to reduce protections. Affected positions and different professional materials must therefore be included, with public reasons why omissions do not affect the current judgment and when the question should reopen. One must not count only operators' costs while ignoring the price others bear. Risk-sensitive simplification differs substantively from evading responsibility. [T-152; T-protection]
argumentSteps: Premise: both the consequences of mistaken judgments and the price of procedures themselves vary with purpose, power and context.
Connection: a uniform maximum intensity creates unnecessary burdens, while a uniform minimum intensity permits high-impact risks; review should therefore address actual gaps and protection needs.
Conclusion: strengthen proportionate review for insufficient evidence, power asymmetry, irreversible consequences and high-pressure conditions; ordinary understanding need not run every contract.

Qualification: simplification does not mean removing necessary protections, more formalities do not mean more reliable judgments, and supported local conclusions can coexist with other unresolved matters.

Evidential and normative responsibility: risk descriptions need grounds; permissions and rights cannot be offset by an overall risk score; people's experiences do not require terminological competence for admission.

distinctions.leftText: Adjusting review to actual consequences and protection gaps.
distinctions.rightText: More formalities are not necessarily better; procedures can also create burdens.

distinctions.leftText: No supportable numerical value is available; keep it unknown.
distinctions.rightText: A danger must not be deemed small merely because it has not been measured or quantified.

distinctions.leftText: It can be recognized within the scope supported by existing evidence.
distinctions.rightText: Other dependencies may remain unresolved and must be reported separately.

distinctions.leftText: Differences in expression or training.
distinctions.rightText: Linguistic form must not be used to dismiss someone's experience and justified needs.

boundaries: Constructed conditional counterexample: the same automatic summary has different real consequences when used for personal reading notes and when used to decide whether to discontinue a service; the same review intensity must not simply carry over.
Constructed conditional counterexample: requiring a complete family history to verify a low-risk appointment time may add privacy burdens with no corresponding value to the judgment.

Constructed conditional counterexample: the overall recommendation stays the same, but new materials show that one position cannot exit safely, so protections should change. One must not call review worthless because “the main conclusion did not change.”

Procedural costs do not automatically establish that all review should stop. When substantive rights or irreversible harm are involved, necessary procedures still need to be retained while unnecessary burdens are reduced as far as possible.
questions: A review did not change the preferred option but changed the route for appeal. Was it worthless?
If probability lacks reliable data, may one write “probably very low” to complete the process?
If the person concerned does not understand structural terminology, must they take lessons before their predicament can be addressed?
Does not running every contract for ordinary reading mean that unverified materials may be presented as facts?

caseNotes.title: An actual methodological text: risk prioritization and scarce resources
caseNotes.text: AI RMF 1.0 §1.2.3 treats higher risks in a concrete context as more urgent and requiring more extensive management, while warning that unrealistic expectations of zero risk can waste resources. The additional focus here is proportionality in review effort. [R-NIST]

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: changing the use of the same output
teachingExamples.text: Suppose a fictional system summarizes a service record as “repeated no-shows.” If it merely helps the person find records, check that the summary corresponds to the original. If it is instead used to suspend services automatically, further checks are needed of what nonattendance means, recording errors, prior notification, the person's explanation, applicable rules and review authorization. The same text can serve both purposes without carrying the same risk. The entire scenario is a teaching construction, not a report about a real system.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Only the output text and its two uses are stipulated; actual numbers or causes of missed appointments, eligibility rules and lawful authorization are not assumed.
teachingExamples.boundary: This example must not be used to judge a real user untrustworthy or to conclude that an institution may discontinue service; the missing conditions are precisely what must not be silently invented.

questionAnswers.question: A review did not change the preferred option but changed the route for appeal. Was it worthless?
questionAnswers.answer: No. Protection arrangements are also outcomes this section explicitly requires prioritizing; explain what changed rather than considering only the name of the option.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source, line 139.

questionAnswers.question: If probability lacks reliable data, may one write “probably very low” to complete the process?
questionAnswers.answer: No. Retain the unknown, explain the consequences, window and materials needed, and do not lower risk through fabricated numbers.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source line 137 and the limits on expressing risk.

questionAnswers.question: If the person concerned does not understand structural terminology, must they take lessons before their predicament can be addressed?
questionAnswers.answer: No. Listen and clarify in comprehensible terms, retaining supported local content; terminology training must not become a prerequisite for recognizing experience.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source, line 139.

questionAnswers.question: Does not running every contract for ordinary reading mean that unverified materials may be presented as facts?
questionAnswers.answer: No. Proportionately reducing procedure does not remove honesty or grounds; corresponding responsibilities must also be added when actual use escalates.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source, lines 137–139.

figures.alt: Insufficient evidence, power asymmetry, irreversible consequences and high-pressure contexts call for stronger review. At the same time, consider costs in time, care, privacy and expression, retain local conclusions and provide comprehensible entry points.
figures.caption: A proportionality diagram created by the explanatory author; it does not add risks into an overall score or treat procedural cost as permission to omit protections.

1.5.2.diagramBrief: Figure 2 presents four types of escalation conditions alongside four types of procedural cost, placing “changes judgment or protection” in a shared checking box; it supplies neither unsupported risk scores nor a one-dimensional ranking.

openQuestions: Whether a particular procedure reduces risk without excessive burdens requires actual process information, affected people's experiences and outcome materials; this task has not conducted that comparison of use.

1.6.title: 1.6 Ten Questions for Strong Judgments
1.6.lead: The ten questions locate gaps that actually limit a conclusion; nine points cannot offset one act beyond authority.
explanation: Source location: Chinese source lines 149–154, titled “1.6 Ten Questions for Strong Judgments”; assembly route /theory/part-01#section-1-6 is a preset entry point. Short quotation, translated from the Chinese: “not a checklist for adding points to conclusions” (line 153). This section presents ten kinds of gaps that may invalidate a judgment or exceed authority, requiring dependencies to be located and proportionate measures taken rather than a pass rate calculated. [T-16]

A “strong judgment” must not be identified by tone alone. A sentence beginning “I think” may still carry substantial use responsibilities if it actually determines someone's eligibility. A tightly bounded mathematical conclusion stated with certainty does not mean all its premises are claimed to hold in reality. Examine what the conclusion claims, what it depends on and how it will be used, together with §1.1's output distinctions and §1.5's risk requirements. [T-16; T-output; T-risk]

First question, whether the object is established: first check that its boundary, members, states, time window and identity fit the current question, then examine support for the empirical object claimed. Calling a group of people “a system” or grouping materials into a category does not by naming alone establish relatively independent structural effects. A candidate may continue to be explored; a gap affecting formal instance eligibility in this framework must not be disguised as support already obtained. This does not cancel the independent knowledge provided by existing domain materials. [T-16; T-object]

Second question, whether the evidence is sufficient: sufficiency is relative to the particular claim and purpose, not the number of sources. Whether materials actually observe the outcome asked about, are independent, have changed their generation process, and address missingness and counterevidence all affects support. Multiple citations of the same report must not be added as independent observations. When these questions cannot be answered, narrow assertions dependent on the evidence or obtain more materials without erasing unrelated reliable parts. [T-16; T-evidence]

Third question, whether a causal bridge exists: moving from observation or correlation to the causal effect asked about requires proportionate identification conditions. Claiming a particular mechanism further requires corresponding channels, temporal order and discriminating materials. Identifying a total effect need not first exhaust every mediator; conversely, several independently real local links do not automatically establish the net effect of the chain as a whole. Without a bridge, retain description or a bounded effect rather than filling out a story into a supposedly proven mechanism. [T-16; T-cause]

Fourth question, whether scale has been substituted: judgments about individuals and groups, local and aggregate conditions, and short and long periods may require different materials. An accurate average does not imply that everyone matches it, and a response in one window does not automatically support a long-term trend. State the original units, target and distinctions preserved by the mapping. If a bridge is missing, limit extrapolation without necessarily rejecting the conclusion at the original scale. [T-16; T-scale]

Fifth question, whether alternative explanations have been compared: confront competing mechanisms, changes in measurement or simpler explanations capable of accounting for the same key materials. Listing their names without comparing expectations with materials is insufficient, but exhaustive consideration of every imaginable alternative is not required. When the materials cannot yet discriminate, specify which observation would change the judgment and retain the particular unresolved issue. [T-16; T-cause]

The sixth question asks whether rights are harmed. Average benefits or institutional efficiency alone are insufficient; affected positions, basic protections, conditions for information and expression, distribution, and the price of refusal must also be identified. Possible harm calls for specific review. It does not mean that every conflict of interests has already been judged unlawful, nor may this question be reduced to a negative score offset by high scores elsewhere. [T-16；T-protect]

The seventh question asks whether authorization is valid. Who authorizes whom, for which action, within what scope and validity period, and whether the authorizing party holds the relevant decision-making position must all match. An analyst's access to data does not confer authority to act on a person; confidence in an explanation does not permit choosing for someone else; and authorization for one occasion must not transfer unconditionally to a new use. Missing permission generally blocks the relevant real-world action, but need not block a grounded analytical recommendation. [T-16；T-action]

The eighth question asks whether the action can be stopped. It requires more than writing “pause if necessary”: what triggers stopping, which monitoring sources apply, who can give the order, who can actually stop it, and how stopping will affect people must be examined. If shutting down the system itself causes harm, proportionate arrangements for safe stopping are needed. Claiming that an action can be paused without an accessible control, responsible person, or alternative uptake does not establish that it is controllable. [T-16；T-action]

The ninth question asks whether consequences can be remedied. Restoring a configuration and restoring people's circumstances are not equivalent; time already lost, disclosures, or missed opportunities may not be fully reversible. Specify which losses can be recovered, which can only be reduced or compensated, and who bears responsibility. A remedy plan is not permission to cause avoidable harm first, and subsequent compensation does not automatically erase earlier rights issues. [T-16；T-action]

The tenth question asks whether the conclusion can be appealed. Affected people should have understandable reasons, an entry point for correcting errors and submitting contrary material, and an actual mechanism capable of changing erroneous decisions. Receiving an appeal letter is not the same as effective feedback or error correction. Nor does only changing a decision count as serious review: retaining the original judgment may be justified, but the reasons must be answered and proportionate channels retained. [T-16；T-appeal]

The second paragraph explains how to use the ten questions: identify the specific unanswered question, state whether it limits a factual judgment, mechanism account, scope of extrapolation, eligibility for publication, or real-world action, then downgrade or stop only the parts that actually depend on it. Lack of authority to execute may stop an action while leaving analysis intact; an unidentified mechanism may leave a credible description intact; when a population average cannot be extrapolated to individuals, retain the population conclusion. An unknown in one item does not invalidate all the work, while nine satisfactory items do not permit bypassing one indispensable gap. [T-16]

The actual historical material here examines only the specificity of authorization. The memorandum establishing the Apollo 13 Review Board lists investigation, reporting, and recommendation duties, while separately assigning management organizations to study corrective actions. Being responsible for an investigation must therefore not be confused with being entitled to execute any action independently. This supports only that fact about the division of tasks; one document is not being used to declare all ten questions satisfied. [R-AUTH]

The strongest criticism is whether the ten questions might become a permanent obstacle to conclusions. That risk does exist if every question mechanically requires an unconditional yes. Proper use identifies which questions concern the present claim, which do not apply because the task involves no real-world action, and which unknowns actually limit the conclusion. Required protections must not casually be marked inapplicable, while local judgments that do not depend on a gap should not be delayed indefinitely. [T-16；T-risk]
argumentSteps: Premise: a strong claim may depend simultaneously on conditions concerning objects, evidence, identification, scale, norms, and actual use. These dependencies serve different responsibilities.

Inferential connection: when a necessary condition is missing, even abundant satisfaction of unrelated conditions cannot supply it. Local conclusions that do not depend on that gap may nevertheless be retained.

Positive conclusion: locate gaps question by question, clarify whether facts, mechanisms, extrapolation, eligibility for publication, or real-world actions are limited, and respond proportionately by gathering evidence, narrowing scope, downgrading, or stopping.

Qualification: the ten questions are not a universal truth algorithm, nor must ordinary understanding mechanically run the entire set. Inapplicability must be explained by the present task, not used to conceal an actual high-impact use.

Evidential responsibility: factual questions require corresponding materials; norms and authorization need separate explanation; whether procedures can actually correct errors or stop actions depends on available channels, not certification through a self-completed checklist.

distinctions.leftText: Locate which dependency limits which kind of conclusion.
distinctions.rightText: An overall score must not offset missing authorization or essential evidence.

distinctions.leftText: May limit only a particular mechanism explanation.
distinctions.rightText: Independently reliable material about the phenomenon may be retained.

distinctions.leftText: Limits specific actions.
distinctions.rightText: A grounded recommendation may still inform deliberation; execution must not be smuggled in.

distinctions.leftText: The original judgment may remain after the material has been addressed.
distinctions.rightText: An unchanged outcome alone does not establish that the procedure was ineffective.

boundaries: Constructed conditional counterexample: a report marks nine items checked but lacks valid authorization to suspend service. Nine points must not authorize the suspension. Permission is not a numerical quantity that other scores can compensate for.

Constructed conditional counterexample: research credibly identifies an average effect for a population but has no information about individual effects. Extrapolation to individuals should be restricted; the population result need not be withdrawn.

Constructed conditional counterexample: an appeal ultimately leaves a decision unchanged, but each basis for the original decision has been reviewed and contrary materials addressed. The unchanged result alone must not be used to declare the appeal a sham. The effectiveness of the actual channel still requires separate checking.

The ten questions cannot certify themselves. A form showing stopping or remedy arrangements does not mean they can already be executed on site. Nor does this inquiry claim that all ten items have been verified for the historical case.

Does an unknown mechanism mean that the event records are also unreliable?
Does answering every question mean that the facts are true and the action safe?
How should conceptual reading that involves no real-world action handle questions about stopping and remedy?

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: carry the same gap through to the correct conclusion
teachingExamples.text: Suppose a fictional study provides reliable records of overall waiting times for a service, but has neither causal identification nor authorization to change other people's eligibility. It may retain a description of waiting times within this window. The claim that a particular staff member's attitude caused them remains an unproven mechanism; the conclusion that their service eligibility should therefore be suspended lacks both factual and permission bridges. These three statuses must be reported separately. Adding authorization later would not automatically supply mechanism evidence; identifying a cause later would not automatically confer authority to execute an action. All materials and circumstances are teaching assumptions.
teachingExamples.assumptions: The reliability of the records is stipulated. The absence of causal identification and authorization is explicit. No actual person or institution is assumed to exist.
teachingExamples.boundary: Shows only the scope of dependencies. It does not estimate actual service effects or the lawfulness of real disciplinary action.

questionAnswers.question: If nine of the ten questions have supporting grounds but authorization is not established, can a majority pass suffice?
questionAnswers.answer: No. Examine what the gap limits: the relevant real-world action must stop or be narrowed, while grounded analysis may remain.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source, line 153.

questionAnswers.question: Does an unknown mechanism mean that the event records are also unreliable?
questionAnswers.answer: Not necessarily. Material reliability and mechanism identification are different questions and should be reported separately.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source, lines 151–153 and §2.4.

questionAnswers.question: Does answering every question mean that the facts are true and the action safe?
questionAnswers.answer: No. Answers require proportionate evidence and effective procedures; complete paperwork does not certify correctness in the real world.

questionAnswers.question: How should conceptual reading that involves no real-world action handle questions about stopping and remedy?
questionAnswers.answer: Explain that the current work concerns conceptual understanding only and has no corresponding action to execute, rather than fabricating execution records. If the use changes to high-impact adoption, add the corresponding responsibilities.

1.7.title: 1.7 The Protection Floor
1.7.lead: Protections must be usable within the specific option. Silence, remaining, or disclosing little must not automatically be treated as consent.
explanation: Source location: Chinese source, lines 155–160, headed “1.7 The Protection Floor”; the assembled route /theory/part-01#section-1-7 is the designated entry point. Short quotation, translated from the Chinese: “must not remain merely a statement of objectives” (line 157). This section sets out six protections, specifies three easily misjudged situations, and limits the conversion of analytical confidence into greater authority to act. [T-17]

Floor denotes basic constraints that should remain in options and their use, not an appendix that can be skipped when the framework claims to pursue good outcomes. These are normative requirements, not empirical facts that automatically exist whenever a system persists. Check who specifically receives protection, where the channels are, what price must be paid, and who can change arrangements when problems arise, rather than merely whether documents mention respect and safety. [T-17；T-norm]

First, human subjecthood: treat affected people as persons with purposes, understanding, feelings, and reasons, rather than variables with only predictable responses. Recording their circumstances and preferences can aid understanding, but the analyst's model must not be treated as the person themselves. Nor may the model's prediction that someone would consent substitute for that person's expression of consent. [T-17；T-human]

Second, channels for objections: people should have an opportunity to learn reasons sufficient to understand the effects, express disagreement, add material, and request correction. Whether a nominal mailbox, an incomprehensible appeal format, or an arrangement permitting only a plea to the original decision-maker suffices requires specific examination. Receiving views and genuinely changing an adjustable subsequent process must also be distinguished. Retaining the original decision after review may be well justified, but an automated reply must not masquerade as a substantive response. [T-17；T-feedback]

Third, the possibility of exit: examine whether people actually have accessible exit or alternative arrangements, rather than merely writing voluntary. Whether exit would mean losing essential services, bearing excessive costs, or facing improper pressure changes what remaining can demonstrate. Inability to exit provides even less basis for presuming consent. A specific institution may have separately restricted exit conditions; these must be explained and the applicable protections strengthened. Analysts must not independently invent unlimited powers of detention or coercion. [T-17；T-norm]

Fourth, minimum harm: examine avoidable harm, the distribution of impacts, and less harmful alternatives within the objectives, rights, and available options. This promises neither zero risk nor that burdens on a minority can be decided solely by average benefits. Waiting and non-action may entail losses, but that alone does not justify any action whatsoever. Proportionality, permission, and remedy still require explanation. [T-17；T-intervene]

Fifth, traceable responsibility: judgments and actions should be traceable to the relevant reasons, responsible parties, permissions, and time windows, so that when errors arise, it is clear who can explain, correct, stop, and remedy them. Traceability does not mean collecting unlimited personal information or instituting comprehensive surveillance. Necessary records must be compatible with minimum disclosure, and access to sensitive material should also be protected. [T-17；T-cost]

Sixth, genuine rollback: beyond technically restoring a state, check whether effects are actually reversed, support continues to be taken up, and affected people still bear unrecoverable losses. If some parts are irreversible, state this honestly and change the option or restrict its scope. A button labeled reversible cannot make past disclosures or missed opportunities disappear. The ability to compensate does not automatically mean recovery has occurred, and remedy alone cannot erase earlier permission problems. [T-17；T-intervene]

The three situations in Chinese source line 159 each dismantle an erroneous inference. Inability to exit does not imply voluntarily remaining; difficulty expressing a view does not imply having no objection; unwillingness to disclose does not imply no loss. Each shows that observation is constrained by conditions. None proves the reverse claim that every silent person necessarily objects or has been harmed. The appropriate status may be unknown, unobserved, or disclosure withheld by the person concerned. Offer safer means of expression where needed, rather than guessing on another's behalf. [T-17；T-boundary]

These protections should enter the option and the conditions for execution. For example, do not merely say appeals are allowed: specify an accessible entry point, processing responsibilities, and time window. Do not merely say exit is possible: examine dependence on services and transition costs. Do not merely name a responsible person: establish that they can actually stop or remedy the action. This is an operational explanation of the source's requirements, not a claim that they have already been implemented in any actual institution. [T-17]

The actual historical case is PNAS's 2014 editorial expression of concern about research involving Facebook. The editors distinguished the applicability of rules at the time from ethical concerns about informed consent and opportunities to opt out, while retaining the qualification that the arrangements might not have been fully consistent. This shows that discussing protections in data research must not end merely because formal arrangements exist. This inquiry has no basis for upgrading that concern into a finding of unlawfulness or harm to every participant. [R-PNAS]

The final sentence limits exchanging knowledge for power. Gathering more information and developing a more precise explanation may improve an analyst's factual judgments, but does not thereby expand their authority to act. Actions requiring consent, authorization, or review must still establish these separately. Conversely, lacking authority to execute does not prevent clearly explaining materials, proposing protective recommendations, or drafting institutions, provided the status and use of the work are not concealed. [T-17；T-choice]

The strongest counterargument is that exit, objections, and rollback can sometimes be difficult to provide fully in highly dependent environments: does that make all research impossible? This section does not treat difficulties in protection as proof that information is invalid. It requires that consent not be inferred from constrained behavior and that actual limitations enter comparison of options. Which protections are indispensable and which alternatives suffice require specific normative and institutional reasons; technical convenience or the value of research alone must not decide them. [T-17；T-norm]
argumentSteps: Premise: people's behavior and disclosures are affected by exit costs, conditions for expression, dependencies, and pressure.

Inferential connection: when these conditions are unspecified, silence or continued participation can be compatible with multiple states of willingness and loss. Neither automatically identifies consent, absence of objection, or absence of loss.

Normative conclusion: subjecthood, objections, exit, minimum harm, responsibility, and rollback must be implemented in options and execution conditions. Protection is more than a slogan about objectives.
Qualification: this does not infer from silence that everyone objects. Retain unknowns and protected clarification; do not compel disclosure to satisfy a model.
Permission boundary: more evidence and confidence in an explanation may affect judgments about knowledge, but must not independently generate new authority to act.

Evidential responsibility: whether protection is genuinely usable requires checking actual channels and affected positions; a historical editorial expression of concern establishes only what it published and does not substitute for determinations of effects, legality, or harm.

distinctions.leftText: The observation that a certain expression has not been received.
distinctions.rightText: Opportunities and costs of expression and the coverage of records must also be checked; these cannot automatically be equated.

distinctions.leftText: Continuing to participate under the given exit conditions.
distinctions.rightText: Requires the corresponding conditions of information, willingness, and authorization; outward behavior alone is insufficient.

distinctions.leftText: May reflect preservation of privacy or constraints on expression.
distinctions.rightText: Nondisclosure does not establish that loss is absent.

distinctions.leftText: Reasons, roles, and duties to correct errors can be located.
distinctions.rightText: Traceability cannot excuse collecting sensitive information without boundaries.

distinctions.leftText: Stronger support for a particular factual or mechanistic judgment.
distinctions.rightText: Authority to act still requires an independently valid basis.

boundaries: Constructed conditional counterexample: leaving a trial means losing the only essential service available. Even if nobody leaves, zero exits cannot directly establish that everyone is voluntarily satisfied.

Constructed conditional counterexample: complaints are accepted only in person during working hours. The absence of complaints from people unable to attend does not establish that they have no objections.

Constructed conditional counterexample: a system restores its old configuration, but sensitive material has already been seen by unauthorized people. Rolling back the technical state cannot undo information exposure that has occurred.
The source rules out automatic inference, not imposes an automatic counteraccusation: no disclosure is not equivalent to no loss, nor does it establish that loss exists.

An editorial expression of concern is not a retraction, a court judgment, or a definitive conclusion that all participants were harmed. This lesson does not turn historical publication-ethics material into current personal legal advice.
questions: If nobody exits, can we declare that everyone consents?
To make responsibility traceable, may we require disclosure of all unrelated personal experiences?
If an analyst's model predicts more accurately than the person concerned, may the analyst authorize something on that person's behalf?
Does observing zero complaints in the mathematical example establish that the 80 people actually have objections?

caseNotes.title: Historical editorial expression of concern: informed consent and exit cannot be assessed by form alone
caseNotes.text: On July 3, 2014, PNAS published an editorial expression of concern about Facebook-related research, stating that its data-collection practices might not have been fully consistent with principles of fully informed consent and opting out, while explaining limits on the applicability of the rules at the time. This was a qualified ethical concern, not a ruling that illegality or harm had occurred. [R-PNAS]
