4.5.title: 4.5 Historical formation, current carriers, and G3 conditional increment
4.5.lead: “The past has an effect” can ask at least three things: how it shaped the present, how the present continues to carry that effect, and what the past adds after the present is already known. G3 addresses only the third; each needs separate evidence.
explanation: Chinese source line 663 states these three questions and emphasizes, in translation, “the first two may hold while the third does not.” Historical formation asks how earlier experiences change the current state; carrier transmission asks how current records, skills, damage, organizational arrangements, and so on retain or update effects and influence what follows; conditional increment asks what information or effect historical material adds given the currently registered representation. G3 specifically tests the third; it does not provide a single new definition for all historical causation, learning, accumulation, persistence, or reproduction. [T-45]

The distinction is necessary because the same fact can be questioned from different temporal positions. Practice may form a skill, and the skill may change later performance. If the current skill already carries sufficient target-relevant information, adding practice history will not improve prediction. Disappearance of extra predictive information does not erase formation; conversely, “no extra information” cannot establish that the skill formed or transmission occurred, since both causal chains still require their own material. [T-45]

G3a tests predictive path dependence, with historical_conditional_predictive_gain as its sole permitted success criterion. Historical variables must be defined before observing future outcomes; after controlling for the registered current state, environment, and measurement protocol, they must still supply a reproducible out-of-sample conditional increment for the predefined future target. The comparison is between two information sets, not between having or lacking a historical story: the current representation and relevant controls, versus these plus historical variables. Additional accuracy must not result from future-information leakage, opportunities for model selection, or deliberate omission of known current variables. [T-45; T-41]

“Conditional” means asking whether knowing history still helps on top of the current information already known. Here the current state is a registered representation actually available, not an omniscient observer's complete world state. Results must be tied to representation, target, window, error, and comparison method; changing the target or adding current variables may alter the increment. That does not automatically falsify the earlier bounded predictive result; it means the question it answers has a scope. [T-45]

G3b tests causal path dependence. In addition to the out-of-sample conditional increment above, exactly one of history_erasure_effect, history_restoration_effect, and equivalent_intervention_effect must be preselected, and the corresponding erasure, restoration, or equivalent intervention must exceed the predefined threshold. Correlational prediction using history cannot simply be labeled causal, nor may all three operations be tried and the most favorable afterward presented as the original criterion. [T-45]

For these causal operations, researchers must explain exactly which carrier/record is erased or restored, how this is implemented, which current conditions change, and how an identifying comparison is made. The names do not mean that the already-occurred past is literally changed, nor guarantee arbitrary alteration of history while all relevant current conditions remain fixed. If an operation only changes current skill, storage, or damage, its effect may answer the carrier question; whether it additionally satisfies G3b's conditional-increment and selected-operation criteria must still be tested, not conferred by the word “erasure.” [T-45; T-causal]

The null models for both G3a and G3b include the registered current state being a sufficient statistic for the specified target, with history supplying no further conditional increment. G3b additionally requires that its own preselected intervention criterion produce no outcome change; unselected operations do not count toward this instance's success or failure. Sufficiency here is target-relative conditional informational sufficiency: it does not require recovering every past detail or imply sufficiency for other tasks. [T-45; T-F1]

If historical variables are defined only after future outcomes have been seen, current-state information is clearly omitted, or subtype and success criterion were not uniquely preselected, the source requires suspension of the instance. Suspension does not delete historical records; it prevents packaging this material as predefined confirmation. Exploratory findings can retain their status and motivate an independent test. Omitting known relevant current skill so that practice history appears especially predictive is precisely the increment this section forbids manufacturing. [T-45; T-41]

If history supplies no positive increment after controlling for the relevant current state, environment, and measurement protocol, or if G3b's preselected operation fails the positive gate, the default is not supported or unresolved. A bounded refutation or zero conclusion still requires the frozen equivalence or sufficiency, power or sensitivity, and tolerance rules. Nonsignificance, small samples, or coarse measurement cannot automatically constitute proof of sufficiency. Favorable results from unselected operations cannot rescue the original instance. [T-45; T-41]

The H→S→Y example in Chinese source line 675 uses H for earlier experience, S for current skill, and Y for subsequent outcome. H may affect Y through S; once sufficient S is given, H adds no predictive information, while the total historical effect still exists. The conditional question answered by controlling for a mediator differs from the total-effect question. More observational controls are not automatically better: choose them according to the estimation target and causal design instead of adding every measurable variable to the model. [T-45; T-causal]

The carrier-transmission route needs four kinds of positive material: measurement of the current carrier or state; how earlier inputs or changes entered it; how it was retained or updated within the declared window; and longitudinal material on its continued influence on the predefined outcome. Merely observing that a file remains or an outcome persists cannot complete all four links. A file may never be used; a persistent outcome may result from uninterrupted external exposure; a carrier with the same name at two times may have been replaced. [T-45]

A further claim of causal carrier effects requires a proportionate comparison, such as interruption, replacement, restoration, or natural variation with identification conditions, addressing common inputs, continued exposure, selection, attrition, and measurement change. Association without corresponding identification grounds stops at cross-time description or a mechanism candidate. Not every question requires an experiment, but the adopted historical reconstruction, observational, or comparative design must disclose what it can and cannot distinguish. [T-45; T-causal]

Applying for formal mechanism support through later carrier branches in this book also requires a corresponding qualified G2-instance or interface-specified H-instance covering the channel and outcome. H5 supports only trace retention in the selected carrier and window; it cannot alone supply subsequent effects or a causal gate. This requirement concerns the formal-support route; domain research may still have bounded conclusions under its own design and does not lose its original grounds merely because it did not use this book's contracts. [T-45; T-H5; T-domain]

Coverage cannot exceed the original instance: an immediate effect is not automatically long-term, nor is short-window retention automatically reproduction across periods. Several separately supported local links cannot directly be combined into a complete same-case chain: an upstream change must actually reach the object, state, and time to which the next link can respond. A total effect identified by a qualified comparison can be retained without first exhausting every microscopic mechanism; add the corresponding connections only when seeking a more specific propagation explanation. [T-45; T-causal]

The carrier-transmission and G3-increment routes must each independently state evidence, competing explanations, failure conditions, and conclusion ceilings. Carrier support with G3 unsupported is a possible combination; G3 failing does not imply carrier support. Failure of increment cannot justify relabeling the same material “carrier-route success” and automatically closing the original inquiry. If independent carrier evidence exists, honestly report a different proposition without switching the original question. [T-45]

Chinese source line 683 further expresses representation dependence as x_t, z_t=π(x_t), and h_t: x_t is the model's complete current state, π compresses it into registered representation z_t, and h_t is retained history. If π merges different current states that affect the future, history may distinguish those merged states, producing historical gain conditional on z_t. Yet the complete-state dynamics may not actually require an additional historical term. This is a competing explanation that must be examined, not proof that the real world necessarily lacks memory. [T-45; T-C11]

Make proportionate comparisons of current-carrier availability, measurement error, and model complexity. Coarse measurement of relevant current variables may let history serve as a proxy; greater fitting freedom for the history model may also create an unfair advantage. Conversely, complete real-world states are usually unavailable; “the state can always be expanded in principle” cannot substitute for case-specific evidence to declare no historical increment. Honestly record how much current information can be obtained, when it is obtained, and whether its use is permitted. [T-45]

Appendix C.11 gives an exactly calculable two-queue example. The complete current pair of queues determines the next state, while the current mean merges different allocations; the historical initial mean helps reduce error caused by this merging. The two positive errors in the original manuscript are not accidental performance of fitting software, but minimum risks over the complete constructed state domain under specified weights and squared loss. This lesson shows why the conditional mean is optimal, two particular trajectories, and calculated values for four input sets, without treating artificial enumeration as real-world samples. [T-C9; T-C11]

Three practical conclusions may therefore differ: history-assisted prediction is useful; how history formed the current carrier has an independent explanation; and whether the narrow G3 instance meets formal-support requirements remains a separate judgment. Any positive G3 result permits registering only predictive or causal path differences within the preregistered window, not historical destiny, absolute irreversibility, responsibility, or real-world authorization. With insufficient data, identify precisely which question remains unresolved instead of concluding “history determines everything” or “the present suffices, so the past is irrelevant.” [T-45]
argumentSteps: First separate historical formation, continued current-carrier effects, and conditional increment beyond the currently registered representation, avoiding one kind of evidence answering all three questions.
For G3, define historical variables, current representation, controls, target, window, and the unique G3a or G3b criterion before outcomes; fix comparison rules and data splits.
Compare out-of-sample target performance using current information alone and with history added; examine omitted known current states, measurement error, leakage, and model complexity.
Beyond conditional increment, G3b requires identification and an above-threshold effect for its selected erasure/restoration/equivalent intervention; unselected operations cannot rescue it.

The carrier route separately checks input entry, retention/updating, longitudinal consequences, and proportionate causal comparisons; formal mechanism support additionally requires G2 or a specified H instance covering the object, outcome, and window.

Formally, a projection merging current states can generate historical predictive increment. This counterexample refutes the unconditional inference that “increment must come from additional memory in the complete dynamics,” not real-world memory.

Report only bounded combinations supported by current material; G3 failure neither cancels historical formation nor automatically establishes a carrier mechanism, and positive support generates neither destiny nor authorization.

boundaries: Counterexample from the source: in H→S→Y, a sufficient current skill state S can absorb H's predictive information; a zero additional quantity under G3 does not negate historical formation or learning in general within the model.

Counterexample from the source: in C.11, the historical mean can supplement the current mean, but the complete current queues already determine the future; historical gain alone does not establish an additional historical term in the complete dynamics.

Author-constructed conditional counterexample: H, S, and Y are mutually independent, with no causal arrow from H to S or from S to Y; H has no predictive increment given S, yet the claimed transmission through a carrier is also absent. Failure of G3 therefore cannot establish the carrier route.

Author-constructed conditional counterexample: a file has been preserved for years but never subsequently read or used. Its existence and persistence alone do not establish that it changed a decision.

Author-constructed conditional counterexample: deliberately leaving a known, available skill unmeasured and then obtaining predictive improvement from practice history cannot secure qualified G3 support through that artificial omission.

Author-constructed conditional counterexample: treating recollections classified after an outcome as a prior historical variable risks carrying future information back into the past; the corresponding confirmatory instance should be paused, and the materials' actual timing preserved.

Failure of the formal carrier route or G3 route does not automatically revoke well-supported historical research within a domain; likewise, this lesson does not retrospectively certify an actual accident reconstruction as a formal G3 instance.

caseLinks.title: Apollo 13: earlier ground operations, the damaged state during flight, and the later failure

caseNotes.title: Apollo 13: earlier ground operations, the damaged state during flight, and the later failure
caseNotes.text: The section ‘Preflight Damage to Tank Wiring’ in NASA's investigation report of June 15, 1970 records prolonged heating during the special detanking operations of March 27–28; the investigation concluded that the protective switches most probably welded closed under a 65-volt DC load. Subsequent tests supported the finding that overheating could severely damage wire insulation, which the report connected with the later risk of a short circuit. This reuses the accident but adds a focus on how earlier operations left a physical state that continued to have effects, rather than examining only inputs on the day of the accident. The report also retains probabilistic wording about the ignition mechanism and the limitation that telemetry could not establish every detail.
caseNotes.sourceLabel: NASA, Report of Apollo13 Review Board
caseNotes.sourceLocator: Report dated 1970-06-15; Chapter 5, ‘Preflight Damage to Tank Wiring’, printed pages 5-9—5-11 (PDF pages 175—177); ignition assessment on 5-6 (PDF page 172), and telemetry limitations on 5-8 (PDF page 174)
caseNotes.boundary: This is a bounded historical causal judgment formed by the investigation from logs, telemetry, tests, and reconstruction, not a G3 study testing additional historical increments while holding the complete pre-failure state fixed. No comparative result establishes whether G3 holds or fails in this case, nor can it be said that the damaged state was fully known at the time. This lesson does not reassign individual responsibility.

teachingExamples.title: Mathematical teaching construction: the total historical effect and the conditional residual can be separated
teachingExamples.text: Let H equal 0 or 1 with equal probability, skill S=H, and outcome Y=10S, and assume that H can be intervened on while the other equations remain unchanged. do(H=0) gives Y=0, and do(H=1) gives Y=10, so the total effect within the model is 10. Given S, Y is uniquely determined, and the minimum squared prediction error using S and using (S,H) is 0 in both cases. Thus a formation chain H→S→Y and no additional predictive quantity from H given S can coexist.
teachingExamples.assumptions: The distribution, structural equations, domain of operations, and sufficient measurement are all teaching assumptions; this is not an actual experiment on human training.
teachingExamples.boundary: Whether controlling for a mediator is appropriate in reality depends on the estimation target; this construction does not certify actual learning, G3 qualification, or permission to intervene.

teachingExamples.title: Expanding a mathematical example from the book: how omissions in a current projection produce a historical increment
teachingExamples.text: Following Appendices C.9/C.11, let the initial state (q1,q2) range over the 961 ordered combinations in {0,…,30}², with each initial state weighted 1/961. There are no new tasks in any round, and service actually follows F(q1,q2)=(max(q1−5,0),max(q2−5,0)); this is not merely an uncertain upper bound of ‘at most 5’. Let h be the initial mean, z the mean after the first round, and Y the mean after the second round. Trajectory A: (0,20)→(0,15)→(0,10), with h=10, z=7.5, and Y=5; trajectory B: (10,15)→(5,10)→(0,5), with h=12.5, z=7.5, and Y=2.5. The same z merges different values of Y, while h distinguishes these two trajectories. For any input V and output a, E[(Y−a)²|V]=Var(Y|V)+(a−E[Y|V])²; the second term is nonnegative, so prediction by the conditional mean attains the minimum loss on that fiber. Advancing each original initial state individually and preserving its original weight gives the following minimum MSEs for the four input types: z: 0.579016561; (z,h): 0.271143397; complete current two-queue state x: 0; (x,h): 0 (rounded to 9 decimal places). History improves the coarse representation but no longer improves the already complete current queues.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Uniformity applies to the original initial states, not to means, states after the first round, or distinct input fibers; the numbers are rounded from exact fractional calculations over a finite artificial domain. Squared loss, absence of noise, symmetric service, and availability of the inputs are all stipulated.
teachingExamples.boundary: This is mathematical risk, not prediction error in a real service system or empirical G3 evidence. Distinguishing the means in one case does not establish that history is fully sufficient for every sample; the MSE of (z,h) over the whole domain remains greater than 0.

questionAnswers.question: Practice did form a skill, but current skill predicts the next score equally accurately. Does this mean history never played a role?
questionAnswers.answer: No. The formation process and additional information given skill are different questions; the total historical effect can be realized through current skill.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source, lines 637 and 675; teaching structural equations.

questionAnswers.question: If G3a has passed, can causal path dependence be registered?
questionAnswers.answer: No. G3b additionally requires proportionate identification and threshold results for a preselected erasure, restoration, or equivalent intervention.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source, lines 667—673.

questionAnswers.question: If H5 establishes that an archive persists, does that directly support a claim that it changes subsequent action?
questionAnswers.answer: No. Evidence of reading or entry into transitions, longitudinal effects, and proportionate comparisons is required; the formal carrier branch also needs specified G2 or H support covering the corresponding claim.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source, lines 677—679.

questionAnswers.question: Two queues both have a current mean of 7.5. What are their respective next means?
questionAnswers.answer: A is 5 and B is 2.5; the mean omits the current allocation. The initial means of 10 and 12.5 distinguish these two examples, but history plus the mean is still not fully sufficient over the entire domain.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source, Appendix C.11, line 4956, and the complete calculation.

questionAnswers.question: Can the original table be reproduced by reassigning equal weights to the distinct states after the first round?
questionAnswers.answer: No. The weight of 1/961 for each of the 961 original initial states must be preserved; when several initial states converge on the same current state, their probabilities must be added.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source, Appendix C.11, line 4956.

questionAnswers.question: Since all history can theoretically be packed into a state, must G3 fail in this case?
questionAnswers.answer: No. The representation actually available in this case is not an omniscient state; comparisons should follow the registered representation, target, and window, and be retested when the representation changes.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source, lines 683—685.

questionAnswers.question: If G3 has not passed, can the carrier route be declared to have passed instead?
questionAnswers.answer: The judgment cannot be changed automatically. If independent carrier evidence exists, a separate bounded conclusion may be drawn, but its evidence, competing explanations, and stopping point must be explicit.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source, lines 637 and 681.

figures.alt: Historical formation asks how H changes S; carrier transmission asks how S continues to affect Y; G3 asks what additional quantity H provides given the current representation. The G3a predictive gate and the G3b causal gate are listed separately.
figures.caption: Created by the author based on §4.5; these three questions do not form a single linear staircase that must be passed in full, step by step.

figures.alt: The initial states (0,20) and (10,15) advance to (0,15) and (5,10), respectively, both with a current mean of 7.5; after another advance, the target means are 5 and 2.5. The initial mean distinguishes these two trajectories.
figures.caption: An openly presented calculation of the book's mathematical example in Appendix C.11, with no new tasks and service in each round following the given equation.

figures.alt: Under 961 equally probable original initial states, the minimum MSE for the current mean is approximately 0.579016561, or approximately 0.271143397 after adding the historical mean; it is 0 for the complete current state and remains 0 when history is added.
figures.caption: The author recalculated the book's artificial state domain using exact fractions; these are not real observational data. The MSE values apply only to the specified distribution, target, and loss.

4.5.diagramBrief: Figure 1 places historical formation, carrier transmission, and the G3 conditional increment side by side, while explaining the difference between G3a and G3b. Figure 2 shows the two exact queue trajectories in C.11, highlighting different futures despite the same current mean. Figure 3 lists the minimum MSE for four input types under the same artificial distribution, explicitly stating that the original initial states are equally probable and specifying the model boundaries of the zero values. All figures are currently static; if switching is implemented in the future, it may switch input representations with weights explicitly unchanged, without generating real-world data or treating an updated representation as though the original test had never changed.

applicability.reason: This section involves actual historical formation and physical carriers. It uses newly checked material on preflight damage in the NASA investigation while preserving uncertainty in the reconstruction, and uses an explicit mathematical model to distinguish total effects, carriers, and conditional residuals.

openQuestions: The complete current state is usually unavailable in reality; specific historical predictive value and causal paths require data proportionate to the task. This lesson has not conducted a G3 test on Apollo 13 controlling for the current representation.

4.6.title: 4.6 G4 representational closure and object or intervention conversion
4.6.lead: An aggregate representation may describe the current total correctly yet omit the composition that determines the next step or the response to a particular intervention. G4 must first specify which failure or conversion is being tested; closure itself can also be a valuable result.
explanation: Lines 689—691 of the Chinese source distinguish G4a closure failure from G4b object or intervention conversion. G4a asks whether variables excluded by the scale representation still provide a predetermined conditional increment once the retained variables are given; G4b asks whether a selected conversion difference arises between scale transformation and dynamics, intervention, object identity, or related features. Neither is established merely by observing that two levels are ‘related’; each has explicit comparisons, thresholds, and stopping points. [T-46]

G4a permits three success criteria, one of which an instance must preselect: conditional_information_gain asks whether excluded scale variables increase the specified conditional information; conditional_predictive_gain asks whether they improve specified conditional predictive performance; conditional_intervention_gain asks whether they improve specified intervention-evaluation performance. Information, prediction, and intervention are not the same metric; a positive result on one cannot count as success on another. The null model concerns only the selected criterion: given the retained variables, the excluded scale variables provide no corresponding increment above the predetermined threshold. [T-46]

G4b permits five criteria, again with only one preselected. object_dynamics_non_commutation asks whether advancing the dynamics and then converting differs from converting first and then advancing proportionate target dynamics; intervention_non_commutation asks whether the order of intervention and conversion makes a difference; identity_criterion_violation asks whether the target mapping no longer satisfies the prefrozen K; effective_relation_change asks whether the effective relation changes beyond tolerance; intervention_response_change asks whether the intervention response changes beyond tolerance. Each requires named mappings and actual objects; the five cannot be combined into a fallback of ‘something is bound to differ’. [T-46]

G4b null models likewise match the preselected criteria one to one: object dynamics commute, interventions commute, the target mapping satisfies K, the effective relation stays within tolerance, or the intervention response stays within tolerance. Unselected criteria neither rescue nor refute this instance. For example, if a preselected change in relations does not meet the threshold and K is later found not to hold, that issue should be recorded separately and accurately; the original claim about relations cannot be reclassified as having passed. [T-46]

D3/E5 requires specifying the source and target scales, retained/changed/lost variables, operators, errors, scope of applicability, comparison targets, and competing explanations. Without this inspectable bridge, repeated terms and similar narratives are merely parallel descriptions. E5 does not require G4 to be true first; rather, a G4 instance must pass E5. This avoids wrongly making ‘cross-scale research can be conducted’ depend on ‘cross-scale failure must first be found’. [T-D3；T-E5]

General correlation, unconditional coupling, similar narratives, and omitted variables at the same scale are insufficient to support G4. The key is what the declared scale transformation discards and whether it still changes the selected target conditional on the variables already retained. If the original model has merely omitted a variable at the same scale, analyze that omission first; do not label it cross-scale closure failure merely to fit the terminology. [T-46]

An instance is paused if a unique subtype/criterion was not specified before results, or if the D3/E5 mapping, comparison model, positive threshold, null_decision_rule, power or sensitivity gate, and tolerance were not frozen. This prevents observing a difference first and then changing the scale, K, or threshold to guarantee success. Reasonable exploration may remain exploration, and existing domain results retain their standing according to their designs, but a nonexistent confirmatory contract cannot be backfilled. [T-46；T-41；T-domain]

If the positive gate passes, G4a registers only closure failure within the preregistered variables, metrics, scales, and window; G4b registers only the selected conversion candidate within the predetermined mapping, K, scales, and window. Failure to pass the positive gate defaults to unsupported or unresolved. Only when preregistered equivalence/sufficiency tests, power/sensitivity gates, and tolerance gates actually pass may G4a register criterion-bounded closure, or G4b register that the preselected conversion was not found. Nonsignificance is not proof of closure, much less of equivalence across all interventions. [T-46]

This makes both closure and nonclosure researchable outcomes. If a concise representation is already sufficient for the current task, criterion-bounded closure supports continuing to use it; if nonclosure is detected, then consider revising the representation or narrowing its uses. supported and null_supported are relative to the preselected factual assertion: when the assertion is ‘closure failure’, null_supported may favor retaining the concise model. They are not rankings of methodological quality, theoretical progress, or the superiority of scales. [T-46]

Sufficiency must be relative to the target, horizon, environment, and permitted operations. A representation sufficient for prediction under natural evolution may become insufficient under an added intervention, because the compositions merged into the same macroscopic state may respond differently. When insufficiency is found, one can add necessary variables, retain composition or history, restrict the set of actions, shorten the horizon, or narrow the use; recovering every microscopic detail is unnecessary. Conversely, emergence, aggregation, same-scale omissions, and cross-boundary transmission do not universally presuppose G4 closure failure; a well-closed model can still correctly represent cross-boundary effects. [T-46；T-D3]

The A1/A2 probability example at the end of this section addresses only a specified one-step target. Under natural evolution, both have probability 0.2 of entering B, so predicting ‘whether B is reached at the next step’ need not distinguish composition. After intervention, the probabilities become 0.8 and 0.1, making the mixture response 0.8p+0.1(1−p)=0.1+0.7p, where p is the share of A1. Adding p alone answers this mixture's one-step probability, but does not specify how p itself subsequently updates, how other target blocks change, or whether other interventions remain applicable. [T-46；T-461]

Subsection 4.6.1 further supplies exact formal closure and approximate error bounds, explaining why static queries, one-step targets, multistep dynamics, and intervention operations must be separated. Mathematical criteria can establish relationships in a given model; they cannot dispense with measurement, mappings, samples, and positive/null gates for real-world G4. Crossing scales does not automatically expand authority to act on the J axis either. [T-461；T-E5]
argumentSteps: First declare the mapping M and source/target scales, target, horizon, environment, and permitted operations, explicitly identifying retained and excluded variables.
Freeze G4a or G4b and a single success criterion; establish a matching N0, comparison method, positive and null thresholds, sensitivity, and tolerance.
Check the selected increment conditional on retained variables, or compare the selected order of dynamics/intervention, K, relation, or response; do not substitute general correlation.

Passing the positive gate supports only the corresponding closure failure or conversion candidate; failure leaves the instance unsupported/unresolved, and a null conclusion requires independently completing every gate.

Use the result to choose whether to enrich the representation, restrict operations, shorten the horizon, or retain an already sufficient concise model; do not equate higher scales or positive statuses with superiority.
Separate formal models, empirical support, and actual authority; the construction in this section demonstrates logic only and does not automatically certify real G4 instances.

caseNotes.title: Actual experiment: overall density and local congestion patterns on the same circular track
caseNotes.text: Sugiyama et al.’s 2008 paper reports arranging 22 cars on a circular track with a circumference of 230 meters. They initially traveled at nearly uniform spacing, after which stop-and-go waves emerged. Figure 3 compares the initial scene with the scene after 3 minutes, and Figure 4 gives vehicle trajectories. The bounded inference here is that an aggregate description such as a fixed number of cars divided by track length can remain unchanged while local traffic patterns change. Thus ‘the overall-density statistic is correct’ must be separated from ‘this information suffices to answer questions about local congestion or the next response’.

teachingExamples.text: Let p=P(A1|A) and 1−p=P(A2|A). Under natural conditions P(B|A1)=P(B|A2)=0.2, so P(B|A)=0.2p+0.2(1−p)=0.2. Knowing A without knowing p cannot yield the same intervention probability for all mixtures; adding p can restore this time point’s one-step target.

4.6.1.title: 4.6.1 Formal Closure, Approximate Closure, and Empirical Qualification
4.6.1.lead: The formal question of closure is whether the same simplified state can determine the same next simplified state. Approximate closure adds a question: how does per-step error accumulate over the required horizon?
explanation: Chinese source line 705 gives a source-state domain X, a representation π:X→Y with Y=π(X), and deterministic one-step dynamics F:X→X. Exact closure requires a macroscopic update F̄:Y→Y such that π(F(x))=F̄(π(x)) for every x. The left side advances at the source level before aggregating; the right aggregates first and then advances at the macro level. Only equality allows the macro representation to update independently. Taking Y as the actually attainable image avoids imposing irrelevant conditions on representations without sources. [T-461; T-C8]

Explicit proof of necessity: if such an F̄ exists, choose any π(x)=π(x′). Then π(F(x))=F̄(π(x))=F̄(π(x′))=π(F(x′)). The same current representation cannot split into two different next representations; otherwise the same input would require F̄ to output two values simultaneously, so no such function exists. This is a logical contradiction independent of sample size or fitting algorithm. [T-461; T-C8]

Explicit proof of sufficiency: conversely, suppose π(x)=π(x′) always implies π(F(x))=π(F(x′)). For each y∈Y, define F̄(y) as π(F(x)) for any source state satisfying π(x)=y. Since the condition ensures that all such x give the same value, the definition does not depend on the representative chosen. Since Y=π(X), each y has a source; F(x) remains in X, so the output is also in Y. Thus π∘F=F̄∘π holds. [T-461; T-C8]

If this condition holds over the whole state domain for fixed F, multistep closure follows by induction: at t=0, π∘F⁰=π=F̄⁰∘π; if π∘Fᵗ=F̄ᵗ∘π, then π∘Fᵗ⁺¹=(π∘F)∘Fᵗ=F̄∘π∘Fᵗ=F̄ᵗ⁺¹∘π. Finding no conflict in a few visited states cannot replace the whole-domain premise: future trajectories may reach unchecked states sharing a representation but differing in response. [T-461; T-C8]

Sufficiency for a static query cannot substitute for dynamical closure. If the current question asks only for the sum of two queues, retaining the sum is of course exact; under service saturation, however, different allocations with the same sum can update to different sums. The target has changed from ‘the current total’ to ‘the next-step total’. This is a task change, not a mathematical contradiction; F1 static recovery and F2 dynamical closure each have their own conditions. [T-461; T-D3; T-C9]

If multiple operations are permitted, specify the source update F_u for each operation version u and test the projection condition separately. A proof for natural F cannot directly be applied to F_u. If one macroscopic operation name admits several microscopic implementations, check whether they produce the same macroscopic response or responses within tolerance. If an operation is feasible only in some collapsed states, check common implementability or restrict the domain. A shared operation name does not eliminate these differences. [T-461; T-C8]

Following Appendix C.8, this guide develops the case of a finite stochastic system with a given partition; comparing means alone is insufficient. For any two states in the same source block, compare the sums of conditional transition probabilities into each target block. Equality defines a macroscopic transition kernel independent of hidden composition. Accidental equality for one initial mixture may fail when the mixture changes. Nor can ‘the same probability of reaching B’ be expanded into ‘the same distribution over all target blocks’; the example in 4.6 therefore claims only one-step sufficiency for the specified target. [T-461; T-C8]

Approximate closure first fixes a metric d, ε≥0, L≥0, operations, operating range, initial state, and horizon. Every step must satisfy the projection-deviation bound d(π(F(x)),F̄(π(x)))≤ε; the macroscopic update must satisfy the Lipschitz condition d(F̄(y),F̄(y′))≤L·d(y,y′) at the comparison points involved. These are bounds for every relevant state and step, not a single average error; all points used by the actual and macro trajectories must remain within the range where the premises hold. [T-461; T-C8]

Let the actual projection be π(x_t), the macro-model state be y_t, and e_t=d(π(x_t),y_t), starting from the same initial representation with e_0=0. The triangle inequality separates ‘one-step projection deviation’ from ‘existing error amplified by the macro update’: e_{t+1}≤d(π(F(x_t)),F̄(π(x_t)))+d(F̄(π(x_t)),F̄(y_t))≤ε+Le_t. Starting from e_0=0 gives e_1≤ε and e_2≤ε+Lε; induction gives e_t≤ε∑_{j=0}^{t−1}L^j. [T-461; T-C8]

For 0≤L<1, the geometric sum is (1−Lᵗ)/(1−L), so e_t≤ε/(1−L) at times satisfying the premises; for L=1, e_t≤tε; for L>1, e_t≤ε(Lᵗ−1)/(L−1), and the bound may grow rapidly. These are upper bounds, not assertions that actual error must attain them. Nonzero initial error adds Lᵗe_0; changing per-step error or L requires rewriting the recursion rather than mechanically applying the fixed formula. [T-461; T-C8]

Adding a composition proportion may repair a one-step probability at one time without supplying that proportion’s own update. The approximate formula also cannot be applied directly from a short-run average fitting error. Leaving the operating range, changing operations, or encountering omitted errors requires rechecking premises. With only finite empirical material and insufficient sensitivity, ‘no departure yet detected’ remains unresolved; it is not a mathematical proof of exact closure. [T-461]

This subsection establishes conditional relations within a model and does not award support to a real G4 instance. Actual applications still require independent checks of measurement, source-to-target mapping, samples, operation implementation, and error conditions, plus the positive and null gates. Proof of exact closure, finite-domain enumeration, numerical estimation, and real-world testing each retain their own status; numerical checking adds no real-world observations and creates no authority to act. [T-461; T-form]
argumentSteps: Necessity: the same represented input into a single F̄ must yield the same output, so its projections after source-level updating must agree.
Sufficiency: define F̄ by the common next projection of source states sharing a representation; the image condition ensures total definition, and agreement within each fiber ensures unambiguity.
Multiple steps: with fixed dynamics over the whole domain, start at t=0 and repeatedly apply the commutation relation to obtain any nonnegative integer number of steps.

Operation/stochastic branches: test each permitted operation and microscopic implementation separately; for a finite stochastic system with a given partition, test every target block’s probability, not just the mean.
Approximation: the triangle inequality, per-step ε bound, and Lipschitz condition give e_{t+1}≤ε+Le_t; with e_0=0 the recursion yields a geometric sum.
Boundary: all premises must hold throughout the required horizon and operating range; mapping the mathematical conclusion to reality, measurement, and instance eligibility require separate evidence.

teachingExamples.title: Mathematical teaching construction: a static total cannot advance independently
teachingExamples.text: Let X be pairs of nonnegative integer queues, π(q1,q2)=q1+q2, and let F subtract the actually serviceable min(q,5) at each position. Both x=(0,6) and x′=(3,3) have π=6; F(x)=(0,1) gives π=1, whereas F(x′)=(0,0) gives π=0. If a macro function F̄ existed, F̄(6) would have to equal both 1 and 0, a contradiction. These two states witness failure of exact closure, although π still answers the current total accurately.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Queues, service equations, absence of arrivals, and deterministic operations are all stipulated; no actual queueing effect is estimated.
teachingExamples.boundary: Other representations or dynamics may be closed; a counterexample targets only the specified π and F.

teachingExamples.title: Mathematical teaching construction: identical one-step error bounds, different multistep guarantees
teachingExamples.text: Let ε=0.1 and e0=0, comparing fixed L=0.5,1,2. The geometric-sum upper bounds for t=1 through 4 are: L=0.5: (0.1,0.15,0.175,0.1875), with long-run uniform bound 0.2; L=1: (0.1,0.2,0.3,0.4); L=2: (0.1,0.3,0.7,1.5). Values follow from B_{t+1}=0.1+LB_t and B0=0; they are conditional guarantees, not three actual error trajectories.

teachingExamples.boundary: This does not establish that these L or ε exist in reality; L>1 says only that the bound can amplify, not that every actual error grows exponentially.

questionAnswers.answer: A function can give only one output for the same input; the two conflicting requirements already constitute a counterexample.

questionAnswers.question: Why is agreement of the next representation within each fiber also sufficient?
questionAnswers.answer: The common value can define that macrostate’s update; every macrostate has a source, and choosing a different representative does not change the result.

questionAnswers.answer: No. Uncovered compatible states or operations may split; whole-domain conditions or an explicit valid subdomain and reachability are required.

questionAnswers.question: Why do random 0/2 in A and constant 1 in B have equal means without distributional closure?
questionAnswers.answer: A assigns 0.5 each to 0 and 2; B assigns 1 to 1. Target-block probabilities differ, and the mean 1 erases that distinction.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source line 707 and the counterexample.

questionAnswers.question: With ε=0.1 and L=2, must the fourth-step error be 1.5?
questionAnswers.answer: No; 1.5 is an upper bound while the premises hold, and actual error can be smaller.
questionAnswers.basis: The recursion and teaching values.

questionAnswers.question: Can a training mean error of 0.1 be used directly as ε=0.1?
questionAnswers.answer: No. A uniform bound for the relevant states and steps is required, along with Lipschitz and operating-range conditions.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source line 709.

4.7.title: 4.7 A Fictional Group of Root Instances
4.7.lead: These four fictional cards are not four experimental reports. They place G1–G4's preceding evidential responsibilities in one setting to examine how the questions connect and how they cannot substitute for one another.
explanation: Chinese source line 715 explicitly states, in translation, “No external observations are cited.” m1–m4 demonstrate contracts within a fictional multilayer transport model, not an actual organization, engineering accident, or collected dataset. Readers can learn what each must ask and how it can fail, but cannot add the four to an empirical-support inventory. Conditional results expressed with “if” and “suppose” do not imply actual occurrence. [T-47]

These are teaching abbreviations, not four formal instances with every field and evidential artifact supplied. Full eligibility still follows §4.1: two record sections, prior freezing, mode, splits, four outcome states, departure disclosure, and resolvable evidence, among other requirements. For example, m1 lists only some object fields; that does not permit permanent omission of D0's relations R and interfaces I. Actual research must still explain these under the full object contract. Parameters, samples, or measurement precision absent from the original must remain unspecified, not invented for the author. [T-47；T-41；T-D0]

m1/G1a asks about predictive grouping gain for a candidate group of units. Freeze beforehand the candidate group, B/X/T/SP/K, grouping method, complexity-matched N0 without that grouping information, the single out_of_sample_predictive_gain criterion, and its metric and threshold. Excellent training-set performance means only fit to those data, not out-of-sample gain. Loss of gain after a slight boundary perturbation fails the predetermined robustness requirement; replication in independent time blocks is another requirement selected by this example. Read m1's “failure” with the preceding section as noncompletion of positive-support conditions, not automatic proof of the null model. [T-47；T-G1]

If m1 passes under the teaching premise that all conditions hold, it yields only bounded grouping-gain support within the corresponding window. It does not show aligned intentions within the group or identify which route caused the target change. Using this candidate object to pose m2 next is a continuation of research, not automatic completion of G2 causal identification by G1 grouping performance. [T-47；T-G1]

m2/G2a first specifies a channel and target transition, selects only controlled_perturbation_effect, and uses controlled blockage as the perturbation. Only if a proportionate design excludes shared-input, alternative-channel, selection, and measurement explanations, and blockage produces a target-transition difference exceeding the threshold, does the channel receive candidate causal-carrier status. “Different before and after blockage” cannot be cut out of those complete comparison conditions and treated as sufficient causal proof in every situation. [T-47；T-G2]

m2 specifically assumes only delay was measured. Readers must retain one positive result alongside four gaps: delay is measured; capacity, reliability, controllability, and loss remain unknown. Unknown is neither 0 nor infinity, nor proof that the channel has no effect. Evidence of producing an effect and the extent of measurement across performance dimensions are separate matters. [T-47；T-G2]

m3/G3a predefines “backlog in the preceding three rounds” as its historical variable and selects only historical_conditional_predictive_gain. Controlling the current queue, environmental inputs, and measurement protocol, it asks whether that variable adds out-of-sample predictive information about the next round's target. The study must specify which times “the preceding three rounds” includes and how they are summarized. This section supplies no such calculation rule; it cannot be claimed already frozen as an actual data field. [T-47；T-G3]

If m3 obtains a proportionate conditional increment, it registers only predictive path dependence. No qualified causal erasure or restoration operation is supplied here. §4.5 also permits G3b to use one uniquely preselected equivalent intervention, but this likewise requires additional causal conditions and a selected outcome exceeding its threshold. This example cannot upgrade to G3b merely because G2 supplies a channel or G3a supplies predictive gain. Nor should its mention only of erasure/restoration be misread as §4.5 removing the equivalent-intervention route. [T-47；T-G3]

m3 also retains a representational boundary: if the current queue already sufficiently carries the relevant historical information, an additional historical variable may add no gain. That does not negate how the past formed the backlog or how the current carrier continues to act. Conversely, historical predictive information may supplement insufficiently measured current differences. Do not deliberately omit a known current queue to manufacture gain, or infer an established carrier backward from a zero increment. [T-G3]

m4/G4a asks only about conditional_information_gain in closure failure. Before results, freeze micro and aggregate scales, mapping M, retained and excluded variables, the metric, and threshold; then ask whether excluded local timing carries conditional information exceeding the threshold given the aggregate variables. Conditional information is not general correlation. An unfavorable result cannot prompt replacement with predictive or intervention gain, or a jump to G4b object conversion. [T-47；T-G4]

If m4 fails its positive-support check, its own null rule still governs; it cannot automatically be called “aggregation is closed.” Corresponding equivalence/sufficiency, sensitivity, and tolerance conditions can support bounded, criterion-specific closure. Without that material, the result remains unresolved. This example has neither an actual results section nor power testing, so this explanation invents no final supported/null_supported states for the four items. [T-41；T-G4]

The final sentence is the section's key point: the four instances can suggest subsequent questions for one another but do not substitute for one another. Useful grouping does not guarantee that the selected channel is effective; an effective channel does not guarantee historical increments beyond current state; historical gain relative to one representation does not guarantee that variables excluded by the selected scale mapping satisfy G4's information criterion. The latter two may concern different variables, representations, windows, and targets. Similar names do not create automatic inference. [T-47]

This separation does not prevent the same material from supporting several different facts, but specify exactly which step it supports and retain the shared-source relationship rather than counting independent reviews repeatedly. When one instance is unresolved, other independently grounded conclusions may remain; only higher-level claims actually dependent on that gap must stop. The cards clarify local responsibilities, rather than requiring the world to traverse G1→G2→G3→G4 as universal mandatory stages. [T-47；T-missing；T-source]

m1's teaching conclusion should be called “bounded grouping-gain support within the corresponding window.” It creates no fact of candidate-unit existence and supplies no evidence in place of m2's channel effect, m3's additional historical information, or m4's representational closure. Independently established object facts remain on their original grounds if any one item fails.
argumentSteps: First label m1–m4 as fictional teaching instances, without external observations or empirical truth assigned to them.
m1 freezes a predictive grouping comparison and checks out-of-sample performance, boundaries, and independent time blocks. At most it answers bounded grouping-gain support.
m2 separately freezes the channel and controlled perturbation to identify candidate causal carriage. Retain the measured delay alongside the four unknown dimensions in this example.

m3 separately freezes the preceding-three-round historical variable and conditional prediction rules, controlling the current queue and other relevant information. Predictive support does not replace causal operations.
m4 separately freezes the cross-scale mapping and single conditional-information criterion; neither changing the criterion nor switching to object conversion is allowed.

Passing one item does not directly complete the next, and failure limits only conclusions actually dependent on it. Formal results and null judgments still require complete contracts and actual material.

boundaries: Boundary in the original: m1 cannot obtain the example's required positive support if effective only on training data or if gain disappears after a slight boundary perturbation.
Boundary in the original: m2 measures only delay; the other four dimensions remain unknown.
Boundary in the original: m3 supplies no additional causal-operation evidence and cannot upgrade predictive gain to causal path dependence.
Boundary in the original: m4 cannot change criterion or switch to G4b after seeing results.

Author-constructed conditional counterexample: in the same object, channel c changes next-step state Y, while Y is determined entirely by a sufficiently registered current state and historical records add no information. Channel effects and G3 increments need not both hold.

Author-constructed conditional counterexample: an artificial simulation is run one thousand times, then m1–m4 are said to have one thousand real-world reviews. Computational repetition does not create external observations.
This section provides no actual samples, effect sizes, numerical thresholds, evidential artifacts, or final outcome states. Explanation must not disguise these missing items as executed research.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: a channel can have an effect while historical residuals remain zero
teachingExamples.text: Use artificial equations to isolate the logic: historical H is equally likely 0/1, and current state S=H. A controllable channel switch c∈{0,1} gives next-step Y=S+c. Holding S fixed, changing c from 0 to 1 changes Y by 1, so the within-model channel effect is nonzero. Given (S,c), Y is uniquely determined, and adding H contributes no predictive information. Thus m2's channel effect can coexist with zero additional historical information of the kind m3 concerns.
teachingExamples.assumptions: The structural equations, distribution of H, control operation, and current information set (S,c) are artificial assumptions, without noise or omissions. No formal m2 or m3 contract was executed.
teachingExamples.boundary: It refutes only “a channel effect necessarily implies an additional historical increment,” not establishes the result of any actual G2 or G3 instance.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: cards with numbers must still retain material status
teachingExamples.text: Suppose one illustrative m2 card reads “delay=2 seconds,” while another reads “delay unknown.” If the former is merely a constructed assumption, it still cannot become an actual measurement. The latter honestly retains an unknown without denying a possible channel effect. Actual use of the former requires separate material on clocks, starting and ending points, logs, and comparison conditions.
teachingExamples.assumptions: 2 seconds and both cards are teaching assumptions, not observed values reported by the original.
teachingExamples.boundary: No actual channel experiment is conducted, and invented numbers do not fill the original instance's results section.

counterexamples.effect: Rejects the claim that channels necessarily imply historical residuals.

questionAnswers.question: After m1 passes, what must m2 still examine?
questionAnswers.answer: A channel, single perturbation criterion, proportionate identification comparison, and target difference are still required. Useful grouping prediction does not establish effectiveness of that channel.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source lines 691–695 and 725.

questionAnswers.question: If m2 measures only delay, should reliability be recorded as 0 or 100%?
questionAnswers.answer: Neither. The material supplies no reliability value. Retain unknown status and explain the missing trial denominator, conditions, and success definition.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source line 719; §4.4.

questionAnswers.question: When is the preceding-three-round backlog variable defined? Why not select the most favorable three rounds afterward?
questionAnswers.answer: Define it before seeing future outcomes and specify the window/calculation rule. Post-result selection changes the confirmatory question and may introduce selection or leakage.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source line 721; §4.5.

questionAnswers.question: Is m3's historical predictive gain sufficient for G3b?
questionAnswers.answer: No. A uniquely preselected erasure, restoration, or equivalent intervention and corresponding causal-identification/threshold conditions are also required. This example lacks that material.
questionAnswers.basis: §4.5, Chinese source lines 667–673.

questionAnswers.question: What if m4's information criterion lacks support but its predictive criterion performs well?
questionAnswers.answer: Retain the original information-criterion result and label the predictive discovery as another question or exploration. The original success conditions cannot be replaced afterward.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source line 723.

questionAnswers.question: Does repeated execution of a fictional model increase the count of real empirical support?
questionAnswers.answer: No. It can test code or within-model relations, but creates no external observation.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source line 715; §4.17.2.

questionAnswers.question: In the teaching equation Y=S+c, why does H add no information once S and c are known?
questionAnswers.answer: Current information already uniquely determines Y. Adding H cannot further distinguish the answer to this target, although c's within-model effect on Y remains 1.
questionAnswers.basis: The explicit structural equations in this section.

4.8.title: 4.8 Epistemological constraints E1–E5
4.8.lead: These five constraints govern “on what grounds we judge”: clarify the object, visible scope, and whether observation participates; retain competing explanations; and test cross-scale connections.
explanation: The original parent section at Chinese source lines 727–728 contains only a heading, without additional body text. What follows is navigation to five independent subsections, not a new empirical law. E1 limits object declarations; E2 limits what records and models can see; E3 requires an actual causal channel for observational participation; E4 compares competing explanations that would alter judgment and retains residuals; E5 checks cross-scale transfer. [T-Eintro；T-E1；T-E2；T-E3；T-E4；T-E5]

These epistemological and methodological constraints first govern analysts' reasoning. Following a methodological rule does not automatically cause a real mechanism to occur. Complete fields, coherent explanations, and cross-scale diagrams cannot replace specific evidence. Conversely, insufficient material on one item should limit only conclusions actually dependent on it, rather than declare the whole world unknowable. [T-roles；T-missing]

The five constraints are not a checklist for mechanically increasing costs. Locate object-field gaps by inference rather than expanding material endlessly. Do not demand more viewpoints when the representation already suffices for the current task. Do not invent competing explanations merely to reach a count when none is reasonable. Transfer testing also does not require first finding G4 closure failure. Each subsection specifies when to add evidence, narrow, retain, or stop. [T-E1；T-E2；T-E4；T-E5]
argumentSteps: First identify the object, observation, and comparison grounds required by the current claim.
Review the distinct responsibilities of the five constraints without treating methodological compliance as mechanism evidence.
Limit gaps locally while retaining independently established bounded conclusions.

4.8.1.title: 4.8.1 E1 Object-Declaration Constraint
4.8.1.lead: First clarify whom, which period, which scope, and what you are judging; then ask whether the material is sufficient. Identify the specific effects of missing fields rather than invalidating evidenced facts along with them.
explanation: Chinese source line 731 requires explicit specification of the object, scope, scale, time window, necessary variables, and identity. An object is more than a name: should an institution with the same name be compared by the same standards before and after restructuring? Can one week's logs represent the entire year? Are individual averages, organizational aggregates, and regional totals answering the same question? These matters must be stated first; otherwise apparently consistent statements may refer to different objects. [T-E1; T-D0]

Comparative claims separately declare a baseline or N0. For example, “faster processing” must specify faster than which process, under which identical task and window. A receipt record only establishes that a record exists at a particular time; a control group need not be invented merely to state this limited fact. A null model belongs to a specific comparison contract. It should not be inserted into the D0 object vector and used to declare that all facts must first pass the same test. [T-E1; T-D0; T-41]

The key is to locate gaps relative to inferences. If a log gives dates and items but no identity criterion across years, it may still support “this item was recorded on this day” while failing to support “the same mechanism operated throughout ten years.” Where scale or boundaries are missing, an analyst's convenient grouping cannot directly be declared an objective structure; this does not make sourced people, events, or texts vanish. [T-E1; T-missing]

Ordinary facts, textual meaning, and mathematical proofs are reviewed under their respective responsibilities. Textual interpretation checks versions, context, and argument; mathematical propositions check domains, assumptions, and derivations; empirical effects check objects, design, and material. A complete mathematical counterexample cannot be required to undergo real-world sampling before its logical force is recognized; nor can the rigor of mathematical expressions perform measurement for an empirical object. [T-E1; T-form]

E1 thus guards against both upgrading “I drew a boundary” into “it is an entity” and overreaching from “one field is blank” to “all material is invalid.” Supplementing information should focus on the inference actually disputed, not endlessly expand collection. Actual adoption also requires separate checks of necessity, protection, and permissions. [T-E1; T-missing]
argumentSteps: Specify the object, scope, scale, window, variables, and K of the current judgment.
If claiming comparative advantage or difference, separately list a matching baseline/N0.
For each gap, identify the inference it blocks while preserving sourced facts that do not depend on it.
Continue review under the distinct responsibilities for ordinary facts, textual interpretation, formal proof, and empirical effects.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: one record can support a small fact without supporting a broad comparison
teachingExamples.text: Suppose a reliable teaching log explicitly records “document A received on day 5,” but provides no completion time, alternative process, or records for other months. Within the assumptions, one may say that A was received; one cannot say that processing was faster than process B or that all months were the same. Missing comparative and extrapolation material limits the latter two questions without canceling the first.
teachingExamples.assumptions: The log's reliability and content are teaching assumptions; no actual document A or institution exists.
teachingExamples.boundary: In reality, the log's source, terminology, and record-generation process require checking; assumed reliability cannot be treated as empirical certification.

counterexamples.text: Constructed conditional counterexample: because it is unknown whether an institution meets an identity criterion after restructuring, someone declares that evidenced documents issued before restructuring do not exist. This wrongly cancels independent facts through an intertemporal gap.
counterexamples.effect: Limits the unconditional chain of inference addressed in this section while preserving evidenced, bounded conclusions.

counterexamples.text: Constructed conditional counterexample: dividing a list into three color groups and then claiming three objective mechanisms have been identified. Color labels supply no evidence of grouping gain.

questionAnswers.question: Without data from another process, can an existing receipt log still be confirmed?
questionAnswers.answer: The log's own provenance may support a limited fact of receipt; it cannot establish comparative process quality.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source line 731.

questionAnswers.question: If D0 lacks K, which conclusions are especially affected?
questionAnswers.answer: Comparisons depending on the same object across periods or changes are especially affected. The specific effect must still be explained claim by claim, without indiscriminately canceling other evidenced facts.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source line 731 and §3.1.

questionAnswers.question: Can a mathematical counterexample undermine the unconditional logical inference it targets without a real-world experiment?
questionAnswers.answer: Yes, provided the model's premises and derivation hold; whether reality satisfies that model requires separate evidence.

It is currently static. Future task switching may change only the required material, not the original log.

4.8.2.title: 4.8.2 E2 Observational Position and Model Limits
4.8.2.lead: Every observation reveals some things and leaves others unseen. Whether to look again depends on whether the omission could change the answer to the current task.
explanation: Chinese source line 735 says, in translation, “One kind of record cannot be treated as the object's entire state.” Position affects who and which stages can be reached; the measurement channel determines what is recorded; model choice determines which differences are preserved. A customer-service phone line covers only callers; an instrument measures only its designed quantities; an aggregate model may not retain positional differences. These scopes require item-by-item checking. “We have data” cannot bypass how those data were generated. [T-E2; T-measure]

But E2 does not presume that every task needs an additional viewpoint. If the current question asks only for a recorded total of like items, a reliable, complete aggregate table may suffice; if the question changes to which position is overloaded, that same total may be insufficient. Sufficiency depends on objectives, deadlines, environment, and permitted operations. More observations are not inherently better, and extra information may add cost, delay, or privacy burdens. [T-E2; T-D3]

“Invisible does not mean nonexistent” limits inference from a blank record to negation in the world. Treating absence as counterevidence requires reasons to expect that the event would generate a record, that the record would be preserved, and that it could be found in this search. Conversely, invisibility is not evidence of existence either. Mark unknown or unobservable states; “it may be hidden” cannot exempt every conjecture from testing. [T-E2; T-evidence; T-source]

When task-relevant blind spots are substantial, three justified responses are available: supplement with proportionate evidence, narrow the use, or remain unresolved. For example, inability to identify affected positions can halt a claim of harmlessness across the whole domain while preserving facts about measured positions. Supplementing evidence need not mean collecting more personal information; it may mean adjusting the question, using public aggregates, or obtaining credible review. The choice is constrained by protection, costs, and authorization. [T-E2; T-evidence]

Whether probing is permitted is a separate decision. A high-risk operation does not automatically gain permission because “trying it will tell us”; waiting may also miss a window or cause harm. Compare known risks, reversibility, deadlines, and authorization, choosing proportionate protection or evidence collection under current evidence. E2 must not be misread as requiring permanent inaction or complete knowledge before action. [T-E2]
argumentSteps: Record observational positions, measurement channels, models, and data-generation processes.
Compare observed information with the current objective, deadline, environment, and operations to assess whether blind spots are relevant.
Do not infer nonexistence directly from lack of a record, or existence from possible invisibility.
If blind spots materially affect the task, supplement evidence, limit use, or remain unresolved; probing separately requires checking risk windows and permissions.

boundaries: Constructed conditional counterexample: an aggregate table completely answers “what is the total,” yet private details about every person are demanded before that total is accepted. This confuses task sufficiency with reconstruction of the entire state.

caseLinks.title: NASA investigation: what an electrical test can establish, and what it still cannot see

caseNotes.title: NASA investigation: what an electrical test can establish, and what it still cannot see
caseNotes.text: Determinations (4), in the continuation of item 7 on printed page 5-13 of the Apollo 13 investigation report, states that an external 500-volt withstand test could not reveal the extent of possible internal insulation damage. It showed only that, with the relative wire positions at the time of the test, that potential could be withstood without breakdown. This section adds attention to the measurement channel and current use: a test can produce a genuinely valid bounded result while not covering the full internal state.
caseNotes.sourceLabel: NASA Apollo 13 Review Board report
caseNotes.sourceLocator: 1970-06-15, Chapter 5, item 7 continued, Determinations (4), printed 5-13, PDF p. 179
caseNotes.boundary: This is the report's limitation on a particular electrical test, not a universal claim that withstand testing is invalid. The passage is not extended into the entire accident mechanism or any individual's prior knowledge, nor does it require unlimited testing for every task.

teachingExamples.title: Mathematical teaching construction: the same total has different sufficiency for two questions
teachingExamples.text: Counts at two positions may be (4,6) or (0,10), both totaling 10. If only the total is asked, the representation 10 suffices. If the question is “does the first position contain any quantity,” the two states give different answers, so the representation 10 is insufficient. Adding positional observations must be justified by the latter task's requirements, not by the belief that finer data are inherently more advanced.
teachingExamples.assumptions: The states and queries are constructed; the quantities are of the same kind, and the recorded total is error-free.
teachingExamples.boundary: No actual institution is simulated, and this does not establish the necessity of, or authorization for, collecting personal details in reality.

questionAnswers.question: If the total is correct but positions are unknown, which answers can still be retained?
questionAnswers.answer: The answer about the total may be retained; position-dependent judgments are limited, and whether to supplement evidence depends on the task.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source line 735 and the teaching counterexample.

questionAnswers.question: Why does failure to find a log not always refute an event?
questionAnswers.answer: First check whether this kind of event should have left a record, whether that record should have been preserved, and whether this search should have found it; otherwise absence may reflect a channel blind spot.
questionAnswers.basis: §2.7.1, Chinese source line 371.

questionAnswers.question: May risky probing be conducted directly to fill a blind spot?
questionAnswers.answer: No. Probing requires comparing risks, windows, and authorization; the need for more evidence does not automatically confer permission to operate.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source line 735.

figures.alt: The same total of 10 may come from 4/6 or 0/10. The total query has an answer; the first-position query is limited. Evidence may be supplemented, scope narrowed, or the result left unresolved; probing requires separate review.
figures.caption: A mathematical illustration constructed by the explanatory author; the actual NASA measurement boundary is precisely cited separately in the main text.

4.8.2.diagramBrief: The diagram places the current objective, observed scope, blind spots, and three responses side by side, using two states with the same total to show task differences. It is currently static. Future query switching could show whether positional information is necessary, without automatically permitting additional collection.

applicability.reason: This section directly addresses actual measurement limits. The original NASA report's qualification of a specific electrical test illustrates bounded validity, while a mathematical example shows that not every question requires another viewpoint.

4.8.3.title: 4.8.3 E3 Conditional Observational Participation
4.8.3.lead: Observation, naming, or rating sometimes enters an object's environment for action, but “a change occurred after observation” is insufficient. E3 requires finding the actual connection and explaining what would happen without this kind of observation.
explanation: The limiting phrase in Chinese source line 739 is, in translation, “only ... actual causal coupling.” An analyst privately writing a name does not automatically change the studied object merely through naming. A testable candidate for participation arises when, for example, a platform displays a rating, an institution adopts a classification, or an observation device changes measured conditions. One must still record what information or operation traveled through which channel, reached whom, and caused what change when. [T-E3; T-causal]

Temporal order is one necessary check, but not sufficient proof. Behavioral change after publication may result from simultaneous policy, environmental, or sample changes; “people care about evaluations” is only a possible mechanism. Locate the actual channel, then establish counterfactual comparisons involving no observation, alternative observation, or blockage. Whether using experiments, natural variation, or another design, disclose identification conditions and limits. [T-E3; T-causal]

The three comparisons serve different purposes: a no-observation condition compares the presence and absence of the observational arrangement; alternative observation compares different display, notification, or measurement methods; blockage compares outcomes when the signal cannot arrive or cannot continue to act. This does not require dangerously removing oversight or protection to obtain a control, nor does it mean every object can safely undergo these operations. Research design and eligibility for actual implementation require separate arguments. [T-E3]

The target of participation may be behavior, expression, material distribution, or subsequent feedback. A change in one target cannot settle every target. Sending a notice does not mean it was received; receipt does not mean behavior changed; and behavioral change does not automatically support a psychological explanation. Actual causal coupling may occur through physical or informational paths; it does not assign intentions to devices, platforms, or statistical indicators. [T-E3; T-H4]

Thus neither the unconditional claim that all observation changes objects nor the view that observers are absolutely external is acceptable. E3 requires a conditional, fallible judgment: if a channel does not reach its target, alternative inputs explain the difference, or the comparison lacks identification, retain a candidate or unresolved status. Further action involving publication and feedback also requires separate checks of protection, permissions, and consequences. [T-E3; T-causal]
argumentSteps: Define the specific version of observation, naming, rating, or publication and the target change.
Locate the channel through which it actually reaches the object and enters subsequent processes.
Use proportionate no-observation, alternative-observation, or blockage comparisons to distinguish shared conditions and selection explanations.
Register only the supported scope of participation. Separate receipt, behavioral change, and psychological mechanisms; actual operations require separate permission checks.

caseNotes.title: A real randomized experiment: how prior ratings enter the environment for subsequent ratings
caseNotes.text: Muchnik, Aral, and Taylor's 2013 Science paper reports randomly assigning new comments on a social-news website to a positive-vote, negative-vote, or control group. The paper explains that users see a comment's current score alongside the comment. The experiment thus makes visible prior ratings the channel of change, rather than merely comparing naturally occurring high and low scores. The paper reports that prior ratings changed subsequent rating behavior. This section concerns ratings actually entering the environment for later observation and choice; it does not generalize ‘a researcher is watching’ into an all-purpose reflexivity claim.
