teachingExamples.title: Mathematical teaching construction: more rows, no more independent samples
teachingExamples.text: Let two original observations be 0 and 2, with mean 1. Copy each five times to create ten rows; the mean remains (5×0+5×2)/10=1. The new table has ten rows but only two original records; whether those two are independent requires separate examination of the original measurement design. Repeated display may support checking or formatting, but cannot be called ten new measurements. If actual repeated measurements exist, reassess them by their real dependencies rather than row counts alone.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Explicit mechanical duplication of the same two records, without a new measurement process.
teachingExamples.boundary: Not a real data analysis, and not a claim that all repeated measurement is uninformative.

counterexamples.text: Source boundary: reprocessing the same material cannot be registered as a new independent observation.
counterexamples.effect: Repeated processing adds no independent material.

counterexamples.text: Source boundary: recursion depth itself increases neither empirical support nor capability level.
counterexamples.effect: Model depth does not replace empirical evidence.

counterexamples.text: Teaching counterexample: copying two measurements five times creates ten rows but still only the original two observations; estimating uncertainty as if there were ten independent draws misstates the data-generation process.
counterexamples.effect: Duplicated rows do not replace independent sample size.

counterexamples.text: Teaching boundary: a “received” acknowledgment can support a receipt record but cannot itself establish understanding, changed rules, or actual effects.
counterexamples.effect: Receipt support has a limited scope.

questionAnswers.question: Does running the same simulation to step 1000 provide 1000 real-world tests?
questionAnswers.answer: No. It produces a trajectory of the given model; real-world testing requires independent material and an appropriate comparison.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source line 1018.

questionAnswers.question: Is finding an old calculation error through a new proof valueless?
questionAnswers.answer: It has value: the gain comes from checkable reasoning, but cannot be relabeled a new real-world sample.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source line 1018.

questionAnswers.question: Does an explicit recommendation in a report establish that it was executed?
questionAnswers.answer: No. Recommendation text and actual execution require different material.
questionAnswers.basis: Material-status rule; C11.

4.17.3.title: 4.17.3 Rule 3: facts, values, and eligibility to act must be established separately
4.17.3.lead: Knowing how to do something, its being worth doing, and permission to do it are three different questions. The reverse also holds: a target worth protecting does not automatically make an unverified mechanism true.
explanation: Chinese source line 1022 confines facts, predictions, formal feasibility, and technical capability to their respective roles. Facts address current conditions or relations; predictions give conditional consequences; formal feasibility supplies possible actions within a model; technical capability states what can be implemented. None alone produces value rankings, responsibility, or authority to act. [T-law3; T-formal]

Analytical recommendations should disclose normative targets, evidence, prices to be paid, and objections. A recommendation may say “under this target and these constraints, option A is more suitable,” without presenting a conditional evaluation as a value-neutral necessity or prohibiting supported deliberation merely because execution permission is still absent. [T-law3; T-C12]

Real-world adoption separately requires valid permission, a protection floor, implementation resources, stopping, and remedy. Sufficient resources do not mean authority; authorization does not mean technical feasibility. Permission must cover the actual action, object, territory, and duration. An application or recommendation cannot itself turn pending review into approval to implement. [T-law3; T-J]

Normative premises constrain permissible choices; they do not establish an empirical mechanism's truth in reverse. For example, explicitly targeting protection of a population does not establish that an intervention will provide it; proportionate material on effects, risks, alternatives, and distribution is still needed. Weaker empirical grounds require revising the proposal and its uncertainty, not lowering the evidence gate because the target is important. [T-law3; T-C12]

Responsibility and sacrifice also require assessment by specific human positions and independent grounds; “the system needs it” or “it is more efficient” cannot forcibly assign uptake to someone. Existing bounded responsibilities are not universally canceled by this distinction either; state their source, scope, duration, and safe handoff. The methodological boundary prevents both unauthorized additional burdens and unsupported exemptions from independent duties. [T-N]
argumentSteps: List separately what facts, predictions, formal feasibility, and technical capability each support.
Specify the normative targets, evidence, prices to be paid, and objections of an analytical recommendation.
Real-world adoption separately requires permission, protection, resources, stopping, and remedy.
Normative grounds do not establish empirical truth in reverse; empirical changes should return to deliberation over the proposal.

caseNotes.title: The Belmont Report: consent and justice responsibilities beyond scientific benefits
caseNotes.text: Part C of the 1979 Belmont Report separates informed consent into information, comprehension, and voluntariness, and separately discusses risk-benefit assessment and subject selection. The point here is that these requirements each have their own reasons: potential research benefits do not automatically make being informed and voluntary factual.

caseNotes.sourceLocator: 1979-04-18; opening of Part C, first two paragraphs of C.1 and its Voluntariness passage; headings and openings of C.2 and C.3.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: three cards for target, capability, and permission
teachingExamples.text: A fictional system can already generate candidate lists: the capability card. Its user wants to reduce omissions: the target card. Whether disclosure to a particular recipient is allowed, for which use, and for how long is a separate permission-and-protection question. The three cards may independently be present or absent. Even with an explicit target and permission, list accuracy needs independent evaluation; good intentions and permission do not determine it.
teachingExamples.assumptions: The system, list, and target are fictional; no real personal data are included and no disclosure was made.
teachingExamples.boundary: Provides no actual authorization or advice on interventions concerning individuals; specific information-processing rules require verification against the actual institutional arrangements.

questionAnswers.question: If the target is protecting people, does that make the measure effective?
questionAnswers.answer: Effects cannot be inferred from a target; check the actual mechanism, risks, and distributional consequences.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source line 1022.

questionAnswers.question: If an algorithm can generate a result, may it be published externally?
questionAnswers.answer: Capability alone cannot justify the conclusion; publication separately has requirements for permission, protection, use, and duration.
questionAnswers.basis: Rule 3 and the J axis.

questionAnswers.question: Must a recommendation for deliberation pretend execution permission has already been obtained?
questionAnswers.answer: It need not and must not. Disclose norms, evidence, prices to be paid, and objections while retaining its status as a recommendation.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source line 1022; C12.

4.17.4.title: 4.17.4 Method effectiveness and framework evaluation
4.17.4.lead: Testing a case and testing whether a whole framework is worth using involve different denominators and questions. Even if every case makes sense, ask what the framework adds over professional or simpler methods and how much extra it costs.
explanation: Chinese source line 1026 explicitly states that the number of G questions does not establish adequate coverage and completeness of C contracts does not establish real-world reliability. Many questions, cards, publications, or successful cases show only the scale of organized content; whether the method helps users reduce substantive errors remains an independent empirical question. [T-eval]

Fair comparison first fixes common targets, material, and budgets. Comparators should be adequate professional methods or simpler alternatives, not deliberately weak baselines. Declare users' training, experience, accessible information, time and tool limits, and the tasks and evaluation rules; otherwise improvements due to extra information or time may be miscounted as framework effects. [T-eval; T-evidence]

Evaluation cannot ask only whether forms are complete or users like the method. The source requires asking whether substantive errors decrease, necessary distinctions are preserved, explanation or decisions improve, and costs are proportionate. Tasks can record types of misjudgment, important boundaries missed, calibration or answer quality, time spent, and learning costs; these are evaluation proposals made here but not implemented. Specific metrics and weights must be disclosed beforehand, and no existing educational effect is claimed. [T-eval]

Three empirical targets must be separated. An individual-instance effect asks about a bounded difference for a particular object, treatment, and outcome; the applicability rate of a question family within an object set asks which objects qualify under specified sampling and gates; the framework's net gain asks about differences in outcomes and costs on common tasks between use of this framework and a control. Their sampling units may respectively be individuals/objects, candidate objects, and tasks or users; denominators, extrapolations, and evaluations cannot be borrowed across them. [T-eval]

Collecting only successful instances changes the applicability-rate denominator; giving easy tasks to people familiar with the framework and hard tasks to controls mixes in differences in personnel and tasks. A study could retain the complete task set and records of failures/withdrawals in advance, balance personnel and tasks through a reasonable design, use blinded scoring, and disclose uncertainty. Whether randomization, matching, or another design is appropriate depends on the actual tasks; no actual recruitment, assignment, or testing took place here. [T-eval；T-evidence]

Net gain also requires explicit evaluation objectives; heterogeneous quantities such as errors, minutes, and risks to rights cannot be added without explanation. If weighted loss is used, the weights are choices for this evaluation and should have units, reasons, sensitivity analysis, and noncompensable protection floors. A method that makes fewer errors but takes more time may yield different conclusions for different uses; ‘more comprehensive’ is not proof of superiority without cost. [T-eval；T-law3；T-C2]

Without a proportionate comparison under common objectives, materials, and budgets, claims should stop at intended uses, inspectable public derivations, and supported local results. The present section-by-section explanation, structural validation, graphic checks, and independent content reading each serve a purpose, but they have not established learning gains for real readers or net benefits of the framework relative to professional methods. These remain unevaluated, rather than zero-benefit or proven effective. [T-eval]
argumentSteps: Select separately among individual effects, applicability rates, and the framework's net benefits; do not mix denominators.
For framework evaluation, freeze common tasks, materials, budgets, user conditions, and adequate controls.
Predetermine metrics for substantive errors, necessary distinctions, understanding/decisions, and costs, explaining weights and hard protective constraints.
Use a proportionate design to address differences in personnel, difficulty, information, and training, retaining failures and uncertainty.
If the comparison has not been performed, report only intended uses and checked local results; do not fabricate effects.

boundaries: Boundary in the source: the number of questions, completeness of contracts, or a collection of successful instances does not establish universal effectiveness.
Boundary in the source: without a proportionate comparison, only intended uses and checked local results may be claimed.
Teaching counterexample: calculating 100% applicability from 10 successful instances cannot establish the applicability rate for a set of 100 objects if another 90 candidate objects were excluded.

Mathematical teaching boundary: a method with fewer errors but greater time costs may have different net rankings under different explicit cost weights; one set of weights cannot be written as a universal fact.
Current actual limitation: this lesson has conducted no real-reader test or evaluation of the framework's net benefits.

If all 10 displayed cases succeeded, may all 100 candidates be called applicable?

caseNotes.text: In §6.2, Ribeiro and colleagues set up a separate task of ‘choosing the classifier that generalizes better’, comparing greedy and LIME explanations and random/submodular instance selection. Each condition limited both the number of words in each explanation and the number of documents viewed to 6, randomized algorithm positions and instance order, and recorded choices. This provides a bounded example of an actual method-evaluation design.
caseNotes.sourceLabel: Ribeiro and colleagues' original paper, v3
caseNotes.sourceLocator: §6.2, PDF pages 7—8, especially the continuation on page 8 and Figure9; version dated 2016-08-09.
caseNotes.boundary: This is the authors' experiment on a specific task, not an evaluation of this framework, and it does not establish that every training, computation, or implementation cost was fairly accounted for. Its results are not transferred into actual reader effects of this explanation. Reusing the same paper as Law 1 does not constitute independent verification.

teachingExamples.title: Mathematical teaching construction: the same errors and time, different cost weights
teachingExamples.text: Suppose a common budget ceiling is 60 minutes, with fictional method A producing 4 equally weighted errors in 40 minutes and B producing 6 in 20 minutes. The evaluation loss is L=错误数+λ×分钟 (L = error count + λ × minutes), where λ has units of equivalent error cost per minute. At λ=0.05, A=6 and B=7; at λ=0.1, both are 8; at λ=0.2, A=12 and B=10. Which method is more suitable depends on disclosed task-cost weights, not on the word ‘more meticulous’.
teachingExamples.assumptions: All errors have equal weight, both methods use the same task and materials, and neither violates an independent protection floor; all numbers and weights are artificial stipulations.
teachingExamples.boundary: No experiment was conducted. Harms to rights or different error types are not automatically converted into minutes; actual weights and hard constraints must be stated separately.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: fix the denominator of an applicability rate first
teachingExamples.text: Suppose the predetermined set contains 100 candidate objects, of which only 10 successful cases are displayed. The success proportion among displayed cases is 10/10; the applicability rate across the complete set cannot be determined from this because the remaining 90 have not been evaluated. Only after evaluating the complete set or a proportionate sample by uniform criteria, while retaining unevaluated statuses, may an estimate for the declared population be reported.
teachingExamples.assumptions: The numbers 100 and 10 and the unevaluated statuses are teaching stipulations, not actual object statistics from this book.
teachingExamples.boundary: The 90 unevaluated objects are not treated as failures, and no inference is made about the framework's actual applicability rate.

counterexamples.text: Boundary in the source: the number of questions, completeness of contracts, or a collection of successful instances does not establish universal effectiveness.
counterexamples.effect: Quantity does not substitute for methodological effectiveness.

counterexamples.text: Boundary in the source: without a proportionate comparison, only intended uses and checked local results may be claimed.
counterexamples.effect: Without comparison, do not claim net benefits.

counterexamples.text: Teaching counterexample: calculating 100% applicability from 10 successful instances cannot establish the applicability rate for a set of 100 objects if another 90 candidate objects were excluded.
counterexamples.effect: The display denominator does not substitute for the population.

counterexamples.text: Mathematical teaching boundary: a method with fewer errors but greater time costs may have different net rankings under different explicit cost weights; one set of weights cannot be written as a universal fact.
counterexamples.effect: Net rankings depend on evaluation choices.

questionAnswers.question: Can organizing 100 papers prove the framework's net benefits?
questionAnswers.answer: No. The volume of material is not a controlled evaluation under common tasks and budgets.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source, lines 1026—1028.

questionAnswers.question: If all 10 displayed cases succeeded, may all 100 candidates be called applicable?
questionAnswers.answer: No. The remaining 90 are unevaluated; unevaluated objects also cannot directly be counted as failures.
questionAnswers.basis: The teaching example of denominators.

questionAnswers.question: What are the losses for A and B when the cost weight λ=.1?
questionAnswers.answer: A=4+.1×40=8 and B=6+.1×20=8; the tie applies only under the stipulated weights and conditions.
questionAnswers.basis: Teaching construction.

questionAnswers.question: This explanation has been read and validated; does that prove readers necessarily learn better?
questionAnswers.answer: No. Checking content and comparing actual learning effects are different tasks.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source, lines 1026—1028, and the scope not actually carried out in this lesson.

4.18.title: 4.18 Conditional formal propositions
4.18.lead: This group of propositions turns questions such as ‘is the summary sufficient?’, ‘can the next step be advanced?’, and ‘can a qualified action be selected now?’ into provable conditions. Their certainty comes from stated premises, not from attaching the same labels to the real world.
explanation: Line 1032 of the Chinese source explicitly states that the following propositions ‘hold within explicitly specified mathematical objects’ (translated from Chinese). State domains, representations, targets, dynamics, permitted operations, and error conditions are all part of the argument. F1—F5 respectively address static task recovery, closure of dynamics and interventions, common feasible actions, preservation of the same task through successive conversions, and approximate error propagation; they cannot replace one another. [T-418]

A formal proof supplies ‘if these conditions hold, the conclusion holds’, or a two-way characterization of conditions. A counterexample can directly refute the unconditional inference it targets even without a real-world experiment; whether a real object satisfies the conditions still requires measurement, variable mappings, and error materials. The number of exhaustive checks within a model cannot be counted as a real-world sample size. [T-formal]

The existence of a set-theoretic function, computability, computation within budget, timely data availability, practical implementability, and authority to adopt it are separate judgments. A recovery function can be mathematically unique while the actual system uses an incorrect rule; original materials may be preserved but fail to arrive when a decision is made. The formal conclusion is not thereby invalidated, nor does responsibility for application disappear. [T-formal；T-F4A]

The numbers, states, and actions in this lesson are mathematical constructions with labeled assumptions; arrows in the figures represent functions or conditional relationships, not actual causal evidence. Real adoption must still comply with corresponding norms, protections, and bounded authority; in particular, the set of qualified actions in F3 cannot itself generate actual authorization. [T-F3A；T-C12]
argumentSteps: Specify the mathematical objects, domains, targets, and premises.
Use a proof or explicit counterexample to determine the conclusion within the model.
For real-world application, separately check variables, measurement, errors, availability, and the range of operations.
Continue checking implementation resources, authority, and protections under the corresponding contracts.

questionAnswers.question: Why are real-world materials still needed once the mathematical proof is complete?
questionAnswers.answer: The proof guarantees a conditional relationship; whether the real object's quantities, domains, and operations match the premises still requires materials.

questionAnswers.answer: It does not answer directly; dynamics, permitted operations, and action qualification are checked through other conditions respectively.

applicability.reason: This unit presents conditional propositions within explicitly specified mathematical objects, using complete public proofs and mathematical constructions. Real cases cannot certify premises in their place, so historical events are not forcibly matched to them, and no existing real-instance test is claimed.

4.18.1.title: 4.18.1 F1 task recovery
4.18.1.lead: Someone seeing only the same summary must give the same answer. If that summary merges states that should receive different answers, even the smartest decoder cannot distinguish them using the summary alone.
explanation: Let X be nonempty, π:X→Y with Y=π(X), and the target q:X→V. Y includes only representation values that actually occur. For y, the fiber X_y={x:π(x)=y} comprises all source states merged by the same representation. g can read only y; it cannot secretly read source-state numbers, identity labels, or undeclared history. The question is when q=g∘π holds. [T-F1；T-F1A]

Necessity: if q=g∘π, take any π(x)=π(x′)=y; then q(x)=g(y)=q(x′). Thus if a fiber contains two target answers, every deterministic decoder reading only y faces a conflict. This is an information-level impossibility, not something solved by replacing the operator with a more skilled one. [T-F1A]

Sufficiency: if q is constant on every fiber, define g(y) as that fiber's common target value. Y=π(X) makes every fiber nonempty; constancy makes the definition unambiguous. For any x, g(π(x)) is exactly q(x), so recovery holds. Uniqueness: every y has a source state x, and any feasible g must equal q(x), so g is unique on the actual image Y; extended representation points that never actually occur are not constrained by this result. [T-F1A]

This does not require π to be one-to-one. Multiple states can safely be merged as long as their answers to the current target agree; a change of target requires another check. Existence also does not guarantee an algorithm that always halts on an infinite domain, still less finite running time, data availability, or actual authority. Formal ‘losslessness’ is always relative to a specified task, not recovery of every detail of the world. [T-F1；T-formal]

The appendix gives an exact finite-scalar approximation bound. Add the assumptions that X is finite, q is real-valued, g may output any real number, and the loss is worst-case absolute error over the full domain. Let a_y and b_y be the minimum and maximum target values on a fiber. Any output c satisfies |b_y−a_y|≤|b_y−c|+|c−a_y|, so at least one endpoint has error ≥(b_y−a_y)/2. Choosing the midpoint c=(a_y+b_y)/2 puts every fiber value between the endpoints, yielding error ≤ half the range, attained at the endpoints. Hence the optimal full-domain worst-case error is (1/2)max_y(b_y−a_y). [T-F1A]

Thus, given ε≥0, a decoder with full-domain error ≤ε exists if and only if every fiber's range is ≤2ε. Finiteness guarantees the existence of endpoints and the maximum; arbitrary real-valued output makes the midpoint available. Infinite domains, vector targets, integer-only outputs, average loss, and nonuniform probabilities all require new analysis; half the range cannot be treated as a universal information-loss score across domains. [T-F1A]

The appendix also gives the answer for a binary target, zero-one loss, and a uniform distribution over finitely many states: if each fiber contains n_y0 zeros and n_y1 ones, selecting the majority label produces min(n_y0,n_y1) errors, so the minimum error rate is Σ_y min(n_y0,n_y1)/|X|. Randomized output produces a convex combination of the error counts of the two fixed labels and cannot improve on the smaller one. This optimizes average classification error; it does not replace the preceding worst-case absolute error or estimate frequencies in a real population. [T-F1A]
argumentSteps: Necessity: the same π value enters the same g, so its q values must agree.
Sufficiency: define g by the common q value on each nonempty fiber, obtaining q=g∘π.
Uniqueness: every y has a source, and any recovery function must take this common value at y.
In the finite-scalar setting, the triangle inequality on the two endpoints gives the half-range lower bound; choosing each fiber's midpoint attains it.
In the binary uniform case, choose the majority label on each fiber and sum the minimum error counts; randomization cannot improve on the endpoints of the convex combination.
Bound each conclusion to its own domain, output restrictions, and loss; check its real-world correspondence separately.

teachingExamples.title: Mathematical teaching construction: optimal recovery of a finite scalar target
teachingExamples.text: Partition five states into A={x1,x2,x3} and B={x4,x5}, with q values 0,2,4,10,12 respectively. A has range 4; setting g(A)=2 yields errors 2,0,2. B has range 2; setting g(B)=11 yields errors 1,1. The worst error over the domain is 2, and A’s endpoints force any output to have error at least 2, so this is optimal. Tolerance ε=1.5 is unattainable; ε=2 is attainable.
teachingExamples.assumptions: The five states constitute the entire domain; targets are exact real numbers, outputs may be any real numbers, and loss is worst-case absolute error.
teachingExamples.boundary: This is not an estimate of empirical measurement error; average loss or restricted outputs require recalculation.

teachingExamples.title: Mathematical teaching construction: another loss for a binary task
teachingExamples.text: Now take five uniformly distributed states: labels in fiber A are 0,0,1 and in fiber B are 1,1. Outputting 0 for A misclassifies only one state, and outputting 1 for B misclassifies none, so the minimum average error rate is 1/5. Exact recovery within A remains impossible; only one error in this finite domain does not mean correctness at every state.
teachingExamples.assumptions: This is a separate artificial binary task: five uniform finite states, zero-one loss, and deterministic or independently randomized output.
teachingExamples.boundary: 1/5 is not a real classifier’s error rate and must not be conflated with scalar error 2 in the preceding construction.

questionAnswers.question: If π is not injective, must exact recovery fail?
questionAnswers.answer: Not necessarily; recovery remains possible if q is constant within each fiber.
questionAnswers.basis: Proof of sufficiency.

questionAnswers.question: Why emphasize that Y is the actual image?
questionAnswers.answer: It ensures every fiber is nonempty, definitions have sources, and the recovery map is unique on Y; an extended domain has no such uniqueness guarantee.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source line 1036.

questionAnswers.question: If the target values in A are 0, 2, and 4, what is the optimal worst-case error?
questionAnswers.answer: 2, attained by midpoint output 2; the two endpoints give the lower bound.
questionAnswers.basis: Appendix C.6 and the construction.

questionAnswers.question: After restricting outputs to integers, is the optimal error for targets 0 and 1 still .5?
questionAnswers.answer: No. Any integer output has worst-case error at least 1, attained by 0 or 1; the premise permitting arbitrary real outputs has changed.

keyTerms.text: π:X→Y is a deterministic representation, with Y=π(X).
For any y∈Y, the preimage X_y={x:π(x)=y} is called a representation fiber.

4.18.2.title: 4.18.2 F2 Closure under Dynamics and Permitted Interventions
4.18.2.lead: Whether a summary can update forward by itself depends on whether states merged by the summary still yield the same summary after one step. Natural evolution doing so does not mean added interventions do so too.
explanation: Continue with nonempty X and π:X→Y=π(X), and fixed deterministic one-step dynamics F:X→X. Macroscopic closure requires F̄:Y→Y such that π(F(x))=F̄(π(x)) over the whole domain. The left side updates in the source domain and then summarizes; the right updates using only the summary. Agreement gives the macrostate a deterministic update independent of hidden detail. [T-F2; T-F2A]

The two-way proof applies F1 directly with task q=π∘F. If F̄ exists, x and x′ with the same π pass through the same F̄ and give the same result, so π(F(x))=π(F(x′)). If this fiber condition holds, define F̄(y) as the common next-step representation; F1 ensures unambiguity and uniqueness on the actual image. The static task q0=π is always recoverable by the identity decoder, but this does not guarantee recovery of the new task π∘F. [T-F2A; T-F1A]

The whole-domain condition supports finite-step induction. At t=0, π∘F⁰=Id_Y∘π. If π∘F^t=F̄^t∘π, then π∘F^(t+1)=(π∘F)∘F^t=(F̄∘π)∘F^t=F̄∘F̄^t∘π=F̄^(t+1)∘π. Since F maps X back into X, every step stays in the checked domain. Checking a few visited states or short trajectories cannot replace this whole-domain premise. [T-F2A]

With a permitted action set U, check equality of next-step representations within each fiber separately for every specific version F_u before composing any predetermined finite action sequence. If actions are implementable only in some merged source states, common implementability or an explicit domain restriction is also required. If one macro action name includes several micro implementations, exact F2 requires identical macro responses across those implementations; calling them all ‘reset’ does not make them one F_u. Closeness within tolerance instead belongs to an approximation problem requiring separate errors, regions, and horizons and propagation under conditions such as F5. Tolerance cannot establish the exact commutation or arbitrary finite-step equalities here. [T-F2A; T-F5A]

A finite stochastic system instead uses a transition kernel P and a given partition. For x and x′ in the same source block, every target block B must satisfy Σ_{z∈B}P(x,z)=Σ_{z∈B}P(x′,z). Define the common value as the macro kernel. Even if conditioning on the past changes the distribution within the source block, any weighted average remains this common value, so the macro next-step distribution is independent of hidden composition. If the same macro law must hold for all initial distributions, starting with point masses at x and x′ shows necessity as well. [T-F2A]

The preceding paragraph applies only to finite stochastic systems with a given partition; it does not generalize pointwise probabilities to continuous states. Equal next-step means do not imply equal distributions, and coincidence under one fixed initial mixture is not closure for all initial states. Natural dynamics, intervention dynamics, action feasibility, and normative adoptability each have separate gates; these mathematical conditions also do not directly award support to an actual G4 instance. [T-F2A; T-G4]
argumentSteps: Replace F1’s target with π∘F to obtain necessary and sufficient conditions for a macro update to exist.
Define the common next-step representation on each fiber to obtain F̄.
Start at t=0 and use one-step commutation to prove every finite t by induction.
Verify each specific F_u and common implementability, then compose a predetermined action sequence.
For a finite stochastic partition, construct the macro kernel from target-block probability sums; point-mass distributions establish necessity for all initial states.
Independently test empirical measurements, the permitted operation set, and formal G4 gates.

teachingExamples.title: Mathematical teaching construction: natural closure, intervention nonclosure
teachingExamples.text: Partition states a,b,c,d into A={a,b} and B={c,d}. Natural F is a→c, b→d, c→a, d→b, so A always goes to B and B to A; the macro update swaps the blocks. Add action u: a→c, b→a, c→c, d→d. Both a and b initially represent A, but afterward they represent B and A respectively, so u is not closed. The natural-closure proof remains valid; the new action simply fails the same conditions.
teachingExamples.assumptions: The four states are the entire domain, the two deterministic functions are exact, and all listed actions are implementable within the model.
teachingExamples.boundary: This represents no actual system and does not imply failure of all interventions.

teachingExamples.title: Mathematical teaching construction: equal means, different distributions
teachingExamples.text: A finite system has source states a,b and three absorbing states c0,c1,c2. a and b share block A; each c has its own target block with numerical label 0,1,2 respectively. a reaches the three target blocks with probabilities 1/2,0,1/2; b with probabilities 0,1,0. Both next-step label means are 1, yet probabilities of reaching, for example, the c1 block are 0 and 1, violating the blockwise probability-sum condition.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Five finite states, partition, and probabilities are given; c0/c1/c2 are each absorbing, completing the kernel.
teachingExamples.boundary: This only refutes substituting means for distributions and estimates no actual stochastic process.

questionAnswers.question: Why does F2 follow from F1?
questionAnswers.answer: Set the recovery target to the next representation q=π∘F; F1’s fiber constancy is exactly the closure condition.
questionAnswers.basis: Appendix C.8.

questionAnswers.question: What is the macro rule for natural dynamics in the four-state example?
questionAnswers.answer: A and B swap, so any finite number of steps alternates by parity.
questionAnswers.basis: The given F and induction.

questionAnswers.question: Why does the added action u fail?
questionAnswers.answer: a and b in block A go to B and A respectively; the single macrostate A cannot determine the next step.
questionAnswers.basis: The construction.

questionAnswers.question: Can equal next-step means establish stochastic closure?
questionAnswers.answer: No. Check every target-block probability; the construction already conflicts at c1, with probabilities 0 and 1.
questionAnswers.basis: Finite stochastic kernel condition.

4.18.3.title: 4.18.3 F3 Jointly Feasible Actions under Information Constraints
4.18.3.lead: Incomplete information does not always prevent action. The key is whether every state still possibly true now admits at least one common qualified action; each state having a solution differs from being able to choose the right solution now.
explanation: F3 addresses only finite, single-round, deterministic tasks. Current representation y is compatible with a nonempty state set X_y, and each A_ok(x) has already been determined by task targets, protections, resources, and valid authority. It is neither a list of imaginable actions nor merely technically executable actions. Including real-world qualification in the set is a premise of applying the model; the theorem approves nothing for people. [T-F3; T-F3A]

The action may depend only on current y and therefore cannot vary with the still-undistinguished actual x. Qualification for every compatible state requires finding an a belonging simultaneously to every A_ok(x). This is a common-intersection problem, not a matter of finding each state’s optimal action separately and declaring execution possible now. [T-F3A]

Proof of necessity: if a depends only on y and is qualified for all x∈X_y, then a∈A_ok(x) for every x, so a belongs to the intersection and the intersection is nonempty. Proof of sufficiency: if the intersection is nonempty, choose an a from it; it belongs to every set and is therefore qualified for all states without knowing which x is actual. This proof concerns one choice at fixed y, not strategies involving future observation. [T-F3A]

This yields limits in both directions. Identifying all states is not a universal prerequisite for bounded action: a common qualified action suffices. Each state separately having a feasible action is also insufficient: {left} and {right} are both nonempty, yet their intersection is empty. Both statements are set-theoretic results, not policies of ‘always wait first’ or ‘always act immediately’. [T-F3A]

Waiting, additional observation, or preservation may change information and action sets, but these actions can themselves consume resources, alter risks, or require authority; they cannot be assumed safe and lawful. An independently verified preservation action satisfying the current bounded target, protections, resources, and authority may enter the common intersection. If it merely defers the original target without meeting the current task, establish a corresponding sequential or staged task separately rather than silently changing qualification. [T-F3A; T-C12]

The theorem covers only listed compatible states and does not guarantee that unknown states will never arise. Probabilistic choice with risk tolerance, randomized strategies, and action following multiple rounds of observation have different optimization targets and guarantees and require their own conditions. An empty intersection means only that the current representation admits no ‘single-round, deterministic action qualified for all listed states’; it does not prove that every probabilistic or sequential strategy is unsolvable. [T-F3A]
argumentSteps: Specify a nonempty compatible-state set and A_ok already incorporating targets, protections, resources, and authority.
If a common action exists, it belongs to every set, so the intersection is nonempty.
If the intersection is nonempty, selecting an action from it qualifies for every compatible state.
Check whether relevant possibilities are missing from the state set and whether waiting/observation carry separate costs or authority requirements.
Do not generalize a single-round all-state guarantee into conclusions about randomized risk or sequential strategies.

teachingExamples.title: Mathematical teaching construction: changed conditions turn an empty intersection nonempty
teachingExamples.text: In the first scenario, X_y={xA,xB}, A_ok(xA)={left}, and A_ok(xB)={right}; the intersection is empty. In another explicitly conditioned scenario, action H has been independently verified to meet the same current bounded target, protections, resources, and authority in both states. The sets are then {left,H} and {right,H}, whose intersection is {H}. The latter permits choosing H without knowing the actual state; it does not backfill qualification absent from the first scenario.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Two finite states, one deterministic round, and given sets; H’s full qualification is an explicit mathematical premise of the second scenario.
teachingExamples.boundary: No actual preservation, waiting, or intervention is authorized; if H only defers the task without meeting its target, a different task must be constructed.

teachingExamples.title: Mathematical teaching construction: another possible state shrinks the intersection
teachingExamples.text: Continue the second scenario. If new material shows that state xC is also compatible and A_ok(xC)={right}, intersecting the original {H} with {right} makes the intersection empty. The original conclusion covered only the two originally listed states and cannot remain a guarantee for three states.
teachingExamples.assumptions: xC and its action set form another artificial extension scenario.
teachingExamples.boundary: This does not claim that reality always contains omitted states; it only shows that guarantees change with the declared domain.

counterexamples.text: Counterexample in the original text: {left} and {right} are each nonempty but have an empty intersection; separate solutions do not guarantee the right choice can be made now.
counterexamples.effect: Statewise existence is not common existence.

counterexamples.text: Boundary in the original text: a common, already-qualified preservation action may exist without complete state identification, but the theorem cannot fabricate its qualification premises.
counterexamples.effect: Complete information is not a prerequisite for all bounded action.

counterexamples.text: Teaching counterexample: if waiting misses a mandatory deadline in one state, it is absent from that state’s qualified set; ‘waiting is safest’ cannot insert it into the intersection.
counterexamples.effect: Waiting’s qualification requires a separate check.

counterexamples.text: Boundary in the original text: unknown states, risk tolerance, randomization, and sequential strategies are not all handled by the current single-round theorem.
counterexamples.effect: A single-round guarantee cannot be generalized.

questionAnswers.question: If every possible state has a qualified action, does that make action possible now?
questionAnswers.answer: Not necessarily; the sets’ common intersection may be empty.
questionAnswers.basis: Necessary and sufficient condition.

questionAnswers.question: When can there still be a deterministic qualified action without knowing the true state?
questionAnswers.answer: When an action belongs to the qualified-action sets of all compatible states.
questionAnswers.basis: Proof of sufficiency.

questionAnswers.question: Can ‘wait’ always be placed in every qualified set?
questionAnswers.answer: No. Waiting itself must satisfy targets, deadlines, resources, protections, and authority.
questionAnswers.basis: Appendix C.12 and the teaching boundary.

questionAnswers.question: Does an empty intersection rule out all randomized strategies?
questionAnswers.answer: No. It only rules out the currently bounded single-round deterministic action qualified in every state; other targets need separate analysis.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source line 1044.

4.18.4.title: 4.18.4 F4 Task Preservation through Successive Transformations
4.18.4.lead: Successive transformations must address the same final question. The first step may preserve distinctions needed for the answer while the second merges them; each step ‘completing its task’ does not guarantee a correct final answer.
explanation: Let f:X→Z and h:Z→W, with the first stage already satisfying q=g∘f. The final target remains the same q throughout. Whether the second stage is usable depends on whether intermediate states merged by h into the same w all share the same g value within the actually reachable intermediate set f(X), not whether each step independently accomplishes some local task. [T-F4；T-F4A]

Necessity: suppose a final decoder k satisfies q=k∘h∘f. Take any z,z′∈f(X) with h(z)=h(z′), and source states x,x′ with f(x)=z and f(x′)=z′. Then g(z)=q(x)=k(h(z))=k(h(z′))=q(x′)=g(z′). Thus g is constant on each fiber of h restricted to f(X). [T-F4A]

Sufficiency: if that constancy condition holds, define k(w), for every actual final representation w∈h(f(X)), as the fiber's common g value. This is unambiguous, so k(h(f(x)))=g(f(x))=q(x). The decoder need only be defined on the actual image. If a larger W is used, it may be extended arbitrarily at unused points into a nonempty target domain. Unreachable intermediate values must neither be mistaken for obstacles nor quietly added to the original state domain to change the question. [T-F4A]

In the original binary-position counterexample, the first step retains (x1,x2), the second retains only the sum, and the final question still concerns x1. Storage and counting each succeed, but their composition merges (0,1) with (1,0). Keeping the first bit's Boolean value repairs this task without restoring every detail. Changing the final target to the sum is a different successful task, not repair of the original question. [T-F4A]

Representational sufficiency must also be distinguished from correct execution of the actual rule. In the appendix's three-state example, f=(0,0,1), q=(0,1,1), and the actual rule outputs 0 for both representations 0 and 1. The first two states share a representation but require different answers, establishing insufficient information. The third state's representation 1 already determines the correct answer 1, yet the rule outputs 0, separately demonstrating an incorrect execution rule. Correcting the output at representation 1 to 1 repairs only the third state, not the conflict between the first two. The first state's correct result is not canceled by failures elsewhere. [T-F4A]

F4 is a proposition about preservation by functions, not proof that a causal chain or resource schedule connects. Causal chains require joint responses within the same case; average edge effects cannot simply be multiplied. With shared resources, separate feasibility does not imply joint feasibility. Even if a function can recover the answer, access before action, use of the correct implementation version, resources, and authority each require material. Unknown internal representations or contemporaneous rules do not justify forced unique attribution. [T-composition；T-formal；T-F4A]
argumentSteps: Fix the same final q and first check q=g∘f.
Necessity: a final decoder gives the same answer for the same h value, implying constant g on actual intermediate fibers.
Sufficiency: define k by each actual final fiber's common g value to obtain q=k∘h∘f.
Constrain only reachable f(X); do not mix unreachable states into the condition.
Separately check insufficient representation, incorrect actual rules, material timing, and causal/resource/authority responsibilities.

teachingExamples.title: Expanded mathematical counterexample from the original: local counting cannot replace the final position target
teachingExamples.text: X={0,1}², f preserves the state identically, g(x1,x2)=x1, and h(x1,x2)=x1+x2. Certainly q=g∘f holds. But z=(0,1) and z′=(1,0) both map under h to 1 while their g values are 0 and 1, violating F4's condition. If the second stage additionally stores x1, the final task becomes recoverable. Asking for the count instead changes the target rather than repairing the original query.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Exactly four states, deterministic functions, and a final target fixed to the first bit.
teachingExamples.boundary: A mathematical construction that does not erase counting's success at its own task.

teachingExamples.title: Mathematical teaching construction: check only the actual image
teachingExamples.text: Let X={a,b}, f(a)=u, f(b)=v, and let the intermediate space also contain unreachable w. Set g(u)=g(v)=7 and g(w)=99, while h maps u,v,w all to 0. The actual final target is 7 for both a and b, so k(0)=7 recovers it. Although g is not constant on the h fiber throughout Z, it is constant on actual f(X)={u,v}, satisfying the real condition.
teachingExamples.assumptions: w is explicitly unreachable from X, the target domain is nonempty, and all mappings are artificial assumptions.
teachingExamples.boundary: If X is later expanded so that w becomes reachable, recheck the condition rather than ignoring it permanently.

teachingExamples.title: Mathematical construction from the original: witnesses to two different failures
teachingExamples.text: For states a,b,c, f is respectively 0,0,1 and q is 0,1,1. The actual rule g_actual(0)=g_actual(1)=0 produces outputs 0,0,0. a and b witness insufficient representation; c witnesses an incorrect rule despite sufficient information. Changing the rule to g_actual(0)=0 and g_actual(1)=1 yields 0,0,1, repairing c while b remains wrong and a remains correct throughout.
teachingExamples.assumptions: The original finite three-state model has known input representations and actual rules. It does not satisfy F4's initial exact-recovery premise; it separately illustrates diagnostic distinctions between representation and execution.
teachingExamples.boundary: If internal representation or contemporaneous inputs are unknown in reality, retain the gap rather than mechanically applying failure labels.

questionAnswers.question: If step one stores and step two counts correctly, what happens when the final question asks about the first bit?
questionAnswers.answer: It may fail: sum 1 merges states whose first bits are 0 and 1.
questionAnswers.basis: The public counterexample.

questionAnswers.question: Why does F4 not require g to be constant over the relevant fibers throughout Z?
questionAnswers.answer: Only actual f(X) is used; unreachable values do not affect recovery of the original task.
questionAnswers.basis: The necessity-and-sufficiency proof.

questionAnswers.question: After correcting the rule at representation 1 in the three-state example, is everything recovered?
questionAnswers.answer: No. c is repaired and a remains correct, but b's conflict with a at shared representation 0 remains.
questionAnswers.basis: The three-state item-by-item results.

questionAnswers.question: Does answer recovery through function composition establish sufficient resources for execution?
questionAnswers.answer: No. Functions, causality, and joint resource feasibility require separate checks.
questionAnswers.basis: Appendix C.12.

4.18.5.title: 4.18.5 F5 Error propagation under approximate closure
4.18.5.lead: If every step is only slightly off, how large can the difference become over many steps? The answer depends on one-step discrepancy, whether the macro update amplifies or contracts existing error, and how long those conditions remain valid.
explanation: Given a metric d, the actual model state advances by x_(t+1)=F(x_t), while the macro approximation advances by y_(t+1)=F̄(y_t). Assume every reached x at every step satisfies d(π(F(x)),F̄(π(x)))≤ε, and in the comparison region d(F̄(y),F̄(y′))≤L d(y,y′), with ε≥0 and L≥0. Initial states match: y0=π(x0), and e_t=d(π(x_t),y_t). This requires bounds state by state and step by step, not a training mean-squared error. [T-F5；T-F5A]

The triangle inequality splits next-step error into two terms: e_(t+1)=d(π(F(x_t)),F̄(y_t))≤d(π(F(x_t)),F̄(π(x_t)))+d(F̄(π(x_t)),F̄(y_t))≤ε+L e_t. The first term is this step's projected-model discrepancy; the second propagates existing representation error through the macro update. Both points and their relevant updates must remain inside the checked region. [T-F5A]

Recursing from e0=0 gives e1≤ε, e2≤ε+Lε, e3≤ε+Lε+L²ε. Inductively, if e_t≤εΣ_{j=0}^{t−1}L^j, substitution gives e_(t+1)≤ε+εΣ_{j=1}^{t}L^j=εΣ_{j=0}^{t}L^j. Thus the bound holds for every finite t over which the premises remain valid. For t=0, the empty sum gives bound 0. [T-F5A]

For 0≤L<1, the geometric sum is (1−L^t)/(1−L), so e_t≤ε/(1−L). For L=1, step discrepancies add to tε. For L>1, the bound is ε(L^t−1)/(L−1) and may grow rapidly. A growing bound does not mean actual error necessarily grows. If actual and macro updates agree exactly, for instance, actual error may remain 0 despite using a loose positive ε and large L as bounds. [T-F5A]

If initial error is nonzero, the same recursion adds L^t e0; the formula without that initial term no longer applies. If ε or L varies by step, recurse through e_(t+1)≤ε_t+L_t e_t instead of replacing fixed stepwise bounds with averages. Initial perturbations, measurement error, or external noise not included in the premises cannot be claimed covered by the original formula. [T-F5A；derivational extension]

Small average fitting error does not ensure small error at every step. Large discrepancies at rare states, or trajectories leaving the training region, may invalidate the original ε/L premises. Short-term bounds cannot be extrapolated indefinitely without conditions. A numerical formula also does not establish that actual-system measurements, operation sets, and applicability ranges were checked. F5 supplies a conditional error budget, not evidential eligibility for an actual G4. [T-F5；T-G4]
argumentSteps: Define actual and approximate trajectories, metric, and common initial state; specify statewise ε bounds and the L bound over the relevant region.
Use the triangle inequality to separate current-step model discrepancy from propagation of existing error.
Obtain e_(t+1)≤ε+Le_t.
Induct from e0=0 to the geometric-sum bound, simplifying separately for L<1, L=1, and L>1.
When initial error or time-varying parameters occur, retain the corresponding terms and recursion instead of mechanically applying the fixed formula.
Check that each step remains within the region and original operation set. Average fit and real-world mapping carry separate evidential responsibilities.

Mathematical counterexample: of 100 teaching errors, 99 are 0 and one is 10. Mean absolute error is 0.1 but the maximum is 10; the average cannot justify statewise ε=0.1.

teachingExamples.title: Mathematical teaching construction: a family of models attaining the error bound
teachingExamples.text: Use the real domain, identity π, absolute distance, F(x)=Lx+0.1, F̄(y)=Ly, x0=y0=0, and L≥0. The one-step discrepancy is always 0.1, and F̄ has Lipschitz constant L. y_t remains 0 and x_t=0.1Σ_{j=0}^{t−1}L^j, so actual error exactly attains the bound. For t=0 through 4: L=.5 gives 0,.1,.15,.175,.1875; L=1 gives 0,.1,.2,.3,.4; L=2 gives 0,.1,.3,.7,1.5.
teachingExamples.assumptions: The entire real domain, exact equations, constant parameters, common zero initial state, and no additional noise or operation changes.
teachingExamples.boundary: Entirely mathematical constructions. Attaining the bound shows it can be tight, not that every system attains it or grows in the same way.

teachingExamples.title: Mathematical teaching construction: average error cannot guarantee the worst step
teachingExamples.text: Suppose an artificial table has 100 errors: 99 are 0 and one is 10. Mean absolute error is 10/100=0.1, while the maximum is 10. If the next step reaches the large-error state, substituting 0.1 for a uniform ε violates F5's premise. Accuracy on the other 99 items cannot compensate for this failure.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Only a specified finite error table; no actual visitation probabilities or data-generation process are given.
teachingExamples.boundary: Does not estimate actual frequency or imply that average metrics are worthless. They answer a different loss question.

counterexamples.text: Boundary in the original: average one-step fitting error cannot replace statewise, stepwise error bounds.
counterexamples.effect: An average does not replace a worst-case bound.

counterexamples.text: Boundary in the original: the old ε/L guarantee does not automatically continue when trajectories leave the relevant region or the operation set changes.
counterexamples.effect: Guarantees are limited by domain and operation conditions.

counterexamples.text: Mathematical boundary: an L>1 bound can grow while actual error is 0. Do not treat the bound as a necessary trajectory.
counterexamples.effect: An upper bound is not the actual trajectory.

counterexamples.text: Mathematical counterexample: of 100 teaching errors, 99 are 0 and one is 10. Mean absolute error is 0.1 but the maximum is 10; the average cannot justify statewise ε=0.1.
counterexamples.effect: A small average can still contain a large step error.

questionAnswers.question: With L=1, ε=.1, and a common initial state, what is the four-step bound?
questionAnswers.answer: 0.4, the sum of four one-step bounds.
questionAnswers.basis: Geometric sum tε.

questionAnswers.question: With L=.5 and ε=.1, what is the uniform bound?
questionAnswers.answer: 0.1/(1−.5)=0.2; the tighter four-step bound is .1875.
questionAnswers.basis: Geometric sum and upper bound.

questionAnswers.question: If the bound increases for L=2, must actual error increase?
questionAnswers.answer: Not necessarily. A bound is only a guarantee; model discrepancies may be zero or cancel.
questionAnswers.basis: Distinction between bound and actual quantity.

questionAnswers.question: How must the formula change for initial error e0>0?
questionAnswers.answer: The recursion gives L^t e0+εΣL^j; the initial term cannot be omitted.
questionAnswers.basis: The same triangle recursion.

questionAnswers.question: Can mean error .1 directly register ε=.1?
questionAnswers.answer: No. Statewise, stepwise bounds are required; the counterexample's maximum error is 10.
questionAnswers.basis: F5 premises.

4.19.title: 4.19 Task families and dynamic refinement
4.19.lead: Finer state distinctions are not inherently better. Preserve distinctions the specified tasks and permitted actions actually discriminate. A complete finite model permits proof of the coarsest necessary partition; changed horizons, added actions, or allowed error require renewed checking.
explanation: Chinese source line 1056 first returns simplification to its use: finer representations may retain more distinctions while increasing measurement, storage, explanation, and maintenance costs. F6 seeks the coarsest sufficient partition relative to given states, tasks, actions, and horizon, not nature's uniquely correct level or automatically the cheapest or lowest-parameter model. [T-419]

The premises must be complete: X is nonempty and finite; Q is a finite set of target functions, each q:X→V_q; U is a finite permitted-action set, each u corresponding to a total deterministic update F_u:X→X. Every action is feasible in every state, with no unregistered external disturbance. Action string w=u1…uk applies u1 first, then u2, through uk, so F_w=F_uk∘…∘F_u1. The empty string makes no update and ensures current tasks are also compared. An identically named real operation does not automatically meet these conditions. [T-419]

For H≥0, define x∼_H x′ when every q∈Q and every permitted action string w of length ≤H satisfy q(F_w(x))=q(F_w(x′)). This compares an entire family of answers to “ask the task after operations.” H=0 compares only current Q. If Q is empty, the condition is an empty conjunction, so all states may form one class. That merely reflects no registered tasks, not satisfaction of all actual needs. [T-419；direct inference from the definition]

The equivalence-relation proof follows item by item from equality: each answer equals itself, giving reflexivity; exchanging x and x′ preserves equality, giving symmetry; if x and x′, and x′ and x″, give equal answers for every (q,w), so do x and x″, giving transitivity. Represent by equivalence classes [x]_H. Each q∘F_w is constant within a class, so F1 supplies the corresponding decoder. Any other deterministic representation merging two nonequivalent states has a witnessing (q,w) with different answers, violating F1; its partition can therefore only be finer or equal. This proves coarsest sufficiency. [T-419；T-F1]

“Coarsest” refers to refinement order among state partitions, not label names or code lengths. Representations merely renaming the same blocks count as the same partition. The minimum necessary state distinctions do not imply fewest parameters, cheapest measurement, simplest explanation, or irreplaceability of a natural-language concept. Costs require separate modeling and evaluation. [T-419；T-eval]

Finite-horizon sufficiency does not automatically give dynamic closure at that same horizon. In the original four-state example, q(a)=q(b)=q(c)=0, q(d)=1, F(a)=c, F(b)=b, F(c)=d, F(d)=d. a and b both give 0 now and after one step, so a∼1b; but their successors c and b give 1 and 0 after another step, so c is not ∼1-equivalent to b. Generally, for H≥1, x∼_H x′⇒F_u(x)∼_(H−1)F_u(x′): prefixing any successor string v of length ≤H−1 with u gives uv of length ≤H, so the original relation guarantees equal answers. Advancing consumes remaining horizon, unless closure of the fixed partition is separately checked. [T-419]

If all targets must remain recoverable after any finite action string, define ∼_*. Its classes are closed under every F_u: prefixing any successor string v with u still gives a finite string, so successors remain equivalent; the empty string ensures current Q is recoverable too. Conversely, a representation recovering Q and closed under every F_u can advance through any finite string and then recover q, so it cannot merge states nonequivalent under ∼_*. Therefore ∼_* is the unique coarsest partition satisfying Q recovery and closure under every action, with uniqueness by equivalence classes rather than names. [T-419；T-F2]

The algorithm initially partitions by the current target vector (q(x))_{q∈Q}, producing P0. At round h, retain the whole previous P_h and synchronously repartition using only sig_h(x)=([x]_{P_h},([F_u(x)]_{P_h})_{u∈U}), producing P_(h+1). Including the old block in the signature ensures splitting without merging. Read every successor block from the old partition; do not update one block and pass its new numbering off as old-layer information. [T-419]

Induction shows synchronous layer h equals ∼_h. P0 corresponds to empty-string targets. If P_h corresponds to answers for lengths ≤h, equal signatures mean the states retain their common old block and successors under every first action u give equal answers for all later strings of length ≤h, hence all strings of length ≤h+1 give equal answers. Conversely, agreement on all strings of length ≤h+1 includes old-layer questions and every u followed by a length-≤h string, so signatures match. Thus algorithmic layer count genuinely represents a horizon; the number of asynchronous blockwise operations has no such meaning. [T-419]

Let n=|X| and let P0 contain k0 nonempty blocks. Each strict refinement adds at least one block, up to at most n blocks, so the number of strict refinements is ≤n−k0≤n−1. When a complete round produces no split, current targets remain preserved and successor blocks for each action agree within each block, so closure holds. This stable partition recovers all finite strings by closure; moreover, no finite level separates ∼_* equivalent states, so it equals ∼_*. The round confirming stability may contain no strict split. This bound is not a guarantee of total computational steps, runtime, or budget. [T-419]

Adding targets, permitted actions, or a longer horizon adds same-answer conditions to satisfy simultaneously, so the partition can only remain unchanged or become finer. Restricting actions, shortening the horizon, or narrowing uses may make a coarser representation sufficient. Resetting the task may legitimately answer a different question, but success on that new task cannot establish completion of the original one. Whether actions are lawfully permitted and which targets cannot be omitted remain matters of domain requirements, norms, and permissions. [T-419; T-C12]

Closeness within a tolerance is not a ready-made equivalence relation. Take ε>0: 0 and ε are at distance ≤ε, as are ε and 2ε, but 0 and 2ε have distance 2ε>ε, so transitivity fails. Even requiring each block's diameter to be ≤ε may admit multiple valid coarse partitions that do not refine one another; unique coarseness cannot automatically be inherited. Optimal solutions, stability, and costs for worst-case recovery error, probabilistic loss, or dynamic approximation each require their own proofs. “Approximately equal” cannot simply replace F6's equality. [T-419; T-F1; T-F5]

Chinese source line 1074 connects this section to Moore's input-string discrimination and recursive refinement, and to literature on controlled dynamical abstraction. This mathematical connection has specific objects and scope: Moore's cited minimal-machine discussion has its own machine-class conditions; Ravindran and Barto's SMDP model includes stochastic transitions, rewards, and state-dependent action recoding, unlike the finite deterministic model here with fixed U and actions feasible at every state. This section's conclusions rest on its own proof; it borrows no additional optimality or complexity results from other models. [P-Moore; P-RB; T-419]

Stopping points remain important in application. Computability from a complete finite table does not mean incomplete observations identify actual states, nor that a large table can be processed within the available time. If reality involves state-dependent action feasibility, unknown disturbances, continuous quantities, or measurement error, the model must be changed and its new premises tested. Mathematical indistinguishability also cannot reduce people's justified claims to existing prediction targets. Responsibility for selecting Q, U, and tolerances must remain public rather than being automatically decided by the refinement algorithm. [T-419; T-formal; T-C12]

The task family Q, permitted operations U, and horizon H determine what this formal proposition answers; the algorithm cannot decide on participants' behalf whether these conditions are appropriate. Through §2.14, v2 adds a reopening route: if Q omits a legitimate claim, register the challenge, retain the original refinement result, and reanalyze the new task. Formal sufficiency for the old task and insufficiency for the new one may both hold.
argumentSteps: Freeze finite X, Q, U, total functions F_u, common feasibility, and the absence of additional disturbances.
Define the finite-horizon same-answer relation across all targets and action strings, proving reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity individually.
Use F1 to prove the sufficiency of equivalence classes; use differing answers as witnesses excluding every coarser sufficient representation.
Distinguish the countdown guarantee for finite H from closure of a fixed partition; prove closure and unique coarseness for the relation over all finite strings.
Form P0 from current targets; in each round, synchronously refine using signatures from the old P_h only.
Prove by induction that P_h equals ∼_h; use the block-count bound to prove finitely many strict refinements and explain why the stable partition equals ∼_*.
Check monotonic refinement under target/action/horizon expansion item by item; prove approximate relations separately rather than directly substituting them for equivalence.
Use the literature only as mathematical references with explicit scope; separately check real-world mappings, costs, norms, and authorization.

caseNotes.title: Moore's 1956 original text: the mathematical history of equivalence classes and recursive discrimination
caseNotes.text: On printed page 143, Moore's original text constructs a reduced machine from equivalence classes of indistinguishable states; pages 145–146 recursively refine states by finite experiment length. Page 129 already explains that this is not a report of actual physical experimental results. It supports the mathematical connection stated in this section, but its minimal-machine theorem has its own conditions and cannot directly endorse this section's entire scope.
caseNotes.sourceLabel: Edward F. Moore，Gedanken-Experiments on Sequential Machines
caseNotes.sourceLocator: Automata Studies, 1956; printed pp. 129, 143, 145–146; PDF including cover, pp. 2, 16, 18–19.
caseNotes.boundary: Facts about the content of original mathematical literature are used here, not described as real machine experiments. F6's coarsest partition rests on this text's conditions and proof; no additional optimality conclusions for Moore's class of strongly connected machines are borrowed.

caseNotes.title: SMDP homomorphisms in 2003: a related but different abstraction contract
caseNotes.text: In §3, Ravindran and Barto define SMDP homomorphisms with state mappings, state-dependent action recoding, and preservation conditions for transition probabilities and rewards. Their introduction also notes that reducing state counts need not reduce descriptive parameters. This provides a specialist reference for state/action abstraction; its stochastic and action-recoding model cannot simply be renamed this section's deterministic F6 with fixed actions.
caseNotes.sourceLabel: Ravindran and Barto, SMDP Homomorphisms
caseNotes.sourceLocator: IJCAI 2003, printed pp. 1011–1013/PDF 1–3; especially the §3 definition and explanation below it, printed 1012/PDF 2.
caseNotes.boundary: A mathematical reference, not evidence of this framework's real-world effectiveness. Its policy optimality, minimal state-action pair, and complexity conclusions are not transplanted.

teachingExamples.title: Original mathematical construction expanded: finite horizons and synchronous refinement
teachingExamples.text: Order the four states a,b,c,d, with q=(0,0,0,1) and F=(c,b,d,d). Current values give P0={a,b,c}|{d}. One-step answer pairs are a:(0,0), b:(0,0), c:(0,1), d:(1,1), so P1={a,b}|{c}|{d}. Two-step answer triples are a:(0,0,1), b:(0,0,0), c:(0,1,1), d:(1,1,1), so P2 has four singleton blocks. P3 remains the same as P2, confirming stability. There are two strict splits, exactly n−k0=4−2=2, plus another round to confirm stability.
teachingExamples.assumptions: One action, a complete deterministic four-state table, operations feasible at every state, and an exactly specified target.
teachingExamples.boundary: An exact enumeration of the original model, not a measurement of a real system. Two splits do not mean an actual program requires only two operations.

teachingExamples.title: Mathematical teaching construction: stability need not mean singleton blocks
teachingExamples.text: Alternatively, set q(a)=q(b)=0, q(c)=q(d)=1, F(a)=c, F(b)=d, F(c)=a, and F(d)=b. P0={a,b}|{c,d}. Every state in the same block enters the other block, so the first round produces no split and the partition is already stable. The two blocks' outputs alternate at every subsequent step, and states within a block always give the same answers. Since the two blocks have different current outputs, they cannot merge, so the coarsest partition has two blocks.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Another complete four-state, single-action model, whose task contains only this binary q.
teachingExamples.boundary: Recovering a/b or c/d identities is not required; adding a target that distinguishes them requires renewed refinement.

teachingExamples.title: Mathematical teaching construction: tolerance rules do not automatically ensure uniqueness
teachingExamples.text: Let static target values be 0, 1, 2, with tolerance 1 and each block required to have diameter ≤1. P={{0,1},{2}} is valid, as is R={{0},{1,2}}, and neither refines the other. Any partition coarser than both must put 0 and 1 together because of P, and 1 and 2 together because of R. Transitivity forces all three into one block, whose diameter 2 is invalid. Thus no unique coarsest valid partition exists.
teachingExamples.assumptions: A finite three-value static task; the diameter constraint is a separate approximate objective defined for this example, not F6's exact equivalence.
teachingExamples.boundary: This does not deny that valid approximation methods can be developed for other losses; it only rejects automatic inheritance of unique coarseness.

counterexamples.text: Original-text counterexample: in the four-state model, a∼1b but F(a)=c is not ∼1-equivalent to F(b)=b. Finite-horizon sufficiency does not mean closure at that same horizon.
counterexamples.effect: Finite horizons do not replace fixed closure.

counterexamples.text: Original-text boundary: coarseness is relative only to X/Q/U/H; it does not establish the fewest parameters, minimum cost, or a unique natural hierarchy.
counterexamples.effect: The coarsest partition is not optimal in every respect.

counterexamples.text: Original-text boundary: asynchronous operation counts cannot be treated as synchronous horizon H; n−1 bounds only strict refinements.
counterexamples.effect: Iteration counts must retain their mathematical meaning.

counterexamples.text: Original mathematical counterexample: for ε>0, 0≈ε and ε≈2ε, but 0 is not ≈2ε; tolerance-based similarity is not transitive.
counterexamples.effect: Tolerance relations are not automatically equivalence relations.

counterexamples.effect: Approximate constraints may lack a unique coarsest solution.

questionAnswers.question: Why must F6 include the empty action string?
questionAnswers.answer: It ensures that current targets must also agree; comparing only futures could omit answers that need to be distinguished now.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source lines 1058–1060.

questionAnswers.question: In the original four-state example, why can a and b merge at H=1 but not continue under the same H after progression?
questionAnswers.answer: Their current and one-step values are both 0; their successors c and b reach q=1 and 0 respectively one further step later. Only H−1 remains of the original guarantee.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source line 1064 and the enumeration.

questionAnswers.question: What are synchronous P1 and P2 respectively?
questionAnswers.answer: P1={a,b}|{c}|{d}; P2 consists of four singleton blocks.
questionAnswers.basis: Target sequences and signatures from the old partition.

questionAnswers.question: Does n−1 guarantee that the program executes at most n−1 operations?
questionAnswers.answer: No. It bounds only refinements that strictly increase block counts; reading tables, comparing entries, and confirming stability incur additional costs.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source line 1068.

questionAnswers.question: Can adding targets or permitted actions make the coarsest sufficient partition coarser?
questionAnswers.answer: No. Additional same-answer conditions can only preserve or refine it; removing targets or restricting actions may make it coarser.
questionAnswers.basis: The conjunction in the definition.

questionAnswers.question: With tolerance 1, if 0 is close to 1 and 1 to 2, may all three directly be treated as one class?
questionAnswers.answer: No. 0 and 2 exceed the tolerance, so the approximate relation is not transitive; two valid coarse partitions may also be incomparable.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source line 1072 and the three-value construction.

questionAnswers.question: Does coarsest sufficiency prove it justified to merge all people into predictive equivalence classes?
questionAnswers.answer: No. Whether people's justified claims and protective targets must be preserved, and whether actions are permitted, requires normative and permission-based grounds; the algorithm does not decide.
questionAnswers.basis: Chinese source line 1074.
