caseLinks.title: Cash and Counseling: domain comparisons retain their bounded conclusions

caseNotes.title: Cash and Counseling: domain comparisons retain their bounded conclusions
caseNotes.text: Carlson and colleagues' 2007 report presents randomized comparisons among voluntary participants in three states, evaluating care through telephone interviews nine months after assignment. The authors report improvements in paid care, satisfaction, or unmet needs in most states and age groups, while noting lower actual allowance receipt and weaker related effects among older participants in Florida. It illustrates that empirical conclusions depend on specific comparisons and implementation scope, not directly on the label ‘autonomy’ or H2 typing.
caseNotes.sourceLabel: Carlson, Foster, Dale, and Brown, original authors' 2007 abstract
caseNotes.sourceLocator: The original authors' abstract on PubMed: Study setting, Data sources, Methods, and Principal findings; Health Services Research 42(1 Pt2):467—487, 2007-02
caseNotes.boundary: This section cites bounded results only from the checked original authors' abstract; the full paper's methods/data were not obtained for independent review. Nonrecipients cannot be excluded and the result relabeled a randomized comparison; individual wishes are not diagnosed, nor is formal H1/H4/H5 instance status retrospectively granted.

argumentSteps: Identify whether the present assertion is an H1/H4/H5 empirical hypothesis, H2/H3 typing, or an H6 normative boundary.
Specify each item's permitted object and outcome registrations and prohibited overreach; applying a rule requires factual materials, but the rule itself does not become causal evidence.

Before results, an empirical instance uniquely preselects its subtype and criterion and freezes comparisons, thresholds, null models, and necessary analysis rules; H5 additionally checks consistency between family and the single carrier atom.
At the result phase, link materials, artifacts, and deviations item by item and close with one of four statuses; do not use unselected outcomes to rescue the claim.
Ask separately about H5 traces, current-carrier aftereffects, and additional historical increments, supplying materials for whichever route is needed.
Retain bounded domain-study results without automatically granting formal H-instance qualification from a paper's label.
When moving from description to actual adoption, separately register normative premises, protection floors, J scope, option comparisons, and procedures for execution and error correction.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: one appeal can produce results at different levels
teachingExamples.text: A fictional appeal is accepted on day 1; on day 3 a draft field revision is produced but is not yet effective and the authoritative record remains unchanged. On day 5 the revision is formally written and actually adopted by a downstream procedure, and it is still being used on day 30. Day 1 gives acceptance only; day 3 gives only a draft, still lacking implementation; day 5 permits checking H3 write-back under the stipulations. If another case targets only the authoritative record itself and that record was actually corrected on day 3 with an implementation record, its write-back may be established earlier without waiting for downstream results. Continued use on day 30 supports further examination of carrier continuation, but predetermined tasks and comparisons are still needed to judge learning, and one month of records cannot establish long-term repair.
teachingExamples.assumptions: The timeline and implementation facts are fictional; day 3 is explicitly an ineffective draft only, to compare judgment levels. Target states and implementation positions are declared separately; no actual appeal or administrative change was performed.
teachingExamples.boundary: This cannot establish that any real case has achieved write-back, learning, or lawful correction.

teachingExamples.title: Mathematical construction: one successful outcome cannot rescue another preselected target
teachingExamples.text: A fictional H1-style comparison uniquely preselects an effect on resource allocation, with a positive threshold of 0.05 standardized units. Let the resource effect be 0.04 and a separately measured action effect be 0.30. Since 0.04 does not exceed 0.05, the unselected action result of 0.30 cannot reclassify this instance as supported. If the predetermined null rule requires the resource effect's uncertainty interval to lie entirely within [-0.02,0.02] and the sensitivity gate to pass, but the given interval is [-0.06,0.12], that interval is not contained in the tolerance band, so the null conclusion also fails. In this construction the status remains unsupported_or_undecided.
teachingExamples.assumptions: The values, intervals, and rules are explicit author-made stipulations, not results of a sampling experiment; the other qualification conditions are assumed satisfied solely to illustrate the nonequivalence of the two result gates.
teachingExamples.boundary: The interval was not estimated from real data; the example certifies no actual H1 instance and does not claim that 0.05 is a universal threshold.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: leaving a record, using it, and additional history
teachingExamples.text: A record D forms after a fictional event and is preserved across three windows. The trace question checks only whether D persists under the preselected rule. If subsequent personnel never read D, preservation cannot imply an actual effect; if reading D does change a decision, current-carrier aftereffects require a separate check. Further explicitly assume that D is already sufficient for this task's future target Y: given D, Y is conditionally independent of past-event label E, that is, Y ⟂ E | D. Including D therefore leaves E with no additional information about Y, without denying that D was formed or used; ‘the record is complete’ alone cannot establish that sufficiency.
teachingExamples.assumptions: D is a fictional single textual record whose family may be registered as institutional_or_textual_record; Y ⟂ E | D is explicitly assumed for the predetermined future target, not inferred from record completeness. This is only an atomic illustrative example, not a submitted actual H5 instance.
teachingExamples.boundary: In reality, both retention and effects require evidence; disappearance of the additional historical increment holds only under the stipulated sufficient representation.

counterexamples.text: H3 classification holds, so the person's records and rights may be changed directly.
counterexamples.effect: Classification does not grant actual modification authority; action bridging requires a separate check.

counterexamples.text: H5 includes ten carriers at once and treats any one remaining at the end as success of the prior claim.
counterexamples.effect: This violates responsibilities for a unique family, single carrier, and preselected persistence criterion; selecting the best result afterward is prohibited.

counterexamples.text: Someone incurs huge costs and helps the organization succeed, so they have love and must continue.
counterexamples.effect: Costs and effects cannot replace voluntariness, refusal, and grounds for obligation; H6 prohibits such requisition.

counterexamples.text: The resource target failed, but the action target improved significantly, so the original resource target is supported.
counterexamples.effect: Different outcome families cannot rescue one another; an unselected outcome may become a later candidate under its actual status.

questionAnswers.question: If H2 distinguishes performers, beneficiaries, and responsibility positions, has intertemporal reproduction been established?
questionAnswers.answer: No. Typing clarifies the questions; continued supply, maintenance, replacement, and actual continuation still require materials.

questionAnswers.question: In the mathematical example, the resource effect is 0.04 and the threshold 0.05. Why does this not support a null?
questionAnswers.answer: Failure of the positive gate means only that this positive gate did not pass; the given interval [-0.06,0.12] is not contained in the tolerance band [-0.02,0.02], so the null gate also failed.

questionAnswers.question: If a record is preserved for three years, may it directly be called a historical path effect?
questionAnswers.answer: No. Persistent traces, current-carrier subsequent effects, and historical increments beyond the current representation require separate evidence; only the last additionally requires G3.
questionAnswers.basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

questionAnswers.question: May the results of a randomized study using no Xikari format be retained?
questionAnswers.answer: Yes, within its design and evidence scope; H-instance status is not automatically granted, nor does lacking that status invalidate its conclusion.
questionAnswers.basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

questionAnswers.question: If a rewrite was actually implemented but worsened outcomes, does it still count as write-back?
questionAnswers.answer: It may be classified as write-back according to the actual change; error correction, learning improvement, and normative justification require separate checks. Occurrence of an event cannot be acknowledged only when outcomes are good.

questionAnswers.question: H6 requires checking rights to stop. Does it authorize the analyst to stop every arrangement immediately on behalf of those concerned?
questionAnswers.answer: No authorization is granted. It generates normative requirements and gaps; actual protection or stopping still requires corresponding norms, authority, and procedures.

7.2.title: 7.2 Three groups of strong types that must not be mixed
7.2.lead: A project obtaining resources, someone beginning work, an event occurring, someone continuing maintenance, and someone needing to take responsibility often appear in one story but are different judgments. Strong types separate them so evidence addresses the question actually being asked.
explanation: Chinese source location: lines 1572—1575; source anchor section-7-2; short quotation: ‘establishment of one type alone cannot close the case for other types’ (translated from Chinese). The current source appears in the corresponding subsection on this page; the downloadable original research excerpt preserves the historical manuscript.

This section has three groups with eight items in total: GC/GS/GE separates generative conditions, generative subjects, and generative events; CV/RS separates actual uptake from grounds for responsibility; IS/IM/IB separates sources, mechanisms, and observable behaviors of destabilization. The three groups are neither three inevitable timelines nor a division of people into eight mutually exclusive identities.

Types specify subsequent questions, materials, and responsibility boundaries; definitions alone cannot declare facts in the world established. Seeing resources in place does not yet imply agent action; seeing an event occur does not allow a specified agent to be inferred backward from the result; seeing someone execute a task does not mean they bear all responsibility. Every arrow requires additional corresponding materials to hold.

Direct grounds for each claim do not require every field to come from a statistically independent document. A timestamped record may support both ‘who operated’ and ‘when the state changed’, but its shared provenance must be stated rather than counted as two independent replications. Different questions may share material while retaining separate support responsibilities and source dependencies.

One case may receive multiple types, and one person may hold GS, CV, and some RS roles; each needs its own grounds. Separating types prevents automatic inference, not overlap of actual roles. An unknown item does not erase other established facts.

Formal independence relations use full type names prefixed human_strong_type:, such as human_strong_type:CV and human_strong_type:RS. Bare CV, Chinese display names, or ‘uptake group’ cannot replace formal references. The prefix makes references resolvable, but correct spelling still proves no fact. The eight independent units below explain the most likely substitution within each type.

distinctions.leftText: Different questions carry their own evidentiary responsibilities.
distinctions.rightText: Actual people may not hold multiple roles; this section imposes no such requirement.

distinctions.leftText: One record contains two kinds of checkable information.
distinctions.rightText: Require independent sources or design grounds; reuse cannot increase the count.

distinctions.leftText: The name can be resolved explicitly.
distinctions.rightText: Still requires object material; the prefix provides no truth value.

boundaries: The three groups are not a necessary causal chain; definitions create no factual arrows exempt from evidence.
Multiple types in one case do not cancel classification responsibilities; one established type does not establish all others.
A missing mechanism does not cancel an observed event, and missing grounds for attribution do not cancel incurred losses.
questions: Does one person holding three roles violate strong typing?
Can one video showing who pressed a button and the changed screen support two facts?
Does correctly writing human_strong_type:RS establish responsibility?
argumentSteps: First split a mixed narrative into questions of conditions, subjects, events, uptake, responsibility, sources, mechanisms, and acts.
For each, list direct material, object, and window; leave unknowns unknown rather than filling them automatically from adjacent types.
Mark shared and independent sources; field counts do not increase validation counts.
Permit multiple types per case and multiple roles per person, explaining the grounds for each.
Use complete type names in formal references, separating parseable syntax from factual support.

teachingExamples.title: Logical construction: role sets may intersect without being equal
teachingExamples.text: Suppose fictional person A initiates and executes, B only executes, and C only approves. The GS candidate set={A}, and CV={A,B}. If a separate explicit responsibility rule assigns approval duties to C, RS may include C. Thus GS∩CV is nonempty, while CV equals neither GS nor RS. Specific RS assignments depend only on the responsibility grounds given in this construction, not automatically on set names.
teachingExamples.assumptions: These sets represent only roles supported by fictional material; omission does not mean every other actual role has been ruled out.
teachingExamples.boundary: Illustrates ‘may overlap without equivalence’, not a prescribed role distribution for all actual objects.

counterexamples.effect: An intersection in one case does not establish equivalence between two kinds of judgment.

7.2.1.title: 7.2.1 GC (Generative Conditions)
7.2.1.lead: Power, tools, and institutional access may enable something to begin; yet ‘conditions are available’ does not mean ‘someone intends to do it’ or ‘it has been accomplished’. GC first separates potentially operative conditions from human intentions.
explanation: Source location: Chinese source lines 1576–1579; source anchor section-7-2-1; short quotation translated from Chinese: ‘But conditions have no intention.’ See the corresponding section on this page for the current original text; the downloadable original research excerpt retains the historical draft.

GC asks which conditions make generation possible or more likely. Resources, technology, institutions, relationships, trauma, crises, and opportunity windows can be candidates, but listing them only identifies positions to check and assigns no desires, purposes, or choices to conditions themselves.

The first layer of material concerns timing and exposure: when conditions appeared, changed, or were removed, and which objects actually encountered them. A citywide opportunity announcement does not mean every position can use it, and nominal resources need not be obtainable when required. Record candidate-condition existence separately from actual exposure.

A further claim that a condition raises generation probability requires proportionate comparisons, outcome differences, candidate channels, and competing explanations. Shared external causes, selection into exposure, concurrent reforms, or measurement changes may explain why the ‘condition-present group’ differs. Earlier appearance or coexistence is only part of process material.

GC, GS, and GE require separate tests. Conditions may exist with no action; a subject may act while key conditions are missing; an event may form while its mechanism remains unidentified. These can be recorded separately. Confirming GC does not automatically identify the initiator, much less confirm a particular generative event.

distinctions.leftText: A resource or entry point exists.
distinctions.rightText: A specific object can actually access or use it in a specific window.

distinctions.leftText: A possible supporting factor worth checking.
distinctions.rightText: Proportionate comparisons and channel material support its bounded effect.

distinctions.leftText: Changes possibilities or feasible sets.
distinctions.rightText: Anthropomorphically inferring purpose from effect is disallowed by GC.

boundaries: Crises, technologies, and resources do not become generative subjects because their effects are strong.
Correlation between condition and outcome does not automatically mean the condition causes the outcome.
Usable conditions may genuinely exist without initiating action; failure of the event to occur does not negate all preparation.

argumentSteps: List candidate conditions and when, where, and to whom they are actually available.

teachingExamples.title: Mathematical construction: a correlated condition may merely mark a shared external cause
teachingExamples.text: Let U be equiprobably 0 or 1, candidate condition C=U, and generative-event bit E=U. Then P(E=1|C=1)=1 and P(E=1|C=0)=0, an extreme observational association. But E depends only on U in the equations: fix U=1 and externally set C=0, and E remains 1. In this model C is not a channel causing E to change.
teachingExamples.assumptions: The binary structural equations are constructed; externally setting C leaves U and E’s equation unchanged. Whether reality matches requires evidence.
teachingExamples.boundary: Shows only that association cannot determine causation, without denying that actual conditions may have enabling effects.

counterexamples.text: A group with a new tool succeeds more often, so the tool must be the generative subject.
counterexamples.effect: Correlation does not independently identify the tool’s effect, and a useful tool does not acquire human intention.

questionAnswers.question: An opportunity notice is published; may everyone be said to face the same opportunity?

questionAnswers.question: If C and E match perfectly in the model, why might changing C leave E unchanged?

7.2.2.title: 7.2.2 GS (Generative Subject)
7.2.2.lead: ‘Who actually initiated this step?’ requires checking people and their actions, not answering with an opportunity, machine, or completed outcome. Identifying the actor also does not automatically place all responsibility on that person.
explanation: Source location: Chinese source lines 1580–1583; source anchor section-7-2-2; short quotation translated from Chinese: ‘GS does not automatically equal all responsible parties.’ See the corresponding section on this page for the current original text; the downloadable original research excerpt retains the historical draft.

GS asks who can understand and perform initiation, translation, or ceding actions. Initiation brings an arrangement into actual process; translation turns meanings or requirements from different positions into executable form; ceding involves giving control, a position, or room to act to another subject. These identify question types only; actual events still require identity and process checks.

Check subject identity, capability, resources, actual action, and authorization status separately. Capability is not performance, resources are not authority, and acting is not necessarily lawful or justified. Unknown authorization must remain unknown; an actual action cannot be deleted merely to avoid endorsing overreach.

Technology, crises, platforms, metrics, and resource windows cannot be registered as GS. They may be conditions, tools, or carriers, but significant outcomes do not give them understanding and intention; anthropomorphic narratives conceal actual decision-making and work positions.

An event’s occurrence cannot reverse-guarantee a specified generative subject. Whole-system emergence without a subject may occur; where subjects participate, they may be only some among many conditions. GS does not equal all RS; decision, authorization, oversight, conduct, and remedy responsibilities need separate grounds, scopes, and periods.

distinctions.leftText: Has the corresponding understanding and resources.
distinctions.rightText: Specific action records exist; neither substitutes for the other.

distinctions.leftText: Someone actually performed an action.
distinctions.rightText: Whether that action was permitted, with separate grounds and scope.

distinctions.leftText: The action position for initiation, translation, or ceding.
distinctions.rightText: Require responsibility-by-responsibility attribution; GS status cannot settle all of it.

boundaries: An event may occur without identifying the specified GS; do not invent a personified starting point.
A subject may actually act with unclear authority; facts, authority, and legitimacy require separate judgments.
A platform’s or tool’s function neither erases human actions nor attributes all outcomes to the most visible operator.

argumentSteps: First identify the specific initiation, translation, or ceding action in question.
Check identity, capability, resources, action, and authorization separately, retaining each known and unknown item.
Exclude subject labels that directly personify technologies or crises.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: one of five fields cannot replace them all
teachingExamples.text: Fictional A completed training and has tools but has not initiated the task. B pressed the start button, with identity and action recorded, but authorization documents have not been obtained. A’s capability and resources can be recorded, while actual action is unproved; B’s action can be recorded, while authorization remains unknown. One cannot say A ‘could do it, so did it’, or B ‘lacks verified authority, so never acted’.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Purely fictional record configurations; unknown does not mean unauthorized, and no complete search for other subjects has been conducted.
teachingExamples.boundary: This endorses no actual unauthorized act and does not treat a capability test as full qualification of a subject.

counterexamples.text: A system develops a new structure on its own, so there must be a hidden generative subject.
counterexamples.effect: Inferring a personal subject from an outcome ignores subjectless emergence and material gaps.

questionAnswers.question: What do a training certificate and an actual operation log each support?
questionAnswers.answer: The former supports evidence of a particular capability; the latter supports occurrence of a particular action. Neither replaces the other.

7.2.3.title: 7.2.3 GE (generative event)
7.2.3.lead: We may know clearly that a state changed without yet knowing why. GE first preserves that observable occurrence, leaving causes to corresponding mechanism tests.
explanation: Source location: Chinese source lines 1584–1587; original anchor section-7-2-3. Short quotation translated from Chinese: “An unidentified mechanism cannot be rewritten as nonoccurrence of an observed event.” See the corresponding section on this page for the current original; downloaded original research excerpts retain the historical draft.

GE asks which state transition formed and when. It requires prior state, event time, subsequent state, and criterion under the same measurement contract. Changing only a name, statistical definition, or data unit does not automatically constitute the claimed transition in the object itself.

Event time should track actual occurrence as closely as possible. Announcement, detection, and execution may occur at different times. If occurrence can only be located within an interval, retain that interval rather than inventing an exact occurrence time from first detection.

Concurrent competing events and mechanism bridges explain why the transition formed. Unresolved causes do not invalidate direct state material already available. Conversely, an established event does not prove any explanatory story. Separating description from explanation preserves both known and unresolved aspects.

GE may arise from a subject's action or emergence without a unified generative subject. Multiple actors following local rules do not guarantee a subject designed the overall state; an event itself does not “intend” or “choose.” GS existence requires separate checking and cannot be invented through GE's definition.

distinctions.leftText: Prior and subsequent states are checkable under a consistent contract.
distinctions.rightText: Further explains channels and competing factors.

distinctions.leftText: The time or interval in which state actually changed.
distinctions.rightText: When the observer learned of it, possibly later.

distinctions.leftText: May arise from local interactions.
distinctions.rightText: Needs separate subject and plan evidence, not backward inference from the whole.

boundaries: Unclear causation cannot cancel an established event, and an established event cannot endorse a specified cause.
Align changed dimensions, definitions, or scope first; otherwise apparent change may not be the same event.
Retain an occurrence interval when temporal resolution is insufficient; invent no exact time.
questions: With 9 items at time 0 and 12 at time 2, may one assert entry into sufficiency at time 1?
What comes first when measurement definitions change?
Does an observed overall pattern prove a unified generator exists?
argumentSteps: Fix state variables, measurement units, rules, and comparison scope.
Obtain prior and subsequent states, distinguishing actual event, detection, and announcement times.
Judge transition under the predetermined criterion. Report an interval when that is all the material supports.
Explanations of cause separately examine concurrent events, channels, and alternative mechanisms.
Retain the possibility of no unified generative subject; do not personify events.

teachingExamples.title: Mathematical construction: an event and measurement interval under the same threshold
teachingExamples.text: Fictional inventory counts intact items of the same type, with “sufficient” defined as n≥10. Measurements give 9 at time 0 and 12 at time 2. A transition from insufficiency to sufficiency between the observations is established. Without intermediate records, the first crossing can only be located within (0,2], not at time 1. If the second measurement also counts damaged items, restore a consistent definition before using 9→12 to establish the original criterion.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Counts are error-free, and the same object is observed at both ends. No monotone path is assumed, so multiple crossings may occur, but at least one entry from insufficiency into sufficiency occurs.
teachingExamples.boundary: Only an abstract counting model, not actual inventory observations or identification of restocking, repair, or reclassification as the cause.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: local choices produce an overall distribution
teachingExamples.text: Six fictional participants each select locations under the same declared local crowd-avoidance rule, ending in a dispersed layout. If records establish before/after layouts, GE may describe the transition. When no one proposed an overall layout objective, a tool or participant cannot be named the overall generative subject merely to complete the story.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Layouts and behaviors are stipulated. No claim is made that the rule necessarily produces a particular distribution from every initial state.
teachingExamples.boundary: Illustrates evidential roles, not an actual group's emergence mechanism.

counterexamples.text: Because the cause of inventory growth is unknown, the verified change from 9 to 12 under the same definition is denied.
counterexamples.effect: This mistakes an explanatory gap for absence of a descriptive fact.

questionAnswers.question: With 9 items at time 0 and 12 at time 2, may one assert entry into sufficiency at time 1?
questionAnswers.answer: No. Existing material locates at least one entry within (0,2] only.
questionAnswers.basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

questionAnswers.question: What comes first when measurement definitions change?
questionAnswers.answer: Align variables, units, inclusion rules, and object scope before judging an actual transition.
questionAnswers.basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

questionAnswers.question: Does an observed overall pattern prove a unified generator exists?
questionAnswers.answer: No. GS requires independent action material; subjectless emergence cannot be filled out through personification.
questionAnswers.basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

figures.alt: Prior state: same object and measurement contract, e.g. n = 9. Event interval: at least one entry into n ≥ 10, located only within (0,2]. Subsequent state: same-type intact items, e.g. n = 12. Formation causes require separate investigation of competing events and mechanism bridges; unknowns do not erase the event. GS requires separate investigation; an overall state cannot manufacture unified intention. Abstract inventory teaching diagram: under the same counting rule, entry into sufficiency within the interval is established without specifying an exact time or cause.
figures.caption: Abstract inventory teaching diagram: under the same counting rule, entry into sufficiency within the interval is established without specifying an exact time or cause.

7.2.4.title: 7.2.4 CV (uptake carrier)
7.2.4.lead: What actually takes a task up may be a person, position, procedure, or device. CV asks who or what realizes the function; performing a function cannot directly be translated into moral or legal responsibility.
explanation: Source location: Chinese source lines 1588–1591; original anchor section-7-2-4. Short quotation: “CV ≠ RS.” See the corresponding section on this page for the current original; downloaded original research excerpts retain the historical draft.

CV asks who or what actually executes, transmits, maintains, records, cares, or repairs. People, positions, procedures, facilities, and technical systems may all be carriers. Merely stating that a position or system exists does not establish actual task performance.

Material should connect task logs, resource and capacity flows, costs, rights to stop, and functional changes after replacement. Whether inputs arrive, outputs form, someone fills in during interruption, and nominal positions match actual labor all affect carrier judgments. Similar function after replacement may indicate substitutability, but actual causal effects still require comparisons of concurrent changes and compensation.

CV and RS ask different questions. Devices and procedures may execute functions without thereby becoming moral or legal subjects of responsibility. An organization, however, cannot simply be classed with equipment because it “is also a system”; institutional or legal responsibility requires checking its subject status and specific rules.

A human CV does not have an unlimited duty to continue merely because they can. Retain capacity, costs, stopping rights, support, and alternatives. Maintaining output while exhausting its bearer does not establish sustainably reliable uptake. CV identifies functional positions but cannot alone determine responsibility, sacrifice obligations, or compensation.

distinctions.leftText: A position or system is assigned responsibility in the design.
distinctions.rightText: Supported by material on execution, transmission, maintenance, and similar functions.

distinctions.leftText: A causal or operational role.
distinctions.rightText: Requires subject status and specific rules; it cannot be merged with the equipment category.

distinctions.leftText: Output is maintained within a window.

caseNotes.title: STS-114: repairers and functional equipment are different carriers
caseNotes.text: NASA's August 1, 2005 EVA2 entry records that Noguchi and Robinson removed failed CMG-1 and installed its replacement; the mission record subsequently lists four working CMGs. This section adds observation of two functional positions—repair labor and attitude-control equipment—without inferring responsibility from working equipment.

argumentSteps: Specify the task and actual output. Job titles and equipment lists are not completion records.
Trace resources, capacity, costs, stopping, and alternative paths; distinguish nominal from actual uptake.
Compare function after replacement or interruption while retaining concurrent conditions and compensation.
Check carrier function separately from subject status and specific responsibility rules.

teachingExamples.title: Mathematical construction: two carriers' capacities differ from responsibility
teachingExamples.text: A fictional task requires human verification followed by program processing, both measured in items/day. Human capacity is 4 and program capacity 10. With other conditions sufficient and no backlog loss, maximum serial output is min(4,10)=4. Upgrading the program to 20 leaves 4; raising supported human capacity to 7 gives maximum 7. Both are functional carriers. This minimum calculation determines neither who owes overtime, who has approval authority, nor who bears legal responsibility.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Capacities are fixed available ceilings. Maximum output assumes both stages are fully utilized and matched; the maximum is not treated as completed output.
teachingExamples.boundary: Shows only a capacity bottleneck, not actual job measurements or a responsibility-allocation rule.

counterexamples.text: Equipment completes a task automatically, so it is said to assume all the organization's responsibility.
counterexamples.effect: Functional execution cannot transfer or eliminate organizational responsibility established under specific rules.

questionAnswers.question: With human capacity 4 and program capacity 20, why is maximum output still 4?
questionAnswers.answer: Every item must pass both serial stages, so human capacity is the ceiling. This does not mean software upgrading has no value; it means the total-output ceiling in this model remains unchanged.
questionAnswers.basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

questionAnswers.question: Does an organizational chart showing a successor directly establish successful uptake?
questionAnswers.answer: No. Check knowledge, authority, resources, actual execution, and whether the original bearer truly exited or had their burden reduced.
questionAnswers.basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

questionAnswers.question: Does separating CV from RS mean organizations bear no responsibility?
questionAnswers.answer: No. Organizational subject status and specific responsibility rules require separate checking; organizations cannot be treated as equipment.
questionAnswers.basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

7.2.5.title: 7.2.5 RS (responsible party)
7.2.5.lead: After a problem, the easiest person to find may not be the one who decided the rules. RS requires stating “on what grounds, for what, and to what extent responsibility is borne,” rather than making one visible position absorb every accusation.
explanation: Source location: Chinese source lines 1592–1595; original anchor section-7-2-5. Short quotation translated from Chinese: “Low-authority implementers must not become default primary bearers of responsibility merely because they are most visible.” See the corresponding section on this page for the current original; downloaded original research excerpts retain the historical draft.

RS asks who bears which responsibility, for what, and on what basis. Register behavioral, decision, authorization, supervisory, benefit-related, and remedial responsibilities separately. A person or organization may have several or only some of them. Parallel registration assumes neither identical grounds for all six nor a necessary single overall responsible party.

Knowledge, control, scope, period, appeal, and remedies are key material. State the rule or norm invoked, what could be known, what could actually be controlled, which duties applied when, and how judgments can be challenged and corrected. The object of responsibility cannot merely be “something went wrong,” nor its period extended indefinitely backward or forward.

Visibility, uptake, and bearing consequences are insufficient grounds for RS. Frontline personnel may execute rules without authority to change them, and those bearing costs need not have caused them. Benefit is a responsibility-related connection to examine, not automatic comprehensive moral or legal responsibility for anyone who benefits.

Independence from clues such as visibility means responsibility grounds must directly answer the responsibility question, not that every document must originate in statistically independent data. A specific responsibility may require both process facts and normative grounds; accurate facts do not remove normative argument and appeal.

Identifying RS does not itself authorize punishment, public accusation, resource deductions, or compulsory remedies. One may identify duty positions requiring review, evidential gaps, and reasons, but actual attribution and disposition still need relevant norms, authority, and procedures. Distinguish equipment's functional position from an organization's institutional subject status; automation cannot excuse disappearing responsibility.

distinctions.leftText: The position performing an action or completing work.
distinctions.rightText: May involve another decision-maker and different responsibility grounds.

distinctions.leftText: Bears a consequence.
distinctions.rightText: Requires specific causal and normative grounds, not backward inference.

distinctions.leftText: Explains potentially applicable duties and material.
distinctions.rightText: Additionally requires authority, procedures, and conditions for redress.

boundaries: Insufficient attribution material does not prove no one is responsible, and existing harm does not disappear.
Low-authority implementers are not necessarily exempt, but visibility alone cannot make them default primary bearers of responsibility.
Benefit, position, and control may be relevant material, each still requiring a responsibility basis rather than becoming an automatic score.
questions: Does low authority necessarily mean no responsibility?

argumentSteps: Separate six questions: behavior, decision, authorization, supervision, benefit, and remedy.

Check implementation, benefit, and cost positions separately; no one position automatically establishes primary responsibility.
Retain counterevidence, appeal, and remedy paths. Missing evidence differs from a conclusion of exemption.
Separate analysis from actual disposition. The name RS does not automatically create punitive authority.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: a duties matrix is more useful than “who appears in public”
teachingExamples.text: Fictional rules specify that A is responsible for allocation decisions, B for identity checks during execution, and institution C for supplemental payment after authorized error correction. A approves the allocation, B operates at the service counter according to that allocation, D receives resources, and E bears waiting costs. These assumptions permit separate examination of A's decision, B's checks, and C's supplemental payment. B's being the only person visible cannot transfer every other duty to B; D's benefit or E's loss alone cannot make either fully responsible. If B independently changed the allocation, that new fact requires separate examination; “low permission” cannot preemptively exempt all conduct from judgment.
teachingExamples.assumptions: The rules and people are entirely fictional. Responsibility rests only on this lesson's explicit assumptions, not purported current law. Scope is limited to allocation, identity checks, and supplemental payment in this instance.
teachingExamples.boundary: No responsibility of actual people or institutions is adjudicated; actual jurisdictions, contracts, and procedures require their own verification.

counterexamples.text: The front desk receives the most complaints, so its staff are primarily responsible for every institutional error.
counterexamples.effect: Visibility in complaints cannot replace grounds concerning decisions, authorization, control, and oversight.

counterexamples.text: Responsibility material is insufficient, so costs that actually occurred may go unrecorded.
counterexamples.effect: Unresolved attribution and factual consequences are different questions.

questionAnswers.question: Does low authority necessarily mean no responsibility?
questionAnswers.answer: No. Actual conduct, knowledge, control, and specific rules still matter, but visibility cannot directly establish primary responsibility.

questionAnswers.question: If D benefits and E suffers harm, can those facts alone assign responsibility to both?
questionAnswers.answer: No. Benefit and cost positions must be recorded, while responsibility types and grounds require separate checking.
questionAnswers.basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

questionAnswers.question: Does explaining who should bear remedial responsibility already authorize deductions?
questionAnswers.answer: No. Actual measures require separate normative, permission, and operational-procedure checks.

The six questions may involve different or overlapping parties. This diagram neither automatically assigns responsibility nor authorizes any actual action.

7.2.6.title: 7.2.6 IS (Source of Destabilization)
7.2.6.lead: The first person to report a problem may merely be the first to see it. IS traces where disturbances enter or accumulate; reporting positions, conspicuous identities, and dissent itself cannot serve as proof of a source.
explanation: Chinese source location: lines 1596–1599; original anchor: section-7-2-6; short quotation, translated from the Chinese: “A source's existence does not imply malice, a mechanism, or full responsibility.” See the corresponding section on this page for the current original text; the downloaded original research excerpt preserves the historical manuscript.

IS asks where a disturbance enters or accumulates. Material includes its first appearance or accumulation position, entry point, temporal order, exposure differences, and alternative sources. Incoming shocks and gradual internal accumulation may both matter; one should not search only for an external “bad actor.”

First distinguish the actual origin, earliest recorded position, and first public reporting position. Incomplete log coverage, measurement delay, or non-disclosure for protection may make the earliest visible position later than or different from the actual origin. Existing early records provide clues; uncovered areas remain unknown.

Exposure differences help examine sources: did the same input reach affected and unaffected positions, does entry order match state changes, and are there other sources? Proximity to the scene, temporal co-occurrence, or group membership cannot replace these checks.

Confirming a source does not identify a mechanism, malice, or full responsibility. One input may produce consequences through different mechanisms; disturbances may occur without malice, and malice requires independent material. A dissenter presenting counterevidence may increase a problem's visibility; that does not permit registering the dissenter's identity as IS.

distinctions.leftText: Where the earliest visible public material comes from.
distinctions.rightText: Where a disturbance enters or forms; it need not be the same position.

distinctions.leftText: Determines an input or accumulation position.
distinctions.rightText: Determines how it changes subsequent states.

distinctions.leftText: Expressing or reporting a problem.
distinctions.rightText: Requires entry and exposure evidence; it cannot follow from identity.

boundaries: The earliest available log does not guarantee coverage of the actual earliest event; missingness must be explicit.
A source may be a shared input or internal accumulation, without a unified intention.
A source judgment is neither a malice judgment nor a complete determination of responsibility.
questions: If the earliest record is at C, may C be recorded as the actual origin?
If an error is confirmed to have entered at A, does this prove someone there created it deliberately?
Can gradually increasing internal backlog become an IS question?
argumentSteps: Define the disturbance and observation window before choosing someone to blame.
Separate actual entry, recording, and reporting times, explaining visibility at each position.
Trace first appearance and accumulation positions, exposure paths, and alternative sources.
After a source gains bounded support, mechanisms, intentions, and responsibility still require separate judgments.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: an error enters at A but is reported at C
teachingExamples.text: A fictional system's complete logs show that input port A receives erroneous data at time 0, it reaches B at time 1 and C at time 2, and C's duty operator reports it at time 3. Under the construction's complete-coverage assumption, A is the known entry point and C the reporting position. If logs for times 0–1 are missing, only the error's presence at C and later report can be confirmed; A cannot still be recorded as an established entry point.
teachingExamples.assumptions: A conditional comparison of two log configurations. Transmission facts are verified by assumption in the complete version; this does not represent a real system.
teachingExamples.boundary: The entry point determines neither the inputter's malice nor full responsibility, and temporal order alone is not claimed sufficient to prove actual transmission.

counterexamples.text: A complaint makes a problem visible, so the complainant is its source of destabilization.
counterexamples.effect: Confuses increased visibility with entry of a disturbance and bypasses direct source material.

questionAnswers.question: If the earliest record is at C, may C be recorded as the actual origin?
questionAnswers.answer: Not necessarily. First check earlier coverage, delays, and alternative entry points. If material reaches only C, retain the source gap.
questionAnswers.basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

questionAnswers.question: If an error is confirmed to have entered at A, does this prove someone there created it deliberately?
questionAnswers.answer: No. Source, intentions, mechanism, and responsibility each still require material.
questionAnswers.basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

questionAnswers.question: Can gradually increasing internal backlog become an IS question?
questionAnswers.answer: Yes. IS includes accumulation positions, not only external shocks.

7.2.7.title: 7.2.7 IM (Mechanism of Destabilization)
7.2.7.lead: “It is all that group's fault” does not explain how events occurred. IM specifies inputs, mediators, temporal order, state changes, and possible failures segment by segment, making a mechanism supportable or refutable by material.
explanation: Chinese source location: lines 1600–1603; original anchor: section-7-2-7; short quotation, translated from the Chinese: “A mechanism story must not replace causal evidence either.” See the corresponding section on this page for the current original text; the downloaded original research excerpt preserves the historical manuscript.

IM asks through what causal path a disturbance changes states, boundaries, feedback, rhythm, or orientation. A mechanism is neither a person's name nor an overall verdict such as “poor management”; it requires identifiable operations, constraints, and mediating processes.

Each segment should specify mediators, temporal order, bridging evidence, failure conditions, and competing mechanisms. If resource delay is said to cause backlog and then slower feedback processing, separately check when resources arrive, when processing volume changes, and how backlog enters feedback. Drawing three lines cannot replace this material.

Specific human actions may participate in a mechanism, but people, groups, or dissenters themselves must not directly be named as mechanisms. One may test how a particular refusal, rule change, or information blockage acts through a specified channel; identity or disagreement cannot count as a completed causal account.

The same appearance may arise from different mechanisms: backlog can reflect increased arrivals, reduced available capacity, or changed statistical definitions. Timing and variable records help distinguish them, but causal explanations still require proportionate comparisons and counterexamples. Whole-chain effects also require checking continuation in the same cases, capacity, and terminal outcomes; average effects of segments cannot directly be combined into the complete effect.

distinctions.rightText: Channels, comparisons, and failure conditions checkable segment by segment.

distinctions.leftText: An event that may enter a causal path.

distinctions.rightText: Substituting identity for an effect-producing process; prohibited here.

distinctions.leftText: A bounded result within a specified window.

teachingExamples.title: Mathematical construction: two ways of generating backlog
teachingExamples.text: Let end-of-day backlog Bₜ₊₁=max(0,Bₜ+aₜ−cₜ). Each round's arrivals first enter the queue, nonempty tasks are processed fully within capacity, with no discards or priority differences. With B₀=0, daily arrivals a=10 and capacity c=8 give B₁=2, B₂=4, B₃=6. Changing to a=12 and c=10 gives the same sequence. Thus backlog alone cannot distinguish “insufficient original capacity” from “more input”; arrival and actually available capacity records are needed. Changing c to 10 while retaining a=10 keeps backlog at 0 in the model, but this is only a conditional derivation under this equation.
teachingExamples.assumptions: All values are constructed. Work conservation, synchronous daily steps, no discards, and fixed rules are explicit; capacity is what can actually be used in the current round.
teachingExamples.boundary: This does not claim that every actual organization's backlog obeys this equation; eliminating backlog in a model cannot directly authorize greater employee workloads.

counterexamples.text: There is backlog and someone publicly opposes the plan, so “the dissenter” is designated the backlog mechanism.
counterexamples.effect: Identity and co-occurrence supply no evidence of arrivals, capacity, rules, or channels.

counterexamples.text: Two different systems both have backlog sequences 2,4,6, so their causes are declared identical.
counterexamples.effect: The two input/capacity combinations refute this unique identification.

questionAnswers.question: Why is the same sequence 2,4,6 insufficient to identify IM?
questionAnswers.answer: Different arrival/capacity combinations give identical outcomes; material on mediators and competing mechanisms is needed.
questionAnswers.basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

questionAnswers.question: May we study how a particular person's specific action produces an effect?
questionAnswers.answer: Yes, with actions, context, and channels located; a person's or group's name cannot alone replace a mechanism.

questionAnswers.question: If two local segments each have an average effect, may we multiply them directly to obtain the whole chain?
questionAnswers.answer: No. Check same-case correspondence, shared support, joint responses, timing, capacity, and endpoints; see §7.3.6 on whole-chain limits.

7.2.8.title: 7.2.8 IB (Behavior of Destabilization)
7.2.8.lead: An action in a log may be a real fact without explaining why it occurred. Failure to see an action also need not mean no action occurred. IB preserves observational records while preventing direct leaps from behavior to source, mechanism, malice, and responsibility.
explanation: Chinese source location: lines 1604–1609; original anchor: section-7-2-8; short quotation, translated from the Chinese: “Silence and absence must also distinguish nonoccurrence, unobservability, and concealment for protection.” See the corresponding section on this page for the current original text; the downloaded original research excerpt preserves the historical manuscript.

IB asks which actions, omissions, or outputs were actually observed. Original records, logs, or multisource observations should preserve the subject or carrier, context, scale, and time window. “Someone did not respond” is not even a clear behavioral statement if the object, channel, and window are missing.

Recording inaction especially requires specifying expected opportunities and observable scope. Nonoccurrence, unobservability, concealment for protection, and noncollection must not all be coded 0. A person's silence may mean only no public expression; it does not imply consent, no objections, or no private action. Safety boundaries do not disappear because a form needs completion.

Observed behavior does not automatically determine IS or IM, nor directly imply malice or full RS. First establish that an output actually exists, then separately examine its input source, process mechanism, and grounds of responsibility. Missing higher-level explanation should not erase behavioral facts.

IS/IM/IB is a cross-cutting typology, not merely an attachment to HV09 structural load. Within HV02 boundaries and interfaces, ask separately where a refusal signal originates, through what filtering path it travels, and what refusal output actually appears. Within HV06 the drive–uptake chain, ask where interruption enters, how it spreads, and who actually stops or changes work.

Within HV07 feedback write-back, ask separately where a problem or return enters, how it is blocked or continued, and which records and actions actually occur. Within HV08 the conditional potential field, ask about sources of changing conditions, channels affecting evidence or action, and visible expressions and behavior.

Within HV09 structural load, ask where task pressure or accumulation originates, how a gap forms, and what delays and outputs occur. Within HV10 evolutionary phases, ask about disturbance sources, mechanisms of state change, and specific actions. Every interface requires separate material for the source, mechanism, and behavior claimed. Distinguishable information from one source may be shared, but must not be counted as independent replication.

Recording IB therefore does not label someone a “destabilizer.” Observing behavior, judging channels, attributing responsibility, and acting have separate responsibilities. Dissent, refusal, exit, or non-disclosure for protection is not presumed malicious or a target for removal merely because it falls within the discussion window.

teachingExamples.title: Mathematical construction: a zero visible record has three possible states
teachingExamples.text: Let a∈{0,1} indicate whether a behavior occurs, and v∈{0,1} whether it is visible through this observation channel, with simplified record r=a·v. The result r=0 is compatible with (a,v)=(0,1), (1,0), and (0,0), so no visible record does not uniquely imply a=0. Only r=1 requires a=v=1 in this no-false-positive model. Reality may also involve missing records, misrecording, or fabricated records, requiring an additional measurement model.
teachingExamples.assumptions: The binary-visibility model is entirely constructed and initially assumes no false positives or noise; v=0 may include lawful or protective nondisclosure.
teachingExamples.boundary: This is not a privacy-investigation method and does not require forcing increased visibility to determine a; current uncertainty may be retained.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: three questions about the same rejection record
teachingExamples.text: A fictional service system has a checkable ‘application rejected’ output, which IB can record as a fact. Which rule version supplied the rejection input is an IS question; how conditions change the outcome through filtering is an IM question. If the applicant subsequently objects, that objection is another behavioral fact. The applicant cannot simply be relabeled the source or mechanism of the original rejection.
teachingExamples.assumptions: The output and objection are fictional, with no real eligibility, responsibility, or legal judgment provided.
teachingExamples.boundary: This only demonstrates question boundaries, not whether an actual rejection is justified or unjustified.

counterexamples.text: The record is r=0, so there was no action and no objection.
counterexamples.effect: Visibility 0 also produces a zero record; the inference about objection additionally crosses to a different target.

counterexamples.text: Seeing the applicant object, registering them as the system's IM of destabilization.
counterexamples.effect: Behavioral status cannot replace a specific channel and causal evidence.

Retain existing IB facts; check IS / IM / RS separately, without letting behavior settle everything. 7.3.title: 7.3 A unified interface for the eleven variables
7.3.lead: A unified interface is like a comparable set of question fields: everyone can see who is being discussed, what is asked, on what grounds, and how far judgment can go. It neither fits every person onto one scale nor certifies reality once the form is completed.
explanation: Chinese source location: lines 1610–1619; source anchor section-7-3; short quotation, translated from Chinese: ‘All eleven variables are defined as H-World interfaces.’ See the corresponding section on this page for the current source; the downloadable original research excerpt preserves the historical draft.

This section gives common interface discipline for the following eleven variables. They address the human structured world, not a universal ontology. An application first selects the conclusion it intends to make, then supplies the evidence necessary for that conclusion; irrelevant, unknown, and protected-unavailable portions each receive their own reasons. Completeness of 39 fields means every field's status can be explained, not that personal information must be obtained for all 39, and certainly not that submitting all information becomes a condition for ordinary help or lawful services.

The first group of 8 fields specifies identity and the question: id is a local identifier, qualified_id a formal namespaced identifier, and name a display name; proposition states the specific claim, scope its object and scope, claim_type the selected conclusion type, contract_role this card's role, and pause_condition the gap or risk that pauses the claim. What pauses is the corresponding judgment or operation; independently established facts and service eligibility cannot be unconditionally canceled.

The second group of 7 fields specifies inferential position: inferential_requires lists only hard prerequisites shared across levels; protocol_requires only shared methodological or normative-procedural gates; specializes lists definitional, classificatory, or normative qualifications; applies_to lists applicable objects. conditional_support_routes contains conditions added only at a particular level; allowed_inference and prohibited_leap respectively state how far inference may go and which leaps are forbidden. Content entering input_dependencies is not automatically a hard logical dependency.

The third group of 7 fields concerns scale and transfer: scale_profile records the nine-axis profile; effective_object specifies the actual object referred to by the variable; scale_invariants states what must remain across scale changes, required_scale_additions what must be added, and changing_semantics how meanings change. non_applicable_objects excludes inapplicable objects, while forbidden_elevation prevents unauthorized elevation of local conclusions to larger wholes. The nine axes are not merely observational resolution.

The fourth group of 9 fields concerns observation and effects: state records the current state, observables lists visible signals, and evidence lists actual grounds; input_dependencies and output_effects record inputs, outputs, and variable flows; time_window_and_lag specifies windows and lags, uncertainty errors and unresolved matters, local_exclusion_zone the scope of bounded exclusion, and affected_positions affected locations. One visible position cannot represent everyone by default; unobserved also does not mean excluded.

The fifth group of 8 fields concerns carriers and limits: carrier specifies where content is stored or executed; responsible_subject specifies to whom responsibility is attributed and on what grounds; normative_status retains normative standing, judgment_ceiling limits judgment strength, and action_ceiling limits authority to act. counterexamples supplies evidence that could change judgments, appeal preserves avenues of appeal, and rollback preserves withdrawal arrangements. Proximity in the fields does not make carrier and responsible_subject synonymous. The five groups total 8+7+7+9+8=39.

Each conditional route must additionally list 7 items in full: route_id identifies the route, claim_level specifies its conclusion level, and when specifies applicability; additional_inferential_requires and additional_protocol_requires respectively add formal prerequisites and methodological gates; allowed_conclusion and result_ceiling state permitted conclusions and their limits. One cannot combine route A's convenient entry requirements with route B's higher ceiling into an unregistered third route. A candidate description may hold while an advanced mechanism remains unresolved; advanced conclusions also cannot follow merely from filling candidate fields.

G/H instances, HV, and CM conditional mechanisms are inferential prerequisites; they must not be moved into protocol to reduce substantive proof requirements. Protocol fields use only E, CAUSAL, EVIDENCE, ANALOGY, SOURCE, or explicit N/O gates. H2/H3/H6 are classificatory or normative qualifications and belong in specializes, not empirical support. Formal names include human_variable:HV05, human_strong_type:CV, and scale_axis:O; organizational hierarchy O and operational procedures O1–O4 cannot be mixed as bare O. Correct identifiers aid tracing; they create no evidence. Appendix A implements these distinctions card by card, and the following eleven units develop them individually.

distinctions.leftText: Every field contains content or explicit reasons for missingness/inapplicability, with traceable references.
distinctions.rightText: The empirical conclusion in question still requires appropriate evidence.

distinctions.leftText: An interface receives some meaning or resource.
distinctions.rightText: Without this premise, the conclusion at that level cannot be made; the two are not automatically identical.

distinctions.leftText: Constrain classification or prevent normative overreach.
distinctions.rightText: Must come from specific observations and designs; qualification rules cannot replace it.

boundaries: Required evidence varies by claim; a unified interface is not an unlimited personal-information collection form.
Formal references and schema validation cannot certify reality; protected unavailability must be honestly retained.
Each route's conditions and ceilings must correspond as a whole; favorable fields cannot be selected after the fact.
The action ceiling cannot rise automatically from an established judgment; procedures and lawful service eligibility also have their own grounds.
questions: If some of the 39 fields are protected and unavailable, should the person's eligibility for help be canceled?
If input_dependencies lists HV03, does every route necessarily have a hard dependency on HV03 holding?
Why can bare O not directly enter a dependency field?
argumentSteps: First fix the proposition, object, window, scale, and conclusion level, rather than first collecting all personal information.
Check each group of the 39 fields for content or a reasoned status; distinguish content flows from formal dependencies.
Check four categories—common prerequisites, common gates, qualifications, and applicable objects—then the selected route's additional conditions.
Judge evidential support and gaps item by item; higher-level gaps do not erase established lower-level facts.
Limit conclusions and actions, retaining affected positions, appeal, and withdrawal; completing a form cannot confer authority to act.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: content inputs do not automatically become shared hard prerequisites
teachingExamples.text: A fictional uptake card receives a project's target narrative as input_dependencies. It is known that person A actually performed a task for 30 minutes, while whether the target narrative is shared by the group remains undetermined. HV05's basic action classification may retain the execution fact without waiting for an effective HV03 anchor to hold. Only a further claim that the anchor caused the outcome through uptake should select the corresponding complete-chain and causal route.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Assume the execution record genuinely supports that fact; neither identified motivation nor effectiveness of the whole chain is claimed.
teachingExamples.boundary: This illustrates only field and conclusion responsibilities; it certifies no real uptake card.

teachingExamples.title: Counting construction: 39 fields and 7 route items are two structural levels
teachingExamples.text: Divide the 39 fields into the 5 nonoverlapping groups above, yielding 8+7+7+9+8=39. conditional_support_routes is itself one field, within which each route has 7 items. With 3 routes, the form cannot be described as 39+21 mutually independent kinds of evidence: this is a data-organization hierarchy, not a count of independent support.
teachingExamples.assumptions: The five groups only organize reading in this lesson; they do not change the source fields or card contents.
teachingExamples.boundary: Counting does not establish that any variable applies or holds in reality.

counterexamples.text: An HV09 basic-margin record lacks G3, so no burden facts may be recorded.
counterexamples.effect: This incorrectly imposes a higher-level historical-increment prerequisite on lower-level direct description.

counterexamples.text: Move G2 into protocol, and all that is needed is ‘procedure followed.’
counterexamples.effect: Moving fields does not cancel a G2 instance's substantive empirical responsibilities.

questionAnswers.question: If some of the 39 fields are protected and unavailable, should the person's eligibility for help be canceled?
questionAnswers.answer: No. The interface should record gaps according to necessity and protective boundaries; missing material does not automatically cancel lawful services or eligibility to be heard.

questionAnswers.answer: Not necessarily. Formal common dependencies and each route have their own explicit registrations; content flow does not replace them.

7.3.1.title: 7.3.1 HV01 Structural domain
7.3.1.lead: After calling something “a team,” ask what this grouping actually helps us understand. HV01 permits first specifying who the object is, then separately testing whether grouping genuinely adds predictive or extrapolative value.
explanation: Source location: Chinese source lines 1620–1625; source anchor section-7-3-1; brief quotation translated from Chinese: “Naming does not create a community.” See the corresponding section on this page for the current source; the downloadable original research extract preserves the historical draft.

D0 gives a candidate object's complete contract, including boundaries, identity criterion K, states, and applicable window. K is only the identity criterion, not the whole contract. D0 makes the object discussable without automatically establishing an effective structural domain supported by G1 gain. Appendix A1's common formal premise is D0; its common gates are E1, EVIDENCE, and SOURCE.

The R0 candidate-object route preserves traceable boundaries, time windows, uncertainty, member entry/exit, differences in relations and constraints, common problems, and coexistence of institutional rules. Robustness of grouping gain after changes in grouping rules is also material to check. R0 can supply candidate-object references to HV02–HV11; it neither suspends every object-existence claim nor defaults group will to fact.

The R1 bounded effective-structural-domain route adds a preregistered G1-instance and E4. Match the comparison to N0 and examine out-of-sample or extrapolative gain from the candidate grouping under a preselected outcome, model class, sample or extrapolation unit, and threshold. This is gain within that question, model, and scope; it cannot become innate group unity across every scale and task.

Failure to pass positive G1 does not automatically support the zero conclusion “no structure exists,” still less negate legally constituted organizations, actual relations, or service populations independently established by documents and observation. Bounded exclusion also requires sensitivity, equivalence ranges, and other corresponding zero-result conditions. A shared situation may genuinely exist; shared member will remains a separate evidential question.

HV01's R1 registers G1 grouping gain on the preselected outcome and its robustness to boundary perturbations. R0 candidate references and independently supported object facts may continue serving other variables; withdrawing R1 does not automatically withdraw membership, legal identity, or affected positions. Report the two routes in separate columns so “untested” is not read as “these people do not exist.”

argumentSteps: First use D0 to specify the candidate object, K, window, boundaries, and unresolved positions.
Preserve organizational or relational facts supported by independent documents and observation.
Check matched N0 and the prior comparison contract only when the question concerns a structural domain supported by G1 gain.
Register bounded support, rejection, or unresolved status according to testing, without jumping from failure of a positive gate to global nonexistence.
Provide later HV interfaces with bounded object references, not untested unified will.

teachingExamples.title: Mathematical construction: grouping gain misses the threshold while roster facts may hold
teachingExamples.text: A fictional task predefines comparison using mean loss on the same held-out sample. Matched N0 has loss 10; the grouping model has loss 9; only a reduction greater than 2 passes the positive threshold. The actual decrease, 10−9=1, fails. If a verifiable roster independently establishes that these people attended the same course, this prediction comparison does not negate that fact. Nor does 1 failing to reach 2 establish that true gain is exactly 0.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Comparison objects, outcomes, samples, and error definitions are fixed for both models. Numbers are a teaching construction with no fabricated statistical significance.
teachingExamples.boundary: Judges only the given threshold; it cannot declare a real group unorganized or produce a global zero conclusion.

counterexamples.text: A school roster is official, so this grouping must add predictive gain for every outcome.
counterexamples.effect: Document existence and predictive gain have different evidential responsibilities.

questionAnswers.question: Why does shared risk not establish shared will?
questionAnswers.answer: Risk describes external circumstances; will concerns members' expression, representativeness, and action, requiring separate evidence.

7.3.2.title: 7.3.2 HV02 Boundaries and interfaces
7.3.2.lead: Permission to enter often differs from actually reaching, obtaining, and exiting. HV02 examines both eligibility on paper and actual channels, avoiding declarations of universal accessibility based only on the sign above the door.
explanation: Source location: Chinese source lines 1626–1629; source anchor section-7-3-2; brief quotation translated from Chinese: “formal–actual boundary differences.” See the corresponding section on this page for the current source; the downloadable original research extract preserves the historical draft.

A boundary is not merely a circle drawn around something, but an arrangement selecting among flows of resources, information, rights, or responsibilities. Observe membership, entry and exit, cross-boundary flows, gatekeeping nodes, refusal reasons, and whether formal and actual boundaries align. Boundaries for different flows may not coincide.

Appendix A2's common inferential premise is the HV01 object interface; basic R0 does not mandate G1 or G2. Even without tested grouping gain, one can honestly register who is eligible, receives resources, cannot understand a notice, or encounters exit barriers. Registering unknowns and risks is not identification of discrimination or another particular causal mechanism.

R1 boundary-selection effects additionally require a G2-instance, CAUSAL, and E4, specifying the channel, window, and position where selectivity occurs and addressing appropriate alternatives. Separate eligibility differences, actual resource differences, and their causal sources; headcount differences cannot establish a gatekeeper's motives.

Local members, formal representatives, and highly visible positions cannot speak for everyone affected. Excluded people, those who exited, and those indirectly bearing costs may also fall within scope. Being affected does not automatically give someone all decision-making authority; specific authorization must still match action, object, window, and conditions.

distinctions.leftText: Permitted to enter under the rules.
distinctions.rightText: Able to use the relevant resource or entrance within the required window.

distinctions.leftText: Observed different outcomes at two positions.
distinctions.rightText: A specified channel causes the difference, requiring separate testing.

distinctions.leftText: Has a particular source and scope of representation.
distinctions.rightText: May also include positions outside the boundary or with low visibility.

boundaries: Actual nonuse may have multiple causes and cannot directly mean refusal, no need, or discrimination.
One admission does not guarantee sustained resources or safe exit.
A risk inventory may remain while stronger mechanisms are unresolved, preventing specific barriers from being erased because mechanism evidence is missing.
questions: If A contains 4 people and B contains 2, can a 50% causal exclusion rate from the same gate be calculated?
Does formal representation naturally cover people bearing costs outside the boundary?
Can entry rules and actual flows be recorded without G1 support?

caseLinks.title: Cash and Counseling: assignment to a program opportunity versus actual allowances

caseNotes.title: Cash and Counseling: assignment to a program opportunity versus actual allowances
caseNotes.text: The abstract of Carlson and colleagues' 2007 paper reports random assignment of volunteers in three states to a program option or usual services, compared using telephone interviews at nine months. The authors note that fewer elderly Florida participants actually received an allowance, and effects were smaller for that group. This section uses it to distinguish an opportunity to participate from actual allowance receipt.
caseNotes.sourceLabel: Carlson et al., Health Services Research, 2007
caseNotes.sourceLocator: Abstract：Study design、Data collection、Principal findings
caseNotes.boundary: Only the original abstract was checked; full-text methods were not independently reviewed. Nonreceipt is not all attributed to one gate, group differences do not identify a single mechanism, and this framework's G2 eligibility is not retrospectively awarded.

argumentSteps: First fix the object, resource or rights flow, and time window.
Separately register nominal eligibility, actual access, gatekeeping, and refusal material, retaining uncontacted positions.
The basic inventory stops at observable differences; add a qualified causal route only for a selective-effect claim.
Check who is not covered by current member or representative records.
Explain actual accessibility and lawful permission separately.

teachingExamples.title: Set construction: eligibility, resource receipt, and affected people differ
teachingExamples.text: Within a fictional window, eligibility set A={a,b,c,d}, receipt set B={a,c}, and affected people additionally include e, who helps d without payment. A∖B={b,d} warrants checking each reason, but the set difference itself does not show that both faced the same exclusion gate. Interviewing only B omits the two nonrecipients and e's costs.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Fictional sets with eligibility and receipt records assumed verifiable; actual reasons for nonreceipt remain unknown.
teachingExamples.boundary: Set difference cannot identify motives, all causes, or current rights eligibility.

counterexamples.text: Only recipients report satisfaction, so everyone eligible can use the service smoothly.
counterexamples.effect: A sample selected from users cannot cover entry barriers facing nonrecipients.

questionAnswers.question: If A contains 4 people and B contains 2, can a 50% causal exclusion rate from the same gate be calculated?
questionAnswers.answer: No. This fictional window's nonreceipt share is 2/4, but causes and counterfactuals are unidentified.
questionAnswers.basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

questionAnswers.question: Does formal representation naturally cover people bearing costs outside the boundary?
questionAnswers.answer: Not automatically; check the scope of representation and omitted positions.
questionAnswers.basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

questionAnswers.question: Can entry rules and actual flows be recorded without G1 support?
questionAnswers.answer: Yes. The basic route uses HV01's candidate interface; G1 is not a hard premise.
questionAnswers.basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

A, B, and personal labels are teaching sets; the real case supports only separating program opportunity from actual allowances.
