12.5.title: 12.5 Calibration and Evaluation
12.5.lead: Evaluation first asks what is evaluated, for which population, response regime, and horizon. A score answers a specified prediction question, not additionally how many outcomes action saved or who may act.
explanation: Source location: Chinese source lines 2660–2688; source anchor section-12-5; short quotation translated from Chinese: ‘Do not fill missing labels with zero.’ See the corresponding section on this page for the current original text; the downloadable original research excerpt retains the historical draft.

Foresight capability comes from preregistration, comparable outcomes, and continuing comparison, not fluent retrospective explanation. Freeze original targets, horizons, success rules, and information cutoffs. A single case can be scored but cannot certify long-term calibration. Outcome-material formation, missingness, and entry/exit also form evaluation conditions.

Measures depend on the task: probability forecasts may use Brier scores, log loss, calibration curves, and resolution; prediction intervals also need coverage and width. Rankings use predetermined ranking measures, event detection precision/recall or proportionate domain measures, and timing predictions window coverage and lead time. An attractive number cannot replace the originally relevant target.

This guide uses the binary single-event Brier convention L=(p−y)², lower being better; log loss uses natural logarithms, L=−[y ln p+(1−y)ln(1−p)], with infinite loss for probabilities 0 or 1 facing opposite labels. The original multiclass-vector form may differ by a constant factor from this convention; align definitions across reports first. Unsupported probabilities should not be invented just to use a measure.

Calibration asks whether long-run probabilities correspond to observed proportions among comparable forecasts; resolution asks whether objects of differing risk can be distinguished. Reporting one population rate for everyone may be overall calibrated yet have no discriminatory resolution. Chance bin agreement in finite samples does not establish future calibration; sample size, uncertainty, binning, and applicability also matter.

Each of the original’s six evaluation dimensions has a corrective direction. Failed calibration may change expression or downgrade probabilities; weak resolution may remove unhelpful variables or return to baseline; poor coverage may revise intervals or mechanism clocks; no baseline gain stops the complex model’s gain claim; instability across times/locations narrows the domain or retires the model; recurrent underestimation or false alarms at specific positions require affected-party review, remedies, and stronger protection. Wider intervals may improve coverage while losing usefulness; do not optimize one number alone.

Use determines error costs and required reports. Observation reminders and coercive measures may share a score but impose different false-alarm burdens; low-probability high-harm tasks cannot report overall accuracy alone. Show errors by burden-bearing position, population, and phase so averages do not hide sustained false denials, delays, or misses. Excellent measures prove neither correct mechanisms nor normative legitimacy.

Published forecasts may affect action, which may alter actual events; specify the response regime. Preserve reach, actual execution, entry/exit, data formation, and institutional-change records. For targets defined as actual events under the current response regime, score actual labels normally. ‘The model affected reality’ cannot cancel a valid score, nor must every prediction evaluation be converted into intervention-effect research.

Three parallel questions do not replace one another: prediction performance for a frozen target, using comparable labels for loss/classification/coverage; how publication or action changed outcomes, requiring proportionate causal comparison; and appropriateness of prediction/response, requiring explicit norms, protection, costs, distribution, and authority. ‘No event observed’ alone proves neither false alarm nor successful protection; return to target, label, and response definitions.

Specifically, if the preregistered target is the actual event under the current response regime, p=0.8 with complete endpoint label y=0 gives Brier=0.64; with a prior threshold 0.5, this target’s false positive may also be recorded. The calculation says nothing about what would happen without action. If monitoring is offline and y unknown, do not substitute 0. Complete labels only for service recipients directly support only that group, not labels for unreached, rejected, or exited people.

After institutional change, first ask whether the question remains the same. With unchanged targets, report performance changes and comparability limits honestly; a target under a different regime or population needs new registration, preserving old predictions and scores. Do not post hoc change ‘will occur under the current regime’ to ‘would occur without response’ to rescue an erroneous prediction.

teachingExamples.title: Mathematical construction: why Brier prefers true probability within a fixed generative model
teachingExamples.text: Let Y be Bernoulli with parameter q and prediction p. Expected loss q(1−p)²+(1−q)p²=p²−2pq+q=(p−q)²+q(1−q). The second term is independent of p; the first is nonnegative and zero only at p=q, so expectation is minimized at p=q. This algebraic proof within a specified generative model does not infer true model parameters backward from one low score.
teachingExamples.assumptions: One fixed target and distribution, p,q∈[0,1]; mathematics only, no actual trial.
teachingExamples.boundary: Regime changes, selective labels, or mismatched targets prevent direct reuse of one q; this property certifies neither causal explanations nor action authority.

teachingExamples.title: Mathematical construction: bin calibration can match while resolution differs
teachingExamples.text: Construct 20 complete labels: 2 of 10 low-risk items and 8 of 10 high-risk items are 1. The model predicts 0.2 and 0.8 respectively. Each group’s Brier sum is 2×0.8²+8×0.2²=1.6, giving overall mean 3.2/20=0.16. A baseline predicts 0.5 for all; 10 of 20 events match 0.5 overall, but each loss is 0.25 and risks are not distinguished. This finite construction only illustrates bin frequencies versus resolution.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Labels, groups, and probabilities are stipulated; no actual fitting, calibration sample, or independent test.
teachingExamples.boundary: Exact matching over 20 items is not long-term calibration; groups must be predetermined and evaluation labels must not select models retrospectively.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: 0.64 is calculable, how much was prevented is not
teachingExamples.text: A fictional warning contract explicitly predicts events under the current response regime, registering p=0.8, threshold 0.5, and complete endpoint label y=0. Brier=(0.8−0)²=0.64 and log loss −ln0.2≈1.609; predicted positive and actually negative permits this target’s false positive. If action occurred and observed Y(action)=0, Y(no action) may be 0 or 1: the former means occurrence was unchanged, the latter one event prevented. The current observation cannot distinguish these two constructed worlds.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Pure teaching construction; potential outcomes illustrate identification boundaries, with no actual action or randomized trial.
teachingExamples.boundary: If monitoring was offline and y unavailable, this calculation fails; if the original target was not an event under current response, evaluate under its original contract rather than changing labels to fit the formula.

counterexamples.text: No event followed the warning, so it must have been a false alarm.

counterexamples.text: The warning triggered a response, so erroneous predictions should never be scored.
counterexamples.effect: A frozen target with complete labels remains scoreable; identify response effects separately.

counterexamples.text: Twenty perfectly matching bin frequencies prove permanent calibration.
counterexamples.effect: A finite construction establishes only this sample’s relation; long-term, subgroup, and transfer properties still need testing.

counterexamples.text: Observing only recipients’ outcomes permits reporting the same accuracy for all applicants.
counterexamples.effect: Without nonrecipients’ labels or valid identification grounds, direct generalization fails.

questionAnswers.question: Why does p=0.8,y=0 give loss 0.64 rather than 0.2?
questionAnswers.answer: This guide’s binary Brier squares probability error: (0.8−0)²=0.64; 0.2 is the predicted probability of nonoccurrence.

questionAnswers.question: Which two causal situations are both compatible with no event?
questionAnswers.answer: Either the event would not have occurred anyway, or it would have occurred but response prevented it. A zero after action alone cannot distinguish them.

12.6.title: 12.6 Early signals, contrary signals, and trigger points
12.6.lead: Useful lead time runs through completion of protection, not merely appearance of an alarm on a screen. Signals trigger review; they cannot replace path explanation, normative judgment, or authority to act.
explanation: Source location: Chinese source lines 2689–2696; original anchor section-12-6. Short quotation translated from Chinese: “Early algorithmic detection does not guarantee that the last affected person can receive protection before harm.” See the corresponding section on this page for the current original; downloaded original research excerpts retain the historical draft.

Early signals should precede outcomes through the discussed path's mechanism and have observable definitions. For a backlog path, an early change might be arrivals persistently exceeding processing, not a smaller number restating the final backlog in advance. Register observation position, definition, window, and relationship to the path. Without those bridges, any preceding phenomenon could retrospectively be packaged as a precursor.

Contrary signals concern failure of key conditions or support for competing paths. They need not prove the final outcome impossible; they weaken the current path's grounds. Register both signal types before outcomes, specifying which records count as observation and which reflect missing monitoring. Searching only for support removes foresight's possibility of failure.

Trigger points connect observation to review of object identity, path conditions, probability expression, norms, and authorization. A detected signal does not automatically permit action. If an explicitly lawful preauthorization procedure exists, act within its conditions and limits; this section's abstract rule cannot create authority by itself.

High-risk veto triggers should be explicit beforehand: a breached protection floor, key affected people unable to exit, distorted data sources, deteriorating calibration, and so forth. Applicable rules require suspension or veto of the corresponding option and protection review, not merely a slight confidence reduction while continuing unchanged. They also need not stop every task unrelated to the defect.

The clock ends at completed action or effective protection. Detection, verification, issuance, reach, understanding, funding or allocation, transfer, and onset may each take time, differently across positions. Average reach cannot establish completion for the last or hardest-to-reach person. Parallel stages need dependency-based critical-path calculations; only serial delays add directly. Retain unknown delays as unknowns or grounded intervals.

Algorithmic lead time is hazard time minus detection time. Actual protection margin also subtracts time needed for downstream completion. Technical advance notice does not mean every affected person has enough time; communication, understanding, resources, and actual capability can bottleneck. Addressing bottlenecks requires more than greater predictive precision: examine endpoint conditions and protective responsibilities.

No harm after an alarm still returns to frozen targets and labels. If the target is the actual event under the current response regime, with complete labels and predetermined thresholds, an operational false positive may be registered. Whether response prevented harm needs a separate causal comparison. Unreached people and missing records cannot default to safety, and “successful protection” cannot retrospectively rescue every warning.

Three easily confused rates require numerators, denominators, population, and window. Under a fixed binary classification, operational false-positive rate FPR=FP/(FP+TN), false-alarm fraction among alerts FAR=FP/(TP+FP), and false-negative rate FNR=FN/(TP+FN). Names vary across domains; formulas matter more than abbreviations. A zero denominator makes the rate undefined, not zero. Precision TP/(TP+FP) and recall TP/(TP+FN) may be reported separately and must not be interchanged.

caseNotes.text: WMO's 2023 overview of the Early Warnings for All action plan lists four pillars: risk knowledge, monitoring and forecasting, warning dissemination and communication, and preparedness and response capability. This public design retains dissemination and response as separate areas of development, reminding readers that completed detection is not completed end-to-end protection.

argumentSteps: First explain why the path generates the preceding change, registering observable signals and contrary evidence.
Fix thresholds, windows, missing-data handling, and veto triggers before outcomes.
Observation triggers review, not automatic action. Check object, path, expression, norms, and authority individually.
End the clock at completable protection; check critical paths and resources for every bearing position.
Compute operational metrics under frozen targets and report denominators separately. Identify prevented-harm effects independently.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: early and contrary signals must connect to mechanisms
teachingExamples.text: A fictional queue starts with backlog 6. Over the next two hours, arrivals are 2/hour and processing 1/hour, giving backlogs 7 then 8. Preregister an early signal of complete first-hour records showing 2 arrivals and 1 completion, and a contrary signal of second-hour evidence that capacity rose to 3 and 3 were actually processed. If the latter occurs, the endpoint is 6 rather than the original path's 8. Seeing only “capacity-expansion application submitted” does not establish increased actual processing.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Queue, values, and criteria are teaching constructions, with no actual system experiment.
teachingExamples.boundary: Unrecorded arrivals or false completion records invalidate signal status and require source checks. The contrary signal revises the current path, not proves backlog impossible forever.

teachingExamples.title: Mathematical construction: a 30-minute warning can still be late
teachingExamples.text: Let hazard time be minute 30 and signal detection minute 0. Fully serial verification 3, issuance 2, reach 8, understanding 4, resource allocation 6, and action onset 10 total 33 minutes, leaving protection margin 30−33=−3. Another object requires only 2 minutes for reach, totaling 27 with margin 3. Both have the same 30-minute algorithmic lead, yet timely protection cannot be claimed for both. Reducing the first object's reach to 4 gives total 29 and margin 1. This is only clock arithmetic under stated conditions.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Every time and serial dependency is artificial; no actual drill or disaster response occurred.
teachingExamples.boundary: Actual stages may overlap, delays have distributions, and hazard times have error. Check critical paths and uncertainty. This calculation is not emergency-operating advice.

teachingExamples.title: Mathematical construction: the same 18 false positives, three different denominators
teachingExamples.text: Construct 100 consistently defined, fully labeled objects: TP=8, FP=18, FN=2, TN=72. Operational false-positive rate is 18/(18+72)=20%; false-alarm fraction among alerts is 18/(8+18)=9/13≈69.23%; false-negative rate is 2/(8+2)=20%. Precision is 8/26≈30.77%, recall 8/10=80%. The two 20% values coincide only in this example; the metrics are not identical.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Threshold, target, response regime, population, and horizon are fixed. All 100 labels are constructed.
teachingExamples.boundary: If labels cover only response recipients, this complete-population confusion matrix cannot be reused directly. Classification does not identify the number saved by intervention.

counterexamples.text: The warning is issued 30 minutes early, so everyone has 30 minutes to act.
counterexamples.effect: Verification, reach, understanding, resources, and onset consume time, and endpoint capabilities differ across people.

counterexamples.text: 18 false positives necessarily mean a 20% false-alarm rate.
counterexamples.effect: Specify the denominator: this construction gives FPR 20% but approximately 69.23% false alarms among alerts.

counterexamples.text: After a contrary signal appears, only material supporting the original path continues to be collected.
counterexamples.effect: Contrary signals must substantively enter review, withdrawing the path or weakening expression when necessary.

questionAnswers.question: Why is protection for the first object 3 minutes late?
questionAnswers.answer: Total serial delay is 3+2+8+4+6+10=33; hazard occurs at 30, leaving protection margin −3.

questionAnswers.question: With FP=18, TN=72, TP=8, what are the two false-alarm measures?
questionAnswers.answer: False positives among actual negatives: 18/90=20%. Among alerts: 18/26≈69.23%.

questionAnswers.question: Do trigger points prohibit every preauthorization procedure?
questionAnswers.answer: No. Applicable existing preauthorization may be used under its conditions, but observation itself creates no new authorization.

questionAnswers.question: Does absence of harm after an alarm establish a causal warning effect?
questionAnswers.answer: Not by itself. Compare corresponding outcomes without that response; the original forecast remains evaluated under frozen targets and labels.

12.7.title: 12.7 Failure semantics for foresight
12.7.lead: Forecast honesty lies not only in cautious publication but in allowing the original record to be judged unsupported, unresolved, or unevaluable at expiry. Giving failure a vague new name does not improve accuracy.
explanation: Source location: Chinese source lines 2697–2702; original anchor section-12-7. Short quotation translated from Chinese: “Unresolved is not a compromise between success and failure.” See the corresponding section on this page for the current original; downloaded original research excerpts retain the historical draft.

This section gives five meanings for evaluation at expiry: supported, unsupported, unresolved, target invalidated, and cannot evaluate. Return to the prior contract's target, identity criterion, window, material, and success rules rather than selecting face-saving labels. Rules must also specify overlap handling beforehand; the five names are not an automatic classifier needing no explanation.

Supported means obtained material meets the original contract's support rule, only within the original scope, not proof of every mechanism, probability, or extension. Unsupported means the original support criterion did not hold; complete observations contradicting the original assertion may be explicitly reported as failure. One occurrence or nonoccurrence does not automatically validate or invalidate a probability. Use the original scoring and long-term evaluation.

Unresolved is a defined, contract-permitted state of insufficient evidence. For example, a measurement-error interval crosses the predetermined threshold, so the available complete material cannot distinguish the sides. It is not half a success or permission to extend deadlines indefinitely until favorable material arrives. Any allowed supplementary observation procedure must be registered beforehand, retaining the original expiry status.

Cannot evaluate must identify the failed prerequisite, such as permanently lost key data, an untraceable object, an inoperable horizon definition, or unclear execution records. The contract should distinguish it from unresolved: the former may mean the evaluation procedure's entry conditions are unusable, the latter that entry remains usable but evidence cannot decide. This operational distinction is this lesson's contract illustration, not an assertion that the original supplies one exhaustive, unique algorithm.

Target invalidated means the original forecast object or identity criterion actually converted. If a specified service unit is abolished and its tasks and members absorbed elsewhere, and the original contract specifies no uptake relation, the new organization's outcomes cannot masquerade as a hit for the old object. Object change needs material; unfavorable results cannot declare identity change.

Changing targets, horizons, or circle scope after outcomes, or merging competing paths into “something happened a little,” cannot retain the original foresight's success eligibility. Acknowledge the original result and create a version for a new question, object, or conditions. Old registration, evidence, and scores remain, with traceable revision reasons.

Failure semantics is a correction interface, not evasive language. Unresolved specifies missing distinguishing material; cannot evaluate explains why evaluation cannot run; target invalidated demonstrates identity conversion and states continuing monitoring and remedial responsibilities. Excluding difficult objects en masse cannot improve claimed hit rates. Summaries should show counts for all statuses, total original registrations, and the evaluable subset, avoiding selective denominators.

distinctions.leftText: Contract-defined evidence insufficiency; the answer remains unknown.
distinctions.rightText: Converting unknowns into hits without a definition distorts results.

distinctions.leftText: Required procedural, material, or object conditions cannot be met.
distinctions.rightText: Insufficient material cannot become positive evidence.

distinctions.leftText: Material supports conversion of object or identity criterion.
distinctions.rightText: Moving forecast scope to preserve success.

distinctions.leftText: Separately establishes targets and conditions while retaining old results.
distinctions.rightText: Backfilling new conditions into an expired old record.

distinctions.leftText: Supports a specific classification or case-specific loss.
distinctions.rightText: Requires corresponding comparable registrations and calibration evaluation.

boundaries: The five statuses are not arbitrary defensive words; judgment grounds must be reviewable.
This lesson illustrates the contract boundary between unresolved and cannot evaluate without turning it into the theory's sole necessary definition.
Object-identity conversion and data loss both need factual support; failure itself cannot establish either.
Reporting accuracy only among evaluable cases while hiding other statuses misleads about the full registration set.
questions: Why does B's valid interval [7,9] remain unresolved under this contract?
Why is destruction of logs not automatically unsupported?
May both 4/6 and 4/10 be reported for the ten items?
Are new explanations prohibited?
argumentSteps: Check target, object identity, window, material, and decision criteria under the original contract.
If material meets support rules, mark support within scope. Record complete contrary outcomes honestly as unsupported.
Mark insufficient evidence unresolved under predetermined rules; explain cannot evaluate when procedural entry is broken.
If identity converted without contractual uptake, record target invalidated rather than a false hit.
Give new explanations separate versions, retain old records, and disclose all statuses and denominators in summaries.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: five expiry records under one threshold contract
teachingExamples.text: Fictional registration: backlog B≥8 in specified unit A at the end of hour 2. The contract permits direct judgment from exact records with matching definitions; a valid error interval crossing 8 is unresolved; unrecoverable loss of core count data makes evaluation impossible; abolition of A without a succession definition invalidates the target. Five independent hypothetical cases are: complete B=9, supported; complete B=6, not supported; valid interval [7,9], unresolved; destroyed logs with no reconstruction, unable to evaluate; unit A abolished and merged without continuity of the original identity, target invalid. These are alternative cases, not five simultaneous outcomes in one run.
teachingExamples.assumptions: All objects, numbers, contract rules, and events are teaching constructions; the original prediction is a threshold assertion, not a probability statement.
teachingExamples.boundary: Actual contracts may use other explicit criteria; identity succession and credible error intervals require separate material.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: changing the deadline creates a new result, not rescue of an old prediction
teachingExamples.text: The original registered prediction is B≥8 at t=2. Complete observation B2=6 leaves it unsupported. Later B3=9 at t=3 does not let the author change the t=2 record to success by saying “it will eventually reach 8.” New information may support a new registration for t=3 or later, but its registration time must be explicit; after knowing B3=9, it cannot be presented as a prior prediction.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Times and values are constructed, with no actual queue observations.
teachingExamples.boundary: If the original contract had predicted a 2-to-3-hour window, evaluate under that original window. Here the original target is explicitly t=2 only.

teachingExamples.title: Mathematical construction: disclose status distributions instead of counting unknowns as half-success
teachingExamples.text: Suppose 10 registrations resolve: 4 supported, 2 not supported, 2 unresolved, 1 target invalid, and 1 unable to evaluate. Under this construction's prespecified rules, support among the 6 binary-evaluable items is 4/6≈66.67%; supported items among all registrations are 4/10=40%. These answer different questions and both require denominators plus the other four statuses. The two unresolved items cannot each count as half a success to yield 5/10=50% labeled a hit rate, nor may the other four be hidden.
teachingExamples.assumptions: The ten statuses are mathematical constructions, and the binary-evaluable set is explicitly defined in the assumptions.
teachingExamples.boundary: The evaluable support proportion is not overall calibration, causal correctness, or real-world generalizability; unlike tasks cannot be pooled without weighting and separated definitions.

counterexamples.text: An unresolved result at resolution is scored half success and half failure.
counterexamples.effect: Unresolved is an evidence status. Unless the original task has an independently justified, preregistered scoring rule, it cannot arbitrarily be converted into hits.

counterexamples.text: The original unit was abolished and a new team met the target, so the old prediction hit.
counterexamples.effect: First check identity-succession rules; without them, the target is invalid rather than an old success.

counterexamples.text: A hit in hour three proves the hour-two assertion correct.
counterexamples.effect: Time belongs to the frozen target; deadlines cannot be changed afterward.

questionAnswers.question: Why does B's valid interval [7,9] remain unresolved under this contract?
questionAnswers.answer: Threshold 8 lies within the interval, so attainment and nonattainment remain possible. The input material is valid but insufficient to distinguish them.

questionAnswers.question: Why is destruction of logs not automatically unsupported?
questionAnswers.answer: Under this demonstration contract, labels cannot be recovered and evaluation cannot run; absent evidence cannot be entered as a complete contrary result.

questionAnswers.question: May both 4/6 and 4/10 be reported for the ten items?
questionAnswers.answer: Yes, naming them respectively the support rate in the binary-evaluable subset and the supported proportion of all registrations, while disclosing other statuses.

questionAnswers.answer: A new version is allowed, but registration time, target, grounds, and the old failure must remain; original success eligibility cannot be rewritten.

12.8.title: 12.8 The Bridge from Foresight to Bounded Choice
12.8.lead: “This may be better” can become advice for deliberation, but not directly a binding command to others. Conditional consequences, value comparisons, and actual permissions each need their own reasons.
explanation: Chinese source location: lines 2703–2708; original anchor: section-12-8; short quotation, translated from the Chinese: “Recommendation does not generate execution permission.” See the corresponding section on this page for the current original text; the downloaded original research excerpt preserves the historical manuscript.

Foresight states what may happen under conditions; it does not itself decide which consequences deserve pursuit or who should bear costs. High probability strengthens judgment about a consequence without alone expanding authority over others. High average benefits also cannot cancel rights at minority positions.

Before forming an analytical recommendation, make normative premises, evidence status, affected positions, candidate options, costs and benefits, and revision conditions explicit. Reasoned local judgments and conditional advice are possible without banning all analysis because execution is not yet authorized. Clearly mark their deliberative status and unmet conditions for actual adoption.

Before actual adoption, supply the choosing subject and jurisdiction, affected and low-power positions, rights floors, options and cost-benefit distributions, authorization, stopping, appeal, rollback, and remedies. This invokes existing N, PF, J, O, and C12, not a new shortcut from “accurate prediction” to execution.

Under §14.3 (Chinese source lines 3058–3076), N must be explicitly registered at runtime. N1 only prevents explanation from directly authorizing action and supplies no positive objective alone; N2 requires protection not be downgraded; N3 requires corrigibility of high-impact judgments; N4 opposes unlimited, inescapable unilateral sacrifice; N5 prevents treating persistence and selection as justification. Disclose selected principles, whether they are objectives or constraints, and how conflicts are handled rather than silently relying on a benevolent slogan.

PF is a protection floor that cannot freely be traded for efficiency. Section 14.8 (Chinese source lines 3156–3190) requires ten items to connect individually to actual mechanisms, responsibilities, stopping, appeals, review, rollback, and expiry; formal checkmarks are insufficient. Human, sentient, mixed, or unknown objects cannot be declared purely technical to reduce protection. Nor does the floor exhaust substantive rights; specific rights still require independent grounds.

J answers who has valid grounds to perform which action on which object, within what territory and period. Section 14.6 (Chinese source lines 3118–3131) requires one valid atomic tuple to cover an action's full scope. Permission to “read A” and “modify B” cannot combine into “modify A.” Lawful continuation across multiple actors may hold, but each action requires checking its own permissions and input conditions.

O1 freezes description, evidence, and uncertainty; O2 explicitly lists norms, burden bearers, and conflicts; O3 compares options including inaction and checks authorization boundaries; O4 implements bounded execution with monitoring, stopping, appeal, rollback, remedies, and expiry. Under §4.14.1 (Chinese source lines 957–974), C12 checks completeness of bridging components; it neither chooses values for people nor replaces actual institutions' legal validity.

Inaction also requires evaluating consequences and responsibilities: old rules may keep causing harm, waiting may miss a protective window, and existing duties do not disappear because a model recommends no new action. Specify responsibilities for observation, protection, and reopening assessment rather than automatically presenting inaction as neutral, costless, and needing no explanation.

Localize gaps: insufficient evidence blocks corresponding judgments, unclear norms block recommendations depending on them, and insufficient authorization blocks corresponding execution. Independently established descriptions, conditional advice with explicit premises, and evidence needs may remain. Neither execute beyond authority nor refuse all grounded help because one gate fails.

distinctions.leftText: A grounded local or conditional recommendation under explicit premises.
distinctions.rightText: Also requires complete protection, permissions, procedures, and correction conditions.

distinctions.leftText: Strengthens descriptive judgment about the consequence in question.
distinctions.rightText: Requires independent valid authorization and justification.

distinctions.leftText: An aggregate indicator of some benefit or cost.
distinctions.rightText: Who bears burdens, whether refusal is possible, and which floors are not exchangeable.

distinctions.leftText: Whether normative-bridging components are complete.
distinctions.rightTitle: Sources of values and actual authorization
distinctions.rightText: Cannot be created by the checklist itself.

distinctions.leftText: The proposed new action is not implemented.
distinctions.rightText: Existing duties, harms, and protective needs may remain.

boundaries: Lack of authorization does not prohibit analytical recommendations for deliberation, but must prevent their treatment as executable commands.
Positive aggregate net benefit cannot alone override harm to rights at low-power positions.
Several incomplete authorization fragments for an action cannot be assembled into complete valid permission.
N1 is a negative gate, insufficient to choose a positive proposal by itself.
questions: Can C12 replace choosing values?
Why may option B with average +1.5 still be rejected?
If reading A and modifying B are allowed, may A be modified?
What can still be delivered without execution authorization?
argumentSteps: Separate conditional consequences from worthwhile objectives, listing evidence and uncertainty.
Specify positive norms and protective constraints, comparing costs and benefits of candidates and inaction position by position.
Form a bounded recommendation for deliberation with revision conditions, preserving its lack of required permissions.
Before actual adoption, check the subject, J, PF, and O1–O4, then use C12 to check bridging completeness.
Execution must allow stopping, appeal, rollback, remedies, and expiry; inaction also records continuing responsibilities.

teachingExamples.title: Mathematical construction: average benefits can hide concentrated harm
teachingExamples.text: Fictional option A gives utility +2 to each of 9 positions and −30 to 1 low-power position: total 18−30=−12, mean −1.2. Option B gives +5 to each of 9 and −30 to the last: total 45−30=15, mean +1.5. Even with positive mean B, if −30 represents a rights harm the assumptions prohibit shifting, average benefits alone cannot justify adoption. Numerical utilities illustrate aggregation's concealment; the rights constraint is not derived from numerical magnitude.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Utilities, population, and rights constraints are stipulated; no actual harm measurement or proof of interpersonal utility comparability is supplied.
teachingExamples.boundary: Without comparable utilities, even summation cannot serve as an actual comparison. Rights constraints must be independently explicit, not added afterward because the author dislikes a result.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: recommending deliberation is not changing schedules
teachingExamples.text: A fictional team forecasts reduced waiting under voluntary rotation. The analyst explicitly aims to reduce waiting without weakening existing rest protections, compares current arrangements, reinforcements, and voluntary rotation, and identifies who bears extra burdens and what evidence would change the judgment. The analyst may therefore recommend submitting voluntary rotation for deliberation. Without scheduling authority and implemented consent, appeal, and rollback mechanisms, they cannot directly alter actual schedules.
teachingExamples.assumptions: The team, objectives, and prediction are teaching constructions, with no actual personnel or organizational operation.
teachingExamples.boundary: Voluntariness is not treated as established. Actual consent must permit refusal and withdrawal and comply with applicable institutions; no legal judgment on particular labor rules is provided.

teachingExamples.title: Formal construction: permissions cannot be combined across objects
teachingExamples.text: Suppose J1 permits subject A only to read object A this week, and J2 permits that subject only to modify object B this week. The candidate action is modifying A this week. J1 mismatches the action and J2 the object, so neither fully covers it. Taking the Cartesian product of their object and action columns manufactures nonexistent permission.
teachingExamples.assumptions: All subjects, objects, and authorizations are formal constructions; record contents are assumed valid but limited as stated.
teachingExamples.boundary: This does not deny lawful workflows where multiple subjects perform different actions; each action still needs complete coverage of its own.

counterexamples.text: Prediction confidence is 99%, so anyone may be forced to bear preventive costs.
counterexamples.effect: Confidence concerns conditional consequences; cost distribution, rights, and jurisdiction require separate examination.

counterexamples.text: Execution permission has not been supplied, so even conditional recommendations cannot be written.
counterexamples.effect: Evidence-based deliberative recommendations with explicit norms may be written, without presenting them as authorized execution.

counterexamples.text: The model recommends inaction, so protection and observation responsibilities end.
counterexamples.effect: Inaction retains ongoing consequences and existing duties; evaluate them and arrange reopening conditions.

questionAnswers.question: Can C12 replace choosing values?
questionAnswers.answer: No. First register explicit norms and conflicts; C12 checks corresponding bridges rather than secretly creating objectives.
questionAnswers.basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

questionAnswers.question: Why may option B with average +1.5 still be rejected?
questionAnswers.answer: The stipulated rights constraint prohibits shifting that harm onto the last position; the mean cannot cancel an independent constraint.
questionAnswers.basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

questionAnswers.question: If reading A and modifying B are allowed, may A be modified?
questionAnswers.answer: No. One lacks action coverage and the other object coverage; they cannot combine into new permission.
questionAnswers.basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

questionAnswers.question: What can still be delivered without execution authorization?
questionAnswers.answer: Grounded descriptions, conditional recommendations with explicit norms, costs and revision conditions, and outstanding requirements for actual adoption.

12.9.title: 12.9 The Option Set Must Include Action and Inaction
12.9.lead: Comparing options is not finding reasons for a predetermined action. First lay out genuinely available paths worth comparing, especially retaining the no-additional-action baseline and distinguishing active maintenance of current arrangements from doing nothing.
explanation: Chinese source location: lines 2709–2723; original anchor: section-12-9; short quotation, translated from the Chinese: “Inaction may allow the status quo to change naturally.” See the corresponding section on this page for the current original text; the downloaded original research excerpt preserves the historical manuscript.

When the user or task requests a choice, examine six types individually: maintain the status quo, act proactively, delay action, take a small exploratory step, exit or transfer, and explicitly do not act. This checks applicability, not mandatory completion of six buttons. Explain constraints where inapplicable; construct actual comparable options where applicable. Tasks may add options, while pure explanation or verification tasks need no compulsory action list.

Maintaining the status quo may require continuing resources, rules, protections, and costs. Inaction means not implementing this proposed additional action, while existing mechanisms continue changing. Under §14.4 (Chinese source lines 3078–3101), the inaction baseline retains existing maintenance, ongoing conduct, and independent obligations; “no addition” cannot be replaced with “turn off all existing protection.” Specify each difference between active maintenance and baseline rather than merely renaming.

Maintaining the status quo requires checking hidden costs, ongoing harm, and lock-in; active intervention requires checking permissions, irreversibility, and costs spilling across circles. Rapid change is not necessarily worth pursuing, and stability is not necessarily justified. Both directions must disclose normative premises and affected positions.

Delayed action is an option with a clock: specify what material or procedure is awaited, for how long, who observes, and when review reopens. Waiting itself can accumulate harm or miss an opportunity window. Missing evidence cannot justify indefinite delay without responsibility, nor can planned future execution be registered as already having occurred.

A tentative small step must specify what is to be learned, distinguishing signals, scale, deadline, stopping, rollback, and who bears costs. Small scale means only that some quantity is small; it does not guarantee low risk or reversibility. Affected parties, privacy, irreversible information disclosure, and shifted burdens still require checks. Section 12.11 develops the detailed conditions.

Exit or transfer may end an unsuitable relationship or object, but does not automatically erase dependents, existing responsibilities, or history. Check who can exit, who cannot, who takes up the service or responsibility, and how records are preserved. Without qualified uptake, do not invent “just transfer it” to fill an option slot. Nor may exit be held hostage by unlimited responsibility.

Inaction must record the baseline time, expected path, observation plan, reopening conditions, and responsible party. Other actors, resources, and clocks continue moving; the baseline is not a still photograph. Only with this baseline can one compare what additional interference brings; otherwise “we must do something” readily becomes a hidden premise.

The six categories are not naturally mutually exclusive categories of the world. A combined option may begin with monitoring, proceed to a bounded trial, and transfer once a threshold is reached. Registration must distinguish stages, triggers, and resources, without counting the same action's benefits under multiple options or hiding execution-permission gaps behind a combined label. Real-world adoption still requires the bridging in 12.8; an option list does not itself authorize action.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: applicability of six categories in one fictional queue
teachingExamples.text: A fictional service queue has backlog 6 at t=0, 2 arrivals per hour, and existing processing capacity 1 per hour; compare the next two hours. Explicit inaction preserves the original service without adding resources, yielding endpoint 8. Active maintenance adds 1 processing unit per hour to preserve backlog 6. Active improvement adds 2 per hour to the original 1, for total processing 3 and endpoint 4. Delay uses the original processing 1 in the first hour and, after approval, increases it to 3 in the second, taking the backlog to 7 then 6. A small trial increases processing to 2 in the first hour with monitoring, then handles the second hour under a predetermined rule. Exit or transfer is marked inapplicable because there is currently no verifiable receiving party; transfer capacity is not invented. Every additional option remains only a candidate.
teachingExamples.assumptions: The values, capacities, and observation period are all teaching constructions, with no actual service deployment. The original processing capacity 1 is an existing service; inaction does not cancel it.
teachingExamples.boundary: Resource costs and actual authorization have not been compared. Endpoint 4 being smallest does not justify declaring immediate implementation necessary. The trial's second hour still depends on observations and cannot be treated as a fixed endpoint.

teachingExamples.title: Mathematical construction: natural depletion reveals the difference between maintenance and inaction
teachingExamples.text: A purely technical fictional inventory starts at 10, loses 2 naturally each period, and has no other existing inputs. Adding no replenishment for two periods yields 8 then 6. Actively replenishing 2 each period preserves 10 then 10, but requires total additional input 4. Saying the latter option “does not change final inventory” does not mean it “involves no action or cost.”
teachingExamples.assumptions: Depletion, inputs, and the linear update I_next=I−2+replenishment are stipulated assumptions; no actual experiment was conducted.
teachingExamples.boundary: Actual inventories may involve thresholds, demand, and protection obligations. This pure construction should not be used to infer duties of care for people or organizational responsibilities.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: an auditable inaction baseline
teachingExamples.text: Inaction record for the queue above: baseline t=0, B=6; expected values 7 at t=1 and 8 at t=2; check arrivals and actual completions hourly; reopen option review if any complete record shows B≥7; fictional duty role R observes and records. Reopening is only review and does not automatically increase processing resources. If records are missing, mark unknown and trigger a material review; do not treat missingness as low risk.
teachingExamples.assumptions: The observation rules and responsible role are teaching templates only; no work has been assigned to any actual person.
teachingExamples.boundary: Actual responsibility must be accepted by a qualified actor with the capacity, time, and permissions. This template cannot establish that anyone has taken it up in reality.

counterexamples.text: Maintaining the status quo and inaction both ultimately seek stability, so combine them.
counterexamples.effect: Maintenance may require continuous additional input, while the inaction baseline may deteriorate. Distinguish them by actual actions and resources.

counterexamples.text: All six categories must be listed, so mark transfer feasible even without a recipient.
counterexamples.effect: Checking six categories does not make six options feasible; missing uptake should be marked inapplicable or awaiting evidence.

counterexamples.text: Even explaining one concept requires six action options.
counterexamples.effect: Without a request for choice, no action list is mandatory; the task determines output scope.

questionAnswers.question: Why does inaction in the queue yield a backlog of 8 rather than keeping it at 6?
questionAnswers.answer: Existing processing is 1 per hour and arrivals are 2, giving a net increase of 1 each hour: from 6 to 8 over two hours.

questionAnswers.question: What additional conditions are needed to maintain 6?
questionAnswers.answer: Increase processing to 2 per hour, adding 1 unit per hour with separate resources, authorization, and protection conditions.

12.10.title: 12.10 Unified option comparison card
12.10.lead: A unified comparison card unifies questions, baselines, and obligations, rather than forcing every value into one total score. Whether information helps, whether actions jointly qualify, and whether resources support them simultaneously are three questions requiring separate proof.
explanation: Source location: Chinese source lines 2724–2742; source anchor section-12-10; short quotation translated from Chinese: “multidimensional results and openly stated conflicts should be retained.” See the corresponding section on this page for the current source text; the downloaded original research excerpt preserves the historical draft.

Compare each option against the same baseline, target, and deadline. Minimum records include the option description, foresight references, normative premises, affected parties, minimum rights protections, expected path, worst acceptable outcome, cross-circle spillovers, cost-benefit distribution, information value, lock-in risk, reversibility, resource costs, executors, authorization, stopping, rollback, and remedies. “Large benefits and controllable risks” alone provides no reviewable comparison.

Targets and paths must state which mechanism changes. The protection floor must identify unacceptable harm; average benefits cannot substitute for it. Distribution must state who gains, who pays, and when; an aggregate net value is insufficient. Cross-circle spillovers require checking whether costs are externalized; indicators for the main circle cannot monopolize evaluation.

Information value asks whether new observations distinguish mechanisms or paths, or change an evidence-based choice, rather than whether an action is dramatic. Reversibility and lock-in ask whether stopping, withdrawal, and remedy are actually possible; verbal promises are insufficient. Permissions must identify who can decide, execute, and hear appeals, and within what valid scope; a job title or model recommendation is insufficient. Inaction still follows a changing baseline and cannot be assigned zero cost.

Without a reasonable common unit and public trade-off rules, multidimensional results should retain vectors, conflicts, and rankings under different normative premises. A model can explain which option it favors under disclosed norms and what would change that judgment, but cannot make a binding final decision for qualified actors. Forced summation can hide minimum rights protections or silently set interpersonal utility exchange rates.

The bounded information-value formula is EVSI=E_Z[max_a E(U(a,θ)|Z)]−max_a E[U(a,θ)]. Here θ is the state, a the action, Z the information, and U a previously accepted utility with a computable expectation. The formula compares the optimal expectation when the action can respond to Z after learning it with the optimal expectation from choosing one action without Z. Utilities and probabilities need declared status; a conditional model calculation is not a verified real-world benefit.

Nonnegativity requires information to be free and ignorable, with the action set and target unchanged. If the original optimal action remains available after information is acquired, one can do at least as well as before. Actual inquiry takes time, privacy, and resources and may change the object or make actions expire, so gross EVSI is not net value. Unquantified privacy and rights costs cannot default to zero, nor may they be forcibly monetized just to use the formula.

Two clues may each leave the decision unchanged yet be valuable together, so information values need not add up item by item. Knowledge also has value for understanding independent of this action; EVSI=0 in this formula does not make research worthless. Section 12.10.1 further explains when a common action is feasible under uncertainty; 12.10.2 checks shared resources across multiple actions. The parent section's comparison card cannot replace these two tests.

distinctions.rightText: Possible only with additional justified trade-offs and conditions on units.

distinctions.rightText: Also includes inquiry time, resources, privacy, and opportunity costs.

boundaries: The maximization formula does not turn utility premises into natural facts or automatically authorize information collection.
If information is not free and ignorable, gross EVSI's nonnegativity cannot establish that real-world inquiry is always beneficial.
Two individually useless clues need not be jointly useless; information values generally cannot be mechanically added.
Complete comparison-card fields improve reviewability only; they do not certify factual accuracy or real-world permissions.

Why does observing only X give no gain in the XOR example?
What is the net value when cost is 0.6?

argumentSteps: Complete comparison fields for the same baseline, target, and deadline, retaining each burden-bearing position.
Without a reasonable common scale, retain multidimensional results and disclose normative conflicts and conditional preferences.
For information value, first specify states, signals, actions, and utility, then state the calculation's conditional status.
Prove gross information value nonnegative when information is free and ignorable and the action set is unchanged; separately deduct corresponding real-world costs.
Check clues' joint effects, commonly acceptable actions, and shared resources before submitting the choice to a qualified procedure.

teachingExamples.title: Mathematical proof: nonnegativity of bounded EVSI
teachingExamples.text: Assume a finite, nonempty, fixed action set and existing utility expectations; take the no-information optimal action a*. For each signal z, max_a E[U(a,θ)|Z=z]≥E[U(a*,θ)|Z=z]. Taking expectations over Z and applying the law of total expectation gives the left side ≥E[U(a*,θ)]=max_a E[U(a,θ)]; subtraction yields EVSI≥0. Being free and ignorable ensures that feasible strategies after the signal still include the fixed a*. If the action set changes, this step may fail.
teachingExamples.assumptions: A finite probability model, finite action set, and integrable utility are explicit conditions. This is an algebraic argument, not a real-world experiment.
teachingExamples.boundary: Nonnegativity concerns gross expected value. It does not show that every specific signal improves matters, guarantee positive net value for real-world collection, or establish permission.

teachingExamples.title: Mathematical construction: two individually unhelpful clues are valuable together
teachingExamples.text: Independent fair bits X and Y have four combinations, 00, 01, 10, 11, each with probability 1/4; state θ=X XOR Y. Action a∈{0,1} scores 1 for a correct guess and 0 otherwise. Without information, θ is uniform and the best expectation is 1/2. Observing only X or only Y leaves the other uniform, so the expectation stays 1/2 and each individual EVSI=0. Observing X and Y together allows exact calculation of θ, scoring 1 every time, so joint EVSI=1−1/2=1/2. If the two pieces of information cost 0.6 in total on the same utility scale, with nothing else changing, net value is 0.5−0.6=−0.1.
teachingExamples.assumptions: All distributions, utilities, and costs are stipulated; no information was actually collected.
teachingExamples.boundary: This does not imply that real-world information can always jointly resolve ambiguity. Cost comparability is also stipulated; actual privacy and rights constraints cannot be arbitrarily converted.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: multidimensional comparison without forced summation
teachingExamples.text: Fictional option A reduces waiting by 2 hours but adds privacy exposure; option B adds no exposure but reduces waiting by only 1 hour. Without public privacy constraints and time trade-offs, “2−privacy points” should not be disguised as an objective total score. Report waiting, whose information is exposed, difficulty of withdrawal, the protection floor, and resources separately; then exclude A under an explicit premise that specified additional exposure is prohibited.
teachingExamples.assumptions: The options and effects are constructed; no actual user data is described or collected.
teachingExamples.boundary: Exclusion follows from the explicit constraint, not automatically from the numerical time values; compare again if the evidence changes.

counterexamples.text: EVSI is nonnegative, so inquiry is worthwhile however expensive it is.
counterexamples.effect: Nonnegativity concerns only the gross value of free, ignorable information; real-world net value can be negative.

counterexamples.text: X and Y each have zero EVSI, so their joint EVSI must be zero.
counterexamples.effect: In the XOR construction, they jointly reveal the state exactly, giving a gain of 1/2.

counterexamples.text: If no total score can be calculated, no preference can be proposed.
counterexamples.effect: A conditional preference can be offered for deliberation under explicit norms, retaining conflicts without overstepping authority to decide.

questionAnswers.question: What is the key inequality in the EVSI proof?
questionAnswers.answer: The optimal action after the signal is at least as good as retaining a*; then apply the law of total expectation.
questionAnswers.basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

questionAnswers.question: Why does observing only X give no gain in the XOR example?
questionAnswers.answer: Y remains fair, so θ's conditional distribution remains 1/2 for each value; X alone cannot raise the expected success of guessing.
questionAnswers.basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

questionAnswers.question: What is the net value when cost is 0.6?
questionAnswers.answer: Gross value 0.5 minus cost 0.6 gives −0.1, assuming cost and utility are comparable.
questionAnswers.basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

questionAnswers.question: Why need a unified comparison card not produce a unified total score?
questionAnswers.answer: Dimensions may be incommensurable or subject to hard rights constraints. Unified recording is sufficient; trade-offs require additional public reasons.

12.10.1.title: 12.10.1 From identifiable answers to feasible choices
12.10.1.lead: Not knowing which state holds need not prevent all action; yet each state having its own solution does not ensure that one common qualified solution can be selected now.
explanation: Source location: Chinese source lines 2743–2748; source anchor section-12-10-1; brief quotation translated from Chinese: “This gives a positive condition for bounded action while retaining unknowns.” See the corresponding section on this page for the current source; the downloadable original research extract preserves the historical draft.

Let the credible-state set compatible with current material be nonempty. For each state z, A_ok(z) is not an arbitrary imagined list, but qualified actions determined by public targets, protection floors, resources, and valid permission. Otherwise even a nonempty formal intersection contains only paper actions, not real feasibility.

In a bounded single-round deterministic choice, a nonempty common intersection means at least one action qualifies in every listed compatible state. These shared actions can then be compared without first identifying the actual state. This is a positive condition for bounded action with unknowns, not a requirement to wait indefinitely for perfect knowledge.

If the intersection is empty, each set separately being nonempty is insufficient. Knowing z1 would select left and z2 right, but a current representation that does not distinguish them cannot guarantee the right selection with one deterministic rule. Check whether further evidence, waiting, a narrower target, or independently grounded protective actions alter conditions; do not assume those options automatically available.

Conversely, a sufficient answer does not guarantee action. Even if z1 is identified, inadequate resources, failed protection, or missing permission may leave A_ok(z1) empty. Identification, computability, access, implementation, resources, and authority to adopt carry different responsibilities; a correct answer is not a pass for all.

The condition covers only listed credible states and constraints, without guaranteeing no omitted states. Nor does it declare worst-case criteria uniquely rational. Grounded probabilities, risk tolerance, randomization, or sequential strategies may yield other rules, but must state their own targets and conditions rather than extending this single-round deterministic result without bounds.

This matches F3 in §4.18.3 (Chinese source lines 1042–1045) and Appendix C.12 (lines 4968–4972). The comparison card first defines qualification; this section proves whether a common action exists under limited information. The next tests whether multiple shared or separately feasible actions compete for one resource.

distinctions.rightText: The intersection of all sets is nonempty, a stronger logical claim.

teachingExamples.title: Formal proof: common action is equivalent to a nonempty intersection
teachingExamples.text: Necessity: if the same action a is chosen using only current representation y and qualifies for every compatible z, then a∈A_ok(z) for every z, so a belongs to the intersection. Sufficiency: if the intersection is nonempty, take any a in it; a qualifies for every z without identifying the actual z. The proof uses only set definitions, not evidence of real qualification of each set.
teachingExamples.assumptions: A bounded single-round deterministic task, nonempty observation class, and already determined qualified sets.
teachingExamples.boundary: Does not prove necessary/sufficient conditions for sequential, randomized, or risk-tolerant strategies, or certify actual permission.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: a common protective option under unknown state
teachingExamples.text: Fictional z1 has qualified set {left,preserve}, z2 has {right,preserve}; preserve is assumed to have this task's resources, protection, and valid authorization. The intersection is {preserve}, allowing comparison and selection without knowing z1 versus z2. If preserve's permission expires and it leaves both sets, {left} and {right} remain with empty intersection. The previous version's feasibility no longer applies.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Action names, states, and authorization are formal stipulations; no actual preservation action occurs.
teachingExamples.boundary: Preserve is not a magically lawful action; failed premises require rechecking.

teachingExamples.title: Formal construction: knowing the answer may still leave no feasible action
teachingExamples.text: Material uniquely identifies z1, but required action left needs capacity 2 and only 1 exists; all other actions violate stipulated protection constraints. A_ok(z1)=empty, so the state is fully identifiable while the task cannot be executed. Only actual additional capacity and satisfied permission may create a new qualified set.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Capacity and constraints are stipulated; no actual resource request is made.
teachingExamples.boundary: Knowing the resource shortfall does not mean new resources have arrived or the old cutoff automatically extends.

counterexamples.text: Every state has an action, so the right action can certainly be selected now.
counterexamples.effect: {left} and {right} are separately nonempty but their intersection is empty.

counterexamples.text: Since not every state is known, all bounded action must stop.
counterexamples.effect: If an already qualified common action exists, identifying every state is unnecessary.

counterexamples.text: An empty intersection proves randomized and sequential strategies useless.
counterexamples.effect: This condition does not address them; analyze their respective targets and constraints separately.

questionAnswers.question: What is the intersection of {left,preserve} and {right,preserve}?
questionAnswers.answer: {preserve}, provided preserve already meets resource, protection, and permission conditions.

questionAnswers.answer: No. Authorization and related conditions are prior evidential responsibilities for A_ok eligibility.

questionAnswers.question: Why may unique identification of z1 still fail to permit action?
questionAnswers.answer: Insufficient resources or permission may still leave A_ok(z1) empty.

questionAnswers.question: Does a nonempty intersection imply a unique optimum?
questionAnswers.answer: No. It proves only that a commonly qualified action exists; multiple options still need comparison.

12.10.2.title: 12.10.2 Joint feasibility of multiple options
12.10.2.lead: Each task may claim to need just one resource, ultimately promising the same resource twice. Joint feasibility must put capacity, dependencies, personnel, stopping capability, and deadlines into one constraint table.
explanation: Source location: Chinese source lines 2749–2754; source anchor section-12-10-2; brief quotation translated from Chinese: “separately feasible but jointly infeasible.” See the corresponding section on this page for the current source; the downloadable original research extract preserves the historical draft.

Individual feasibility establishes completion when an action uses conditions alone, not enough capacity, budget, personnel, or stopping channels for simultaneous execution. Departments passing separate reviews still need joint-constraint checks if they use the same resource. Differently named resources may depend on one underlying person or platform.

The minimal counterexample has two unit tasks, each occupying the whole current period and both due by its end, with capacity only 1. Each alone needs 1≤1 and is feasible; together they need 2>1 and are infeasible. Additional capacity next period does not change this period's deadline; later completion is not timely completion of the original task.

Adding same-period capacity changes constraints. A grounded and authorized extension of one deadline can also create a feasible new option, preserving the original contract and revision status. If the old deadline was already missed, later successful completion does not erase the late record. Scheduling mathematics cannot erase delay harms or protections for affected people.

Resource scheduling also needs task dependencies. If premise verification, authorization, execution, and effect have serial dependencies, tool concurrency cannot make them all complete simultaneously. Actually independent reads or tasks may run in parallel, but shared write targets, common capacity, version prerequisites, and conflicts need handling rules.

Stopping capability is also a resource. If one person or channel cannot respond to several stop requests within the critical window, separate stopping promises cannot simply become joint stoppability. Rollback, remedy, and monitoring may compete for the same resources and must be checked alongside normal execution.

Task completion must reach the promised affected people and protective outcomes. First-node completion, sending a request, or interface success does not mean the last person is protected; check timing and coverage together. This connects to the end-to-end clock in 12.6, with the unit-capacity counterexample in Appendix C.12, Chinese source line 4966, directly supporting the formal boundary.

distinctions.leftText: An action using resources alone meets constraints.
distinctions.rightText: All actions satisfy shared constraints together under one schedule.

distinctions.leftText: More may be done in the future.
distinctions.rightText: Required sufficient resources and actual completion at the time.

distinctions.leftText: No prerequisite dependency and sufficient resources.
distinctions.rightText: Executes downstream work before its premises hold.

distinctions.leftText: Normal action has resources.
distinctions.rightText: Simultaneous exceptions also require resources and actual mechanisms.

boundaries: Joint-feasibility proofs depend on actual stipulated demand, capacity, and deadlines; mathematics does not certify these inputs.
Extensions require grounds and valid procedures; models cannot rewrite contracts themselves.
Shared resources include personnel, budgets, and stopping channels as well as machine capacity.
A feasible schedule is neither completed execution nor delivery of promised protection to affected people.
questions: Why are demands of 1 each individually feasible but jointly infeasible under capacity 1?
What becomes true after B's deadline is lawfully moved to period 2?
Why must joint comparison list stopping channels?
Can verification, authorization, and execution all run simultaneously for speed?
argumentSteps: List each action's resource use, dependencies, deadline, and actual completion endpoint.
Find shared underlying resources, personnel, and stopping channels, checking capacity jointly for every period.
After individual feasibility, separately check joint inequalities; conflicts prohibit repeated promises of the same resources.
Same-period expansion or lawful condition changes create new options; old deadline results are not rewritten.
Check serial critical paths, endpoint coverage, and stopping/remedy capability; first-node completion does not replace whole-task completion.

teachingExamples.title: Mathematical construction: two current-period tasks compete for one unit of capacity
teachingExamples.text: Tasks A and B each need one full unit of current-period capacity and are both due at period end, with C1=1. Separately, dA=1≤1 and dB=1≤1; jointly, dA+dB=2>1, so both cannot finish on time. If current capacity becomes 2, demand 2≤2 can be scheduled. If only next-period capacity rises to 2 while both original deadlines remain, current-period tasks still cannot be met.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Discrete single period, indivisible unit workloads, and stipulated capacity/deadlines.
teachingExamples.boundary: Divisibility, different durations, or preemption would change the model; those conditions cannot be silently inserted into the original.

teachingExamples.title: Mathematical construction: a lawful new deadline permits a new schedule
teachingExamples.text: Continuing the example, suppose a valid procedure changes B's deadline to the end of period 2, with C1=C2=1. Schedule A in period 1 and B in period 2: each period uses 1 and meets the new respective deadline. Feasibility of the new contract does not complete the old contract requiring both this period; if lateness already occurred before revision, it remains.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Grounds and authorization for extension are explicitly assumed in the construction; no real extension occurs.
teachingExamples.boundary: Real delay may harm a party, still requiring applicable protection, rights, procedure, and remedy judgments.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: stopping promises also conflict over resources
teachingExamples.text: Two fictional pilots run simultaneously, each requiring the same supervisor to perform a manual shutdown taking exactly 1 minute within 1 minute of receiving a stop signal. If both signals arrive together and no other stopping channel is available, one supervisor cannot perform both at once. Individual stoppability does not establish that joint operation meets the same stopping deadline.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Personnel, operation duration, and simultaneous signals are teaching constructions, not descriptions of a real safety system.
teachingExamples.boundary: Real systems may have independent automatic stopping or multiple personnel; verify these rather than assume they exist.

counterexamples.text: A and B each pass individual resource review, so joint implementation also passes.
counterexamples.effect: Shared resources may be promised twice; check constraints under a common schedule.

counterexamples.text: Adding capacity next period proves this period's deadline was not missed.
counterexamples.effect: Future resources cannot restore a past deadline; at most they support catching up and a new option.

counterexamples.text: Each pilot has the same supervisor, guaranteeing joint stopping.
counterexamples.effect: One supervisor may be unable to fulfill several short-deadline stopping promises simultaneously.

questionAnswers.question: Why are demands of 1 each individually feasible but jointly infeasible under capacity 1?
questionAnswers.answer: Individually 1≤1, jointly 2>1; the same original deadlines do not permit borrowing from another period.
questionAnswers.basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

questionAnswers.question: What becomes true after B's deadline is lawfully moved to period 2?
questionAnswers.answer: The new contract has a schedule with capacity 1 per period; this does not mean the old contract was completed on time.
questionAnswers.basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

questionAnswers.question: Why must joint comparison list stopping channels?
questionAnswers.answer: Concurrent faults also compete for personnel and capability; individual promises do not guarantee joint compliance.
questionAnswers.basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

questionAnswers.question: Can verification, authorization, and execution all run simultaneously for speed?
questionAnswers.answer: Not with sequential dependencies; only independent stages with sufficient resources and permission may run in parallel.
questionAnswers.basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

Task B requires 1 this period, individually 1≤1: feasible. Increasing capacity in the same period to 2 permits a new schedule; adding only next-period capacity does not recover this period's old deadline. Lawfully changing B's deadline permits a separate second-period schedule while retaining the old record. Unit tasks and capacities are formal constructions; actual resources, deadlines, protection, and valid authority require separate verification.
