teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: two different status chains
teachingExamples.text: Proposition A would accuse an artificial organization of dereliction. IG1 verifies the object, but IG2 source-status verification fails. Dependent IG3–IG7 are all not_run; even a complete separate eight-item package cannot repair the source break. Proposition B only compares two public definitions in a low-impact classroom setting, with no intervention, eligibility, resource, or substantive reputational consequences for a specific subject. With evidence for other applicable gates, IG6 may be not_applicable for that explicit use reason, continuing to IG7 with description_only. B still has no action authorization.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Propositions, organization, uses, and statuses are artificial, not actual process certification.
teachingExamples.boundary: Retaining B depends on genuine independence; it cannot copy A's accusation under a new name.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: where to reopen after a use change
teachingExamples.text: An artificial L2 report originally compares scheduling models, then is proposed for named employees' promotions. Recheck object and material fit for the new use and reopen at least affected positions, anti-retaliation, reflexivity, and strong-judgment procedures; if object definition changes, restart IG1. Renaming the report L3 or adding a signature on the final page is insufficient.
teachingExamples.assumptions: No actual employees, promotions, or automated decisions.
teachingExamples.boundary: Illustrates reopening at the earliest affected gate, without issuing intervention authority to any organization.

13.4.title: 13.4 Five gates and thirteen steps: the diagnostic expansion layer
13.4.lead: Five gates and thirteen steps lay out material for complex questions, helping the seven gates see grounds clearly. They cannot issue another pass that bypasses the main process.
explanation: Source location: Chinese source lines 2864–2895, original-site location /theory/part-13#section-13-4. See the theory-v2 source for the current full text; historical research originals and extracts remain downloadable in their original editions.

The source positions this as a “diagnostic expansion layer” in translation. Use it for complex objects, high responsibility, high reflexivity, or when seven-gate review needs finer evidence gathering—not for thirteen mandatory steps in every proofreading task. Outputs of the five local gates and thirteen steps return to the sole seven-gate process, creating no second main-process status. [T-main; T-seven]

Preserve gate mappings individually: FG1 object material serves IG1; FG2 signal costs, sources, weights, and review serve IG2; FG3 nine axes, within-scale objects/evidence, and scale change serve both IG1/IG2; FG4 effects on rights/resources, contrary conditions, repair windows, and appeal/review serve IG3/IG4/IG6; FG5 pre-observation baseline, responses during observation and after publication, and recursion caps serve IG5. Calling FG4 a responsibility gate does not allocate responsibility by itself. FG5 stops endless recursive checking rather than allowing “observe the observer again” to expand indefinitely. [T-main]

DS01, question entry, first states in ordinary language who asks what and for which use. “How are erroneous records corrected?” should not begin as “this system belongs to a certain phase.” DS02, object and boundaries, then identifies effective objects, subsystems, higher-level environments, and external channels to bound comparison; objects without corresponding material remain candidates. [T-main]

DS03 separates facts, behavior, resources, feedback, narratives, feelings, conjectures, and noise. One interview may include personal experience and speculation about others; not all of it can be labeled fact or noise. DS04, observation participation, registers observed people's awareness, observer power, publication effects, and possible responses. This concerns both evidence generation and safe expression; people aware of being scored cannot be treated as static objects unaffected by observation. [T-main]

DS05, dominant constraints, retains candidates, selection reasons, and competing constraints. “Dominant” is a contestable task judgment, not selecting the most theory-like cause first. DS06, states and windows, uses S0–S6 only for applicable human intentional collectives, also recording within-state positions, parallel subsystems, and contrary conditions. Technical systems and categories lacking intentionality grounds must not be forced into them; state inapplicability and use the domain's own states and windows. Stages are not maturity or destiny. [T-main; T-HV10]

DS07, core structural scan, checks anchors, uptake layers, transmission chains, boundaries, and feedback write-back. Naming a link does not establish a connected chain; every link needs object and channel grounds. DS08, key protection variables, lists protected objects, damage paths, resources, redundancy, and repair/return paths. Finding importance generates protection needs, not immediate authority for researchers to alter resources or decide for people. [T-main]

DS09, uptake and repayment, separates cost bearers, return recipients, stopping rights, long-term overdraft, and harm transfer. The busiest, most visible, or final-step executor does not thereby become solely responsible or obliged to keep sacrificing. DS10, hidden problems and boundary types, checks maintenance debt, fast/slow mismatch, indicator substitution, distorted summaries, and object-conversion candidates. Each is a checkable question; a full terminology list does not establish every problem occurred. [T-main]

DS11 lists only competing mechanism candidates allowed by material and sufficient to change judgment, stating needed and weakening evidence and elimination rules. Without reasonable alternatives, report search scope and failure conditions rather than inventing stories to fill two or three mechanisms. Candidates remain limited by causal contracts; procedural generation does not make explanations empirical evidence. [T-main; T-causal]

DS12 branch anticipation lists triggers, early signals, reversal conditions, repair windows, and minimum action requirements. Branches are not determined futures, and minimum requirements are not direct execution commands. DS13 outputs in ordinary language with revision triggers, record scope, review, withdrawal, and rollback; without effective review and withdrawal, judgments cannot be entered into organizational records, qualifications, allocations, or public memory. A new explanation also does not automatically correct the downstream effects of old records. [T-main]

The added point from the Knight Capital case here is that accident analysis must separate deployment, request transmission, monitoring, and response. The SEC order lists them separately and records a code-withdrawal operation that worsened the failure. This helps explain why technical states, response timing, and repair conditions need separate columns; it assigns no technical system an S0—S6 label or all responsibility to one person based on their execution position. [P-SEC]

The strongest objection is that thirteen steps become lengthy paperwork. Reuse the same evidence through stable references, explain decisive reasons in the main text, and have procedural checks handle repeated fields; still retain unknowns and conflicts that actually affect the conclusion. Completing every local step neither automatically passes the seven gates nor proves an actual option optimal. Use and materials determine stopping points. [T-main]
argumentSteps: Decide whether expansion is needed, preserving the seven gates as the sole source of status.
FG1—FG5 map details back to corresponding main gates without issuing another overall pass.
DS01—DS04 specify the question, objects, signals, and observation effects.
DS05—DS10 check constraints, applicable states, structure, protection, costs, and hidden hazards.
DS11—DS13 form bounded competing mechanisms and conditional branches, outputting reviewable, retractable text with a defined scope.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: a minimum thirteen-step chain for an incorrect roster
teachingExamples.text: The artificial request is ‘explain why this week's roster assigns A twice and propose review conditions’, limited to internal error checking. DS01 records the request and use; DS02 bounds roster v1, the importer, and the approval interface; DS03 separates observation of two duplicate rows from speculation about ‘deliberate overassignment’; DS04 records that publishing a named conclusion may affect personnel; DS05 compares duplicate import and conflicting merge as two candidate constraints; DS06 does not apply S0—S6 to a technical table, recording v1/v2 and time instead; DS07 traces the chain from file to operational roster; DS08 protects actual rest and correction opportunities; DS09 lists who checks, who bears temporary coordination costs, and rights to stop; DS10 checks old-version caches; DS11 uses import IDs and version logs to distinguish candidates rather than judging motives through guesses; DS12 proposes evidence supplementation and correction requirements if duplicate IDs are confirmed, otherwise retaining an unresolved status; DS13 outputs only a reviewable report and reopening conditions, without changing an actual roster.
teachingExamples.assumptions: People, tables, and logs are artificial; the candidates suffice to change the handling direction, but no actual system was run.
teachingExamples.boundary: This construction displays each step's products, not a seven-gate pass, established causation, or authorization to change schedules.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: the stopping point when independent review is missing
teachingExamples.text: An artificial organization wants to enter the preceding explanation into A's qualification file, but only the diagnosis's author can change the conclusion, A cannot supplement evidence, and old versions cannot be withdrawn. DS13 conditions are insufficient, so this high-impact entry should stop. Even complete DS01—DS12 materials cannot use expansion-layer ‘completion’ to bypass the main process.
teachingExamples.assumptions: No actual personnel or qualification record is involved.
teachingExamples.boundary: This does not claim all internal material organization must stop; only the high-impact use depending on the missing item stops.

questionAnswers.question: Must a technical-system failure be written as S0—S6?
questionAnswers.answer: Do not force it; state inapplicability and retain the domain's own versions, states, and windows.
questionAnswers.basis: DS06。

questionAnswers.question: Are three listed mechanisms more qualified than one?
questionAnswers.answer: Not necessarily. Candidates must be reasonable and potentially change the judgment; do not invent them to reach a count.
questionAnswers.basis: DS11。

questionAnswers.question: If key protection variables have been identified, may others' resources be allocated directly?
questionAnswers.answer: No. Only protection needs are generated; execution authority requires separate checking.
questionAnswers.basis: DS08。

questionAnswers.question: If all thirteen steps are filled, may a failed seven-gate check be ignored?
questionAnswers.answer: No. The expansion layer has no second set of pass statuses.

13.5.title: 13.5 The eight-part strong-judgment package
13.5.lead: The ‘strong’ in strong judgment concerns its use, not how confidently it is worded. A score affecting qualifications, rights, or reputation must permit supplemental evidence, refutation, and actual correction even if called a draft.
explanation: Chinese source location: lines 2896—2916; original-site location /theory/part-13#section-13-5. The current complete text is in the theory-v2 source; the historical research manuscript and excerpts remain available in their original versions for download and checking.

The source defines strong judgment by ‘use and foreseeable effects’ (translated from Chinese). Judgments intended or reasonably foreseeable for action upon people, qualifications, rights, resource allocation, material effects on specific parties' reputations and public memory, or incorporation into automated, organized, or institutional decisions enter the corresponding procedure. Intermediate scores, recommendations, or material filtering also require actual-use checks if transmitted into such decisions; an upstream ‘for reference only’ label does not automatically remove downstream responsibilities. [T-main]

Public dissemination heightens scrutiny but is not sufficient to upgrade every public analysis to L3. Consider the object, factual allegations, identifiability, scope, and consequences. Ordinary argument evaluation, mechanism explanation, or normative opinion can still give clear grounded conclusions when it does not reach those effects. Conversely, titles such as ‘commentary’, ‘research’, or ‘draft’ do not exempt uses actually meeting strong-judgment conditions. [T-main]

SJ1 reversal conditions ask which observable circumstances would weaken, reverse, or withdraw a judgment, not merely ‘we will reconsider if something changes’. SJ2 repair windows ask when correction remains possible, on what grounds, and when it expires. A window cannot be set by wish; if lost qualifications or opportunities are hard to recover, record that irreversibility in the ceiling rather than assuming a later apology suffices. [T-main]

SJ3 evidence requirements separate support, missingness, and contrary evidence. Contrary materials are not decorative appendices; they may change the judgment. SJ4 appeal entry specifies who can enter, who is responsible, processing time, and whether results can change. A mailing address without any possibility of changing records or pausing consequences is not an effective appeal. [T-main]

SJ5 protection against retaliation must define protected conduct, monitoring, independent reporting, and remedies. Merely writing ‘retaliation prohibited’ does not establish that low-power positions can actually speak safely. SJ6 the right to supplement evidence must permit submission, version correction, and downstream synchronization, rather than changing one database while other scores and rosters still implement the old error. Arrange privacy protection and checkable identities by matter; disclosure of all materials cannot be a condition of appeal. [T-main]

SJ7 external-review triggers specify when review starts, who is independent, and whether sufficient materials can be accessed and consequences stopped. A nominal outsider dependent on the assessed party's control of materials, personnel, or dismissal may lack substantive independence; check actual arrangements rather than organizational names. SJ8 rollback and write-back specify the state to return to, who repairs it, the authoritative version, and synchronization. Rollback may not restore already lost opportunities, so residual harms remain separately recorded. [T-main]

Only L3 with all seven gates and all eight items passed permits registering a strong-judgment candidate, still without actual authorization to act. Any missing item fails that judgment's IG6, preventing retention of the original high-impact use. It may be reduced to an internal hypothesis, open assertion, or candidate mechanism within the materials and actual uses allowed, not renamed while continuing the same action upon people. [T-main；T-seven]

Independent L2 comparisons that do not depend on the missing item or trigger strong judgment may remain, preventing local failure from canceling all materials; if a common premise fails, the dependent chain stops together. The eight items are not mutually compensable scores: seven perfect scores and one missing appeal do not qualify through a high average. Strong factual support also cannot offset protection or review gaps. [T-main]

The added point from the Knight order here is that ‘independence’ requires institutional conditions. The historical document requires consultant review and also specifies access to materials, implementation certification, follow-up checks, and restrictions on arbitrary dismissal and later relationships. It illustrates why review cannot stop at a title; the order's text proves neither implementation nor satisfaction of all SJ1—SJ8. [P-SEC]

The strongest objection is that eight items make emergencies too slow to address. Check waiting costs, the narrowest reversible requirements, monitoring, and valid external authority separately, without deleting objects, protection, or stopping conditions. Incomplete items lower the corresponding strong-judgment use; emergencies neither let tools create power nor force independently established low-impact descriptions into silence. [T-main；T-level]
argumentSteps: Determine triggering by use and foreseeable consequences, not tone or title.
Submit SJ1—SJ8 item by item, supporting contrary evidence, appeals, supplemental evidence, external review, and actual repair.
Judge each independently without compensating for missing items through an overall score.
A missing item fails the relevant IG6, stopping strong judgment and its original high-impact use; independent L2 is reviewed separately.
Even completeness yields only a strong-judgment candidate; actual action still requires choice, C12, J, and O checks.

13.6.title: 13.6 Diagnostic levels
13.6.lead: L1, L2, and L3 are levels of responsibility, not credibility rankings. The greater a task's effects, the more it needs traceable, refutable conditions and the ability to stop.
explanation: Chinese source location: lines 2917—2928; original-site location /theory/part-13#section-13-6. The current complete text is in the theory-v2 source; the historical research manuscript and excerpts remain available in their original versions for download and checking.

The source says ‘a higher level is not closer to truth’ (translated from Chinese). The same fact may have a reliable low-impact description, while a complex high-impact judgment may remain factually uncertain. Levels mainly organize use, reversibility, and procedural responsibilities; L3 cannot become a badge of authority, nor L1 permission to write facts carelessly. [T-main]

L1 suits lightweight description and exploratory questions with low complexity, low impact, reversibility, and limited information. Output stops at descriptions, questions, and the next observation—for example, registering a passage's source or identifying a material gap without packaging observation as a mechanism conclusion. It clarifies unknowns rather than using limited information as a back door to high-impact judgment. [T-main]

L2 is a standard reviewable judgment requiring structural comparison without entering action carrying high responsibility. It may offer bounded comparative judgments or candidate mechanisms, with clear conclusions, grounds, and counterexamples, without deliberate vagueness. If intended for named qualification, resource, or automated decisions, actual use has changed; the L2 label cannot be retained while continuing issuance. [T-main；T-SJ]

L3 concerns substantively high-impact judgments and judgments embedded in automated, organized, or institutional decisions; public dissemination also needs review of objects, factual accusations, identifiability, and consequences. Its ceiling is a strong-judgment candidate after the seven gates and eight-part package pass, not final action permission. Selecting L3 cannot skip gates or turn ‘stricter review will occur’ into ‘already passed’. [T-main; T-seven]

Downgrade triggers include reduced evidence coverage, object conversion, uncontrolled reflexivity, and failed appeal or anti-retaliation protections. Downgrading must change actual output and use, stopping dependent conclusions where needed; changing the cover from L3 to L2 while the automated pipeline keeps using it does not suffice. Object or use changes require review from the earliest affected gate, preserving old records and reasons. [T-main; T-seven]

Urgency removes neither object, protection, nor stopping conditions. Where waiting is costly, separately propose the narrowest withdrawable, monitorable action requirement, still subject to corresponding external authorization; ‘act first, fill in later’ is disallowed. If actual conditions prevent withdrawal, state irreversibility and limits rather than making an irreversible act reversible through wording. [T-main; T-record]

The Knight case adds that emergency response is not automatically correct. The SEC order records continuing orders during on-site troubleshooting and a code rollback worsening the problem. Time pressure still requires separating diagnosis, actions, and consequences. This guide does not retrospectively assign L levels or claim that tier rules necessarily prevent accidents. [P-SEC]

The strongest objection is excessive procedure in ordinary discussion. Distinguish actual use: proportionately recorded low-impact explanation can be explicit without all public content becoming L3. Conversely, gently titled scoring used in automated decisions still needs impact-based treatment. Reducing unnecessary burden and preventing evasion of responsibility can coexist. [T-main; T-SJ]
argumentSteps: Select the level by complexity, impact, reversibility, and actual use.
L1 retains descriptive questions; L2 offers bounded comparisons/mechanism candidates; L3 offers only strong-judgment candidates after itemwise gates.
Levels are neither truth values nor confidence; assess evidence separately.
Substantively downgrade and review use after coverage, object, reflexivity, or protection failures.
Urgency permits only the narrowest monitorable requirements; authority and stopping conditions remain.

13.7.title: 13.7 Six Formal Tools
13.7.lead: Each of six tools manages a kind of record. They can locate one another, but cannot serve as one another’s external evidence and circulate an unverified judgment into fact.
explanation: Source location: Chinese source lines 2929–2945, original-site location /theory/part-13#section-13-7. The current full text is in the theory-v2 source; the historical research draft and excerpts remain downloadable in their original versions.

These tools are formats and working methods for recording responsibilities, not a list of installed or necessarily executable software. Formal IDs provide stable references; names do not prove implemented functionality. Tools may share objects, sources, and versions while preserving material status and support scope. [T-main]

TOOL-EVIDENCE-LEDGER separates sources, material, observations, evidence, counterexamples, coverage, and uncertainty. It answers ‘Where are the grounds, which sentence do they support, and to what limit?’ A URL cannot mark a claim supported. Repeated references to one source remain one dependency, not independent validations. [T-main]

TOOL-OPEN-ASSERTION records a temporary judgment target open to challenge, falsification, and withdrawal. Explicitness makes it more testable than vague impressions but does not permit high-responsibility action. TOOL-CLAIM-VALIDATION further checks claim type, evidence, counterevidence, falsification conditions, impact, and ceilings; the former’s ‘registered’ cannot substitute for the latter’s substantive validation. [T-main]

TOOL-FORECAST-REGISTRY freezes predictions, windows, triggers, early and contrary signals, and revision targets. Freezing does not make a forecast correct; it prevents changed goals from contaminating later evaluation. Failed predictions must write back to related claims, not delete failed versions and claim they were always scenarios. Without the foresight contract, retain conditional-scenario status; a registry cannot generate eligibility for a hit. [T-main; T-dynamic]

TOOL-STRESS-TEST uses boundary cases, adversarial explanations, and scale changes to find failures and narrow scope. Internal constructions may refute unconditional logical leaps or reveal format/model defects, but do not establish real parameters or mechanisms. The original calls it ‘a wind tunnel’, a metaphor separating testing from external empirical support, not an actual wind-tunnel experiment. [T-main]

TOOL-AI-BOUNDARY requires disclosure of sources, material gaps, human responsible parties, uncertainty, prohibited uses, and review/withdrawal. It cannot cleanse unqualified content with a disclaimer: body text and actual use must respect ceilings. Responsibilities follow division of labor rather than assigning everything to the last person who clicks. [T-main; T-AI]

Automatic validation suits closed fields, resolvable references, consistent versions/states, and recalculation; it cannot replace material authentication, affected-party testimony, causal identification, or value choice. An openable source path establishes at most accessibility; source support and factual grounds still need checks. Logs may remain separately locatable from the text so readers see decisive reasons, not only pass counts. [T-main]

The Knight order adds a distinction about what certification wording claims: a process’s existence differs from controls meeting requirements. Text inspection may locate a statement difference, while actual control quality needs further material. This does not mean a regex can certify compliance or complete logs eliminate risk. [P-SEC]

The strongest objection is duplicated work across six tools. Shared record IDs can avoid copying the body six times, but circular self-certification is forbidden. If a ledger cites only a validation form and that form cites only the ledger, the closed loop adds no empirical support without external material. Reuse preserves dependencies and copying adds no independence; tools expose gaps rather than eliminate their names. [T-main]

The ledger preserves source-to-claim support chains; open assertions retain temporary status.
Assertion registration does not replace claim validation; failed foresight writes back to the original version.
Stress tests and AI boundaries expose failure conditions without using internal processes to certify reality.
Programs check form and arithmetic; people check material/testimony/causation/value; cross-tool references cannot self-certify circularly.

13.8.title: 13.8 Boundaries on AI Use
13.8.lead: AI may produce complete analyses, recommendations, and plans, while making material, inference, responsibility, and use explicit at every step. Generating text is neither consenting for people nor gaining authority to act in reality.
explanation: Source location: Chinese source lines 2946–2955, original-site location /theory/part-13#section-13-8. The current full text is in the theory-v2 source; the historical research draft and excerpts remain downloadable in their original versions.

The original does not limit AI to copying tables and checking formats. It may organize material, check fields, compare versions, generate questions, compare mechanisms, list alternatives, and, where evidence and normative premises permit, form refutable judgments, recommend options, and draft complete institutional plans and commentary. Boundaries come from material and use, not permission to output only blank templates or never conclude. [T-main]

Each prohibition targets a different overreach: fabricated sources undermine traceability; training memory treated as current evidence confuses versions and timeliness; consenting for people or equating silence with consent removes their expressive position; replacing decision or authorization bodies confuses advice with authority; hidden uncertainty expands judgment ceilings; independent high-risk real decisions cross protection and execution responsibilities. AI’s usefulness cannot erase these differences, nor does risk justify rejecting every low-impact analysis. [T-main]

Each output should identify used material, gaps, observation/inference/analogy, final judgment responsibility, permitted uses, and review/withdrawal timing. Not every process log must enter body text, but key reasons and limits must be visible and details locatable. A final ‘for reference only’ does not repair unsupported definite accusations in the body or actual high-impact use. [T-main; T-tools]

Separate protective omission from absent evidence. Identity exposure, retaliation risk, or justified opacity may require withholding details; a public version should safely mark limits rather than fill protected positions as nonexistent. Conversely, ‘privacy’ cannot universally shield uncheckable claims; appropriate controlled verification routes and conclusion ceilings are needed. [T-main; T-missing]

Responsibility falls, according to the actual division of work, on material providers, those who determine goals and authority, system maintainers, executors, and reviewers. Technical facilities and programs do not become subjects capable of bearing moral or legal responsibility simply by producing recommendations or performing actions; organizations with particular institutional status must be assessed separately for the matter concerned. Neither anthropomorphize programs nor infer from this that organizations bear no responsibility. [T-main]

“A human clicks at the end” is not enough to establish effective review. Reviewers must have sufficient materials, time, capability, and stopping authority that can actually take effect; organizations must provide resources. If workloads exceed checking capacity, the system withholds original grounds, or irreversible action has already occurred by the time of the click, nominal human involvement cannot eliminate these breaks. Nor does this concentrate all responsibility on that reviewer. [T-main]

The 2024 NIST document on generative AI risks also sets out the division of roles, documentation, feedback and remedies, and monitoring and escalation as suggested actions, and discusses confabulation risks. This is an actual example of a public governance text, illustrating that review requires arrangements rather than a slogan. This lesson does not treat the document as an effectiveness trial or certification of any AI product’s accuracy. [P-NIST]

The strongest objection worries that responsibility for materials prevents AI from producing substantive content. The appropriate approach is to state supported bounded conclusions, complete feasible analysis and full drafts, and identify key gaps and conditions that could change the judgment; when real action is involved, proceed under valid authority. Protective boundaries should improve the quality of texts and proposals, not become an excuse to repeat disclaimers without completing the requested work. [T-main]
argumentSteps: Determine the requested content deliverable and its actual use; distinguish analysis, recommendations, and drafts from real decisions.
Use traceable materials; label observations, inferences, analogies, and gaps. Do not present training memory as current verification.
When evidence and normative premises support them, provide complete bounded judgments and texts, not merely frameworks.
Record responsibilities according to the division of work; review requires materials, time, capability, and effective stopping authority.
List protective omissions separately; specify prohibited uses and the practical feasibility of review and withdrawal. Do not consent or authorize on others’ behalf.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: a review-capacity calculation
teachingExamples.text: A human team must review 120 AI summaries per day, with at least 5 minutes per summary required to check original materials: total demand is 600 minutes. One reviewer has 360 working minutes available. Without parallel assistance or a reduced workload, the shortfall is 240 minutes; at most 72 summaries can be reviewed to that standard. Conditional proposals may add resources, limit use, or adjust the workflow, but 120 button clicks cannot count as five minutes of verification for every summary.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Times and staffing are constructed; reviews are sequential and each requires 5 minutes, excluding other work. This is not an actual productivity study.
teachingExamples.boundary: The capacity calculation does not judge whether real employees failed in their duties, nor authorize forced overtime or reductions in necessary review.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: keeping a complete draft separate from authorization
teachingExamples.text: The constructed request is to draft a procedure for supplementing evidence. AI can provide complete provisions on submission scope, recipients, evidence access, deadlines, protection against retaliation, version synchronization, and withdrawal conditions, while marking resources and authority still to be decided. The draft can be reviewed and used, but “the draft is complete” does not mean the organization has adopted it, assigned authority, or obtained the parties’ consent.
teachingExamples.assumptions: A constructed institution; no actual publication or configuration.
teachingExamples.boundary: Complete delivery and actual adoption are different endpoints; boundaries do not justify omitting requested draft content.

13.9.title: 13.9 Execution records and failure semantics
13.9.lead: Execution records let readers see what passed, what failed, what was not run, and the maximum permissible use of a report. They are auditable records of judgment and handoff, not automatically generated licenses.
explanation: Source location: Chinese source lines 2956–2967; original site location /theory/part-13#section-13-9. See the theory-v2 source for the current full text; historical research drafts and excerpts remain available for checking in their original downloadable versions.

“Field closure” in flow_execution_record means that every dimension required for recording has an explicit place; ad hoc notes cannot bypass statuses and ceilings. Object and scale, L1–L3, IT1–IT4, IG1–IG7, diagnostic elaboration and SJ triggering, as well as evidence, alternative explanations, uncertainty, categories, judgment/action ceilings, normative handoff, appeals, rollback, and statuses must all be checkable. Complete fields establish only formal completeness; claims within them still require corresponding materials. [T-main]

The three closed output ceilings are description_only, diagnostic_only, and requirements_only, bounded respectively by description, diagnosis, and requirements. The specific categories allowed at each level must be checked against the fixed rules of the implementation used; callers cannot ad hoc add “execution instructions.” All three fix can_authorize=false and can_execute=false. This section of the original does not enumerate each level’s full category set; this explanation does not invent an official enumeration and present it as the original. [T-main]

action_requirements states conditions that external choice and authorization procedures must satisfy, such as required evidence, protections, responsibilities, and stopping paths. It has no execution effect. Even if free text in a report says “authorized,” it cannot alter the closed Boolean values, still less permit downstream systems to read only that sentence while ignoring authority fields. [T-main；T-seven]

Normative handoff should link to verifiable external choice, C12, and authorization records, or explicitly identify what is missing. Object, action, scope, time, and actual verification grounds must match the current use. “The committee approved it” does not identify which object, when, or which actions were approved; circularly citing this record’s own “verified” status adds no external grounds. Formats may vary across implementations; verification responsibility does not. [T-main]

Statuses first distinguish execution facts: passed means the gate in that record passed, not that a proposition about the world is true; failed means it was actually run and did not pass; not_run means an earlier gate or the scope prevented it from running. When an earlier gate fails, later dependent steps cannot pretend to have been checked; failed especially cannot be rewritten as not_applicable to erase failure. Another judgment with independent grounds still requires independent review; one cannot copy the failed chain and revive it under a new name. [T-main；T-seven；T-IT]

The four missingness states answer different questions: unknown means currently unknown; not_applicable means inapplicable for a stated reason; not_observable means currently unobservable; withheld_for_protection means withheld for protection. These are neither a bad-to-good ranking nor four aliases for a null value. Inability to disclose protected materials does not mean the matter does not exist; protective status cannot automatically be recorded as “nonexistent.” [T-main；T-missing]

authorization_effect is always none. Even with complete external normative choice, C12, J, and O records, the tool only checks and hands off existing grounds. Valid external authority may exist, but this record is not its source. Normative legitimacy, authority scope, execution resources, and stopping conditions still require separate checks. The record’s lack of authorizing effect does not negate genuinely established external authorization; conversely, an external label cannot make this record issue authorization itself. [T-main]

Reviewed outputs must also retain accessible appeals and practical withdrawal/correction paths. Tool conclusions that cannot be withdrawn must not enter high-impact uses that are difficult to reverse. Withdrawal involves more than changing the report title: it must allow correction of records and uses that actually adopted the conclusion. Where consequences already incurred cannot be fully reversed, residual effects must be stated and remedial needs proposed. The strongest objection says rigorous records are cumbersome; the appropriate response is concise main text with locatable details, not deletion of failures or authority checks. [T-main；T-tools；T-endpoint]

Paragraph 51M of the SEC Knight order requires narrative and attachments to support certification of compliance and allows requests for further evidence. This concretely illustrates the difference between “claimed complete” and “checkable grounds.” However, the order specifies external regulatory requirements; it is not an instance of this lesson’s record, and its text alone cannot establish actual completion. The case serves only this local comparison of auditable requirements. [P-SEC]
argumentSteps: Fix the object, scale, use, and level; record conversions, gates, and applicable procedures item by item.
Match each result to its actual execution or missingness status; mark subsequent steps dependent on failure as not_run.
Narrow ceilings according to fixed output categories; authorization and execution Booleans are false at all three levels.
Check external records’ object, action, scope, time, and grounds; explicitly record any missing elements.
Keep authorization_effect as none; provide actually accessible appeals, correction, and withdrawal paths.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: a local record of failure and nonexecution
teachingExamples.text: For constructed proposition Q, IT1 obtains a signal; IT2 is marked failed because source status cannot be verified, and dependent IT3/IT4 are marked not_run. The record may still describe the obtained materials whose status is unverified and the gaps, but cannot form the strong judgment originally dependent on that source. If another proposition R relies on independently verifiable sources, its evidence and use must be listed separately; R’s passing cannot be used to rewrite Q.

teachingExamples.boundary: If the status gap affects a shared foundation, R is also blocked; independence must have grounds.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: conflict between authority fields and free text
teachingExamples.text: A constructed record has output_ceiling=requirements_only, can_authorize=false, can_execute=false, and authorization_effect=none. Its author writes in a note, “All authority has been obtained; execute immediately.” The note conflicts with the ceiling and should be removed or revised into the required external verification conditions. If a separate record A exists, cite it only when object, action, scope, period, and grounds match; false cannot be changed to true.

13.10.title: 13.10 Nine gates for multi-circle projection
13.10.lead: The nine gates dynamically elaborate on the seven gates: from freezing facts through branching, foresight, choice, handoff, and write-back. They make conditional paths open to questioning, but cannot turn conditional stories into validated predictions or permission to execute.
explanation: Source location: Chinese source lines 2968–2985; original site location /theory/part-13#section-13-10. See the theory-v2 source for the current full text; historical research drafts and excerpts remain available for checking in their original downloadable versions.

The seven gates remain the sole main process for explanation and diagnosis. DF1–DF9 are expanded only when the task explicitly requires dynamic projection, conditional foresight, or bounded choice. Ordinary descriptions need not run all nine gates merely to appear comprehensive, nor may the nine gates bypass objects, evidence, affected parties, power, reflexivity, strong judgments, or action ceilings. Every output dependent on upstream failure remains constrained by the main process. [T-main；T-seven]

DF1, fact freezing, first fixes event types, sources, times, the evidence cutoff, and disputes. It freezes the materials available and the judgment version for this run, not a claim that disputes have been settled; later evidence may open a new version. If it fails, provide a list of factual questions to avoid retrospectively rewriting what was originally known after learning the outcome. DF2, the joint object, then checks actors, circles, relations, members, and K; if it fails, retain only candidate groupings or return to a single focus. Lines on a diagram do not create membership binding on other people. [T-main]

DF3, dual channels and clocks, records only task-relevant material and experiential–meaning conditions, their corresponding times, and unknowns. Irrelevant items may be marked inapplicable with reasons; not every task mandates investigating inner experience. Where conditions are missing, retain the snapshot and pause propagation dependent on them, reviewing genuinely independent paths separately. Entering 0 for “unknown experience” replaces missingness with a measurement. A shared date should not conceal different update cycles across multiple clocks. [T-main；T-clock]

DF4 mechanism propagation requires channels, thresholds, delays, feedback, and cascades; drawing arrows between correlated variables does not prove causation. On failure, list candidate mechanisms and observations that could distinguish them. DF5 path branching links conditions, parent/child nodes, and early and contrary signals. Where conditions are insufficiently distinguished, retain parallel paths without forced rankings or invented probabilities. Tool-proposed DF2 circles and DF5 variables remain candidate and cannot automatically upgrade without external evidence. [T-main]

DF6 forecast registration must specify targets, deadlines, simple baselines, calibration, and write-back. Without these, the output is only scenario projection and must not masquerade as prediction through “will” or “expected hit” wording. Registration does not guarantee a hit: outcomes still require comparison under prespecified windows and metrics. One smaller error establishes neither cross-context calibration nor stable gain; failures also enter the record. [T-main; T-tools]

DF7 normative choice checks N, PF, affected people, options, and inaction. Pause recommendations specifically blocked by gaps while retaining independently grounded evaluations, conditional advice with explicit premises, and evidence needs. Do not erase all factual analysis or smuggle in a premise-free uniquely optimal option. Predictive accuracy alone cannot justify choice; a low-error option may still breach the protection floor. [T-main]

DF8 authorization and execution checks J, O, responsibilities, stopping, rollback, and remedies; failure means external handoff without execution. Failed DF7 or DF8 cannot produce executable instructions. Even with conditions complete, §13.9 prohibits the tool from generating authorization; actual execution occurs under valid external permissions and procedures. Action reversibility must be realized in the relevant system; the words “can roll back” are not an operational safeguard. [T-main; T-record]

DF9 outcome write-back records outcomes, baseline comparisons, deviations, downgrading, and retirement. It must preserve failures and open new versions rather than overwrite the original run with corrected normal output. A path weakened by contrary signals should be narrowed or retired, not reinterpret every outcome as “anticipated all along.” New versions may still repair it; one failure is not permanent inability to learn. [T-main]

The Knight order records inconsistent deployment across eight servers, leaving old and new processing paths in parallel, followed by code removal that worsened the problem. This helps locate state, branching, and response-feedback checks, but our reading is retrospective: it cannot backfill DF6 forecasts for participants or prove the nine gates could prevent the accident. The case provides only bounded teaching comparisons against verified historical paths. [P-SEC]

The strongest objection is that nine gates turn analysis into lengthy procedure. The answer is not mechanically filling nine boxes: enable dynamic expansion according to the task, using conditions that actually affect judgment. Explain known non-applicability, preserve unknowns, and deliver explicit conditional branches for pure scenarios. Complexity must yield reviewable boundaries rather than procedural names replacing substantive explanation. [T-main]
argumentSteps: First preserve the seven-gate main process and the current object's evidence and use, confirming that the task needs dynamic expansion.
DF1 freezes material; DF2 checks joint objects; DF3 distinguishes relevant dual channels and clocks.
DF4 establishes testable candidate mechanisms; DF5 retains conditional branches and early/contrary signals.
Without complete foresight conditions, DF6 remains a scenario; registration still requires baseline comparison and write-back.
DF7 independently checks values and protection; DF8 checks external permissions and execution conditions, issuing no instructions on failure.
DF9 preserves original runs, outcomes, and failures, opens new versions, and permits downgrading or retirement.

teachingExamples.text: An artificial service system analyzes only request congestion. Path A: increased arrival rate, with larger arrival counts as an early signal. teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: outcome write-back and a baseline

Changing the forecast to 8 requires new version r2, not overwriting r1 to claim zero error.

13.11.title: 13.11 AI Boundaries in Dynamic Operation
13.11.lead: AI can help clarify, calculate, and compare dynamic problems and write complete recommendations. Its generated classifications, simulations, and self-reports cannot alone certify world facts or determine other people's rights boundaries.
explanation: Chinese source location: lines 2986–2993; original-site location /theory/part-13#section-13-11. See the theory-v2 source for the current full text; the historical research manuscript and excerpts remain downloadable in their original versions.

This section governs two elaborations: 13.11.1 separates evidence for material checking from tool actions, and 13.11.2 grounds task endpoints, concurrency, retries, and stopping conditions in checkable objects. Together they require AI to complete grounded substantive work without treating fluent text as proof that the external world changed. [T-main; T-check; T-end]

Permitted work includes organizing material, checking locatable original text, identifying missing fields, generating and comparing competing paths, checking contract consistency, and calculating registered metrics. Explicit normative premises also permit grounded local judgments, recommendations, and complete texts. Scope is not confined to questions or templates; conclusions must remain tied to supporting objects, information, periods, and uses. [T-main]

A model saying “I verified it,” internal scores, or repeatedly generating the same answer cannot alone certify actual events. External material is not uniformly trustworthy either; distinguish its status, methods, counterexamples, and uses. Faithfully reporting a source establishes reporting accuracy, not automatically the truth of that source's claims. Separating them allows precise statements about completed steps and remaining evidential gaps. [T-main; T-check]

Prohibitions protect facts, subjects, and permissions separately: do not diagnose personality from text, disclose information for others, impose binding circle boundaries through one's own classification, treat simulation as fact, determine disputed value premises for others, or issue authorization. Analyzing observable behavior differs from concluding personality; proposing candidate classifications differs from letting classifications determine treatment. These distinctions enable useful work within boundaries. [T-main]

When AI proposes variables automatically, record their model-candidate status, minimal tests, and prohibited uses. “Communication delay may explain request backlog,” for example, remains a candidate requiring observable timestamps, comparison conditions, and alternative mechanisms; it cannot directly become a capability score for a particular person. Without corresponding external evidence, retain candidate, regardless of attractive graphics or repeated generation. [T-main; T-dynamic]

The NIST 2024 document discusses erroneous generated content, including false logic or citations offered in support, and recommends responsibility arrangements. It is used here as an existing risk-governance text illustrating why evidence checks matter, not to estimate any product's current error rate or infer that all AI output is wrong because risk exists. [P-NIST]

The strongest objection is that AI's inability to certify independently would leave it unable to do anything. Locatable citations, transparent calculations, condition comparisons, and complete drafting are substantive outputs. Certification boundaries require accurate claims of completion, not denial of those outputs. Conversely, where actual external evidence and valid permissions are established, generic disclaimers should not obscure a supportable clear conclusion. [T-main]
argumentSteps: Specify the dynamic task, object, material, and use, keeping normative premises explicit.
Complete locatable checks, candidate comparisons, registered-metric calculations, and required full texts.
Separate observations, model candidates, simulations, and empirical judgments, marking minimal tests and prohibited uses.
Do not disclose for others, settle disputed values, issue permissions, or let classifications determine others' eligibility.
Use 13.11.1 to check material and actions, and 13.11.2 to check corresponding task endpoints.

13.11.1.title: 13.11.1 AI Material Checking and Tool-Action Chains
13.11.1.lead: Finding a source still leaves questions about citation accuracy, whether the original passage supports the statement, and whether world facts have sufficient grounds. Tool actions likewise require separating “completed” in text from actual completed execution.
explanation: Chinese source location: lines 2994–3001; original-site location /theory/part-13#section-13-11-1. See the theory-v2 source for the current full text; the historical research manuscript and excerpts remain downloadable in their original versions.

The four material checks have independent objects. First, does the source actually exist and can it be located? Second, are author, title, date, page numbers, and other citation details correct? Third, does the passage in context and under its limits support the current sentence? Fourth, does the reality described by that sentence have sufficient grounds? Passing one does not automatically carry over to the next: a real article can be miscited, and a faithful quotation can transmit source error. [T-check]

If a given source does not mention a fact, one can only say that this source does not support the statement, not that the statement must be false. An explicit denial backed by method is a different kind of evidence. Local knowledge, oral accounts, and protected material do not cease to exist because they lack a public webpage. Appropriate identity, timing, cross-checking, and controlled access can be designed without requiring all sensitive details to be published for traceability. [T-check]

Retrieval augmentation can help obtain material, and consistency or uncertainty detection may identify some errors, but effects depend on retrieval coverage, shared sources, and error types. This section explains limits of these functions; it supplies no improvement estimate for any system. Reproducible errors can also be highly consistent. Multiple models repeating the same inaccurate source do not constitute multiple independent empirical supports. [T-check]

A formal checker can confirm a derivation under explicit premises. For example, a=2 and b=3 imply a+b=5, but correct calculation does not prove that a real warehouse contains 2 and 3 items. The checker's conditional conclusion remains useful; responsibility for establishing its premises must stay with the corresponding factual verification. Formal correctness and empirical truth must neither be merged nor used to negate each other. [T-check]

The action chain separates recommendation, tool request, application execution, external state, and consequences. A model saying “stopped” is only generated text; check whether a specific stop request exists, whether the executor received it, whether in-flight actions terminated, and what happened to consequences. A deletion status in the interface does not prove downstream copies disappeared, and withdrawing a recommendation does not guarantee taking effect before an irreversible action. [T-check；T-end]

Actual protection and correction permissions must be exercisable in the relevant system. A reviewer with only a comment box and no effective stopping channel cannot treat comments as an execution brake. Even a brake button requires knowing which queues and stages it controls. Human involvement does not automatically mean edits propagated in time. This connects to §13.8's requirements for material, time, capability, and stopping resources. [T-check；T-human]

NIST2024 §2.2 explicitly discusses confabulation that can include logic or citations. This supports verifying explanatory prose too, rather than substituting explanation length for source support. It is itself a risk document, not proof that this lesson's four checks eliminate every error or that a factual audit has been completed. [P-NIST]

The strongest objection is that endless source checking would prevent any conclusion from being delivered. The four checks should target the factual importance and intended use of the task, stating current support and remaining gaps. A task requiring only accurate representation of a document can finish at that representation, but must not incidentally claim that every worldly fact in the document has been verified. A bounded endpoint can genuinely be completed; its conditions must be explicit. [T-check；T-end]
argumentSteps: Locate the source and check citation identity and version.
Return to the original passage's context and check support scope and qualifications sentence by sentence.
Separately verify worldly facts according to their importance to the task; do not equate absence of mention with falsity.
Check source independence, coverage, and counterexamples; formal checking proves only derivations within explicit premises.
For actions, separately verify recommendations, requests, execution, external state, and consequences; stopping and correction must be practically exercisable.

13.11.2.title: 13.11.2 Task endpoints and verifiable execution chains
13.11.2.lead: Completion must match the endpoint the user requested: delivering a draft, changing an external record, and actually delivering a remedy are different tasks. Verifying the required endpoint accurately avoids treating receipts as outcomes or delaying narrow tasks indefinitely.
explanation: Source location: Chinese source lines 3002–3019; original site location /theory/part-13#section-13-11-2. See the theory-v2 source for the current full text; the historical research original and excerpts remain available for download and checking in their original versions.

The task endpoint is determined by the user's request or the institutional task. If only a draft is requested, saving it correctly, making it openable, and satisfying content requirements can complete delivery. Changing an external record also requires checking the target object's state. Delivering a remedy further requires checking that resources, rights, or services arrive. Consequence requirements for a broad task cannot negate completion of a narrow task, and success on a narrow task cannot replace an unfinished broad task. [T-end]

The recommendation-formation layer checks the target, material, object to be changed, and permitted scope, preventing generation from being mistaken for adoption. The tool-request layer checks action, parameters, current version, and permissions, preventing a correct recommendation from being sent to the wrong object. The application-execution layer checks receipt, execution or refusal, and duplicate-request semantics; delivery and queueing are not yet execution success. [T-end]

The external-state layer checks whether the target and dependent objects changed as expected, avoiding a local label update while actual execution still reads old state. The task-consequence layer checks the specified benefit/protection endpoint and residuals: correcting a record may be complete, but a request to remedy a lost opportunity also requires checking whether the opportunity, resources, or service actually recovered. Not every correction fully reverses consequences; residuals must be retained honestly. [T-end]

For concurrency, first distinguish independent reads, independent modifications, and shared writes to the same object. Shared-state modifications require ordering, version preconditions, or conflict handling. Two individually permitted actions do not justify ignoring lost updates from simultaneous overwrites. Before irreversible action, recheck that permissions and stopping conditions remain valid; initial permission does not necessarily cover subsequent changes in object, use, or deadline. [T-end]

A request timeout only means no definite result arrived within the waiting window. Execution may not have happened, may be underway, or may have finished with its receipt lost. Do not assume non-execution and repeat the action. First check by request identifier or object state, then decide whether to retry. Where a system provides an idempotency contract, handle the same request under that actual contract; do not mistake a new identifier for a retry of the old request. All applications need not share one log format. [T-end；P-AWS]

The AWS technical article explains uncertainty after a timeout, introduces client request identifiers for distinguishing duplicate requests, and discusses rejecting different parameters under the same identifier. It publicly describes concrete technical semantics. Its timeout scenario is hypothetical, not an actual incident. This lesson did not operate any interface or verify production performance. [P-AWS]

Stopping has at least four separate items: issuing the stop, executor confirmation, termination of in-flight actions, and remedying consequences already produced. If the first two pass, report only “stop sent and receipt confirmed,” not that all tasks and side effects have disappeared. This does not deny the first two steps' progress; it preserves the endpoints still requiring verification. [T-end]

Stopping the main task does not mean removing all subsequent protections. If safe withdrawal still requires bounded actions, continue under their independent responsibilities, permissions, and actual conditions—for example, checking in-flight status or preserving necessary evidence. Do not restart the stopped main task under the pretext of withdrawal. A repair failure must retain the failed object and real-world consequences; new normal outputs must not overwrite them. [T-end]

The strongest objection is that layered verification might pursue consequences throughout a person's life without end. The source explicitly bounds verification by the requested endpoint: verify the draft for draft delivery, the target and necessary dependencies for a record change, and the specified arrival only for remedy delivery. A good completion report states completed layers, unknowns, and residuals item by item, neither overpromising nor hiding what has actually been completed. [T-end]
argumentSteps: First state the task endpoint and acceptance object, distinguishing content delivery, record changes, and remedy arrival.
Use the five-layer chain to check target parameters, versions, permissions, receipt and execution, target and dependent states, and required consequences.
Distinguish independent reads/independent modifications/shared writes; preserve order or check version conflicts for shared writes.
Record timeout as unknown; verify by request identifier/object before deciding on retry, without blindly repeating actions.
Check stopping item by item: sending, confirmation, in-flight termination, and consequence remedies. Bounded safe withdrawal needs independent grounds.
Report reached endpoints and residuals; retain failures and new versions without overwriting history.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: lost updates and version verification
teachingExamples.text: A constructed shared document v1 contains value 10. A reads v1 intending to add 2; B also reads v1 intending to add 3. If each overwrites the whole value with 12 and 13, the final value may be only 13, losing A's update. If the task requires preserving both increments, the correct total is 10+2+3=15. One approach rejects B's stale write on a version mismatch, rereads v2, and merges under the still-valid task.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Constructed integers and whole-value overwrite semantics. Not every concurrent write loses updates, and no system was actually configured.
teachingExamples.boundary: 15 holds only if both increments should be retained and authorization remains valid; rechecking cannot let the algorithm expand its own permissions.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: genuine completion at different endpoints
teachingExamples.text: Constructed user A requests only a scheduling draft. The saved file opens and meets content requirements, so draft completion can be reported, but not notification of employees. User B wants a system record corrected; besides a success receipt, the target and relevant caches must be read back. User C requests a missed service be made up; even after the record changes, service arrival and residual harm still require checking. The three cannot substitute for one another.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Constructed requests, files, and services; no actual user data or real-world actions.
teachingExamples.boundary: This does not require every draft to be executed; the actual request determines the task endpoint.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: reporting stopping by layer
teachingExamples.text: A constructed queue sends a stop at t=1; the executor confirms at t=2; at t=3, tasks already taken from the queue remain in flight; termination is verified only at t=5. At t=2, report only that the request was confirmed. At t=5, report in-flight termination within the checked scope. If erroneous records were already publicly displayed before t=1, they still require correction on independent grounds and verification of arrival. Stopping the main queue does not establish that all consequences disappeared.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Constructed times and queue; no actual shutdown, deletion, or external sending occurred.
teachingExamples.boundary: Completion can be declared only within the verified scope; separately list grounds for safe withdrawal and residual issues.

intro-14-part.title: Part Fourteen: Normative Choice
intro-14-part.lead: Explaining how an object operates and deciding who may change it in what ways are different questions. Part Fourteen openly brings together the values, protections, permissions, and failure repairs involved in choice for review.
explanation: Source location: Chinese source lines 3020–3035; original site location: this part's introduction (no separately numbered anchor). See the theory-v2 source for the current full text; the historical research original and excerpts remain available for download and checking in their original versions.

The preceding structural grammar, empirical question families, scales, mechanisms, and human variables mainly bear descriptive and explanatory obligations. This part separately asks who may choose, on what grounds, whom the choice constrains, and how failure is stopped and repaired. The former provide important material for choice, but are not the latter's source of authorization. [T-intro]

A reliable explanation may still permit several feasible directions. That a measure improves efficiency does not answer who receives the benefits, who bears the price, who has the right to decide, or whether minimum rights protections are crossed. Widespread support does not erase these questions. Normative choice is therefore an independent contract layer between explanation and real-world action, rather than an appended “implementation recommended” at the end of a report. [T-intro]

The following sections distinguish, in order, facts from oughts; system, actor, and governance selection; N premises; options including inaction; genuine choice and representation; J and O procedures; status correction; the ten PF protections; cross-circle distribution; and non-domination. These are not multiple indicators of one score: strong facts, good objectives, extensive procedures, sufficient authority, and actual protection each require their own grounds. [T-intro; T-main; T-types; T-PF]

“Independent” does not mean that prior factual analysis is useless. Facts and uncertainty determine feasibility, expected consequences, and risks; normative premises select which values warrant pursuit or prohibition; authority determines who may act within what scope. Once these responsibilities are separated, clear, conditional proposals remain possible, rather than stopping indefinitely at “values are complex.” [T-main]

The 1979 Belmont Report is an actual normative document that publicly states ethical premises, distinguishing respect for persons, beneficence, and justice. It provides a textual example of values and protective reasons; it does not automatically derive the justification of all research from scientific benefits. We neither equate these three principles directly with Xikari's N/PF nor use them to approve any specific project. [P-BEL]

v2 divides this part into three levels. Principles of argument apply to normative judgments and analytical recommendations offered for deliberation; valid authorization and the substantive content of the ten protections constrain real-world adoption; recording formats such as field counts and numbering constrain the framework's own authorized records. Other implementations may use different formats but bear equivalent responsibilities for protection, traceability, and review; equivalence must undergo independent review.

The test is not whether a field looks technical: if deleting an item changes who is protected, who bears the price, who has authority to decide, or who can stop or correct an action, it remains a substantive requirement. A bounded recommendation may first present its reasoning in full; passing format checks does not automatically confer real-world authority.
argumentSteps: First distinguish whether the current question concerns explanation or a binding choice.
Retain reliable facts while listing questions about beneficiaries, those bearing the burdens, protection, and authority that still require independent answers.

14.1.title: 14.1 Facts Cannot Yield Oughts
14.1.lead: “More efficient” is an important fact, but “should be adopted” additionally requires publicly stated values, protection, and authority. Facts can change reasons for choice; they cannot supply these premises themselves.
explanation: Chinese source location: lines 3036–3045; original site location /theory/part-14#section-14-1. For the current full text, see the theory-v2 source; historical research manuscripts and excerpts remain available for checking in their original downloadable versions.

Factual propositions describe what is; normative premises specify what merits pursuit, protection, or prohibition. Stability, efficiency, retention, and rising risks cannot individually yield an ought. This does not mean facts and values have no connection; it requires the additional value premises in the inference to be made public. Facts can rule out impossible options and revise expected consequences and risk judgments, but they do not select values or create authorization by themselves. [T-main]

O1 first freezes the facts, evidence, scales, and uncertainties to be used, preventing evidence from being retroactively altered after a favored option is chosen. O2 registers the N1–N5 premises adopted this time, value conflicts, beneficiaries, and those bearing the burdens. This identifies which N premises are actually adopted and their roles; merely writing all five terms does not complete it. N1 is only a veto gate preventing a direct leap from facts to action; it cannot independently generate a positive proposal. [T-main; T-N; T-C12]

O3 compares options including inaction and checks the J axis, authorization, jurisdiction, duration, and conflicts of interest; an independent normative-choice record then freezes the decision. Options may differ in the distribution of benefits and the price paid in rights. A single ranking by overall efficiency cannot justify ignoring those who bear the burdens. [T-main; T-options]

Only O4 turns an approved option into bounded execution: reversible, monitorable, stoppable, open to appeal, capable of rollback, and subject to expiration. This does not require a draft recommendation to have been implemented before drafting can be completed; it specifies the conditions for moving from a recommendation pending review to real-world adoption. A grounded recommendation must disclose premises, evidence, and prices to be paid; the absence of real-world implementation permission does not justify providing only a blank template. [T-main; T-C12]

“A severe diagnosis” does not cancel the conversion chain, and “a highly confident model” does not expand authority. Stronger evidence may raise the ceiling for descriptive judgment, but the action ceiling remains constrained by independent norms, protection, J, and O. If an independently valid external duty exists in an emergency, it should be handled within its own scope; severity of diagnosis does not create emergency powers out of nothing. [T-main; T-J]

C12 checks whether the bridge is valid; it does not decide values for people. It requires descriptive conclusions, current evidence, explicit N premises, conflicts, protection, authorization, options including inaction, O procedures, an action ceiling, and provisions for stopping, review, rollback, and remedy. Minimal harm and proportionality must be explicitly selected, explained, and reviewed in the specific choice record; they are not universal value answers silently embedded in C12. [T-main; T-C12; T-options]

The randomized comparison in Cash and Counseling provides empirical material about a combined opportunity within a specific volunteer sample and a nine-month window, with proxy and generalizability limitations. Recommending service arrangements on that basis still requires normative reasons such as valuing autonomy or reducing unmet needs, local feasibility, protection, and authority. The study's effects cannot be presented as requiring everyone to enter this model, and a combined opportunity certainly cannot be decomposed into a single-factor effect of choice alone. [P-CC]

The strongest objection is that saying facts cannot yield oughts invalidates every recommendation. A proper, complete argument is: under the stated values and constraints, given these bounded facts and the consequences of inaction, this option has these advantages and risks; actual adoption then requires verification of valid authority and execution conditions. Such reasoning can make a clear recommendation while accepting revision under different value premises or new facts. [T-main]
argumentSteps: Identify factual statements and normative premises; do not use efficiency, stability, or risk to fill in values.
O1 fixes facts, evidence, scales, and unknowns; O2 discloses the N premises actually adopted, conflicts, and cost-bearing positions.
O3 compares options including inaction, checks J/authority/jurisdiction/duration/conflicts, and independently freezes the choice.
Explicitly select minimal harm and proportionality, checking the C12 bridge item by item without letting it select values on anyone's behalf.
After approval, O4 bounds execution, correction, and expiration; a recommendation pending review can still be fully explained.

14.2.title: 14.2 Three Kinds of Selection Are Not the Same Process
14.2.lead: System selection, a person's decision, and collective governance can all be called “selection” or “choice,” yet cannot use the same reasoning about actors, consent, and authority. First ask which kind it is, then what makes it valid.
explanation: Chinese source location: lines 3046–3057; original site location /theory/part-14#section-14-2. For the current full text, see the theory-v2 source; historical research manuscripts and excerpts remain available for checking in their original downloadable versions.

SEL-SYS is a process of differential retention without a unified decision-making actor: variants receive different outcomes through mechanisms such as environments, feedback, competition, and replication. Register the unit of selection, environment, retention mechanism, time window, and random null model. A unit's retention is a fact requiring explanation; it does not mean “the system considers it better,” nor does it establish the normative justification of popularity, survival, or efficiency. [T-main]

SEL-SYS has a ceiling of describing selection; it cannot enter authorized status or include an external_action option. Even if people design the retention mechanism, distinguish the designers' decisions from the differential outcomes after the mechanism operates. The former carry separate responsibilities concerning actors and authority; system outputs cannot be treated as one's own ethical judgments or authorization. [T-main; T-options]

SEL-AGT has an identifiable actor, but the actor's decision is constrained by their own authority, genuine options, geographic scope, and duration. Deprivation of information, default lock-in, insufficient capability, unsafe refusal, or obstructed exit prevent apparent choice from being directly interpreted as free consent. Not exiting is not consent, and initial entry is not permanent consent; consenting to one matter does not automatically bind others or extend to other matters. [T-main]

SEL-GOV is procedurally authorized collective governance, not individual preference multiplied by a headcount. Shared affairs still require boundaries, agendas, the source and scope of representation, participation, dissent, minority protection, conflicts of interest, execution and review responsibilities, and authorization expiry to be specified. “Being affected” identifies matters that must enter protection and review; it does not directly turn every affected area into the governor's jurisdiction. [T-main; T-governance]

Numbers, vocal prominence, efficiency, claims to represent others, and legal form cannot individually substitute for bounded public authorization. This does not deny the effectiveness of lawful public procedures; it prevents inferring that all conditions hold from a single marker. External legal validity, normative justification, and internal certification by this framework must also be distinguished. Independently existing rights and powers are not negated merely because the framework's forms have not yet been used. [T-main; T-J]

These are distinct process identities, not developmental stages. A real situation may simultaneously involve system diffusion, individual responses, and governance rule-making, but the different actions must be modeled separately. Diffusion outcomes cannot replace individual consent, nor individual preferences public authorization. Hard boundaries restrict inferential crossings; they do not require a real system to contain only one kind of process forever. [T-main]

The 2020 offline study by Mansoury and colleagues updates recommendation profiles through simulated interactions, offering a locatable example of research on differential diffusion and feedback. The paper explicitly states that the changes concern representations of preferences within the system, not measured inner human preferences. This neither permits anthropomorphizing the algorithm nor supports finding user consent from simulated outcomes. The historical Belmont text, meanwhile, separates information, comprehension, and voluntariness, providing a limited normative comparison for conditions of actor consent; these two types of sources cannot exchange evidentiary identities. [P-SIM; P-BEL]

The strongest objection is that real processes are too intertwined for the three-way distinction to be useful. Precisely because they are intertwined, the subject and force of the current statement must be identified: does it concern content diffusion, an actor's decision, or shared rules binding on others? Once distinguished, clear explanations and recommendations can be offered for each, instead of calling every outcome “everyone's choice.” [T-main]
argumentSteps: Identify whether the current process has a unified decision-making actor and what effect it is intended to produce.
System selection registers units, environments, retention, time, and null models, without anthropomorphism or authorization.
Agent decisions check actual options, information, capability, refusal, exit, and the person's own authority.
Collective governance checks agendas, representation and participation, minority objections, conflicts, execution review, and expiry.
Record distinct processes within the same scenario separately; selection does not replace consent, nor individuals governance.

distinctions.leftText: Differences are retained through a mechanism, without a unified deciding agent.
