caseNotes.sourceLocator: Documentation Tips, introductory paragraph and Think about your safety first item; What might I want to document?, first paragraph
caseNotes.boundary: This is guide text published by a support organization, not a real personal case or an effectiveness trial; this lesson does not confirm victimization or surveillance for any particular reader or prescribe evidence-collection actions.

argumentSteps: Establish the actual conditions of existing review, appeal, and evidence chains; do not register nonexistent provisions as already available.
Organize existing facts, statements, patterns, and unknowns separately, rejecting demands for risky evidence collection.
Form protective open claims with all six components, clearly marking prohibited uses.
Prioritize reducing exposure, connecting with support, and obtaining safe external perspectives, without making proof of who is right a prerequisite.
Continue limiting judgments according to escalation and withdrawal signals; formal action must separately meet applicable grounds and procedures.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: how to write a six-part open claim
teachingExamples.text: Suppose a temporary collaboration group has no independent appeal. Current materials: two received messages changing tasks and a personal diary, but no complete correspondence. Pattern warranting attention: repeated task changes may impose extra workload on one member; motives cannot yet be judged. Prohibited uses: no public labeling, punishment, or disqualification on this basis. Escalation signals: new verifiable threats, withdrawal of support, or continued workload increases. Withdrawal signals: independent materials show that the original messages included an omitted negotiation process, requiring revision of the pattern judgment. Low-risk next step: when the person’s safety and wishes allow, first organize existing materials and consider a trusted external perspective, without creating conflict to obtain more evidence.
teachingExamples.assumptions: All people, messages, and circumstances are constructed; no interviews or investigation were conducted.
teachingExamples.boundary: “Two messages” does not establish a persistent pattern; do not declare the next step certainly safe when actual safety conditions are unknown.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: preservation differs from a disciplinary file
teachingExamples.text: Suppose a member, when safety permits, retains messages they have already received and notes dates and uncertainties; this preserves leads. Another person turns those fragments into a permanent personnel file stating “this person cannot be worked with” and forwards it to recruiters; this exceeds the use ceiling of protective open claims and cannot be justified as “keeping a record.”
teachingExamples.assumptions: This illustrates a use boundary; no real private information was retained or sent.
teachingExamples.boundary: Actual recording and transmission must still comply with applicable privacy, authorization, and safety requirements; this example does not provide legal advice.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: absence of review does not erase local facts
teachingExamples.text: Suppose a verifiable notice explicitly cancels an agreed form of support; the fact of that notice can hold. Whether it constitutes intentional isolation, overall control, or breach of contract requires other materials and procedures. The middle path permits retaining the notice and recording risks, but does not permit claiming the notice never existed because other evidence is missing, or directly finding guilt.
teachingExamples.assumptions: The notice and agreement are conditional assumptions.
teachingExamples.boundary: Multiple interpretations may be possible in reality; a local fact neither automatically obtains an overall interpretation nor is negated by an unresolved overall judgment.

counterexamples.text: Without an independent adjudicator, no signs of harm should be recorded.
counterexamples.effect: Institutional deficiencies limit strong conclusions but do not erase knowable facts and risks.

counterexamples.text: Because the purpose is protection, unverified interpretations may be made public to everyone.
counterexamples.effect: This path explicitly prohibits public characterization; protection does not authorize increased exposure.

counterexamples.text: To receive help, one must stay in a dangerous situation to collect evidence.
counterexamples.effect: The original rejects requiring affected people to collect evidence at personal risk; support should not come at the cost of continued exposure.

questionAnswers.question: What is wrong when a six-part open claim lacks withdrawal signals?
questionAnswers.answer: A provisional interpretation can too easily become permanently fixed as correct; specify what materials would lead to revision or withdrawal, and retain versions.
questionAnswers.basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

questionAnswers.question: Does retaining messages permit creating a negative eligibility file about someone?
questionAnswers.answer: No. Safe documentation and use for disciplinary eligibility are different; the latter is outside this path’s authority.
questionAnswers.basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

questionAnswers.question: Can a trusted friend who has heard the story replace formal independent review?
questionAnswers.answer: Not automatically. An external perspective has local value, but relationships, competence, confidentiality, and authority must be considered.
questionAnswers.basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

questionAnswers.question: Why cannot low risk be defined by a fixed list of actions alone?
questionAnswers.answer: Screenshots, public inquiries, and contacting supporters can all increase exposure in particular circumstances; they must be bounded by safety and the person’s wishes.
questionAnswers.basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

16.12.title: 16.12 GOV-12 Protecting Subjects Who Cannot Exit
16.12.lead: A person may remain in a relationship or arrangement because they have nowhere feasible to go, care cannot be interrupted, or their income is controlled—not because they agree to everything happening. Protection should first reduce harm and preserve choices, without requiring “successful departure” as proof that they deserve support.
explanation: Original location: Chinese source lines 3646–3653; original anchor section-16-12; short quotation, translated from the Chinese: “Not exiting does not equal consent.” A verbatim source excerpt for this topic is separately attached in source-slice.md, keeping explanation apart from the original.

This section lists children, severely dependent people, people whose income is controlled, incarcerated people, people bound by care responsibilities, and subjects with extremely limited resources, noting that they may be unable to exit. This identifies a possibility and an entry point for protection; it does not presume from identity that everyone lacks will or capacity. Exit depends on affordable costs, continuity of support, information, real options, and safety; nominal permission to leave that entails losing necessary care is not feasible exit. Remaining cannot automatically be interpreted as consent, loyalty, or approval of the arrangement.

The six protections are: safety first; trusted proxies; restoration of minimal choice, information, records, and connections to support; low-exposure documentation; local buffers and alternative exits; and prohibiting romanticization of inability to exit as love, loyalty, maturity, sacrifice, or the greater good. They are not six tests for the person to pass, but responsibilities of protective arrangements. Minimal choice may mean an available communication channel, saying no to one step, or a temporary buffer; its value cannot be denied because a complete exit plan is not yet available. Yet small choices must not conceal ongoing restrictions.

People should not be required to remain exposed to prove their situation. The original allows proxy submission, delayed expression, staged disclosure, external uptake, preservation of evidence, and refusal of direct dialogue. Allowing these methods does not declare every method safe in every context, authorized, or legally effective; actual exposure and support conditions must be examined. In particular, “dialogue can solve the problem” must not become a rule forcing someone to face the person being questioned, nor may refusal of dialogue be rewritten as noncooperation.

The goal is to reduce harm, preserve agency, and expand future options under conditions where exit is impossible, rather than force an ideal exit. If moving now would interrupt necessary care or increase danger, first check alternative uptake arrangements and buffers; external support can help expand the conditions available and should not require immediate departure as a prerequisite for help. This connects to the boundaries of X0 and transfer to external uptake: leaving the nominal old environment does not automatically provide safety, support for living, or continuity of responsibility. Protection must not rationalize long-term entrapment either; feasible choices still need to be sought continuously.

Trusted proxies must distinguish four kinds of work by matter: helping a person understand and express themselves, submitting materials on their behalf, handling matters entrusted by them, and making decisions on their behalf. The first two do not automatically include the latter two, and an authorization for one matter does not expand into representation in every domain. Record the grounds, scope, and limits separately; a proxy’s account cannot automatically be written as the person’s own expression or consent. Relatives, professionals, and familiar caregivers may provide important support, but neither identity nor convenience is sufficient standing to represent someone.

Also preserve the person’s available ways of communicating, records of proxy conflicts of interest, conditions for refusing or changing support, review of dissent, and continuity of necessary support. Communication may differ from a formal spoken answer; expression cannot be erased merely because it does not fit a conventional form, nor can a supporter’s guess be passed off as the person’s own words. Changing support should not suddenly interrupt necessities for living, and imperfect records cannot become an excuse to force disclosure or stop necessary support.

If the person’s wishes remain indeterminate after support, state what support efforts were made, the grounds of interpretation, and the remaining uncertainty. “I cannot understand” cannot directly be registered as “the person has no will,” nor may a result be decided first and a proxy statement then sought as consent. Where materials or institutions contain substitute decision-making and emergency measures, check their institutional grounds and normative disputes separately; describing what an institution permits does not establish conformity with this section’s protective principles, still less authorize issuing permission for real people on the basis of this book.

The strongest opposing position emphasizes that, when information and communication are limited and support cannot wait, making no arrangements at all may also harm people. This difficulty requires distinguishing uninterrupted necessary support, revocable bounded arrangements, cautious interpretation of wishes, and actual substitute decision-making, while retaining corresponding grounds, review, and disputes; urgency cannot expand proxy authority without limit. Another objection worries that all proxies are being deemed untrustworthy. This section makes no such presumption; it requires verifiable scope, conflicts of interest, and conditions for the person to change support, so that trustworthiness is more than a self-description.

distinctions.leftText: Real options, resources, safety, or other conditions make departure infeasible.
distinctions.rightText: Requires corresponding expression, information, and conditions; it cannot be presumed from staying.

distinctions.leftText: Helps the person form and express judgments.
distinctions.rightText: Hands decisions to another person; grounds and normative disputes require separate checking.

distinctions.leftText: An account made by the proxy on the basis of their materials and understanding.
distinctions.rightTitle: The person’s own expression or consent
distinctions.rightText: Must not be replaced directly without distinction.

distinctions.leftText: Protects basic living and communication conditions from interruption.
distinctions.rightText: Continuity of support does not mean a proxy can never be changed.

boundaries: Childhood, disability, or dependency must not directly negate agency, nor may inability to leave be interpreted as consent.
Kinship or professional qualifications do not automatically create authority to represent someone in all matters.
Refusal of direct dialogue, staged disclosure, and delayed expression may be protective methods, not automatic evidence of noncooperation.
Record requirements must not interrupt necessary support or force sensitive disclosures.
This lesson does not assess real individuals’ capacities or decide care, guardianship, medical, or legal matters.

caseLinks.title: A real normative text and corrigendum: support is not substitute decision-making

caseNotes.title: A real normative text and corrigendum: support is not substitute decision-making
caseNotes.text: The Committee on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities’ 2014 General Comment No. 1 discusses respect for will, communication support, and safeguards in support relationships in paragraphs 17, 21, and 29. The corrigendum of January 26, 2018, replaces paragraph 27, using “or,” rather than the original “and,” when listing characteristics of substitute decision-making regimes. Interpreters must therefore check versions and cannot mistakenly require all three characteristics simultaneously as the only identification condition.
caseNotes.sourceLabel: CRPD Committee, 2014 GC1 and 2018 Corr.1
caseNotes.sourceLocator: 2014 comment, ¶17 (pp. 4–5), ¶21 (p. 5), ¶29(c)(d)(g)(h) (p. 7); 2018 Corr.1 replaces all of ¶27, with a separate source link
caseNotes.boundary: This is the Committee’s normative interpretive text, not a current compilation of all guardianship rules in any country, nor evidence of real-world implementation effectiveness; this lesson does not judge the legality of proxies or emergency measures for real individuals.

argumentSteps: Check actual exit conditions; do not treat staying or an identity category as proof of consent or incapacity.
Implement the six protections, prioritizing reduced exposure and continuity of necessary support.
Distinguish support, submission, entrusted handling, and substitute decision-making by the four kinds of matter, recording their respective grounds and boundaries.
Preserve the person’s communication, conflict-of-interest records, refusal and changes of support, and review of dissent, preventing proxies from overriding the person.

When wishes are unclear, report support efforts, interpretive grounds, and unknowns; substitute decision-making and emergency measures require separate institutional and normative checks, and do not automatically obtain sufficient authorization.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: submission on someone’s behalf is not consent on their behalf
teachingExamples.text: Suppose a care-service user asks a supporter to submit feedback about daily routines to the service provider. The supporter may submit that matter, but cannot also sign consent to relocation or declare that the person waives an appeal. If the person uses picture cards to express a wish to change one arrangement, preserve the communication materials and context, rather than treating the supporter’s full retelling as a verbatim quotation.
teachingExamples.assumptions: The people, feedback, and picture cards are all teaching assumptions; no real care decision is involved.
teachingExamples.boundary: The effect of a particular delegation or consent must be checked separately against actual institutions, norms, and the person’s expression; this example issues no authorization.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: changing support must not interrupt support
teachingExamples.text: Suppose someone wants to replace a helper with a conflict of interest, but still relies on that helper’s services for daily communication. Proportionate protection requires alternative communication and service continuity, rather than saying “if you reject this person, all support is cancelled.” Conversely, the importance of the service cannot justify permanently locking in the same proxy.
teachingExamples.assumptions: The situation is constructed; no service adjustment was implemented.
teachingExamples.boundary: Whether replacement resources are actually available needs checking; verbal promises cannot establish safety.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: multiple explanations for staying
teachingExamples.text: Suppose a member still lives at the same address: they may prefer to stay, or they may lack financial resources or alternative care. Unchanged residence alone cannot distinguish these possibilities. Protective records should list existing materials, feasible choices, and unknowns; “they did not leave” cannot establish consent, still less justify forcing immediate relocation to complete the proof.
teachingExamples.assumptions: The home, member, and resource conditions are all hypothetical.
teachingExamples.boundary: No blanket finding of control is made about any real co-residential or dependent relationship.

counterexamples.text: They are an immediate relative, so anything they say automatically represents the person’s consent.
counterexamples.effect: Identity does not supply the missing matter, grounds, scope, or the person’s expression.

counterexamples.text: Anyone seeking a new supporter must first have all current care cancelled.
counterexamples.effect: Conditions for changing support and continuity of necessary support must be considered together; refusal must not be punished.

counterexamples.text: Not leaving means the person approves every arrangement.
counterexamples.effect: Feasible exit and consent require separate checks; not exiting does not imply consent.

questionAnswers.question: Can a proxy who helps submit materials also decide relocation?
questionAnswers.answer: Authority cannot expand automatically. Submission and substitute decision-making are different matters; grounds, scope, and the person’s wishes must be checked separately.

questionAnswers.question: What should be written when a person’s wishes are temporarily indeterminate?
questionAnswers.answer: The support efforts provided, interpretive grounds, and uncertainty; do not write a proxy’s guess as the person’s consent.

questionAnswers.question: Why is immediate departure not the goal of protection?
questionAnswers.answer: Safe alternative uptake may not be available in reality; the goal is to reduce harm, preserve agency, and expand future options, not to force an ideal exit.

questionAnswers.answer: The connector between characteristics of substitute decision-making in paragraph 27 changed to “or”; one must no longer mistakenly require all three characteristics simultaneously before identifying the corresponding substitute decision-making regime.

16.13.title: 16.13 GOV-13 Complex Trauma and the Absence of a Healthy Baseline
16.13.lead: “Restoring things as they were” sounds like repair, but the earlier state may never have been safe. Where a healthy baseline is absent, first ask how minimum safety and predictable support can be established today; do not invent an ideal past for someone to fit a repair narrative.
explanation: Original location: Chinese source lines 3654–3663; original anchor section-16-13; short quotation, translated from the Chinese: “The framework cannot use its own theory to invent a healthy past.” A verbatim source excerpt for this topic is separately attached in source-slice.md, keeping explanation apart from the original.

This section first distinguishes four structural histories: a formerly healthier structure that later departed from that state; a nominal anchor that remains but is hollow in practice; an initial-building type in which a healthy anchor never formed; and a trauma-as-building-material type in which rules, identities, boundaries, and relationships formed under traumatic conditions from the outset. They point to different questions: grounded restoration, checking the gap between nominal and actual conditions, establishing conditions for the first time, or reexamining constraints embedded during formation. These four are neither a list of clinical diagnoses nor stages every object must pass through.

A healthier past requires historical evidence; it cannot be inferred solely from “things later became worse.” Even a surviving nominal anchor requires checking current uptake and effects; institutional names or old slogans do not establish continued operation. Both the initial-building and trauma-as-building-material types may lack a healthy state to return to, but they are not identical: not yet having formed does not automatically establish formation through harm, and current behavior cannot substitute for formation history.

For the latter two types, TRAUMA-NO-HEALTHY-BASELINE does not default to returning to the original state; instead it asks in six directions: current minimum safety; whether predictable support is being obtained for the first time; whether expression is possible without punishment; whether small, repeatable trust is available; which strategies once protected survival but now constrain it; and whether new anchors already exist but remain unseen or need to be built together. These questions must connect with the person and specific conditions, rather than define one standard healthy life for everyone.

Predictable support centers on repeatedly dependable conditions, not a single intense promise; an unpunished entry point centers on actual consequences, not merely saying expression is allowed; small, repeatable trust also cannot be produced by forced disclosure, demands for forgiveness, or direct confrontation. Strategies that once protected someone should not casually be dismissed as defects, while whether they now restrict choices can still be discussed through specific materials. This explains research directions; it prescribes no treatment steps and guarantees no effects for anyone.

Discovering new anchors differs from building them together. Discovery requires evidence of existing relationships, commitments, or support; construction is new negotiation and practice, requiring records of participants’ goals, boundaries, conditions for withdrawal, and actual consequences. An analyst’s preferred values cannot be declared the object’s true anchors, nor can minimum safety now be denied because a goal has not formed. “Building together” must not obscure power differences: who has resources, who can refuse, and who bears costs still need checking.

Tasks requiring corresponding qualifications—such as therapy, clinical work, care, child protection, and law—should go through the relevant professional procedures. Framework research cannot itself issue clinical classifications, treatment plans, guardianship arrangements, or legal judgments. Professional knowledge and credentials likewise do not create power to decide every aspect of a person’s life: the person’s valued goals, comprehensible communication, dissent, and refusal still require handling through applicable procedures. Emergency duties and authority over specific matters need independently applicable grounds; explain scope, duration, review, and continuity of support separately, rather than deriving “I understand, therefore I have authority” from theory.

“Trauma-as-building-material type” is only a candidate description of certain structural formation histories, not complex post-traumatic stress disorder or another clinical diagnosis. Present harm requiring protection may be recorded first; formation history, psychological mechanisms, and professional classifications carry separate evidentiary responsibilities. Being harmed today does not imply that all past relationships were constituted by trauma; incomplete history does not require suspending all safety support. Nor must people prove they once had an ideal past to qualify for help.

The strongest opposing position worries that rejecting a healthy baseline makes improvement arbitrary, allowing any new arrangement to be called repair. The response is not to fabricate a past, but to clarify present minimum safety, the person’s goals, normative boundaries, testable improvement, and counterexamples, distinguishing protection, initial construction, and evidence-based restoration. Another objection worries that “it once protected survival” exempts present restrictions from examination; acknowledging a historical function does not mean keeping it forever, and current costs, alternative conditions, and the person’s feasible choices can still be evaluated.

distinctions.leftText: Use real historical and current functional evidence to determine what should be restored.
distinctions.rightTitle: Building safe support for the first time
distinctions.rightText: The corresponding baseline may never have existed; do not pretend this is a return.

distinctions.leftText: A candidate description of structural formation history.
distinctions.rightText: Requires corresponding professional evidence and procedures, not an inference from a framework label.

distinctions.leftTitle: A strategy once had a protective effect
distinctions.leftText: Describes its bounded function under conditions at the time.
distinctions.rightTitle: It should still be retained now
distinctions.rightText: Current costs and alternatives require a separate judgment.

distinctions.leftText: Knowledge and qualifications to undertake specific tasks.
distinctions.rightTitle: Power to decide all aspects of life
distinctions.rightText: Still requires authority over the matter, the person’s goals, and procedures; credentials do not confer unlimited authority.

boundaries: Do not invent a healthy past or assume that all formation history was constituted by trauma because harm exists now.
Recording current protection needs does not require a complete history or clinical diagnosis first.
Do not conflate initial-building and trauma-as-building-material types or treat the four categories as a developmental sequence.
Professional procedures and the person’s expression, dissent, and refusal should all be respected.
This lesson contains no clinical assessment, treatment trial, or case-specific care decision; teaching examples should not be used as treatment plans.

caseNotes.title: A real public-health definition: division of responsibilities between trauma-informed practice and specialist treatment
caseNotes.text: The UK government’s working definition published on November 2, 2022, emphasizes safety, trust, choice, and collaboration; the “Prevent re-traumatisation” section explicitly states that trauma-informed practice focuses on reducing barriers to services, while treatment of trauma-related difficulties is undertaken by specialist services and staff. This provides a real normative text that does not equate service design directly with treatment.

argumentSteps: Check the four candidate explanations of structural history separately; do not infer a healthy or traumatic past from current harm.
Without a healthy baseline, turn to questions of minimum safety, predictable support, expression, small trust, survival strategies, and new anchors.
Distinguish discovery of existing conditions from jointly building new ones, retaining the person’s goals and refusal.
Collect evidence separately for current harm, formation history, psychological mechanisms, and clinical classifications; none replaces another.
Tasks requiring professional qualifications enter the corresponding procedures; credentials and urgency do not automatically expand authority over matters.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: four histories cannot all be called restoration
teachingExamples.text: Suppose mutual-aid group A once had verifiable safe expression and resource support that later stopped; B nominally retains a support committee but accepts nothing in practice; C has just formed and has not yet developed stable support; D’s rules have been built around punitive control from the start. A may study which existing conditions to restore; B checks hollowing out; C needs initial construction; D checks formation history and how to rebuild safer arrangements. The same goal of “returning to the original state” cannot handle all four.
teachingExamples.assumptions: The four groups and histories are teaching constructions; no real organization was assessed.
teachingExamples.boundary: Real situations may be mixed, contain conflicting evidence, or remain unknown; they cannot be forcibly classified by resemblance to a story.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: old strategies and new conditions
teachingExamples.text: Suppose a member has long avoided conflict by not expressing needs, which may have protected them at the time; after entering a hypothetically safer environment, it may also restrict access to help. Analysis should ask whether current expression is truly safe and whether alternative support exists, rather than ordering immediate disclosure of every experience or diagnosing silence as a disease.
teachingExamples.assumptions: A conditional strategy example; no psychological mechanism was judged for a real person.
teachingExamples.boundary: Both historical protection and current restriction require facts; this pattern cannot be imposed on everyone who is silent.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: qualifications still have boundaries
teachingExamples.text: Suppose a professional may conduct a specific commissioned assessment, but cannot therefore decide all of the person’s friends, interests, and life goals. If an emergency arises, independently applicable grounds, time limits, review, and continuity of support still need checking; a theory calling something “dangerous” cannot justify self-expansion of authority.
teachingExamples.assumptions: A construction about authority relationships; no instructions for any real emergency action are provided.
teachingExamples.boundary: Actual clinical and legal authority depends on professional procedures and local rules, not this example.

counterexamples.text: If things are unhealthy now, they must once have been healthy; simply recover that state.
counterexamples.effect: A past baseline needs evidence; without one, initial construction rather than restoration may be needed.

counterexamples.effect: A candidate description of structural formation cannot replace clinical diagnosis.

16.14.title: 16.14 GOV-14 Separating Open-Ended Undertaking, Normative Premises, and Metaphorical Drift
16.14.lead: Whether someone is willing to bear costs, whether it helps, and whether we should praise it are three questions. A good result does not establish that they acted voluntarily, nor does sincerity guarantee a beneficial outcome; still less may everything unexplained be called love.
explanation: Original location: Chinese source lines 3664–3677; original anchor section-16-14; short quotation, translated from the Chinese: “Whether a description holds, an effect holds, and something deserves praise are three questions that can each receive an affirmative or negative answer.” A verbatim source excerpt for this topic is separately attached in source-slice.md, keeping explanation apart from the original.

This section treats love neither as a residual left unexplained by structure nor as an a priori motive label. HV11-R1-voluntary-limited-action describes only bounded voluntary undertaking: check the action, identifiable costs, direction, voluntariness, and actual conditions for refusal, exit, or negotiation, while examining competing explanations such as interests, fear, identity benefits, inertia, dependency, and coercion. Costs may be distributed across positions; do not see only the actor’s apparent contribution while ignoring burdens borne by others. Competing explanations do not mean denying goodwill in advance; they prevent a favored story from replacing materials.

R1 allows outcomes to be achieved, unachieved, harmful, or unknown; successful structural consequences are not an entry condition. If an action has evidence of voluntariness and bounded costs, failure must not erase the attempt by definition; conversely, a coerced action cannot be retrospectively made voluntary because it produced good outcomes. A clear direction does not equal a justified direction; descriptive facts and normative praise must still be stated separately.

HV11-R2-structural-consequence judges whether an action, through specified channels, changes affected positions’ safety, ability to refuse, appeals, resources, or subsequent possibilities. It must follow the corresponding G2/causal contract and check CAUSAL and E4 under the HV11 card (source theory-hv11, A.11, Chinese source line 4674). Before-and-after change does not automatically identify causation, and sincerity or high costs cannot replace effect evidence. R2 is not a second stage requiring prior R1: coerced actions may also have identifiable structural effects, and an affirmative R2 still does not supply R1 voluntariness.

Normative approval separately discloses N premises, the protection floor, and costs to other affected people. An objective may improve one indicator while sacrificing others' right to refuse; whether it merits approval cannot be assessed solely by the net total or the actor's wishes. Protecting low-power actors, opposing the cancellation of responsibility through structural language, and favoring appeal, withdrawal, and reproduction of those able to take up the work are value boundaries the framework explicitly undertakes. They belong in Part Fourteen, rather than being disguised as neutral theorems automatically derived from facts.

Action costs, coercion, or gaps in stopping rights revealed by R0 can directly establish protection needs without waiting for voluntariness and causal effects to be fully confirmed. Here, “establishing needs” does not mean the framework acquires power to implement protection or redistribute resources itself; actual action still requires corresponding authority, procedures, and risk conditions. Nor may failure to meet R1 negate personhood or inner worth, or satisfaction of R1 justify demanding continued sacrifice until the task ends. A bounded undertaking does not automatically generate unlimited obligations; necessary continuity and release from responsibility require separate reasoning for the matter.

These routes do not exhaust love, care, or general goodwill. Low-cost kindness, private companionship, unsuccessful creativity, and the value of everyday relations can hold in appropriate contexts. Greater cost must not be equated with deeper love, nor may the existence of G2 causal identification judge all private meaning. Here the framework limits only how strong its judgments can be about specific undertakings and consequences; it does not monopolize every use of these words.

Broad utility can incorporate concern, identity, and commitment, so utility theory cannot simply be said to permit only narrow self-interest. But representing an observed choice as optimal under some utility function does not independently identify the actual reason or determine its normative standing. If every observed choice is retroactively assigned the highest payoff, the model can fit any outcome but cannot distinguish competing explanations such as interest, fear, or commitment. Exploratory extensions may be retained, but a claim of increased explanatory power must specify which additional possible outcomes are distinguished relative to the original model, on what grounds, and what material would make the explanation fail.

Cross-domain concepts require six identities to be marked: metaphors aid expression; analogies compare bounded relations; candidate mechanisms propose channels for testing; empirical corroboration supplies bounded external material; formal models derive results under explicit assumptions; and validated rules may be used only within their actual validation scope. These six are not labels that can be upgraded merely by polishing language. Something being “like” another system does not mean it “follows” that system's laws; material from physics, biology, or animal behavior does not directly establish conclusions about human institutions.

Each metaphor should state similarities, differences, risks of misuse, and evidence for discontinuing it. For example, “a team is like an immune system” may prompt attention to detecting and responding to anomalies, but members have meanings, rights, dissent, and exit; dissenters cannot be eliminated as pathogens. If the analogy begins concealing these differences or fails to yield new distinguishable questions, discontinue or narrow it rather than using natural phenomena to justify organizational sanctions.

The strongest objection is that separating action, effect, and norms so finely makes everyday goodwill impossible to express. The response is to preserve expressive space in different contexts while clarifying the material required for strong assertions; not all care needs a causal trial. Another objection says that any choice can be represented through utility, so no other explanation is needed. Representability does not mean the cause has been identified. If different explanations have exactly the same predictions and evidence, acknowledge that they remain undistinguished rather than declaring a winner through repeated renaming.

distinctions.rightText: An effect judgment for specified channels, objects, and windows; it cannot disprove or supply missing evidence of voluntariness.

distinctions.leftText: One possible answer concerning outcomes and causal support.
distinctions.rightText: Separately requires public value premises and costs to affected people.

distinctions.leftTitle: A choice is representable as optimal
distinctions.leftText: Some utility representation exists.
distinctions.rightTitle: The reason for action has been identified
distinctions.rightText: Requires distinguishing competing explanations, not retroactive filling-in.

distinctions.leftText: Bounded similarities help formulate questions.
distinctions.rightTitle: A validated rule for human institutions
distinctions.rightText: Requires independent bridging and object evidence; it cannot be inferred directly from natural systems.

boundaries: Failure does not cancel an evidenced R1, and success does not establish voluntariness; coerced actions can also have R2 effects.

These routes do not exhaust everyday love and care, and failure to satisfy a route does not negate personhood.
Broad utility permits more than narrow self-interest, but all-purpose retroactive fitting is not increased explanatory power.
Analogies with natural systems cannot authorize eliminating dissent, requisitioning labor, or depriving actors of rights.

caseLinks.title: An actual theoretical debate: Sen's distinction between consistent choice and reasons

caseNotes.title: An actual theoretical debate: Sen's distinction between consistent choice and reasons
caseNotes.text: On printed page 326 of his 1977 “Rational Fools,” Sen notes that consistent choice still does not resolve the issue of self-interest; pages 326–327 distinguish sympathy from commitment and discuss situations in which a choice happens to coincide with expected personal-welfare maximization without being made for that reason. This provides an original argumentative text distinguishing behavioral representation from identification of reasons.
caseNotes.sourceLabel: Amartya Sen，1977，Philosophy & Public Affairs 6(4)
caseNotes.sourceLocator: Original printed pp326–327 (scanned PDF pages 11–12), opening of page 326 and section IV, first 3 paragraphs of page 327
caseNotes.boundary: I checked the relevant original-journal page images. This is neither an experiment nor proof of any particular person's motives, nor Sen's endorsement of all Xikari routes.

argumentSteps: First check R0 action costs and risks; do not wait for a complete positive route before recognizing protection needs.
For R1, separately check action, cost, direction, voluntariness, and genuine refusal, exit, and negotiation; retain failed and unknown outcomes.
For R2, use a proportionate causal contract to judge specified structural consequences; effects must not fill in motives or voluntariness.
Normative approval discloses N premises, the protection floor, and costs to others; authority for actual action is checked separately.
Utility representations require discriminating power and failure conditions; cross-domain uses must mark their identity, similarities, differences, risks, and evidence for discontinuation.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: different answers to three questions
teachingExamples.text: Suppose A can freely refuse and explicitly agrees to undertake two hours of work to help a colleague, but the method is ineffective. R1's bounded voluntary action can hold while an R2 beneficial effect remains unsupported. B performs the same work under threat, and independent evidence does show improved outcomes: R2 may hold while R1 does not. Whether the arrangements merit approval still requires value premises and costs to others; B's good output cannot justify approving coercion.
teachingExamples.assumptions: People, durations, and evidence conditions are hypothetical; no actual work-effect experiment was conducted.
teachingExamples.boundary: Actual R2 must meet the corresponding contract. The story's “independent evidence” is a conditional premise, not something this lesson has verified.

teachingExamples.title: Mathematical construction: why retroactive payoffs do not identify reasons
teachingExamples.text: Let the choice set be A={a,b}. Defining u(a)=1 and u(b)=0 only after observing choice a makes a optimal; if b were chosen instead, redefining u(b)=1 and u(a)=0 would likewise make the choice optimal. Both retroactive functions match the observed choice, yet neither distinguishes any outcomes in advance, much less fear, interest, or commitment. Utility parameters with prior independent grounds that yield predictions capable of failure would present a different evidentiary situation.
teachingExamples.assumptions: The two options and numbers form a formal construction; they estimate no real person's utility.
teachingExamples.boundary: This does not reject all utility models; it shows only that unconstrained retroactive filling-in lacks the discriminating power claimed here.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: when to discontinue the immune-system metaphor
teachingExamples.text: Comparing a team's problem detection with recognizing anomalies may help ask about feedback channels. But members are not pathogens to be destroyed, and opinions are not diseases. The similarity concerns information recognition and response; differences concern human rights, meanings, and relations open to appeal. The risk of misuse is pathologizing dissent. If the metaphor supports suppression instead of helping distinguish facts, stop using it.
teachingExamples.assumptions: A design example for reviewing metaphors, not a biological mechanism or an actual team study.
teachingExamples.boundary: Without bridging evidence, an immune mechanism cannot be presented as a causal rule for human organizations.

counterexamples.text: The help failed, so it cannot count as any voluntary undertaking.
counterexamples.effect: R1 does not require success for entry; retain a failed outcome rather than deleting the action.

counterexamples.text: A utility function can be written, so the actor has been proved merely self-interested.
counterexamples.effect: Representability does not identify reasons, and broad utility can also contain concern or commitment.

counterexamples.text: Ecological systems eliminate individuals, so organizations should also eliminate dissenters.
counterexamples.effect: Cross-domain facts do not yield norms for human institutions, still less authority to act.

questionAnswers.answer: No. R2 causal effects and R1 voluntariness require separate evidence.

16.15.title: 16.15 GOV-15 Intellectual Genealogy and Source Transparency
16.15.lead: When borrowing others' concepts, the priority is not listing famous names but showing readers what was taken, what was changed, and how far the original author actually supports the claim. Renaming different methods with one common term does not mean their disagreements have been resolved.
explanation: Chinese source location: lines 3678–3685; source anchor section-16-15; brief quotation translated from Chinese: “Connections between bodies of knowledge should preserve where disagreements occur.” An exact source excerpt is separately attached in source-slice.md; explanation and source text remain separate.

For every traceable concept, intellectual genealogy should record intellectual affinities, specific sources, versions, what was retained, modified, and abandoned, cross-cultural and cross-domain risks, and the scope of support and non-support. An intellectual affinity is an explainable connection, not proof of direct inheritance, priority of originality, or the original author's endorsement. Sources that cannot yet be traced should be marked unknown; a familiar name must not fill in a false developmental history. Nor does using a concept require that it have only one permitted ancestor.

Specific sources should be locatable at definitions, arguments, or material in the original text, rather than merely listing an author and year. Versions matter especially: revised drafts, original publications, reprints, translations, and errata may differ, so at least identify the version actually checked. What is retained specifies the scope or relation still used; what is modified specifies the new object, definition, or task; what is abandoned specifies claims no longer made or withdrawn. A prominent term must not be retained while concealing its original qualifications.

Cross-cultural and cross-domain risks require checking context, rather than treating identical translated words as identical concepts or taking roles and rights structures in one place's institutions as defaults everywhere. A concept may be illuminating but still need new object evidence to explain another setting. Acknowledging modifications and differences helps readers locate the bridge and the evidence still missing without undermining the theory itself. Concealing affinities instead can make concepts appear as authority from nowhere and reduce their openness to criticism.

This section states four non-substitutions: theoretical material cannot replace case evidence; a single case cannot replace a universal rule; an internal summary cannot replace original records; and an AI summary cannot replace traceable sources. Each still has uses: theory organizes questions, cases test bounded assertions, summaries aid navigation, and abstracts help locate material. But source chains and identities must remain. Even an accurate summary cannot entitle an author to claim that the full original was checked; the existence of an original file does not mean every part has been carefully studied.

An interoperability interface lets different methods connect within their respective boundaries; it does not declare that all belong to this framework. Before connecting them, specify the objects, outcomes, scales, evidence, errors, or normative premises each uses for the same task. If a domain method is sufficient, it may be used alone; knowledge need not be relabeled with Xikari codes to become valid. Choosing to retain a method requires identifying what is newly distinguishable in the current task, rather than merely comparing counts or complexity of terms.

There are at least three kinds of intellectual disagreement: estimating different outcomes, proposing competing mechanisms for the same outcome, and adopting different value premises. The first may not be contradictory—for example, waiting time and service accessibility. The second requires material that distinguishes mechanisms, not merging them under the same new term. The third requires public normative tradeoffs, not pretending more facts eliminate value disagreements. Units, denominators, time windows, and actual objects also need checking to avoid mistaking differences in measurement basis for mutually exclusive theories.

The strongest objection is that detailed genealogy burdens citation until research becomes mere literary etiquette. A reasonable response retains necessary sources and modification records only for concepts and claims actually carrying the argument, permits references back to specialist records, and avoids decorative reading lists. Another objection says unified naming reduces communication costs. It may serve as an expressive tool, provided the objects, evidence, and conflicts of the methods remain recoverable; memorability cannot justify erasing real disagreements.

distinctions.rightText: Requires separate historical material; similarity does not establish it.

Unified naming offers, at most, expressive convenience; it cannot automatically resolve empirical or normative disagreements.

caseLinks.title: An actual conceptual boundary: the engineering task in Shannon's communication paper

caseNotes.title: An actual conceptual boundary: the engineering task in Shannon's communication paper
caseNotes.text: In the introduction to his 1948 communication paper, Shannon limits the task to reproducing at one point a message selected at another, excluding semantic aspects from that engineering problem. The university-held copy checked here is labeled a corrected reprint, and the official Bell Labs page also preserves the corresponding introduction. This reminds us to retain the original task boundaries when using ‘information’ across domains: transmission theory cannot directly establish human understanding, trust, or value.
caseNotes.sourceLabel: C. E. Shannon, corrected reprint of the 1948 paper
caseNotes.sourceLocator: Version notice at the top of PDF page 1 of the corrected reprint and paragraph 2 of the Introduction; title date and corresponding introduction on the official Bell Labs page
caseNotes.boundary: This lesson checks only the introduction and version information. It does not claim to have read all 55 pages or reproved communication theorems. Limiting an engineering task does not assert that semantics is irrelevant to every problem.

argumentSteps: Record traceable sources and the actual versions for each concept; explicitly retain unknowns where a genealogy cannot be confirmed.
Explain what is retained, modified, and abandoned, and the risks of crossing cultures and domains; limit the support claimed from the original source.
Separate the evidentiary responsibilities of theory, cases, summaries, and AI abstracts, and maintain a traceable chain.
First check disagreements over outcomes, mechanisms, and value premises, then decide which interfaces can connect.
Choose methods for the additional discriminatory power they offer for the current task; allow direct use of domain methods when they suffice.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: an adequate account of conceptual borrowing
teachingExamples.text: A hypothetical study borrowing ‘channel’ to analyze complaint referrals could state: retain questions about transmission positions and blockages; modify the concept for human relationships involving power and safety risks; reject the inference that ‘arrival means understanding and the ability to correct’; require new evidence from affected people's feedback, actual permissions, and write-back. The original information transmission theory can suggest questions; it does not prove that the organization's complaints process works.
teachingExamples.assumptions: This is a design example of a borrowing record, not a real intellectual genealogy or an institutional study.
teachingExamples.boundary: Each actual citation must be checked individually; the presence of entries in the example does not make the sources reliable.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: different outcomes do not directly conflict
teachingExamples.text: Method A reports a reduction in average processing time, while method B finds that members with few resources have greater difficulty accessing the service. Even if both findings are true, they estimate different outcomes; one cannot simply claim that one is fabricated. Only if A goes on to claim that everyone benefits might B's material challenge that extrapolation. How to weigh efficiency against accessibility also requires explicit normative premises.
teachingExamples.assumptions: The methods and outcomes are conditional constructions; no actual survey was conducted.
teachingExamples.boundary: An actual comparison still requires aligning objects, windows, and definitions; different outcomes may also interact.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: the responsibilities of an original publication and a summary
teachingExamples.text: Suppose a hypothetical AI summary claims that a paper proves improvement for every group, but checking the original reveals only specified objects and a limited window. The correct response is to narrow the claim to the original scope and record the summary's overextension. A summary link cannot serve as evidence that the original paper has been read in full. If the original is temporarily unavailable, state that only the summary was obtained and specify its limits of support.
teachingExamples.assumptions: The paper and summary are abstract constructions; no specific publication has been fabricated.
teachingExamples.boundary: When the original is actually accessible, checking should continue; the convenience of a summary cannot excuse avoiding necessary research.

counterexamples.text: Citing ten theorists proves the conclusion about the present case.
counterexamples.effect: Intellectual sources do not replace evidence about the object; citation counts do not certify facts.

counterexamples.text: All schools study structure, so a unified framework has eliminated their disagreements.
counterexamples.effect: Differences in outcomes, mechanisms, and normative premises still need to be preserved separately.

counterexamples.text: Domain methods without this framework's identifiers cannot count as valid knowledge.
counterexamples.effect: The source permits direct use of domain methods when they suffice; identifiers do not confer a monopoly on knowledge.

questionAnswers.question: When borrowing the same term, what changes must at least be explained?
questionAnswers.answer: Record the actual source version, what is retained, modified, and abandoned, cross-domain risks, and limits of support; merely listing names is insufficient.
questionAnswers.basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

questionAnswers.question: If one method examines duration and another accessibility, must one be wrong?
questionAnswers.answer: Not necessarily. The two methods concern different outcomes. First check their respective facts, then examine extrapolation and normative choices.
questionAnswers.basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

questionAnswers.question: Why is an AI summary not equivalent to a traceable original source?
questionAnswers.answer: Summaries select and rewrite material and may omit conditions; return to the actual source or explicitly state the limits imposed by not obtaining it.
questionAnswers.basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

questionAnswers.question: Why does interoperability permit not using Xikari?
questionAnswers.answer: The value lies in additional distinctions. When a domain method is already sufficient, forced translation adds a burden without adding evidence.
questionAnswers.basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

16.16.title: 16.16 GOV-16 Usage-threshold debt and accessibility auditing
16.16.lead: Complex rules can prevent misuse, but they can also exclude those most in need of help. This section requires examining who has time to learn, who can gather evidence safely, who can appeal, and whether people needing help are required to complete the hardest steps independently before receiving it.
explanation: Chinese source location: lines 3686–3695; source anchor section-16-16; short quotation: ‘Accessibility is not completed by adding a simplified version to the full text’ (translated from Chinese). The source slice for this topic is attached verbatim in source-slice.md, keeping the explanation separate from the source.

There are six kinds of usage-threshold debt. Learning consumes time and cognitive resources; meaning may be lost between plain language and technical terms; evidence may not be safe to collect; external review may be entirely unavailable; greater investment may make exit harder; and the identity of someone who ‘understands the framework’ may bring interpretive authority and social capital. Debt here is a metaphor for continuing burdens and power risks, not a single monetary quantity. Complexity has two sides: simpler is not always safer, and more complex is not always more reliable.

The learning burden falls on maintainers and collaborators as well as readers: filling fields, maintaining versions, handling objections, drawing diagrams, and reading in full all require labor. Adding this work shows value only insofar as it clarifies problems, addresses counterexamples, respects the boundaries of transfer, and allows affected people to obtain real correction. Counts and completion receipts do not automatically establish understanding or fairness. Ask which steps are indispensable, which are repetitive, and who bears the burden; maintenance costs must not be covertly shifted onto participants with little power.

Accessibility begins with plain language, but plain language must not remove important restrictions and package what remains as a complete diagnosis. Graded ceilings on use tell users whether they can currently do no more than describe, explore, diagnose, or retain a risk. A simplified version may use fewer technical terms, but it cannot remove protection and correction. Where needed, say directly: you do not need to master the framework before protecting yourself, recording facts, and seeking support. This is a low-barrier protection route, not an exemption from evidentiary responsibilities for high-impact users.

Proxy or assisted expression, routes for nontextual material, and equal weight for appeals require different modes of expression to allow substantive issues into the process. Oral communication, images, and assisted communication do not inherently prove facts, but neither can they automatically be downgraded for failing to resemble a standard academic paper. Check what the material can support, rather than assigning value to speakers by their command of terminology. A proxy must preserve the person's own expression and authorization for the matter at hand, rather than make decisions for them in the name of help.

In particular, people who need assisted expression must not be required to prove their full expressive capacity independently before receiving the support that makes expression possible. That creates a circular barrier: without help they cannot complete the proof, and without the proof they cannot receive help. A proportionate design can first provide a safe, limited assisted route, then address factual and protective requirements for the current task. It cannot claim equivalent opportunities merely because ‘everyone gets the same form.’

Without equivalent routes for appeal, protection, and withdrawal, use must not enter substantive high-impact applications or be embedded in automated decisions. Equivalence does not require every route to look identical; it requires that relevant rights and opportunities for correction are not weakened by mode of expression, learning resources, or identity. Public dissemination should receive greater scrutiny according to the objects involved, factual allegations, identifiability, and consequences; ordinary analysis also needs accessible correction and withdrawal routes. This neither bans all public discussion under one maximum threshold nor makes a claim of low impact an exemption for publicly harming others.

Command of terminology, complete reading, internal certification, and paid learning do not constitute external qualifications. Learning can improve ability, but cannot by itself confer authority to review, diagnose, or sanction others; a paid certificate does not automatically constitute external review either. The risk that greater investment makes exit harder requires withdrawal and exit conditions that do not demand declarations of loyalty, rather than forcing continued burdens because ‘you have already studied for so long.’

The strongest objection is that lowering barriers will admit a flood of erroneous material and make quality impossible to maintain. The response separates accessible entry from the strength of conclusions: ordinary people can submit problems and seek protection, while strong conclusions must carry proportionate evidence. Another objection says that providing a simplified version completes accessibility. This section instead asks whether people can actually express themselves, receive equal treatment, obtain assistance, and withdraw, rather than merely counting words on a page. If actual usability and correction outcomes have not been checked, identify what remains a design and do not claim verified accessibility.

distinctions.leftText: Allow people with different resources and conditions of expression to raise problems and seek support.
distinctions.rightText: Strong conclusions still require proportionate material; low barriers do not mean abandoning verification.

distinctions.leftText: One tool for reducing the burden of understanding.
distinctions.rightText: Also includes assistance, appeals, protection, withdrawal, and actual correction.

distinctions.leftText: Handle appeals on their substantive material, without downgrading them for style or identity.
distinctions.rightText: Truthfulness and scope of support still require checking.

distinctions.leftText: Facts about learning and internal processes.
distinctions.rightText: These require an independent basis and do not arise automatically from proficiency, payment, or certificates.

boundaries: Examine both complexity's value in preventing misuse and its burdens; do not assess it by word count alone.
Assisted expression does not allow a proxy to override the person or reduce protection requirements.
Equivalent routes need not take the same form, but should preserve substantive rights and opportunities for correction.
Ordinary analysis also needs accessible correction; high-impact and automated applications cannot operate without equivalent routes for protection.
This lesson has not conducted an actual accessibility test or awarded any certification or qualification.
questions: Do low barriers mean low evidentiary standards?
Do equivalent appeals require everyone to use the same format?
What is the most defensible thing an internal certificate can establish?
How can we judge whether filling in more fields is worthwhile?

caseLinks.title: Actual accessibility guidance: seeking help should not first require navigating complex menus

caseNotes.title: Actual accessibility guidance: seeking help should not first require navigating complex menus
caseNotes.text: The W3C Working Group Note Making Content Usable states in §4.8.1 that human help should be easy to find, require as few steps as possible, and avoid complex menus. Its abstract and status information also identify it as a Working Group Note providing supplemental guidance, rather than additional requirements for WCAG conformance. It illustrates that access to help itself needs design.
caseNotes.sourceLabel: W3C COGA, Making Content Usable, page dated 2021-04-29
caseNotes.sourceLocator: Heading Working Group Note 29 April 2021; final paragraph of the Abstract and Status; §4.8.1.2 and 4.8.1.4
caseNotes.boundary: Only the specified passages were checked. An actual guidance document does not mean this lesson has performed user testing or certified a system's WCAG conformance; accessibility principles are not automatically generalized into a claim that all institutions are fair.

argumentSteps: Audit the six kinds of entry-barrier debt and maintenance labor, identifying who bears the burden and what risks it creates.
Provide plain language, graded ceilings on use, assisted expression, nontextual routes, and equal weight for appeals.
Avoid the circular requirement to prove complete ability before receiving assistance; retain protection and support routes that do not require completing the learning first.
For high-impact and automated use, check equivalent appeal, protection, and withdrawal routes; increase scrutiny of public dissemination according to identifiability and consequences.
Test value through clarification of problems, handling of counterexamples, and actual correction; reading, payment, or internal certificates do not confer external qualifications.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: the circular requirement to pass an exam before seeking help
teachingExamples.text: A hypothetical appeals system requires applicants to complete a complex terminology test independently before they can request assisted expression, even though their inability to complete that form independently is precisely why they need assistance. The procedure appears identical for everyone but places support behind an inaccessible barrier. Providing proportionate assistance and a usable route first, then examining the appeal according to facts and the task, does not mean all appeals automatically succeed.
teachingExamples.assumptions: The system and participants are a teaching construction; no actual ability test was conducted.
teachingExamples.boundary: Assistance must respect the person's wishes, safety, and permissions concerning the matter; this example cannot establish that a specific system is unlawful.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: a simplified version that preserves stopping points
teachingExamples.text: A hypothetical simplified version renders ‘first retain facts, risks, and unknowns; these do not authorize sanctions against others’ as ‘record what happened; mark what is uncertain; this record cannot yet decide someone else's qualifications.’ If brevity reduces this to ‘see the structure clearly and you can decide,’ an important ceiling on use has been deleted. Simplicity should lower the cost of expression, not covertly enlarge authorization.
teachingExamples.assumptions: This is a design example of rewriting content, not an empirical test of published teaching material.
teachingExamples.boundary: Whether real readers understand it requires separate testing, which this lesson has not performed.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: maintainers also bear entry-barrier debt
teachingExamples.text: Suppose a hypothetical maintenance process requires five equivalent forms to be filled in repeatedly for every objection, leaving volunteer collaborators unable to address actual counterexamples. Examine whether one traceable record could support references from several views, reducing repetition while preserving responsibility. Reducing fields must not incidentally delete crucial counterevidence or protective information, and a heavy workload cannot justify calling unfinished work complete.
teachingExamples.assumptions: The process, number of forms, and personnel are teaching assumptions; no software was deployed.
teachingExamples.boundary: Actual labor savings need to be measured; a design idea is not evidence of increased efficiency.

counterexamples.text: A one-page simplified version has been provided, so appeals and assisted expression are unnecessary.
counterexamples.effect: A simplified version addresses only part of the burden of understanding; accessibility also includes substantive entry routes and correction.

counterexamples.text: After reading the whole book and paying for a certificate, you may independently audit others' qualifications.
counterexamples.effect: Learning and internal certification do not confer external permissions.

counterexamples.text: Anyone who cannot first write a complete appeal in technical language does not deserve help.
counterexamples.effect: People needing assistance cannot first be required to independently overcome the very obstacle that the support is needed to address.

questionAnswers.question: Do low barriers mean low evidentiary standards?
questionAnswers.answer: Not necessarily. Entry allows description and requests for help, while strong conclusions still require proportionate evidence; keep the two separate.
questionAnswers.basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

questionAnswers.question: Do equivalent appeals require everyone to use the same format?
questionAnswers.answer: No. Modes of expression should not weaken rights or the weight given to a case; different accessible forms may be used.

questionAnswers.question: What is the most defensible thing an internal certificate can establish?
questionAnswers.answer: Only the corresponding internal learning or process outcome; it cannot alone establish external professional qualifications or authority to act.
questionAnswers.basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

questionAnswers.question: How can we judge whether filling in more fields is worthwhile?
questionAnswers.answer: Assess whether they actually clarify problems, handle counterexamples, limit transfer, and enable affected people to obtain correction, rather than counting fields or diagrams.

16.17.title: 16.17 GOV-17 Risks of Toolization, Commercialization, Weaponization, and Forking
16.17.lead: Once a framework becomes a course, software, or a paid service, “convenient to deliver” can easily be mistaken for “valid judgment.” This section requires products to preserve evidence, protection, and correction. Persistent disagreements may lead to clearly identified forks, but different rules must not operate under the same name without users being able to tell.
explanation: Source location: Chinese source lines 3696–3701; source anchor section-16-17; short quotation translated from Chinese: “Forking is not betrayal.” The source excerpt for this topic is separately reproduced verbatim in source-slice.md; explanation and source text are kept separate.

Courses, consulting, AI tools, organizational software, scoring sheets, audit forms, and public standards can all turn theory into actual processes affecting people. Different formats do not remove responsibility: evidence tracing, judgment downgrading, protection of low-power positions, appeal entry points, protection against retaliation, human review, stopping, and withdrawal must remain. A lightweight tool may provide limited prompts or organize material; a complete-looking interface cannot equip it to perform an unsupported full diagnosis.

Risks of toolization often involve substitution of status. A lightweight template is sold as a complete diagnosis, internal certification is described as external review, or AI output is packaged as independent investigation: each converts the status of a process or product into that of stronger evidence. Human review cannot consist solely of a confirmation button either; it needs appropriate capability, material, independence, and actual room to correct. Tracing sources is more than listing URLs, and downgrading is more than appending “for reference only” after a strong conclusion.

Customer satisfaction is not evidence of effectiveness. Satisfaction may indicate an evaluation of a particular experience or delivery, but cannot alone establish factual accuracy, a causal explanation, affected people’s safety, or net benefits. The payer may not be the person who bears the consequences of misjudgment. Product evaluation should separately examine whom it serves, whom it affects, which outcomes were measured, and which counterexamples were retained—not merely whether purchasers would recommend it.

Commercial deadlines or contractual pressure cannot force a strong diagnosis into existence. Insufficient material should permit unresolved status, downgrading, stopping, or delivery of limited analysis alone; a customer’s payment is neither evidence nor authorization. Unilateral payer control over material, feedback, and publication framing may filter out unfavorable facts and obscure low-power positions. Appropriate source-control records and independent review arrangements are needed. Charging money does not itself establish impropriety, but commercial relationships cannot cancel these protections.

“Framework certification” must not become a new eligibility monopoly. Completion of internal courses or operational proficiency may be accurately recorded, but does not automatically confer eligibility for professional practice, external review, or sanctioning others. Product descriptions should specify capabilities and limits. Automated decisions affecting actual rights or opportunities still require the corresponding strong judgments, protection, norms, J authorization, and O procedures; a brand cannot bypass them. Weaponization includes more than overt attacks: it also includes making terms into unappealable labels and shifting the costs of explanation and defense onto low-power people.

When users persistently disagree about core commitments, they may create forked versions. Forking is not a moral betrayal; a clear identity makes understanding and comparison easier than surface agreement. If a version changes protective boundaries, empirical questions, or conceptual meanings while retaining the same name and claiming complete compatibility, old authorizations, citations, and evaluations may be wrongly applied to new rules. Forks should have identifiable versions and proportionate descriptions of scope; a name change must not become a way to evade old responsibilities.

Every fork must explain which empirical problem families it retains, which boundaries it abandons, which concepts it modifies, and what new misuse risks it introduces. Retaining a problem family does not establish every conclusion about its instances; publicly abandoning a boundary does not thereby make high-risk conduct justified or lawful. Forks still require their own judgments of evidence, norms, and authority; saying “we are another version” does not exempt them from protecting affected people. Following 16.15, if the transformation offers only different names without added discriminatory power, say so accurately.

The strongest objection is that permitting forks could destroy shared quality standards. The response is to register core disagreements transparently, make each version accountable for its own testable commitments, and retain actual risk thresholds, rather than prohibit disagreement until changes can only happen covertly. Another objection is that protection requirements make tools too heavy. Uses may be narrowed, lightweight entry points retained, and conclusion strength reduced; lightweight tools must not be packaged as full investigations, nor may protection costs simply be deleted while strong powers of action remain.

distinctions.leftText: Organizes material or provides prompts for limited questions.
distinctions.rightText: Requires applicable objects, evidence, scale, and protection; a template’s appearance cannot provide them.

distinctions.leftText: A customer’s evaluation of an experience or delivery.
distinctions.rightText: Target outcomes, factual accuracy, and net effects need corresponding evidence.

distinctions.leftText: A record of a particular internal learning process or procedure.
distinctions.rightText: Actual relationships and authority require separate checks; the seller cannot self-certify them.

distinctions.leftText: Discloses changes in commitments and concepts so users can identify the version.
distinctions.rightTitle: Covert change under the same name
distinctions.rightText: Different rules are mistaken for the same framework, hiding differences in evidence and authority.

boundaries: Commercialization is not automatically unjustified, but neither payment nor deadlines add evidence or authorization.
Satisfaction cannot replace factual accuracy, protection, or causal effects.
Making a tool lightweight should narrow its uses, rather than remove protections while continuing high-impact uses.
Forking is neither betrayal nor exemption from responsibility; publicly abandoning boundaries does not make harm justified.
This lesson has released no tool, course, or certification, and has not evaluated the effects of any real commercial product.
