caseLinks.title: Actual contextualization guidance: NIST risk tolerance and resource allocation

caseNotes.title: Actual contextualization guidance: NIST risk tolerance and resource allocation
caseNotes.text: The About section of GOVERN 1.3 in the NIST AI RMF Playbook explains that governance resources are limited and that risk tolerance may range from negligible to severe losses. Suggested Actions calls for defining impact and likelihood assessments and qualitative or quantitative risk scales, recognizing that risk tolerance and risk levels change over the lifecycle. This illustrates risk-scale arrangements requiring organizational registration and review, rather than providing fixed numerical thresholds shared by every institution.
caseNotes.sourceLabel: NIST official AI RMF Playbook Govern page; accessed 2026-10-14
caseNotes.sourceLocator: First three paragraphs of GOVERN 1.3 About; all five Suggested Actions, especially the final item
caseNotes.boundary: Supports only that the guidance calls for managing risk scales according to organizational context. It does not establish implementation by any organization, nor is NIST’s illustrative risk-combination formula treated as this framework’s universal scoring rule or current law.

argumentSteps: Identify which of the five parameter groups this judgment actually depends on, and locate the specific external determination procedure.
Register organization, jurisdiction, object, risk level, evidentiary basis, validity period, and review conditions.
When parameters or applicability fields are missing, retain downgraded, suspended, or competing status; do not pass off defaults as valid decisions.
Propagate restrictions along dependencies. Independently grounded conclusions retain their original scope; shared gaps must not be evaded by splitting tasks.

Record protective unknown, lack of observational capacity, inapplicability, and pending evidence separately, and compare added records’ judgment benefits with waiting, exposure, and maintenance costs.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: a missing window does not erase a date fact
teachingExamples.text: An imagined original record reliably establishes that a module was suspended on Monday, but the observation window and decision-maker required for restoration have not been determined through an applicable procedure. The fact “suspended on Monday” can be retained. Three elapsed days do not permit independently declaring three days sufficient and announcing restoration. The gap blocks restoration eligibility; it does not erase the independent date record.
teachingExamples.assumptions: The date, module, and three days are hypothetical; three days is not a recommended threshold.
teachingExamples.boundary: If the date source’s identity is itself unverified, that fact needs separate downgrading.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: four kinds of blank are not the same zero
teachingExamples.text: In an imagined table, A omits sensitive details to protect the person; B lacks measurement tools; C is inapplicable because the relevant activity is absent; and D awaits supplementary documents from an authorized source. All four cells may look blank, but should be recorded separately as protective unknown, lack of observational capacity, not applicable, and awaiting supplementary evidence. They cannot all be scored as zero, whether they concern four people or four items.
teachingExamples.assumptions: A, B, C, and D are recording situations, not personality or personnel categories; all are constructed.
teachingExamples.boundary: Necessary state records should also minimize exposure; protective unknowns need not be filled in.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: repeated registration increases exposure
teachingExamples.text: Suppose a check already has valid proof whose reuse is permitted, but a second form demands a complete repetition of a sensitive account that cannot change any decision. Examine whether a secure reference to the existing proof or reduced duplicate collection would suffice, while retaining necessary review entry points.
teachingExamples.assumptions: The situation and proof are hypothetical; no real sensitive information was processed.
teachingExamples.boundary: Reuse is permissible only when reuse itself is authorized and applicable; cost savings must not expand data access.

counterexamples.text: One institution used thirty days, so all restoration windows should be thirty days.
counterexamples.effect: Contextual values require checking object risks and applicable procedures; they cannot be directly universalized.

counterexamples.text: One parameter is unknown, so even an independently established date cannot be stated.
counterexamples.effect: A missing parameter blocks only conclusions that depend on it; independently grounded facts may retain their original scope.

counterexamples.text: A protective unknown is just insufficient evidence; disclosure must be required before an appeal is permitted.
counterexamples.effect: Protective unknowns have safety or privacy grounds; they must not justify forced disclosure or removal of the corresponding rights entry point.

questionAnswers.question: May the framework casually fill in a set of risk-weight numbers to make the procedure run?
questionAnswers.answer: Only for an explicitly assumed demonstration, not as valid parameters for a specific context or for real-world clearance.
questionAnswers.basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

questionAnswers.question: What work can continue when a restoration observation window is missing?
questionAnswers.answer: Independently sourced facts may be checked, candidates and gaps organized, and comparisons prepared. Eligibility for restoration that depends on the window cannot be declared satisfied.
questionAnswers.basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

questionAnswers.question: Why is inapplicability different from lack of observational capacity?
questionAnswers.answer: The former means the object scope does not require the item; the latter means it may apply but cannot currently be obtained. Their subsequent evidentiary responsibilities differ.
questionAnswers.basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

questionAnswers.question: Do more records mean greater safety?
questionAnswers.answer: Not necessarily. Assess whether they can change judgments and reduce harm, alongside waiting, exposure, and maintenance costs; necessary safeguards must not be casually deleted.
questionAnswers.basis: The source text of this section and the public derivation above

figures.alt: Five groups of context-specific parameters: determined through applicable external procedures, not filled automatically by the framework. Seven applicability records: organization, jurisdiction, object, risk, grounds, validity period, and review. Missing information → restrict dependent uses; downgrade, suspend, or retain competing alternatives, while preserving independently grounded conclusions. Protective unknown is separate from lack of observational capacity; genuine inapplicability is separate from awaiting supplementary evidence. Proportionality comparison: judgment and protection benefits versus waiting, exposure, and maintenance costs. Drawn by the author of this guide from 16.25; the diagram contains no universal numerical threshold, and missing does not mean zero.

intro-17-appendix-a.title: Appendix A: Human Variable Interface Cards
intro-17-appendix-a.lead: Appendix A turns eleven human variables into interface cards that can be questioned item by item; its 39 fields are a structure of responsibility, not a gate requiring everyone to supply every item.
explanation: Source location: Chinese source lines 3776–3781, original-site location: introduction to this part, with no separately numbered anchor. The current full text is in the theory-v2 source; the historical research draft and excerpts remain downloadable in their original versions.

Short quotation translated from Chinese: “Completing the table is not a qualification for ordinary services or understanding.” Following HV01–HV11 in Part Seven, the appendix is organized into five areas: A, identity and proposition scope; B, formal dependencies and conclusion boundaries; C, nine-axis object contract; D, states, evidence, and variable flows; and E, uptake, responsibility, normative ceilings, and correction. It helps readers see unfulfilled burdens of argument, rather than using elaborate forms to exclude those who struggle most to express themselves. [T-intro]

Expanding all 39 fields does not mean every real task must collect 39 kinds of personal information. The fields express a contract structure; specific evidence is obtained according to the selected route and task relevance. Ordinary explanation, services, and support do not require completion of a formal root-instance test. Additional evidentiary responsibilities for a route arise only when seeking its particular form of G/H support. [T-intro; T-main]

Not applicable, unknown, not yet collected, and unavailable for protective reasons must remain separate. Not applicable explains why the field is unrelated to the task; unknown means it cannot currently be determined; not collected means it has not yet been obtained; unavailable for protective reasons means acquisition is restricted by privacy, safety, or similar concerns. The last category must not be rewritten as “uncooperative,” nor may contents be fabricated for formal completeness. [T-intro]

An empty dependency set is explicitly written “none (empty set),” meaning only that this type of relationship has no registered objects, not zero evidentiary risk or proof that an empirical claim holds. For example, an empty specializes field does not make the variable unconditionally applicable to any system; each card’s object, proposition, and routes still constrain outputs. [T-intro; T-main]

Read each conditional-support route as a whole: fixed when conditions, additional inferential or protocol dependencies, permitted conclusions, and result_ceiling. Descriptive inventories and conditional causal effects often follow different routes; the weaker entry conditions of a descriptive route cannot be attached to a different route’s strong causal conclusion. Object references passed between interfaces must also carry candidate or supported status and uncertainty. [T-intro; T-main]

This topic first explains how to use the entire card collection, then studies HV01 independently. Subsequent cards should retain their distinctive objects and conditions, rather than compressing eleven variables into one “universal system health score.” This navigation makes no independent real-world causal claim, so no success case is inserted. Teaching examples test confusion between spliced routes and material states. [T-intro]
argumentSteps: First identify the interfaces and routes needed for the task.
Use the five areas to understand the different responsibilities of the 39 fields.
Register not applicable, unknown, not collected, and unavailable for protective reasons separately.
Read conditions and ceilings along the whole route; do not splice across routes.
Preserve candidate and supported states; a completed form is not real-world evidence.

distinctions.leftText: A structure of responsibilities for argument and protection.
distinctions.rightText: Ordinary service users must not be forced to complete every field before receiving support.

distinctions.leftText: No registered dependencies of that kind.
distinctions.rightText: Requires separate judgment from specific material.

distinctions.leftText: Conditions, dependencies, and conclusion as a whole.
distinctions.rightText: Favorable fragments from different routes must not be selected after the fact.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: four blanks, four meanings
teachingExamples.text: In an artificial study, an irrelevant axis is marked not applicable with reasons; an unclear boundary is marked unknown; an interview not yet conducted is marked not collected; and identity information that cannot safely be disclosed is marked unavailable for protective reasons. None means “confirmed absence of risk,” and entering the same none in all four cannot erase the differences.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Artificial record states; no real people are involved.
teachingExamples.boundary: State labels preserve evidence boundaries only; they do not establish missing facts or authority.

questionAnswers.question: Do 39 fields require submitting 39 kinds of private information?
questionAnswers.answer: No. The fields define a contract structure; evidence is obtained according to route and task relevance, subject to protection.
questionAnswers.basis: Appendix introduction.

questionAnswers.question: Does an empty dependency set automatically pass?
questionAnswers.answer: No. It only means there are no registered objects for that dependency type.
questionAnswers.basis: Empty-set rule in the appendix introduction.

questionAnswers.question: Can R0 conditions support an R1 conclusion?
questionAnswers.answer: No. A complete route must not be dismantled and recombined after the fact.
questionAnswers.basis: Final sentence of the appendix introduction.

A.1.title: A.1 HV01 Structural domain (complete interface card)
A.1.lead: HV01 first registers candidate human objects, then tests bounded grouping gain through G1. A shared name does not imply a unified will, still less authority to impose dispositions.
explanation: Source location: Chinese source lines 3782–3865; original site location /theory/appendix-a/a-01#section-a-1. See the theory-v2 source for the current full text; historical research drafts and excerpts remain available for checking in their original downloadable versions.

Short quotation translated from Chinese: “D0 only declares a candidate human object.” HV01 first permits clarification of “which people, materials, boundaries, and window we are studying,” without requiring prior proof that this grouping has become an effective structural domain. It separates candidate naming from preregistered G1-instance support, preventing names, shared locations, or common problems from being substituted for an objectively unified will. [T-main；T-D0]

R0 (HV01-R0-candidate-object), when D0 is complete but no eligible and supported G1-instance exists yet, permits registration of the candidate object, material set, boundary disputes, and needs for supplementary evidence. R0 may pass object references carrying scope and uncertainty to HV02–HV11, so incomplete G1 need not silence all subsequent description; downstream uses must not present the reference as a supported structural domain. [T-main]

R1 (HV01-R1-effective-domain) requires a preregistered G1-instance to achieve supported within the same object, scale, window, K, and generalization unit, and adds the E4 protocol. It supports bounded grouping gain exceeding a threshold on preselected outcomes relative to matched N0, with scope bound to preregistered SP/T/K and generalization_unit. Domain grounds for an object’s real existence differ from predictive/explanatory grouping gain; gain cannot prove ultimate ontology, collective will, or jurisdiction. [T-main；T-G1]

R0/R1 are not rankings of personality or organizational maturity. Existing materials may support meaningful boundary observations without supporting formal G1; conversely, grouping gain for an outcome cannot imply all members’ wishes coincide or permit dispositions against excluded people. Cross-scale use must add units and populations, representativeness, the J axis, and low-visibility positions; local members cannot speak for everyone affected. [T-main]

Appeals focus on boundaries, representativeness, and identity criteria, and must be safely available without retaliation to members and affected positions, leading to review outside the original naming/decision chain. Authorized rollback does more than change the structural domain’s name: it must cancel its effect on downstream object scope, restore the material set, preserve versions, and verify completion. Actual record and rights adjustments still require valid authority. [T-main]

DWP’s FRS 2023–2024 distinguishes household, family/benefit unit, and individual levels within the same survey. This provides a real-world comparison for registering object criteria, but official definitions alone cannot establish G1, nor can a statistical unit define all family rights. The following 39 fields retain every registration in the original card and separately explain their responsibilities. [P-FRS；T-main]
Field-by-field study of all 39 fields (“Original card” below retains the field’s complete content in translation; “Interpretation” specifies its role and irreplaceable responsibility).

01 | Interface ID (id). Original card: HV01. Interpretation: the short identifier within the cardbook tracks the same interface; it does not indicate that a real-world object has been proved. [T-main]

02 | Qualified ID (qualified_id). Original card: human_variable:HV01. Interpretation: the namespace prevents naming collisions; references to this ID must still carry object and evidential status. [T-main]
03 | Name (name). Original card: Structural domain. Interpretation: the name provides a reading entry point, not an automatic label for particular people, groups, or real structures. [T-main]

04 | Claim type (claim_type). Original card: H. Interpretation: H identifies the role of a human-instance/interface proposition; it cannot be upgraded into formal proof or an unconditional law of the world. [T-main]

05 | Contract role (contract_role). Original card: human_variable_interface. Interpretation: this variable-interface contract specifies how to enter analysis; a field’s existence does not mean an empirical instance has been established. [T-main]

06 | Proposition (proposition). Original card: D0 only declares a candidate human object; a bounded effective structural domain is registered within an instance’s scope only when a preregistered G1-instance shows that the candidate grouping achieves out-of-sample or generalization gain above the threshold on preselected outcomes relative to matched N0. Interpretation: there are two levels of eligibility: D0 suffices to declare a candidate; only proportionate generalization gain over matched N0 under preregistered G1 supports a bounded effective structural domain. These cannot be reversed. [T-main]

07 | Scope (scope). Original card: Relationships, teams, organizations, institutions, and public issues. Interpretation: scope lists task domains that may be studied, not empirical support for every object within them. [T-main]

08 | Pause condition (pause_condition). Original card: Object, boundary, scale, time window, or identity is insufficient to support the selected route; when applying for formal G1 support, the corresponding null model or instance contract is incomplete. Interpretation: pausing concerns dependent judgment or adoption; independent descriptions may remain, but failed premises cannot continue to be used. [T-main]

09 | Inferential dependencies (inferential_requires). Original card: 1. D0. Interpretation: inferential dependencies provide upstream content needed for the proposition to hold; upstream candidate/support status must pass through unchanged, without automatic upgrading by citation. [T-main]

10 | Protocol dependencies (protocol_requires). Original card: 1. E1; 2. EVIDENCE; 3. SOURCE. Interpretation: protocol dependencies constrain evidence gathering and expression; completing protocols does not independently prove an empirical proposition true. [T-main]

11 | Qualification / specialization (specializes). Original card: None (empty set). Interpretation: an empty set means only that no such specialization relations are registered, not that evidential responsibility is absent; a nonempty set also does not imply universal validity. [T-main]

12 | Applicable-object references (applies_to). Original card: None (empty set). Interpretation: applicable-object references cannot replace the current object contract; an empty set is explicit registration, not permission to apply to every object. [T-main]

13 | Conditional support routes (conditional_support_routes). Original card: 1. route_id=HV01-R0-candidate-object; claim_level=candidate_description; when=The D0 object contract is complete, but no eligible G1-instance with result_state=supported exists yet.; additional_inferential_requires=None (empty set); additional_protocol_requires=None (empty set); allowed_conclusion=Register the candidate human object, material set, boundary disputes, and G1 supplementary-evidence needs.; result_ceiling=Candidate-object description only; may provide HV02-HV11 with object references carrying boundaries and uncertainty, without treating those references as effective structural domains already supported by G1. 2. route_id=HV01-R1-effective-domain; claim_level=descriptive_classification; when=A preregistered G1-instance achieves supported within the same object, scale, window, K, and generalization unit.; additional_inferential_requires=G1-instance; additional_protocol_requires=E4; allowed_conclusion=Register the bounded effective structural domain within that instance’s scope, strength of grouping-gain support, robustness of that gain to tested boundary perturbations, and applicable window.; result_ceiling=Limited to preregistered SP/T/K and generalization_unit; no judgments of ultimate ontology, unified will, or authorization. Interpretation: R0 may pass candidate objects to other HVs while retaining uncertainty; R1 requires an eligible G1-instance=supported and E4. R0’s weaker conditions must not be connected to R1’s effective-structural-domain conclusion. [T-main]

14 | Allowed inference (allowed_inference). Original card: 1. R0 may register candidate objects, boundary disputes, and bounded descriptive references; 2. Register the bounded effective structural domain supported by its gain and the strength of identification only within the G1-instance’s preregistered object, scale, window, outcome, and generalization unit. Interpretation: these are permitted directions of conclusion; which is actually reached and with what strength remain limited by the selected route and materials. [T-main]

15 | Prohibited leap (prohibited_leap). Original card: 1. Naming means an objective community; 2. Shared circumstances mean shared willingness. Interpretation: these are common boundary violations, not avoided by rewording; inspect actual inference and downstream use, not wording alone. [T-main]

16 | Nine-axis scale profile (scale_profile). Original card: SP=<A,X,T,O,C,R,I,N,J>; A=aggregation level: relationship or event units, candidate member population, distributions inside/outside the boundary, and grouping rules; X=spatial scope: shared places, organizational boundaries, digital platforms, and cross-domain external environments; T=time span: identification window, membership-change cycles, and boundary history; O=organizational level: roles, teams, organizations, institutions, through governance ecosystems; C=causal level: original events, interaction mechanisms, meso-level relational structures, institutional and systemic conditions; R=observational resolution: original interactions, event sequences, individual member cases, boundary distributions, indicators, and summaries, with compression loss registered; I=sphere of influence: direct members, excluded people, indirectly affected people, second-order spillovers, cross-domain and intergenerational positions; N=network-topological scope: member relations, boundary connections, isolated nodes, and cross-domain bridges; J=jurisdiction and authorization scope: register authorization separately for object naming, boundary adoption, and subsequent disposition; inapplicable axes must have reasons for not_applicable registered. Interpretation: register all nine axes individually; particularly, sphere of influence I creates no jurisdictional authority J, and lower observational resolution R requires retention of compression loss. [T-main]

17 | Effective object (effective_object). Original card: The candidate object declared by D0; registered as a bounded effective structural domain within that instance’s scope only after passing the preregistered G1-instance threshold test relative to matched N0. Interpretation: a candidate object is not nonexistent; “bounded effective” here specifically denotes the scope supported by a G1-instance test, not a verdict on the object’s ultimate reality. [T-main]

18 | Cross-scale invariants (scale_invariants). Original card: 1. Object contract; 2. Participating and affected positions. Interpretation: invariants are comparative responsibilities retained during transfer, not a declaration that variable values remain constant at every scale. [T-main]

19 | Required additions on elevation (required_scale_additions). Original card: 1. Units and populations; 2. Representativeness; 3. J axis; 4. Low-visibility positions. Interpretation: elevation is not copying and enlarging the original table. Where materials on new populations, interfaces, responsibility positions, and so on are incomplete, restrict conclusions dependent on them. [T-main]

20 | Semantics changing with scale (changing_semantics). Original card: 1. Effective members, relations, and identity may change with scale. Interpretation: the same word may change meaning when the object or scale changes; reconstruct correspondence rather than assume the original meaning applies unchanged. [T-main]

21 | Inapplicable objects (non_applicable_objects). Original card: 1. Nonhuman systems without interfaces for intention, institutions, or responsibility. Interpretation: inapplicability constraints prevent unconditional projection of human normative, responsibility, and experiential interfaces; they do not deny that other theories can study these objects. [T-main]

22 | Forbidden elevation (forbidden_elevation). Original card: 1. A local group directly representing all affected parties. Interpretation: inference from local to whole requires separate proof; broad impact, a grand name, or formal similarity cannot supply representativeness and authorization. [T-main]

23 | State set (state). Original card: 1. Candidate; 2. Identifiable; 3. Boundary disputed; 4. Not established. Interpretation: states are descriptive classifications requiring evidence, not a maturity ladder for scoring people; state changes require windows, grounds, and versions. [T-main]

24 | Observables (observables). Original card: 1. Differences in relational density and constraints inside/outside boundaries; 2. Records of members entering, exiting, and being excluded; 3. Repeated co-occurrence of common problems, resource channels, or institutional rules; 4. Whether grouping gain remains stable after grouping rules change. Interpretation: observable indications tell us where to seek materials; a single indication’s presence is not proof of a complete mechanism or causal effect. [T-main]

25 | Evidence requirements (evidence). Original card: 1. D0 candidate-object and identity records; 2. G1-instance preregistration form and matched N0; 3. Training and out-of-sample or generalization results; 4. Gain comparisons between candidate and competing groupings. Interpretation: this column includes materials needed when applying for G1; it must not be read as requiring all G1 steps before everyday R0 description or ordinary services. Evidence gathering follows the particular route and task relevance. [T-main]

26 | Input dependencies and interface content (input_dependencies). Original card: 1. D0 provides candidate-object fields only, not evidence that the structure is established; 2. Preregistered G1-instance and matched N0, thresholds, model class, samples or generalization units; 3. Observation positions, competing groupings, and E1 protocol. Interpretation: this states what arrives from upstream and its eligibility; gaps cannot quietly disappear while passing between interfaces. [T-main]

27 | Output effects and variable flow (output_effects). Original card: 1. R0 provides the remaining variables with candidate-object references, boundaries, time windows, and uncertainty; R1 additionally provides the bounded effective scope supported by G1; 2. Grounds for object existence and domain facts remain separate from grouping gain. Interpretation: variable flow identifies downstream judgments that may depend on this interface; passing references guarantees neither downstream conclusions, actual repair, nor authorization. [T-main]

28 | Time window and lag (time_window_and_lag). Original card: Register identification windows, boundary changes, and membership-change lags. Interpretation: occurrence, observation, execution, and arrival of effects may differ in time; short-term materials cannot automatically certify extensions beyond the window. [T-main]

29 | Uncertainty (uncertainty). Original card: Record boundary disputes, absent members, and observational coverage. Interpretation: direct uncertainty toward specific materials and positions; an overall confidence score cannot conceal fundamentally uncovered positions. [T-main]

30 | Local exclusion zone (local_exclusion_zone). Original card: Positions unable to express themselves safely or not sampled must not be represented by the aggregate. Interpretation: exclusion zones limit current inferential coverage, not delete people or facts from the world; unavailability for safety is neither consent nor absence of problems. [T-main]

31 | Affected positions (affected_positions). Original card: 1. Members; 2. Excluded people; 3. Cost bearers outside the boundary. Interpretation: register directly and indirectly affected parties together; visible members do not represent every cost bearer. [T-main]

32 | Uptake carrier (carrier). Original card: 1. Relational networks; 2. Organizational boundaries; 3. Institutional records. Interpretation: a carrier is the structure or process that actually carries something; its name, completed construction, and arrival of the required function are different evidence. [T-main]

33 | Responsible party (responsible_subject). Original card: 1. Analysts proposing structural-domain judgments; 2. Decision-makers using those judgments. Interpretation: identify who proposes, operates, or uses judgments; recording responsibility is not automatically a legal-liability adjudication or new authorization. [T-main]

34 | Normative status (normative_status). Original card: A descriptive H-World interface; generates no justification. Interpretation: distinguish descriptive, normative, and bridging status according to the card. Established facts do not independently determine value rankings; normative reasons do not automatically prove empirical effects. [T-main]

35 | Judgment ceiling (judgment_ceiling). Original card: Only when G1-instance passes, and only within the preregistered object, scale, window, outcome, and generalization unit, may an explanatory-level bounded effective structural domain be registered; otherwise do not register grouping-gain support, while candidate-object references and independently grounded object facts remain as usual. Interpretation: the ceiling here is an explanatory-level bounded effective structural domain supported by grouping gain and bound to preregistered outcomes and generalization units. Without G1 support, candidate references and independent object facts still remain according to their respective grounds. [T-main]

36 | Action ceiling (action_ceiling). Original card: This variable produces only descriptions of candidate structural domains, boundary disputes, and supplementary-evidence needs; it authorizes no inclusion, exclusion, or disposition. Any real adjustment must separately pass C12, explicit runtime N premises, J authorization, and O procedures. Interpretation: the interface itself creates no real-world authority to impose dispositions; actual actions separately require checking choice, C12, explicit N, valid J, O, protections, and periods. [T-main]

37 | Counterexamples (counterexamples). Original card: 1. People repeatedly co-occurring in one location have no stable relations or common constraints; 2. A group delineated by an analyst disappears immediately when grouping rules change. Interpretation: counterexamples restrict unconditional extrapolation; they may require narrowing scope or gathering evidence anew, without automatically negating every bounded use. [T-main]

38 | Appeal (appeal). Original card: Under appeal_and_rollback_rule, members and affected positions may challenge boundaries, representativeness, and identity criteria through safely accessible channels protected against retaliation, triggering review independent of the original naming or decision chain. Interpretation: appeals must be safely accessible, free from retaliation, and capable of triggering independent review; a name alone does not mean authority to correct errors exists. [T-main]

39 | Rollback (rollback). Original card: Under appeal_and_rollback_rule, when rollback is authorized, a designated responsible person must actually revoke the structural-domain registration within the specified period, remove its effect on downstream object scope, and return it to candidate grouping. Independently grounded object facts are not thereby revoked; preserve versions and completion verification. Interpretation: actually cancel erroneous effects within valid authorization, correct downstream uses, and verify completion; changing document wording does not restore rights and resources to the affected person. [T-main]

Read the complete card’s outputs and rollback together: R1 supports only grouping gain and robustness to boundary perturbations within preregistered SP/T/K and generalization units. Revoking the corresponding structural-domain registration and its downstream gain effect does not revoke object facts with other reliable grounds. R0 may still provide candidate references carrying boundaries and uncertainty; the card state “not established” cannot be expanded into denial of people’s existence.
argumentSteps: Use D0 to fix object, boundary, scale, window, and K.
Without an eligible supported G1 instance yet, follow R0 and output only candidate descriptions and supplementary-evidence needs.
When applying for R1, freeze outcomes, model class, matched N0, thresholds, and generalization units, then judge through the G1 instance.
Limit instance support to preregistered scope; downstream recipients receive the same evidential status.
Members, excluded people, and cost bearers outside boundaries can all challenge representation and boundaries.
If a boundary judgment is withdrawn, eliminate downstream effects and verify through valid procedures; do not impose dispositions directly from the interface.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: crossing a numerical threshold is only part of an instance judgment
teachingExamples.text: Suppose an outcome score for which higher is better, a matched N0, and a 5-point threshold are frozen in advance; in the same extrapolation evaluation, the candidate grouping scores 78 and matched N0 scores 70, giving a difference of 8 points, above 5. This completes only the numerical comparison in the setup; conditions including valid freezing, independent evidence, matching of comparisons, error, and decision rules are still required. 8>5 alone cannot establish that a real G1 is supported. If the scope is this type of team this quarter, it also cannot be extrapolated nationwide or to shared will.
teachingExamples.assumptions: All scores and thresholds are teaching constructions, not measured samples or an actual G1 instance.
teachingExamples.boundary: An artificial threshold crossing is not used as formal supported status, still less as real-world authority to include or exclude.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: candidate references can still be used
teachingExamples.text: Constructed materials concern residents of the same building, but G1 has not been conducted. R0 may fix the candidate resident scope and absent people, then pass it to HV02 to describe entrances, exits, and resource interfaces; “a building roster exists” must not be rewritten as everyone’s wishes, nor may ordinary safety support be refused because G1 has not been conducted.
teachingExamples.assumptions: The building and people are fictional; no personal data are involved.
teachingExamples.boundary: An available descriptive entry point does not establish its causal effects or all domain facts.

questionAnswers.question: Does absence of G1 support mean no relationship or boundary may be described?
questionAnswers.answer: No; with complete D0, the R0 candidate-description route can be used, passing references with uncertainty to other HV interfaces.

questionAnswers.question: If grouping gain is sufficient, can a shared will be declared?

A.2.title: A.2 HV02 Boundaries and Interfaces (Complete Interface Card)
A.2.lead: HV02 separates formal boundaries, actual passage, and causal effects of specified channels; neither membership nor influence scope automatically becomes consent or jurisdiction.
explanation: Original location: Chinese source lines 3866–3949; original site location /theory/appendix-a/a-02#section-a-2. See the theory-v2 source for the current full text; historical research manuscripts and excerpts remain available for download and checking against the original edition.

Short quotation, translated from the Chinese: “membership equals consent” is a prohibited leap. HV02 does not merely draw an inside/outside line; it registers members, resources, information, rights, responsibilities, and cross-boundary interfaces together. Formal rosters, actual resource control, technical openness, and real passage may differ; relevant judgments should pause when these are conflated or exclusions are invisible. [T-main]

The upstream inferential dependency is HV01, but inputs may be HV01 candidate objects or supported structural domains, carrying their evidence status. R0 does not require G1 to have passed in advance, so “grouping gain has not yet been established” does not prevent describing thresholds, waiting, and refusals; nor does it permit silently rewriting a candidate object as a unified community. [T-main; T-HV01]

HV02-R0-boundary-inventory permits description of boundary states, interface accessibility, gatekeeping positions, refusal records, and exclusion risks when the six boundary contents and formal–actual differences can be registered item by item. Its ceiling is inventory and description only; it cannot claim that the boundary has produced a causal selection effect. “Selective openness” as a state differs in strength from an established causal effect. [T-main]

HV02-R1-selective-effect requires a preregistered boundary or interface change that, through a qualified G2-instance, shows an above-threshold channel effect on specified cross-boundary flows or admission/refusal outcomes, with CAUSAL and E4 additionally required. Permitted conclusions are limited to the specified channel, window, positions, and distribution of cross-boundary costs; spatial, organizational, or influence scope cannot imply J-axis authority to act. Observed before-and-after change still requires addressing competing explanations and matched comparisons. [T-main; T-G2]

A boundary is not closure. An interface may be open to some information, impose eligibility restrictions on other resources, and have different actual accessibility for different groups; boundaries of rights and responsibilities need not coincide with physical walls. Nine-axis elevation requires adding membership categories, cross-domain interfaces, representative authorization, and inherited protections; especially after gatekeeping nodes change, recheck who can refuse and who can appeal. [T-main]

States, observables, and evidence jointly help locate gaps: roster exceptions, usage records, flows, refusal reasons, waiting times, and formal–actual differences each answer different questions. For positions unable to access, unable to exit, or withheld for protection, “no usage record” cannot imply absence of need or existing consent. [T-main]

Outputs connect to HV05 uptake, HV07 write-back, and PF-9 exit, but the existence of an interface does not establish arrival of resources, write-back of bad news, or safe exit. Authorized rollback must correct membership/refusal records, actually restore corresponding admission or interface states, revoke erroneous actions, and verify completion; merely changing “closed” to “open” in a table is insufficient. [T-main]

The OECD’s urban accessibility method distinguishes the presence of a stop from accessibility of service opportunities, providing a local reference for the difference between formal openness and actual accessibility; it has not performed a preregistered G2 here, and a methodological definition cannot count as causal support for a boundary change. The original 39-field card is preserved in full below, with interpretation limited by the selected route. [P-OECD; T-main]
Field-by-field study of all 39 fields (“Original card” below retains the field’s complete content in translation; “Interpretation” specifies its role and irreplaceable responsibility).

01 | Interface ID (id). Original card, translated: HV02. Explanation: this is a short identifier within the card collection, tracking the same interface; it does not indicate that a real object has been established. [T-main]

02 | Qualified ID (qualified_id). Original card, translated: human_variable:HV02. Explanation: the qualified namespace prevents name collisions; references to this ID must still carry the object and evidence status. [T-main]

03 | Name (name). Original card, translated: Boundaries and Interfaces. Explanation: the name provides a reading entry point, not an automatic label for specific people, groups, or real structures. [T-main]

04 | Claim type (claim_type). Original card: H. Interpretation: H identifies the role of a human-instance/interface proposition; it cannot be upgraded into formal proof or an unconditional law of the world. [T-main]

05 | Contract role (contract_role). Original card: human_variable_interface. Interpretation: this variable-interface contract specifies how to enter analysis; a field’s existence does not mean an empirical instance has been established. [T-main]

06 | Proposition (proposition). Original card, translated: Human boundaries must register members, resources, information, rights, responsibilities, and cross-boundary interfaces together. Explanation: this proposition must be understood together with the conditional routes and ceilings below; unconditional causal or normative conclusions cannot be extracted from one sentence. [T-main]

07 | Scope (scope). Original card, translated: Human structures involving inclusion, exclusion, exchange, or jurisdiction. Explanation: the scope lists task domains that may be examined; it does not mean all objects within it have empirical support. [T-main]

08 | Pause condition (pause_condition). Original card, translated: Formal and actual boundaries are conflated, or exclusions are invisible. Explanation: pausing applies to judgments or adoption dependent on this; independently established descriptions may remain, but invalid premises cannot continue to be used. [T-main]

09 | Inferential dependencies (inferential_requires). Original card, translated: 1. human_variable:HV01. Explanation: an HV01 reference may carry candidate status; this card’s R0 does not require G1 to have passed. An upstream candidate reference must not be elevated by concealing its evidence status. [T-main]

10 | Protocol dependencies (protocol_requires). Original card: 1. E1; 2. EVIDENCE; 3. SOURCE. Interpretation: protocol dependencies constrain evidence gathering and expression; completing protocols does not independently prove an empirical proposition true. [T-main]

11 | Qualification / specialization (specializes). Original card: None (empty set). Interpretation: an empty set means only that no such specialization relations are registered, not that evidential responsibility is absent; a nonempty set also does not imply universal validity. [T-main]

12 | Applicable-object references (applies_to). Original card: None (empty set). Interpretation: applicable-object references cannot replace the current object contract; an empty set is explicit registration, not permission to apply to every object. [T-main]

13 | Conditional support routes (conditional_support_routes). Original card, translated: 1. route_id=HV02-R0-boundary-inventory;; claim_level=descriptive_classification;; when=Members, resources, information, rights, responsibilities, cross-boundary interfaces, and formal–actual boundary differences can be registered item by item.;; additional_inferential_requires=None (empty set);; additional_protocol_requires=None (empty set);; allowed_conclusion=Describe boundary states, interface accessibility, gatekeeping positions, refusal records, and exclusion risks.;; result_ceiling=Boundary and interface inventory only; must not claim that the boundary has produced a causal selection effect.; 2. route_id=HV02-R1-selective-effect;; claim_level=conditional_effect;; when=A preregistered boundary or interface change, through a qualified G2-instance, shows an above-threshold channel effect on specified cross-boundary flows or admission or refusal outcomes.;; additional_inferential_requires=G2-instance;; additional_protocol_requires=CAUSAL, E4;; allowed_conclusion=Register boundary selection effects and the distribution of cross-boundary costs at the specified channel, window, and positions.;; result_ceiling=Limited to tested channels and outcomes; spatial, organizational, or influence scope must not imply J-axis jurisdiction and authority to act. Explanation: R0 only inventories boundaries and interfaces; R1 requires a qualified preregistered G2 channel effect plus CAUSAL and E4. Sharing a task object does not give the two routes equal conclusion strength. [T-main]

14 | Allowed inferences (allowed_inference). Original card, translated: 1. Boundary selectivity; 2. Interface accessibility; 3. Cross-boundary costs. Explanation: boundary selectivity, accessibility, and costs may be described under R0; a claim of causal effect for a specified channel requires R1, and this short list alone cannot bypass the routes. [T-main]

15 | Prohibited leaps (prohibited_leap). Original card, translated: 1. Boundary equals closure; 2. Membership equals consent; 3. Influence scope equals jurisdiction. Explanation: these are common overreaches that cannot be avoided merely by rephrasing; check actual inference and subsequent use, not wording alone. [T-main]

16 | Nine-axis scale profile (scale_profile). Original card, translated: SP=<A,X,T,O,C,R,I,N,J>; A=aggregation level: single cross-boundary events, individual interface-use cases, populations of membership categories, admission/refusal distributions, and aggregation rules; X=spatial scope: physical entrances, organizational boundaries, digital interfaces, jurisdictions, and cross-domain channels; T=time span: boundary effective periods, interface waiting, migration lags, and reorganization cycles; O=organizational level: user roles, gatekeeping teams, organizations, institutions, through to governance ecosystems; C=causal level: cross-boundary events, gatekeeping interaction mechanisms, interface structures, institutional rules, and system conditions; R=observation resolution: raw admission/refusal records, usage sequences, individual cases, flow distributions, service indicators, and summaries, recording compression losses; I=influence scope: direct users, excluded people, positions receiving indirect benefits or bearing costs, second-order spillovers, cross-domain and intergenerational effects; N=network topology scope: interface nodes, gatekeeping bottlenecks, alternative paths, and cross-domain connections; J=jurisdiction and authorization scope: register authorization separately for inclusion, exclusion, interface changes, and adjustments to rights and responsibilities; elevation must record differences on each axis. Explanation: register all nine axes individually; in particular, influence scope I does not produce jurisdictional permission J, and compression losses must be retained when observation resolution R decreases. [T-main]

17 | Effective object (effective_object). Original card, translated: Boundaries that produce selectivity in flows of resources, information, rights, or responsibilities. Explanation: the original card says boundaries producing selectivity; under R0, treat these as objects to describe or test, without using the name to declare a causal selection effect in advance. [T-main]

18 | Scale invariants (scale_invariants). Original card, translated: 1. Inside/outside positions; 2. Cross-boundary channels; 3. Boundaries of rights and responsibilities. Explanation: invariants are comparative responsibilities to preserve during transfer, not a claim that variable values remain unchanged at every scale. [T-main]

19 | Required scale additions (required_scale_additions). Original card, translated: 1. New membership categories; 2. Cross-domain interfaces; 3. Representation and authorization; 4. Inherited protections. Explanation: elevation is not copying and enlarging the original table. When materials about new populations, interfaces, responsibility positions, and so on are incomplete, limit conclusions dependent on them. [T-main]

20 | Changing semantics (changing_semantics). Original card, translated: 1. Boundaries of membership, interfaces, and actual control may change. Explanation: the same word may change meaning when the object or scale changes; rebuild correspondences rather than assuming the original meaning applies unchanged. [T-main]

21 | Non-applicable objects (non_applicable_objects). Original card, translated: 1. Nonhuman boundaries without concepts of membership, rights, or responsibilities. Explanation: non-applicability constraints prevent unconditional projection of human normative, responsibility, and experience interfaces; they do not deny that other theories can study these objects. [T-main]

22 | Forbidden elevation (forbidden_elevation). Original card, translated: 1. Expansion of spatial or organizational scope automatically produces jurisdiction. Explanation: inference from local to whole needs separate support; broad influence, grand names, or formal similarity cannot supply missing representativeness or authorization. [T-main]

23 | State set (state). Original card, translated: 1. Open; 2. Selectively open; 3. Closed; 4. Disputed; 5. Reorganizing. Explanation: states are descriptive classifications requiring evidence, not a maturity ladder for scoring people; state changes require a window, grounds, and version. [T-main]

24 | Observables (observables). Original card, translated: 1. Decisions about membership, admission, and exit; 2. Cross-boundary flows of resources, information, rights, and responsibilities; 3. Gatekeeping nodes, waiting times, and refusal reasons; 4. Differences between formal boundaries and boundaries of actual passage. Explanation: observable leads indicate where to seek materials; a single lead is not proof of a complete mechanism or causal effect. [T-main]

25 | Evidence requirements (evidence). Original card, translated: 1. Membership rosters and exceptions; 2. Interface usage records; 3. Cross-boundary flow and refusal records. Explanation: obtain evidence according to route and task relevance; distinguish unknown, uncollected, not applicable, and unavailable for protection, without forcing disclosure to fill the table. [T-main]

26 | Input dependencies and interface contents (input_dependencies). Original card, translated: 1. HV01 candidate objects or supported structural domains and their evidence status; 2. Roles and authorization; R0 does not require G1 to have passed in advance. Explanation: this specifies what comes from upstream and its qualifications; gaps cannot silently disappear during transfer between interfaces. [T-main]

27 | Output effects and variable flows (output_effects). Original card, translated: 1. HV05 uptake; 2. HV07 write-back; 3. PF-9 exit. Explanation: variable flows indicate which downstream judgments may depend on this interface; passing a reference does not guarantee downstream conclusions, actual repair, or authorization. [T-main]

28 | Time window and lag (time_window_and_lag). Original card, translated: Record lags in boundary effectiveness, change, exit, and appeal. Explanation: occurrence, observation, execution, and arrival of effects may happen at different times; short-term materials cannot automatically certify extension beyond the window. [T-main]

29 | Uncertainty (uncertainty). Original card, translated: Record informal boundaries, proxy access, and drift in digital spaces. Explanation: tie uncertainty to specific materials and positions; a single overall confidence score must not conceal positions that were never covered. [T-main]

30 | Local exclusion zone (local_exclusion_zone). Original card, translated: Positions unable to access an interface, unable to exit, or withheld from public disclosure for protection. Explanation: exclusion zones limit the coverage of current inferences; they do not erase these people or facts from the world, and safety-related unavailability does not mean consent or absence of problems. [T-main]

31 | Affected positions (affected_positions). Original card, translated: 1. Members; 2. Applicants; 3. Excluded people; 4. Those bearing burdens outside the boundary. Explanation: register both directly and indirectly affected people; visible members do not represent everyone bearing costs. [T-main]

32 | Uptake carriers (carrier). Original card, translated: 1. Membership rules; 2. Access mechanisms; 3. Legal or institutional boundaries; 4. Technical interfaces. Explanation: carriers are the structures or processes actually carrying something; the carrier’s name, completed construction, and delivery of required functions are different evidence. [T-main]

33 | Responsible parties (responsible_subject). Original card, translated: 1. Boundary setters; 2. Interface operators; 3. Authorizers. Explanation: specify who proposes the judgment and who operates or uses it; registering responsibility does not automatically adjudicate legal liability or issue new authorization. [T-main]

34 | Normative status (normative_status). Original card, translated: Separate boundary facts from the justification of boundaries. Explanation: distinguish descriptive, normative, and bridging status according to the card. Established facts do not independently determine value rankings, and normative reasons do not automatically establish empirical effects. [T-main]

35 | Judgment ceiling (judgment_ceiling). Original card, translated: Up to diagnostic level when interface and impact evidence are sufficient. Explanation: “up to diagnostic level when evidence is sufficient” is an overall upper bound; R0 still stops at inventory description, and diagnosis cannot issue permission to change admission or resource flows. [T-main]

36 | Action ceiling (action_ceiling). Original card, translated: This variable generates only descriptions of boundary states, interface barriers, exclusion risks, and testing needs; it does not authorize changes to admission, exit, rights, or resource flows. Any real-world adjustment must separately pass C12, explicit runtime N premises, J authorization, and O procedures. Explanation: the interface itself produces no real-world authority to act; actual actions require separate checks of choice, C12, explicit N, valid J, O, protections, and time limits. [T-main]

37 | Counterexamples (counterexamples). Original card, translated: 1. Formal membership boundaries run contrary to actual resource-control boundaries; 2. A digital interface is open, but physical, language, or safety barriers prevent some positions from entering. Explanation: use counterexamples to limit unconditional extrapolation; they may require narrowing scope or collecting evidence again, but do not automatically invalidate every bounded use. [T-main]

38 | Appeal (appeal). Original card, translated: Under appeal_and_rollback_rule, affected people inside and outside the boundary may challenge inclusion, exclusion, and interface barriers through safely accessible anti-retaliation channels and trigger review independent of the original boundary decision chain. Explanation: appeals must be safely accessible, free of retaliation, and able to trigger independent review; a name alone does not mean there is power to correct errors. [T-main]

39 | Rollback (rollback). Original card, translated: Under appeal_and_rollback_rule, when rollback is authorized, a designated responsible person must correct membership and refusal records within the specified time, actually restore affected admission rights or interface states, revoke erroneous boundary actions, and preserve versions and completion verification. Explanation: within valid authorization, actually revoke erroneous effects, correct downstream consequences, and verify completion; changing document wording does not mean rights and resources have been restored to the person concerned. [T-main]
argumentSteps: Fix scope using an HV01 candidate or supported object, retaining its evidence status.
Register formal–actual differences item by item for members, resources, information, rights, responsibilities, and interfaces.
R0 first describes thresholds and exclusions; an inventory must not be treated as a causal effect.
R1 separately uses preregistered G2 and CAUSAL/E4 to test specified channels and outcomes.
When transferring scale, check new members, cross-domain interfaces, representative authority, and inherited protections.
Correct boundaries through safe independent appeals; once authorized, restore actual interfaces and downstream records.

teachingExamples.text: Everyone can open a fictional service’s webpage, but submission requires a particular credential and its sole supported language is incomprehensible to some users. teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: before/after figures are not automatically G2
teachingExamples.text: Before a constructed interface change, 20 of 100 applications succeed; afterward, 40 of 100 succeed. The observed success proportion rises from 20% to 40%, a 20-percentage-point difference. If applicant composition, demand, or other processes changed simultaneously, the difference cannot be attributed to the interface alone. Applying for R1 additionally requires an eligible preregistered G2 and rules for comparison, thresholds, windows, and evidence; there is no formal supported status here.
teachingExamples.assumptions: The numbers are entirely instructional; two sets of 100 do not guarantee the same population or a valid comparison.
teachingExamples.boundary: Correlation or before/after differences cannot replace a causal contract; changing barriers also requires independent authority.
