app-b.title: Appendix B Numbering System and Terminology Table
app-b.lead: An index helps you find a contract; it cannot fulfill it for you. Shared letters, adjacent identifiers, and counts supply no additional evidence or permission.
explanation: Original location: Chinese source lines 4760–4804; original site location: this part’s introduction (no independently numbered anchor). See the theory-v2 source for the current full text; historical research manuscripts and excerpts remain available for download and checking against the original edition.

Short quotation, translated from the Chinese: “This table serves only as a navigational index.” Appendix B answers where to find definitions and contracts, rather than using a prefix to replace the full conditions. Counts are numbers of index entries, not numbers of empirically established items; adjacent identifiers do not imply inferential dependencies or a sequence of maturity. [T-main]

01 | D0–D3 comprise 4 items in Part Three defining structural objects, basic state terms, effective feedback, and scale transformation. Definitions fix language and contracts, but do not independently establish that real objects meet them. [T-main]
02 | U01–U11 comprise 11 universal structural primitives in Part Three. The primitives organize object descriptions; they are not 11 validated universal causal laws. [T-main]

03 | G1–G4 comprise 4 empirical question families in Part Four, with concrete tests established through G-instance; citing a G identifier only indicates the question family and cannot bypass instance qualifications. [T-main]

04 | Laws 1–3 comprise 3 common method constraints in Part Four and Appendix C, governing respectively tasks and representations, material status and scope of support, and facts, values, and action eligibility. “Law” here is not an empirically necessary regularity or real-world legal authorization. [T-main]

05 | F1–F6 comprise 6 conditional formal propositions in Part Four and Appendix C, covering task recovery, closure, joint feasibility of actions, composition preservation, error propagation, and task-family refinement. Conclusions depend on their respective mathematical conditions; social cases do not automatically qualify by sharing an identifier. [T-main]
06 | E1–E5 comprise 5 epistemological constraints in Part Four. Methodological constraints can require how judgments are made, but do not themselves supply real-world effect data. [T-main]

07 | C1–C12 comprise 12 outcome contracts, mechanism propositions, and procedural bridges in Part Four. This C proposition prefix differs from causal-level C in the nine axes; C12 must be used according to its own bridging contract. [T-main]

08 | A/X/T/O/C/R/I/N/J are Part Five’s 9 SP axes and cannot be compressed into a single micro–macro line. J authorization cannot be derived from the scope of the other axes; topological N also differs from normative N1–N5. [T-main]

09 | M01–M09 comprise 9 scale-transformation operators in Part Five. Preservation, losses, and added conditions after transformation must be checked; an operator’s name does not establish valid transfer. [T-main]

10 | CM-* comprises 6 conditional mechanism families in Part Six: FEEDBACK, LEARNING, MAINTENANCE, LOAD, PHASE, and SELECTION. Branches within each family have their own contracts; the word “learning” cannot replace evidence of carriers, temporal order, or effects. [T-main]

11 | H1–H6 comprise 6 human-domain clauses in Part Seven. Check each clause’s status to determine which are empirical instances, classifications, or normative boundaries; do not call them collectively six empirical laws. [T-main]

12 | GC/GS/GE/CV/RS/IS/IM/IB comprise 8 strongly typed labels in Part Seven: generative conditions/subjects/events, uptake carriers, responsible parties, and sources/mechanisms/behaviors of destabilization. The original table calls them “three groups of strong types that must not be mixed,” but this does not mean the eight labels are interchangeable; the same real entity may have different roles, yet evidence for the fields is still collected separately. [T-main]

13 | HV01–HV11 comprise 11 unified interfaces for human variables in Part Seven, with complete cards in Appendix A. An interface’s existence does not mean someone’s variable state has been measured, nor does it directly create authority to adjust it. [T-main]
14 | S0–S6 plus X0 are recorded as 7+1: Part Eight’s seven human state prototypes plus one orderly exit path. 7+1 is not eight stages, X0 is not called S7, and numbering does not rank value. [T-main]

15 | IG1–IG7 comprise 7 gates and are Part Thirteen’s only main workflow; 16 | SJ1–SJ8 comprise 8 strong-judgment materials; 17 | L1–L3 comprise 3 diagnostic levels. Workflow, strong-judgment components, and levels of effort are different dimensions, not one continuous process. [T-main]

18 | TOOL-* comprises 6 formal tools in Part Thirteen: EVIDENCE-LEDGER, OPEN-ASSERTION, CLAIM-VALIDATION, FORECAST-REGISTRY, STRESS-TEST, and AI-BOUNDARY. Tool records can carry checks, but complete forms do not self-validate a judgment. [T-main]

19 | N1–N5 comprise 5 runtime premises for normative choice in Part Fourteen; 20 | O1–O4 comprise 4 bounded-authorization procedures; 21 | PF-1–PF-10 comprise 10 interfaces for normative choice and choice records. Value choices, authorization procedures, and interface records are separate; normative N differs from topological N, and procedural O differs from organizational-scale O. [T-main]

22 | T0–T4 comprise 5 intervention levels in Part Fifteen; 23 | APP-* comprises 9 application modules: REL/FAM/ORG/PLT/INS/OPI/SPC/EMG/ULS. Intervention levels are not empirical confidence levels, and application names do not grant authority in the corresponding domain. [T-main]

24 | GOV-01–GOV-24 comprise 24 governance clauses in Part Sixteen. Governance constraints and application modules cross-reference each other, but the index does not replace each clause’s applicability conditions and action boundaries. [T-main]

Recurring notation must also be read item by item: S*=<B,X,R,I,T,SP,K> contains the seven fields of the D0 candidate-object contract—boundary, state variables, relations or transition constraints, interfaces, time window, scale profile, and identity criterion. These local letters cannot be interpreted directly as the same letters in SP’s nine axes; R in S* is not observation-resolution R, I is not influence-scope I, and X is not spatial-axis X. [T-main]

N0 is a null model, not a zeroth norm preceding N1–N5; K*/F* are repair-target identity and functional criteria. G-instance and H-instance are concrete test instances; an identifier does not mean supported status. F1–F6 are identifiers for formal propositions; standalone F/F* may mean dynamic update, functional criterion, or repair target under local definitions. The same letter does not imply the same object. [T-main]

The final historical boundary is a substantive reminder: G3 tests only historical conditional increment beyond a given current representation. Carrier-mediated learning, accumulation, persistence, and intertemporal reproduction are checked under their respective mechanism contracts; positive G3 support is not their shared prerequisite. When consulting the index, do not attach all these terms to G3 merely because they involve time. [T-main]

In practice, first identify the current sentence’s namespace, local definition, object, and version; then return to the main-text contract; finally check instance materials and permitted conclusions. This appendix makes no external empirical claims; forcing in a historical case would confuse “navigational use” with “theory validation,” so this topic uses explicitly constructed naming-collision exercises without claiming they are historical cases. [T-main]
argumentSteps: Identify the prefix and local namespace, then consult the corresponding main-text part.
Separate the number of identifiers from the number of supported instances.
Distinguish definitional, formal, empirical, normative, procedural, and tool status.
Check local definitions each time for shared letters in S* and SP, F/F*, and N0/N1–N5.
G3 applies only to increment beyond the current representation; check other intertemporal contracts separately.
Cite main-text conditions and instance materials; do not substitute the index for evidence.

intro-19-appendix-c.title: Appendix C Common method kernel and Interdisciplinary Bridging
intro-19-appendix-c.lead: The shared core shares methodological responsibilities without taking away each text’s authority over definitions or letting two texts manufacture independent empirical support for one another.
explanation: Original location: Chinese source lines 4805–4808; original site location: this part’s introduction (no independently numbered anchor). See the theory-v2 source for the current full text; historical research manuscripts and excerpts remain available for download and checking against the original edition.

The introduction states that interoperability across texts can share methodological responsibilities while each text retains its authoritative definitions and operational form. What is shared is how grounds and boundaries are accounted for, not a requirement that all books use the same chapter structure, number of artifacts, or numbering. [T-intro]

“Does not make one text independent empirical evidence for the other” concerns source independence: if A cites B and B cites A in return, without new observations of an object, this cannot count as two external validations. Texts interpreting one another may have interpretive value, but material status must be retained. [T-intro]

Interoperability requires at least declarations of the current text version, cited definitions, corresponding content, and differences. Similar names do not mean identical contracts; the same example may also come from the same upstream source, and changing format does not make sources independent. [T-intro]

This topic has only the user-provided Xikari original and has not obtained the authoritative full text of World Model; it can therefore explain only this book’s proposed interoperability responsibilities, without claiming to have completed a field-by-field comparison of the two books or approved the other book’s definitions. [T-intro]

C.1 below is a list of stable references at the navigation level; it can tell readers what to compare, but does not mean comparison has been completed. Actual joint adoption still requires checking the respective boundaries of definitions, evidence, norms, and real-world authorization. [T-intro; T-main]
argumentSteps: First fix the identities and versions of both texts.
Separate shared methods from each text’s definitions and operational form.
Do not count restatements from the same source as independent empirical evidence.
When the other text is missing, retain unverified status rather than inventing a comparison.

C.1.title: C.1 Methodological Core and Stable References
C.1.lead: A stable reference first locates the relevant level, then returns to the original contract; the six-row table does not merge different materials and responsibilities into one kind of evidence.
explanation: Original location: Chinese source lines 4809–4819; original site location /theory/appendix-c#section-c-1. See the theory-v2 source for the current full text; historical research manuscripts and excerpts remain available for download and checking against the original edition.

The definition level covers objects, states, feedback, scale, circles, information status, and recasting, pointing to this framework’s definitions and World Model’s authoritative definitions. A reference at the definition level means consulting word meanings and object contracts; definitions cannot establish that an object actually exists. [T-main]

Methodological constraints Laws 1–3 point to §4.17, with separate responsibilities for tasks and representations, material status, and facts and action eligibility. Citing a constraint can explain which checks should be made, but cannot establish that following it necessarily improves real-world outcomes. [T-main; T-method]

Conditional formal propositions F point to §4.18–4.19 and this appendix: task recovery, closure, common actions, transformation composition, error, and dynamic refinement. Formal proofs must carry their assumptions; their results are separate from whether real objects satisfy those assumptions. [T-main]

Empirical problem families G1–G4 point to the instance contracts in Part Four: grouping, channels, historical increments, and representational closure, respectively. Stable references need not only a family ID but also the current specific instance and its eligibility. G3 historical increments are not a common threshold for all learning. [T-main]

Result and mechanism contracts C1–C12 point to their respective contracts in Part Four, used for result registration, mechanism composition, and bridges to normative procedures. A seemingly matching story cannot replace a contract, nor can formal rigor alone authorize real actions. [T-main]

Governance invariants concern freezing, evidence, baselines, authorization, protection, and lifecycle, pointing to the two texts’ existing governance provisions. This is a shared checking agenda given by this book, not verified identical provisions or operating results in an actual version of the other text. [T-main]

Stable references should preserve original namespaces and locations, rather than use only similar words such as “method” or “closure.” Mapping a field in A to a field in B requires recording invariants, differences, unknowns, and stopping conditions. The other full text was not read for this topic, so no such mapping is fabricated. [T-main; T-diff]
argumentSteps: Determine each row’s role: definition, method, formal proposition, empirical claim, contract, or governance.
Use the body-text locations in the table to read the actual conditions.
Trace empirical references further to instances and source material.
Keep unverified cross-text differences unverified; shared names cannot fill them in.

C.2.title: C.2 Common method constraints
C.2.lead: Methods 1–3 specify responsible model use; following the procedure does not itself establish a model’s real-world effectiveness.
explanation: Source location: Chinese source lines 4820–4825, original-site location /theory/appendix-c#section-c-2. The current full text is in the theory-v2 source; the historical research draft and excerpts remain downloadable in their original versions.

Method 1 declares task, representation, horizon, environment, operations, and error together. Task specifies what must be recovered or predicted; representation specifies what the model can see; horizon and environment limit the valid domain; operations specify permitted actions; and error defines what counts as good enough. Stating an accuracy rate alone while omitting these conditions may mix different tasks. [T-main; T-full]

Static recovery, dynamical closure, and intervention sufficiency are tested separately. A representation that recovers today’s target need not update to tomorrow; predicting passive evolution does not guarantee that actions chosen under that representation are feasible for every hidden state. These are different questions, not something summarized by “the model is good enough.” [T-main; T-full]

Method 2 requires preservation of material identity, source provenance, inferential premises, and support scope. Real observations, internal teaching examples, simulations, normative claims, and formal proofs do not all become external empirical evidence because the same report contains them. Several charts processing the same upstream observation are not several independent materials either. [T-main; T-full]

At minimum, support scope must be traceable to object, window, and corresponding proposition. Summaries or secondary texts may be the material actually read, but must not stand in for verification of the complete source. Inferential premises should also be listed explicitly to prevent a conclusion from circulating back as its own evidence. [T-main; T-full]

Method 3 requires facts, value judgments, and action eligibility to hold separately. An action’s possible effectiveness does not establish that it is worth doing; a worthwhile goal does not establish effective means or an actor’s authority to execute them. Conversely, lacking execution authority does not prohibit grounded normative recommendations, but those recommendations must not be treated as execution authorization. [T-main; T-full]

These three are responsibilities for model use, not three empirical laws of the world. Whether following them reduces errors or adds unnecessary burdens requires separate evaluation, especially with a specified task and comparison baseline. Tool-completion rates cannot replace outcome testing. [T-main]

Teaching should record “checks complete,” “formal derivation correct,” “real-world premises satisfied,” and “actual net benefit established” separately. This section introduces methods and explicitly artificial examples only; it reports no effectiveness of this framework in any real institution. [T-main]
argumentSteps: Freeze task, representation, horizon, environment, operations, and error.
Separate tests of static recovery, dynamical closure, and intervention.
Preserve material identity and upstream provenance; repeated processing is not independent empirical evidence.
List the respective grounds for facts, normative premises, and execution eligibility.
Evaluate the method’s actual benefits and burdens; compliance does not self-certify effectiveness.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: statically sufficient, dynamically unclosed
teachingExamples.text: Let an artificial state be x=(a,b), representation π(x)=a+b, and current task q=a+b, exactly recovered by g(y)=y. Define one-step evolution F(a,b)=(2a,b). States (1,0) and (0,1) both have current representation 1, but their representations after evolution are 2 and 1. The current sum alone cannot supply one exact next sum for both.
teachingExamples.assumptions: The integer states and specified deterministic evolution are entirely mathematical constructions, not social data.
teachingExamples.boundary: Rejects only exact closure of this representation for this dynamic task; it does not reject its static-sum task.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: effects and authority are separate
teachingExamples.text: An artificial scheduling recommendation may reduce waiting, but changes employees’ shifts. Effects need evidence about the object; fairness rankings need normative reasons; execution still needs specific scheduling authority and applicable procedures. One prediction cannot supply all three.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Fictional scheduling; no real effect is claimed.
teachingExamples.boundary: No scheduling is implemented, and no consent is given on employees’ behalf.

C.3.title: C.3 Shared Governance Invariants
C.3.lead: The nine safeguards protect versions, null conclusions, evidence identity, division of responsibility, parsimony, residuals, lifecycle, and low-power positions. They cannot offset one another through a total score.
explanation: Source location: Chinese source lines 4826–4847, original-site location /theory/appendix-c#section-c-3. The current full text is in the theory-v2 source; the historical research draft and excerpts remain downloadable in their original versions.

Safeguard 1, “freeze before results; append only after results,” protects traceable differences between prior rules and later revisions. Seeing results may prompt a new version of tasks, thresholds, and windows, but the old version must not be overwritten and presented as the original. Revision does not prohibit learning; append-only versioning enables honest comparison. [T-main]

Safeguard 2, “lack of support for a positive claim does not mean support for the null model,” preserves null-conclusion boundaries. Insufficient samples, inapplicable measurements, conflicts, or uncertain outcomes may block a positive conclusion without proving no effect. A null model also needs support through its own test. [T-main]

Safeguard 3 prohibits definitions, contracts, internal teaching examples, and internal simulations from serving on their own as external empirical support. They may clarify logic, test implementation, and reveal counterexamples, but “this holds in the stipulated model” differs from a real object actually being that way. [T-main]

Safeguard 4 treats material identity, proposition role, artifact state, and field absence as orthogonal dimensions. External observation is a material identity; empirical hypothesis is a proposition role; draft/frozen is an artifact state; and not collected/conflicting is a missing-information type. A record may have these values simultaneously; one overall “confirmed” label cannot cover them all. [T-main]

Safeguard 5 separates responsibilities for sourcing, modeling, foresight, evaluation, authorization, and execution. One report may contain several modules, but a real source does not automatically provide predictive eligibility, and completed evaluation does not automatically provide execution authority. Every role transition needs its own grounds. [T-main]

Safeguard 6 requires model complexity to undergo proportionate simplification, deletion, and necessity review. Predictive or empirical capability should be compared against simple baselines and independent evaluation material. Formal proofs, textual explanations, and normative arguments are checked according to their tasks, without a compulsory out-of-sample accuracy measure. Simplicity is not inherently correct either; the question is whether added complexity accomplishes the claimed task. [T-main]

Safeguard 7: “Residuals generate competing candidates only, not real-world variables automatically.” Prediction residuals may arise from omitted mechanisms, measurement, noise, changing objects, or a wrong model. A new name without discriminating material must not turn error into an entity. Retain multiple candidates and their failure conditions. [T-main]

Safeguard 8 binds capability to domain, validity period, drift, suspension, rollback, and retirement. Past effectiveness does not guarantee admissibility in a new environment. Suspension or retirement does not mean deleting historical records; rollback also cannot merely change a label while downstream users retain the old effects. [T-main]

Safeguard 9 preserves low-power positions, privacy, protective nondisclosure, appeals, and exit; aggregate results cannot flatten them. Missing voices may reflect unavailability for protective reasons and must not be filled in as consent. Average improvement cannot erase harm and rights questions at particular positions either. [T-main]

The nine safeguards jointly constrain model use; they cannot be compressed into a single “governance qualification score.” Passing one does not fill another’s gap. Independently grounded local conclusions may remain, but strong judgments depending on missing premises must stop at the corresponding boundaries. [T-main]
argumentSteps: Freeze before results, preserving differences through appended revision versions.
Distinguish unsupported positive claims from support for a null model.
Register material identity, proposition role, artifact state, and absence separately.
Separate responsibilities from sourcing through execution, checking each one’s required evidence and authority.
Review complexity by task, and list competing explanations for residuals.
Continuously examine domain and lifecycle, preserving protective nondisclosure and exit.

questionAnswers.question: Can a model be changed after results?
questionAnswers.answer: A revised version may be appended; old records must not be erased to disguise later success as prior success.

questionAnswers.question: Does orthogonality of the four dimensions mean statistical independence?
questionAnswers.answer: Here it means distinct registration dimensions cannot be merged, not that they are probabilistically independent.
questionAnswers.basis: Typing responsibility in Safeguard 4.

questionAnswers.question: Does every argument need out-of-sample metrics?
questionAnswers.answer: No. Evaluation of predictive empirical capability differs from evaluation of formal, textual, or normative tasks.
questionAnswers.basis: Safeguard 6.

questionAnswers.question: Does nondisclosure mean evidence does not exist?
questionAnswers.answer: No. Protective unavailability and its inferential limits must be retained.

C.4.title: C.4 Preserving Differences Across Texts
C.4.lead: Interoperability must preserve differences. Similar names, similar cases, or complete tables cannot replace actual correspondence between both sides’ contracts.
explanation: Source location: Chinese source lines 4848–4853, original-site location /theory/appendix-c#section-c-4. The current full text is in the theory-v2 source; the historical research draft and excerpts remain downloadable in their original versions.

The first set of checks listed here covers proposition layering, empirical problem-family contracts, null conclusions, scale closure, noncommutation tests, and inferential dependencies. They respectively control what a claim is, how it is tested, what cannot be inferred, whether transformations preserve a task, whether order matters, and which premises a conclusion depends on. [T-main]

The second group of checks covers information identity, artifact systems, typed unknowns, experimental evaluation, capability evidence, and model lifecycles. These govern where material comes from, how records are organized, how missingness is distinguished, whether evaluation is independent, whether capabilities have empirical support, and when to pause or retire a model. Similar terms do not guarantee identical semantics or thresholds. [T-main]

“One side's complete contract cannot be replaced by a similarly named concept or case from the other” means that mapping must examine conditions, outputs, and ceilings, rather than finding a similar picture. If correspondence is incomplete, preserve explicit differences and unknown status instead of assuming equivalence; interoperability also need not force changes to the other side's definitions. [T-main]

The source explicitly does not force alignment between this framework's nine scale operators and the operator steps commonly used in World Models, nor merge this framework's fourteen-section scale-transformation record with the other text's closed artifact system. No one-to-one or many-to-one correspondence is inferred from the numbers here. The other authoritative full text was unavailable for this discussion, so no claim is made to have checked its actual fields or counts. [T-main]

The minimum shared semantics are, item by item: preservation—which distinctions remain; change—which properties are recast; folding—which differences are merged; omission—which items are not carried over; new unknowns—which uncertainties arise after conversion; source genealogy—how material was passed along; domain of application—under which objects and conditions it is valid; residuals—what remains unexplained; and stopping—when it can no longer be used. Different artifacts may answer these common questions separately. [T-main]

More unification is not necessarily better interoperability. Forced unification can conceal different unknown states or support thresholds; no communication at all loses opportunities for shared checks. A practical approach lists source contracts, target contracts, verified preservation, unverified differences, and stopping points item by item. This discussion provides only a constructed demonstration, not a purported actual mapping between the two books. [T-main]

Source genealogy and unresolved status must accompany downstream references: if upstream material states only a candidate, using another system's field name downstream cannot upgrade it to confirmed. Format mapping expands neither the domain of application nor authority; actual adoption still follows each contract's checks. [T-main]
argumentSteps: List both versions and exact contract locations side by side.
Check the 12 responsibilities in the two groups individually; names are no substitute.
The nine operators and fourteen-section record each retain their own organization.
Use preservation/change/folding/omission/unknowns/genealogy/domain/residuals/stopping as minimum common questions.
Explicitly preserve differences where fields cannot correspond, limiting downstream conclusions.

C.5.title: C.5 Methodological Examples of Mathematical Scale Bridging
C.5.lead: Mathematical bridging must carry objects, mappings, initial values, history, errors, and validity periods. Approximate commutation of one statistic cannot be upgraded into equivalence of entire states.
explanation: Chinese source location: lines 4854–4864; original site location /theory/appendix-c#section-c-5. For the current full text, see the theory-v2 source; historical research manuscripts and excerpts remain available for checking in their original downloadable versions.

Let x be a microscopic state, M a coarse-graining map, F_t the microscopic evolution, and F̄_t the macroscopic evolution. The two paths are microscopic evolution followed by mapping, M(F_t(x)), and mapping followed by macroscopic evolution, F̄_t(M(x)). Approximate commutation for the corresponding task can be discussed only if their difference does not exceed ε under specified initial conditions, parameter domains, norms, and time intervals. [T-main]

“The corresponding task” is crucial. If M preserves only a sum, the commutation check concerns the sum's dynamics, not recovery of each component; different source states with the same sum may legitimately be merged. Agreement on one statistic cannot establish equivalence of the entire object; conversely, it does not follow that every compression necessarily harms the current task. [T-main]

A proof must also specify the order of limits, error control, and validity period. Holding at each fixed short time does not mean holding uniformly over an infinite time horizon; taking a parameter to zero and time to infinity may require different arguments. This discussion offers only finite discrete constructions and does not claim to prove any general theorem on exchanging limits. [T-main]

Bridging should carry eight responsibilities together: source object, target object, mapping, scaling law or limit, initial values, retained history, error, and failure boundaries. Two models may use different representations; the key is to explain what is preserved for the current task and what cannot be inferred. [T-main]

A mathematical proof holding, a real object satisfying its premises, and choosing an actual option are three distinct responsibilities. The formal existence of a macroscopic map does not establish it as the actual mechanism of a social object, still less confer intervention authority. Losses in social recasting are not physical entropy either. Applicable quantities and models must be established separately; names alone cannot borrow conservation laws or units. [T-main]

The source's research entries 05.05 “Gödel, Incompleteness, and Computability,” 05.06 “Effective Theories, Scale Closure, and Coarse-Graining,” and 05.08 “Model Selection, Parsimony, and Expressive Power” provide navigation only. Specific conclusions require returning to the original works' assumptions, proofs, and validity domains. These research packages or original works were not obtained here, so no claim is made to have checked their theorems or to use their bibliography as support for social bridging. [T-main]

Appendix D's domain map likewise preserves specialist terminology, measurement, arguments, and boundaries. Teaching examples can illustrate only the structure of conditional counterexamples, not impersonate implemented experiments or actual cases. Topic numbers are not rankings of theoretical importance. [T-main]

The two reproducible constructions below test only paths, statistics, and time windows. Diagram symbols come from this section, while numerical values and update rules are constructed for teaching. What can be proved is the arithmetic of these two models, not processes in actual cities, organizations, or minds. [T-main]

Fix the initial-value domain, parameters, error norm, and validity period.
Calculate the difference between the two paths and specify the only statistic being controlled.
Check extrapolation over time or limits; narrow the domain or rebuild the model on failure.
Separate the three responsibilities of proof, real-world premises, and option/authorization.
Research numbers provide navigation only; do not claim unread original works as verified.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: exact commutation of sums does not recover components
teachingExamples.text: Take x=(a,b), M(a,b)=a+b, F(a,b)=(b,a), and macroscopic F̄(y)=y. M(F(x))=b+a=a+b=F̄(M(x)), so the paths commute exactly at every step. But (1,0) and (0,1) both sum to 1, and the representation cannot distinguish which component is 1.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Ordered pairs of real numbers, swap dynamics, and the sum task are constructed mathematical definitions.
teachingExamples.boundary: This proves closure only for the sum task, not recoverability of the full state or lossless real-world resource distribution.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: a short-window tolerance cannot automatically be extended
teachingExamples.text: Let integer t≥0, F_t(a,b)=(a+0.1t,b), let M take the sum, and let F̄_t(y)=y, with absolute-value error. The difference between the two paths is always 0.1t. Over t=0,1,2,3, the maximum is 0.3, satisfying ε=0.3. At t=4, 0.4>0.3, so the original short-window conclusion cannot extend to the fourth step.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Entirely constructed discrete evolution, with 0.1 treated as exactly one tenth and no measurement noise.
teachingExamples.boundary: This demonstrates a validity window, not a claim that all coarse-graining accumulates loss or fails in the long term.

C.6.title: C.6 F1 Task Recovery and Worst-Case Error
C.6.lead: If states in a representation fiber require different answers, the representation alone cannot recover the task exactly. With error permitted, the answer depends on output space, loss, and distribution.
explanation: Chinese source location: lines 4865–4882; original site location /theory/appendix-c#section-c-6. For the current full text, see the theory-v2 source; historical research manuscripts and excerpts remain available for checking in their original downloadable versions.

First list assumptions: X is nonempty, π:X→Y is deterministic with Y=π(X), and the target is q:X→V. The fiber X_y={x:π(x)=y} contains all source states merged by the representation. The decoder may read only y, without secretly inspecting the source state, identity labels, or undeclared history. The image-set condition ensures every y has a nonempty fiber. [T-main]

Task-recovery proposition: a g:Y→V satisfying q=g∘π exists if and only if q is constant on every fiber. Necessity: if π(x)=π(x′)=y, then q(x)=g(y)=q(x′). Sufficiency: for each y, define g(y) as the common q value of its fiber. Constancy ensures no ambiguity, and substituting any x gives q(x)=g(π(x)). [T-main]

Uniqueness holds only on the actual image Y: every y comes from at least one x, so q(x) fixes every feasible g. If the target representation space is artificially extended to points with no source state, the theorem does not constrain those points. Existence as a set function also does not guarantee always-halting computability on infinite domains or sufficient finite budgets. [T-main]

The finite scalar worst-case-error proposition additionally requires finite X, real-valued q, any real number as a permitted output, and loss defined as worst absolute error over the full domain. Let a_y and b_y be each fiber's minimum and maximum. The optimal risk is (1/2)max_y(b_y−a_y), not a universal formula for all losses. [T-main]

Lower-bound proof: for any output c, |a_y−c|+|b_y−c|≥b_y−a_y, so at least one endpoint has error ≥(b_y−a_y)/2. Every decoder's full-domain risk is at least the largest half-range. Attainability proof: choose c=(a_y+b_y)/2 on each fiber. All target values lie between the endpoints, each error is ≤the half-range, and equality holds at the endpoints. Thus the lower bound is attained, and the infimum is actually achieved. [T-main]

Given ε≥0, a decoder with full-domain error ≤ε exists if and only if every fiber's range is ≤2ε. Infinite domains require suprema and boundedness checks; vectors, restricted outputs, average loss, and probability weights are different optimization problems. The midpoint is one optimal choice; “the exact-recovery g is unique” must not be transferred into “a globally optimal worst-error g must be unique.” [T-main]

The binary version separately assumes uniformly distributed finite source states and zero-one loss, with each fiber's two class counts n_y0/n_y1. Output 0 makes n_y1 errors, and output 1 makes n_y0 errors; majority choice yields min(n_y0,n_y1). Total risk is Σ_y min(n_y0,n_y1)/|X|. Randomized labels produce only a convex combination of the two error counts and cannot do better; ties permit multiple optimal rules. [T-main]

Uniformity applies to source states, not fibers or representation values. Fibers of different sizes have different weights. Even exact arithmetic describes only this given constructed distribution, not error frequencies in an actual population. Without a reasonable mapping and sample, neither half-ranges nor error rates should be attached to real people. [T-main]
argumentSteps: Fix X, π, the actual image Y, and the current task q.
Check whether q is constant on each fiber, proving necessity and sufficiency.
If error is permitted, first state the output space and loss.
For scalar worst-case loss, use the endpoint lower bound and midpoint construction.
For binary uniform zero-one loss, count majority decisions fiber by fiber.
Separate existence, uniqueness, computability, obtainability, and real-world applicability.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: the half-range lower bound and output restrictions
teachingExamples.text: Take three constructed states a,b,c, with π(a)=π(b)=u, π(c)=v, and target q=(2,7,10). The u fiber has endpoints 2 and 7; output 4.5 gives both errors as 2.5. Output 10 on v gives error 0, so the full-domain optimal risk is 2.5. ε=2 is impossible, while ε=2.5 is feasible. If outputs must be integers, choosing 4 or 5 on u gives worst error 3, and 2.5 can no longer be reported.
teachingExamples.assumptions: A finite domain, specified scalar target, and worst absolute loss; all values are constructed.
teachingExamples.boundary: The numbers are not a universal measure of social information loss; integer constraints define a different problem.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: majority classes and source weights
teachingExamples.text: Take 7 constructed, equally weighted source states. The u fiber has labels 0,0,1, and the v fiber has 0,1,1,1. Output 0 on u makes 1 error; output 1 on v makes 1 error. The optimal error rate is 2/7≈28.5714%. Incorrectly giving each fiber weight 1/2 produces (1/3+1/4)/2=7/24, changing the distribution.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Entirely teaching binary states, with zero-one loss and equal source-state weights.
teachingExamples.boundary: This proves risk only under this finite distribution, not actual frequencies.

questionAnswers.question: Why must Y equal the actual image?
questionAnswers.answer: It ensures nonempty fibers and makes the target uniquely determine exact g on all of Y.
questionAnswers.basis: Existence and uniqueness.

questionAnswers.question: Why is the midpoint optimal?
questionAnswers.answer: The endpoint triangle inequality gives the half-range lower bound; the midpoint makes all targets in the fiber satisfy that upper bound.
questionAnswers.basis: A two-step proof.

questionAnswers.question: Can random guessing outperform majority choice?
questionAnswers.answer: Not in this binary zero-one-loss problem with a fixed distribution; its error is a convex combination of the two pure-label errors.
questionAnswers.basis: The specified conditions.

questionAnswers.question: Does the formula apply to arbitrary vectors or average losses?
questionAnswers.answer: No. Another optimization proof for the corresponding space and loss is required.

C.7.title: C.7 F4 Composition of Conversions and Actual Execution
C.7.lead: Each step completing its own local task does not guarantee preservation of a common endpoint; representational insufficiency and an incorrect actual rule can also coexist.
explanation: Chinese source location: lines 4883–4892; original-site location /theory/appendix-c#section-c-7. See the theory-v2 source for the current full text; the historical Chinese research manuscript and slices remain downloadable in their original versions for checking.

Let f:X→Z and h:Z→W, with the final task q already recoverable from the intermediate representation, so q=g∘f. F4 asks whether the composition h∘f still allows recovery of the same q, not whether the second step successfully answers a different question. [T-main]

The necessary and sufficient condition is that g is constant on every fiber of h restricted to the actual image f(X). Necessity: if q=k∘h∘f, then for any reachable z=f(x) and z′=f(x′) with h(z)=h(z′), we have g(z)=q(x)=k(h(z))=k(h(z′))=q(x′)=g(z′). [T-main]

Sufficiency: for each reachable final value w, define k(w) as the common g value on its reachable intermediate fiber. Constancy makes this unambiguous, and substitution gives q=k∘h∘f. The theorem concerns only f(X); unreachable intermediate values need not satisfy the same constraint. Do not turn empty labels in the codomain into additional empirical requirements. [T-main]

The source's Boolean-pair counterexample: X={0,1}², f retains both positions, h retains only their sum, and q asks for the first position. h merges (0,1) and (1,0) into 1, yet they require answers 0 and 1. The first step preserves and the second counts successfully in their own terms, but the same final positional question is not preserved. [T-main]

Adding the Boolean value of the first position makes q recoverable without recovering every source detail. If the final task is instead changed directly to counting, that is a different successful task, not a repair of the original q. Evaluation cannot change the question after the fact and count the original task as passed. [T-main]

Separate representational sufficiency from correctness of the execution rule: for three source states a/b/c, f=(0,0,1) and q=(0,1,1), while the actual g_actual outputs 0 for both representations 0/1. States a/b have the same representation but different q, witnessing representational insufficiency. The fiber containing c unambiguously requires answer 1, so the actual output 0 independently witnesses a rule error. The output 0 for a is still correct in this instance; failures elsewhere cannot erase that local correctness. [T-main]

Changing g_actual to (0,1) repairs only c and cannot simultaneously satisfy the conflict between a/b. This decomposition depends on complete knowledge of source representations, targets, and the actual rule. In reality, if internal inputs or rules are unknown, retain the gaps rather than pretending every failure has a unique classification. [T-main]

An original remaining in existence and a reviewer obtaining it in time are different conditions. Looking back at the original after an error does not establish availability before action. Formal recovery, rule implementation, access timing, and permissions require separate arguments; existence in storage cannot be treated as actual input. [T-main]
argumentSteps: Fix the same final q and first check q=g∘f.
Check whether g is constant on h fibers only within reachable f(X).
Prove both directions and check whether a changed question is being passed off as a repair.
Separate representational conflicts from rule errors on distinguishable states.
Preserve local correctness and internal unknowns, and check accessibility at the time.

C.8.title: C.8 F2 Closure and F5 error propagation
C.8.lead: Exact closure requires consistent projected successors for every merged state; approximate closure additionally requires stepwise errors, amplification constants, and valid regions to remain applicable.
explanation: Chinese source location: lines 4893–4904; original-site location /theory/appendix-c#section-c-8. See the theory-v2 source for the current full text; the historical Chinese research manuscript and slices remain downloadable in their original versions for checking.

Let deterministic one-step dynamics be F:X→X, and let representation π:X→Y use its actual image. There exists F̄ such that π∘F=F̄∘π if and only if x/x′ with the same π still have the same π after updating. Necessity follows because a macroscopic function must give the same output for the same input. For sufficiency, define F̄(y) on each fiber as the common π(F(x)). This applies C.6 with target q replaced by π∘F. [T-main；T-fibre]

If the condition holds throughout the domain, then π∘F^t=F̄^t∘π for every nonnegative integer t. At step zero both sides equal π. Assuming the statement at step t, π∘F^{t+1}=F̄∘π∘F^t=F̄^{t+1}∘π, completing the induction. Holding only in observed samples does not automatically establish validity throughout the domain for arbitrary steps. [T-main]

With allowed actions U, closure must be checked for every explicit F_u before stepwise composition for any prespecified action sequence. Also check whether source states in the same fiber can all implement the macroscopic action, or restrict the available scope. If the same macroscopic action corresponds to different microscopic implementations, consistency of their macroscopic outcomes also requires checking. The same action name does not imply the same implementation map. [T-main]

A finite stochastic system uses a transition kernel P(x,x′). If, for any x/x′ in the same source block, the sums of transition probabilities into each target block B are equal, define the macroscopic kernel by that common value. Sufficiency: even if conditioning on the macroscopic present and past produces different within-block distributions, a weighted average of a constant probability for the same target block remains that constant. The macroscopic one-step update therefore does not depend on the hidden mixture. [T-main]

If the same macroscopic one-step law is required for all initial distributions, equality block by block is also necessary. Start separately from point masses at x and x′ in the same block: the macroscopic present is identical and must have the same distribution over the next block, so the probability sums for every target block must be equal. Preserving only the next-step mean or coinciding by chance under one initial mixture does not satisfy this all-initial-distributions requirement. [T-main]

For the approximate case, let the target space have metric d. Suppose the one-step projection defect d(π(F(x)),F̄(π(x)))≤ε holds for all reached x, and F̄ satisfies a Lipschitz bound L in the region containing the relevant comparison points. Starting from the same initial value y_0=π(x_0), let e_t be the difference between the actual projection and the iterated macroscopic state. The triangle inequality splits the next error into the one-step defect ε and the old deviation amplified macroscopically by Le_t, giving e_{t+1}≤ε+Le_t. [T-main]

Induction from e_0=0 gives e_1≤ε, e_2≤ε(1+L), and e_t≤εΣ_{j=0}^{t−1}L^j. Here L≥0; when L≠1 the sum is (L^t−1)/(L−1), and when L=1 it is t. For L<1 there is a uniform bound ε/(1−L), but this still presupposes continued validity of the domain and stepwise conditions. A large upper bound does not directly prove actual divergence. [T-main；T-bound]

If ε and L vary over time, use the recurrence e_{t+1}≤ε_t+L_t e_t rather than continuing to apply the fixed-parameter formula. Average fitting error is not a per-state upper bound. If a trajectory leaves the working region or a new intervention is outside U, the original guarantee stops where its conditions fail. [T-main]

Exactness, approximation, empirical applicability, and normative usability remain separate. Stochastic closure under ordinary distributions need not cover interventions; a common mathematical update does not establish that an action is feasible or authorized. The kernels, numerical values, and constants below are teaching constructions, not real domain measurements. [T-main]
argumentSteps: Check whether deterministic successors have consistent projections within each representation fiber.
Use step zero and induction to prove finite-step commutation throughout the domain.
For each action, check F_u, feasibility, and microscopic implementations sharing a name.
For stochastic kernels, check probability sums into each target block, distinguishing all initial distributions from a particular mixture.
For approximation, check stepwise ε, regional L, and the same initial value, then apply the recurrence.
Stop using the original bound when drift, new actions, or failure of the valid region invalidates it.

C.9.title: C.9 Differences between tasks in a two-queue system
C.9.lead: The same mean representation can answer total-quantity questions exactly while remaining insufficient for local overload. Adding the maximum repairs some tasks, but does not guarantee closure under location-specific interventions or higher-dimensional dynamics.
explanation: Chinese source location: lines 4905–4920; original-site location /theory/appendix-c#section-c-9. See the theory-v2 source for the current full text; the historical Chinese research manuscript and slices remain downloadable in their original versions for checking.

This is an explicitly constructed model in the user's source: the ordered coordinates (q₁,q₂) each range over 0…30, giving 31²=961 states. The local-overload target is max(q₁,q₂)>15. Only for calculating expected error, give the 961 source states equal weight; the means are not equally weighted, and this is not a real queue distribution. [T-main]

The mean m=(q₁+q₂)/2 maps both (0,20) and (10,10) to 10; the former is overloaded and the latter is not, so exact classification is impossible. Partitioning into fibers by the integer sum s is equivalent to partitioning by the mean, merely avoiding decimal bookkeeping. [T-main]

For s=16…30, there are s+1 states in total. The number with q₁>15 is s−15, and likewise for q₂>15. Both cannot occur simultaneously in this range, so the overloaded count is 2(s−15). The nonoverloaded count is (s+1)−2(s−15)=31−s. For s≤15 all states are nonoverloaded; for s>30 all are overloaded. Thus only the middle fibers conflict. [T-main]

Choose the majority label in each fiber. For s=16…20, overloaded states are the minority, giving minimum errors 2(s−15), which sum to 2(1+2+3+4+5)=30. For s=21…30, nonoverloaded states are the minority, summing to 10+9+…+1=55. The optimal total is 85 errors; dividing by 961 gives 8.844953…%. Independent recalculation of this finite enumeration yields 85 without simulation-based sampling approximation. [T-main；T-binary]

The rule ‘report overload only when the mean>15’ is equivalent to s>30. It misses all overloaded states within s=16…30, totaling 2(1+…+15)=240. There are no false positives, because mean>15 necessarily implies local>15. Its 155=240−85 additional errors above the optimum are excess risk of this rule relative to the optimum; all 240 cannot be attributed to unavoidable representational loss. [T-main]

If the target changes to recovering maximum length, then for a given s the smallest possible maximum is ceil(s/2) and the largest is min(30,s). The greatest range width, 15, occurs at s=30. States (0,30) and (15,15) have maxima 30 and 15, and the real-valued midpoint 22.5 gives worst-case error 7.5; no other fiber has a larger width. Requiring integer outputs gives radius 8 by choosing 22 or 23 for this fiber. Changing the output space changes the problem. [T-main；T-binary]

Add the maximum M: overload is recovered through M>15 and maximum length directly from M, but the larger position remains unknown. With exactly two queues, the smaller value=2m−M. If each position serves at most c items per round, there are no arrivals, and c≥0, then M′=(M−c)_+ and m′=[(M−c)_++(2m−M−c)_+]/2. Thus (m,M) is closed under the specified symmetric model without recovering positional order. [T-main]

Changing position-specific capacities to (15,10) gives (0,20)→(0,10) and (20,0)→(5,0). Both initial representations (m,M) are (10,20), but their successors are (5,10) and (2.5,5), so closure fails. What changes is the symmetry condition of the dynamics; this is not simply a claim that the maximum is useless. [T-main]

Three-queue counterexample: (20,20,5) and (20,15,10) both have mean 15 and maximum 20. After serving 15 at each position, they become (5,5,0) and (5,0,0), with totals 10 and 5 and means 10/3 and 5/3. The mean plus maximum no longer determines the other two values, so the two-queue closure result cannot extend unconditionally to higher dimensions. [T-main]

Retain both positive and negative results: a total-quantity representation could already answer total-quantity questions exactly; adding task-relevant variables can repair some insufficiencies; the same repair does not guarantee tasks involving different operations, positions, or dimensions. Defining success in every task as recovery of all microscopic details would erase the bounded successes that actually hold here. [T-main]
argumentSteps: Fix the 961 constructed ordered states and the equally weighted source distribution.
Partition into fibers by sum s and calculate overloaded/nonoverloaded counts.
Compare the optimal majority decision's 85 errors with the threshold rule's 240.
For maximum recovery, separately check worst-case radii for real/integer outputs.
After adding M, check symmetric two-queue dynamics, then examine position-specific capacities and higher-dimensional counterexamples.
Retain positive tasks such as total-quantity recovery; do not generalize local failure into total loss.

C.10.title: C.10 Strict Stability Conditions for Fixed-Delay Feedback
C.10.lead: Feedback having an effect does not mean stability. The strict threshold in this fixed-delay linear model excludes equality and does not prove real-world safety or repair.
explanation: Source location: Chinese source lines 4921–4944, original-site location /theory/appendix-c#section-c-10. The current full text is in the theory-v2 source; the historical research draft and excerpts remain downloadable in their original versions.

The model is x_{t+1}=x_t−k x_{t−d}, where d is a fixed nonnegative integer, k a fixed real number, and the initial history x_{−d},…,x_0 finite; x is a signed deviation. There is no noise, external input, saturation, or state constraint. The theorem states that the zero solution is asymptotically stable for all initial histories if and only if 0<k<k_c(d)=2sin[π/(4d+2)]. [T-main]

Augment the state to (x_t,x_{t−1},…,x_{t−d}), with characteristic polynomial p(λ,k)=λ^{d+1}−λ^d+k. All roots being strictly inside the unit circle is equivalent to convergence to zero for all initial histories: each mode of the linear recurrence is a power of a root, multiplied by a finite-degree polynomial for repeated roots. If the root modulus is <1, the polynomial times the exponential still decays. A modulus ≥1 provides a nondecaying or growing mode, violating the requirement for all histories. [T-main]

First exclude k≤0: at k=0, root 1 retains a constant mode; at k<0, p(1,k)=k<0, while p>0 for sufficiently large positive λ, so continuity gives a real root >1. For d=0, the sole root is 1−k, and |1−k|<1 directly gives 0<k<2. [T-main]

For d≥1, sufficiently small positive k is stable: the simple root 1 at k=0 moves inside the circle by the implicit-function expansion λ=1−k+O(k²); the other d roots vary continuously from 0 and remain inside for sufficiently small k. Continuity here controls the root set; it does not require each zero root to have the same differentiable expansion. [T-main]

To find boundaries at positive k, set λ=e^{iθ}, 0<θ<2π. From p=0, k=λ^d(1−λ). Since 1−e^{iθ}=2sin(θ/2)exp[i(θ/2−π/2)] and sin(θ/2)>0 on this interval, k=2sin(θ/2)exp{i[(d+1/2)θ−π/2]}. Positive real k requires phase to be an integer multiple of 2π, so θ=(π+4πm)/(2d+1), m=0,…,d. [T-main]

The smallest positive-gain boundary comes from the smallest angle π/(2d+1) and its conjugate angle, giving k_c=2sin[π/(4d+2)]. Roots vary continuously with the parameter and remain bounded at finite parameter values, so leaving the circle requires crossing its boundary. Stability therefore holds from small positive k up to the first boundary. [T-main]

Finding only the first exit is insufficient to prove necessity; restabilization must also be excluded. On the boundary, p_λ=λ^{d−1}[(d+1)λ−d] is nonzero: λ≠0, while (d+1)λ=d would require |λ|=d/(d+1)<1. Thus unit-circle boundary roots are simple and can be differentiated implicitly with respect to k. [T-main]

Using λ′=−1/p_λ and k=λ^d(1−λ), obtain (λ′/λ)=(λ−1)/{k[(d+1)λ−d]}. Take the real part and multiply by the conjugate denominator; the numerator’s real part is (2d+1)(1−cosθ). Hence d log|λ|/dk=(2d+1)(1−cosθ)/{k|(d+1)e^{iθ}−d|²}>0. Every unit-circle crossing at positive k is outward, so the number of exterior roots cannot decrease through inward crossings. There is therefore no region of restored stability at larger gain. [T-main]

At exact equality, a unit-modulus nondecaying mode exists. A floating-point root computed as 0.999999… must not be counted as stability. For k>k_c, a growing mode exists, but an all-zero history remains zero. “Not asymptotically stable for all histories” does not mean every special trajectory must diverge. [T-main]

For the source’s k=0.8 example, the critical values for d=0/1 are 2/1, so both are stable; for d=2/3 they are approximately 0.618033989/0.445041868, so both are unstable. The original guide’s author used numerical characteristic roots for an auxiliary recalculation, obtaining maximum root moduli of approximately 0.2, 0.894427, 1.078049, and 1.129417. This numerical check verifies only these examples and does not replace the strict proof above. [T-main]

With an all-ones initial history, all four cases have the same first step, x1=1−0.8=0.2, showing that feedback has already acted within the model, although convergence properties differ. Even stability does not control transient peaks, costs, human acceptability, or actual repair. Time-varying delay, noise, nonlinearity, or execution constraints require separate analysis; this formula is not a universal recommendation for management gain. [T-main]
argumentSteps: Check assumptions including fixed delay, linearity, no noise, and all initial histories.
Augment the state and use the strict unit-circle root condition.
Exclude k≤0 and prove stability for small positive k.
Find the unit-circle angles and first boundary.
Prove that all positive-k crossings are outward, excluding restabilization.
Use numerics only to assist example checks; distinguish feedback effects, stability, safety, and repair.

C.11.title: C.11 Historical Increments and Omissions in Current Representations
C.11.lead: History improving prediction from a coarse representation need not imply an increment beyond the complete current state. Eliminating an additional predictive contribution also cannot negate effects of early experience transmitted through current carriers.
explanation: Source location: Chinese source lines 4945–4959, original-site location /theory/appendix-c#section-c-11. The current full text is in the theory-v2 source; the historical research draft and excerpts remain downloadable in their original versions.

Retain the 961 equiprobable artificial initial states (a,b)∈{0,…,30}². Each round, each queue serves at most 5 items, with no arrivals: F(a,b)=((a−5)_+,(b−5)_+). “Current” means after round one, and the target is the mean after round two. Do not mistake the initial mean for information after the prediction time, or reset the first-round state distribution to uniform. [T-main]

Compare four inputs: current mean m1; (m1, initial mean m0); complete current ordered two-queue state x1; and (x1,m0). Outputs are real numbers, and loss is expected squared loss under the distribution induced by the given initial-state distribution. This is a different optimization problem from the worst-case absolute error in C.6. [T-main]

Within each input fiber, the target takes values z_i, conditioned using the original initial-state weights. For any output c, conditional squared error satisfies E[(Z−c)²|input]=E[(Z−μ)²|input]+(μ−c)²; the cross term vanishes because E[Z−μ|input]=0. Thus the conditional mean μ is optimal. Weighting by each input’s actual induced probability then gives the global minimum mean squared error. [T-main]

Independent exact recalculation reported in the guide proceeds as follows: enumerate all 31×31 initial states; compute x1=F(x0), x2=F(x1), and target z=sum(x2)/2; group by each of the four input keys; calculate the rational mean of z in each group; sum (z−μ)² for every original initial state in each group and divide by 961. Different original states mapping to the same x1 each still carry probability 1/961; do not deduplicate and assign equal weights anew. [T-main]

The four minimum MSEs are 0.579016561292077, 0.271143397459245, 0, and 0, agreeing with the source’s nine-decimal table. The first two exact rational values are 200877946845133/346929535826874 and 31003222683/114342532304. This is arithmetic on the complete finite model, not estimation from real samples or fitted training performance. [T-main]

Why does the historical mean help? Initial state (0,20)→current (0,15)→next (0,10), with next mean 5; initial state (10,15)→current (5,10)→next (0,5), with next mean 2.5. Both current means are 7.5, but their initial means are 10 and 12.5, respectively. History distinguishes states collapsed by the current mean. Conflicts can remain in other fibers, so adding history lowers MSE without reducing it to zero. [T-main]

The complete current state already determines the next state and target through deterministic F, so minimum MSE is 0. Adding the initial mean cannot improve below 0 and provides no further predictive benefit. This zero result is limited to this model, complete current state, specified target, distribution, and loss; it does not mean every real system is memoryless. [T-main]

Real applications must address measurement, confounding, temporal order, leakage, and model selection. If the current carrier is unavailable altogether, historical increments cannot be said to have been ruled out. The disappearance of a historical predictive increment also does not negate the past’s total effect: if early experiences shape current skills and thereby affect outcomes, the additional predictive contribution disappearing conditional on sufficient current skills limits only the part “beyond the current representation.” [T-main]

This section aligns with G3’s boundary: G3 concerns historical increments beyond a given current representation, without canceling general learning, carrier formation, or early causation. The artificial deterministic queues are not used to judge people’s trauma, skills, or personalities. The discussion of skills explains a conditional structure, not a diagnosis of a real case. [T-main; T-history]
argumentSteps: Fix the original probabilities of the 961 initial states; do not restore uniformity after propagation.
Advance each state two rounds, using the first-round state as input and the second-round mean as target.
Form fibers for the four inputs separately and use conditional means to minimize squared loss.
Accumulate errors using original weights and check all four MSEs.
Distinguish compensation for omissions in a coarse representation from increments beyond the complete current state.
Real-world extrapolation requires separate checks of measurement, confounding, leakage, and availability of current carriers.

C.12.title: C.12 Three Boundaries on Combining Local Successes
C.12.lead: Functional composition, causal chaining, and joint resource feasibility are three distinct checks. Knowing that every state has some solution also does not guarantee that current information permits selecting a jointly qualified action.
explanation: Source location: Chinese source lines 4960–4975, original-site location /theory/appendix-c#section-c-12. The current full text is in the theory-v2 source; the historical research draft and excerpts remain downloadable in their original versions.

This section first separates three kinds of “combination”: whether a transformation preserves the same final answer is a functional condition; whether causal effects can chain through mediators is a joint-response condition; and whether actions can be implemented together within resources is a constraint-set condition. One process may need all three, and a generic “connected” state cannot establish them all. [T-main]

The functional boundary returns to C.7: when q=g∘f, the composition h∘f preserves q only if g is constant on the h-fibers in the reachable intermediate domain. Two steps that separately preserve and count do not guarantee retention of a task about the first position. This is a different failure from the causal or resource obstacles below. [T-main; T-compose]

The source’s causal construction takes equally weighted s=0/1, with m(a)=a(1−s) and y(a,m)=s m. The effect of changing treatment a from 0 to 1 on the mediator is 1−s, respectively 1/0 for the two types, averaging 1/2. At fixed a, the outcome effect of changing mediator m from 0 to 1 is s, respectively 0/1, also averaging 1/2. But the whole-chain effect y(1,m(1))−y(0,m(0))=s(1−s)=0, with mean 0 as well. The product of edge means, 1/4, cannot replace the joint response of 0. [T-main; T-causal]

Different types carrying the two segments explains why unconditional multiplication fails. It does not imply that all chain effects are always zero, or revoke an independently identified total effect. If a real task has directly identified its total effect, retain it according to its grounds rather than requiring recertification through a product of edges. [T-main]

The resource construction has two unit tasks, each exclusively occupying one complete time slot, both due by the end of period one, with capacity 1 in that period. Each can be scheduled alone, but total demand 2>1 makes a joint schedule infeasible. Capacity 2 in the same period permits parallel execution; alternatively, lawfully moving one deadline to period two with capacity 1 there permits sequential scheduling. If both original deadlines remain unchanged, adding period-two capacity cannot fill the original deadline gap. [T-main]

F3 is limited to finite, single-round deterministic tasks. Current observation y is compatible with a nonempty state set X_y, and every state has a qualified-action set A_ok(x). There exists one action selected solely from y that is qualified for every compatible state if and only if the intersection ∩_{x∈X_y}A_ok(x) is nonempty. This guarantees the same action across all compatible states, not secretly selecting different actions according to the true hidden state. [T-main]

Necessity: if a common action a exists, it is qualified for every compatible x, hence belongs to every set and their intersection. Sufficiency: select an a from the nonempty intersection; it is qualified for every compatible x without needing to know which x is real. Each A_ok(x) being nonempty is only necessary: the sets {left}/{right} still have an empty intersection. [T-main]

If both states permit an already authorized preservation action, their intersection can be nonempty while the state remains incompletely identified. Thus full state identification is not a universal prerequisite for every bounded action. However, “preservation” cannot be treated as inherently available: its protections, resources, and authority must first actually be checked into A_ok. [T-main]

Qualified sets must already include task goals, protections, resources, and valid authority. Writing an action mathematically does not establish real eligibility. The conclusion covers only listed compatible states, not a guarantee that unknown states can never appear. Lawful additional observation, waiting, or preservation can change the set of information strategies, but neither happens automatically nor is authorized by this proposition itself. [T-main]

Probabilistic choice under risk tolerance, randomization, and sequential strategies involve different goals and problems. Original F3 asks only for one deterministic action qualified in every state; acceptable average risk cannot quietly replace the original all-state guarantee. intro-20-appendix-d.title: Appendix D Domain explanation and application map
intro-20-appendix-d.lead: This map navigates from domain questions into the framework; it does not compress thirty-two areas of knowledge into one answer. Every domain must still answer with suitable materials, and one source cited across several domains does not become multiple independent validations.
explanation: Source location: Chinese source lines 4976–4979; original anchor part_20. Short quotation translated from Chinese: “Domains do not bear responsibility for validating one another.” The source excerpt for this lesson is separately attached verbatim in source-slice.md; explanation and original text are distinct.

Appendix D’s introduction specifies an order: preserve the domain’s original question first, then connect applicable boundaries concerning representation, evidence, norms, and action from the main text. Preserving questions means economic, legal, care, historical, or artistic questions cannot all be replaced by whether circles advance. A domain may primarily need mechanism explanation, clarification of meaning, normative argument, procedural checking, or formal proof; different tasks have different appropriate materials and endpoints.

The thirty-two domains define the map’s organizational scope, not a count of thirty-two completed independent empirical validations. This section’s “taking up existing research” describes the author’s source lineage. Further assertions about actual historical adoption, data, or conclusions of a study still require its original research and version. This lesson explains connections from the accessible current original, without treating research-entry numbers as proof that all underlying texts were read.

The four connections to the main text have different responsibilities. Representation specifies objects, variables, and scales used to express the question; evidence specifies how materials support particular claims; norms disclose protective and value premises; action boundaries limit who may do what and how to stop and remedy it. These levels are related, but clear representation does not prove facts, sufficient evidence does not eliminate normative disagreement, and value reasons do not create real authorization.

Domains’ lack of responsibility to validate one another means that “feedback exists in physics” cannot prove an organization’s feedback mechanism, nor a similar term in an institutional study prove a psychological hypothesis. Domain materials can complement one another through explicit bridges, but support still comes from their own checkable objects, methods, and conditions, not shared names or inclusion in the map.

When multiple studies cite the same original work, data, or case, retain their related source lineage. Different analyses of the same data may add robustness checks, answers to new questions, or debate; they need not add nothing. But paper or chapter counts cannot accumulate as independent samples or replications. Actual independence depends on data generation, measurement, objects, and inferential relations, not merely author names or page addresses.

When reading the map, ask for each section: what exactly does this domain seek to explain; how far can its methods answer; what distinction does the framework add; what still needs source verification; and is there normative or action overreach? The map organizes questions rather than imposing additional entry barriers on readers. A sufficiently good domain account may remain directly, without first being translated into the whole vocabulary.
