counterexamples.effect: Being found first does not mean greater likelihood of truth; distinguish temporary demand growth, reduced capacity, and common external causes as well.

counterexamples.text: Constructed conditional counterexample: ‘This scheduling system's release notes call its stages “consolidation” and “expansion,” similar to S0 “anchor consolidation” and S2 “first expansion,” so use S0–S6 to stage the system itself.’
counterexamples.effect: State prototypes apply only to human collectives meeting the corresponding conditions. Similar names do not qualify a technical system.

counterexamples.text: Constructed conditional counterexample: ‘The feedback form has reached the department, so the department has learned.’
counterexamples.effect: Returned signals must be distinguished from learning; learning requires a retainable update actually entering subsequent tasks.

counterexamples.text: Constructed conditional counterexample: ‘Five analysts independently completed the same search card and agreed, confirming the mechanism.’
counterexamples.effect: Multiple people using the same order do not prove a mechanism; a shared search procedure can produce shared omissions.

counterexamples.text: Constructed conditional counterexample: ‘Two paths both cite the same waiting-time record, so there are two independent pieces of support.’
counterexamples.effect: Repeated citation of shared evidence does not add independent support.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: searching for candidates when waiting times increase
teachingExamples.text:
Imagine a community service office where, two weeks after a new appointment rule launches, waiting times at the document-processing counter's morning appointment sessions increase markedly. Records distinguish that counter and time slot rather than using only an office-wide mean. First define applicability: the object is the reception process, not a human collective to which state prototypes apply, so S0–S6 are not used. The scale is one counter and one time slot, focusing on the morning document counter while recording other counters and periods as comparisons. The window spans four weeks before to four weeks after launch. The requested output is candidate mechanisms and discriminating observations, not attribution of responsibility. The four input types are queue records by counter and time, the increase in waits, staff service hours plus the appointment system and weekly roster, and undistinguished factors such as the new rule, a seasonal epidemic, and closure of a nearby office.
Candidate A, local overload: under §6.6 CM-LOAD, measure same-type demand and available capacity at the same position and within the same window, recording their locations and distributions. The expected prior change is a gap in which same-type demand exceeds available capacity at that counter and time, before waits become markedly longer. Contrary signals include no measurable gap there, or longer waits distributed uniformly across counters and periods.
Candidate B, a temporary demand increase: office-wide arrivals should rise first. Contrary signals are unchanged arrivals or arrivals increasing only after waits lengthen.
Candidate C, reduced capacity: available service hours should fall first, or individual processing times should rise with arrivals unchanged. The contrary signal is neither changing.
Candidate D, a common external cause: an external factor simultaneously increases arrivals and reduces staffing, aligned in time with the changes. Contrary signals are its absence or lack of temporal alignment.
Simple baseline: the before-and-after difference falls within fluctuations in the same season of previous years.
Do not call ‘waiting starts to increase’ Candidate A's early signal, count the same queue record as independent support for A and B, or default to A because it comes first on the search card.
teachingExamples.assumptions: The office, rule, window, external factors, and all observables are teaching assumptions, not any real institution or event. This example omits each candidate's continuation conditions and stopping points.
teachingExamples.boundary: This illustrates only search and recording structure. It identifies no true candidate and is neither a formal load-mechanism instance nor causal identification. Only part of §6.6's complete conditions is illustrated; actual use requires returning to the source.

questions: Is a candidate found earlier more likely true? On what basis may search order be adjusted?
Where do path candidates and mechanism candidates respectively come from?
Which four items must a candidate path specify at minimum? What can it still do without enabling evidence?
If the expected outcome is markedly longer waits, why is ‘waiting starts to increase’ not an early signal of local overload?
Can complete cards and multiple analysts using the same search order prove a mechanism? What comparison is required when adjusting the order?

questionAnswers.question: Is a candidate found earlier more likely true? On what basis may search order be adjusted?
questionAnswers.answer: No. The source says the order is only for finding candidates, not evidence that earlier ones are more likely true. Search order may be adjusted based on omissions, misjudgments, and cost of use, while preserving the original mechanisms' applicability boundaries and facing comparison with simpler search methods.
questionAnswers.basis: §6.14, second and fifth paragraphs.

questionAnswers.question: Where do path candidates and mechanism candidates respectively come from?
questionAnswers.answer: Path candidates come from state-exit conditions; mechanism candidates come from observed changes. Both then require individual checks of enabling conditions, propagation stages, and minimum evidence.
questionAnswers.basis: §6.14, second paragraph.

questionAnswers.question: Which four items must a candidate path specify at minimum? What can it still do without enabling evidence?
questionAnswers.answer: Continuation conditions, observable changes the mechanism should produce first, contrary signals, and stopping points. Without enabling evidence, it can still organize discriminating observations but cannot become an identified mechanism.
questionAnswers.basis: §6.14, fourth paragraph.

questionAnswers.question: If the expected outcome is markedly longer waits, why is ‘waiting starts to increase’ not an early signal of local overload?
questionAnswers.answer: It merely restates the outcome more mildly. Temporary demand growth and reduced capacity can also lengthen waits, so it fails to distinguish competitors. Under §12.6, an early signal is an observable change the path's mechanism should produce first.
questionAnswers.basis: §6.14, third and fourth paragraphs; §12.6.

questionAnswers.question: Can complete cards and multiple analysts using the same search order prove a mechanism? What comparison is required when adjusting the order?
questionAnswers.answer: No. Adjustments must preserve the original mechanisms' applicability boundaries and face comparison with simpler search methods.
questionAnswers.basis: §6.14, fifth paragraph.

openQuestions: This section requires distinguishing local overload from temporary demand growth, reduced capacity, and common external causes. Specific observational conditions belong to §6.6 CM-LOAD; the lesson does not prescribe a uniform criterion on the author's behalf.
This lesson has not compared this search order with simpler search methods.

applicability.reason: This section specifies a working order for finding candidates. The lesson uses a teaching construction only to illustrate search and recording; it is no formal mechanism instance and adds no figure.

6.14.summary: Search order is only a working order for finding candidates; earlier discovery does not mean greater likelihood of truth. Retain competing candidates and simple baselines when using a candidate. Without enabling evidence, it may still organize discriminating observations, but cannot become an identified mechanism.

16.20.1.title: 16.20.1 Organizing Methods and Sampling Reviews
16.20.1.lead: Sampling some derived entries and finding no errors shows only that no problem has yet been found in those examined. Unexamined categories remain unknown; the author's permission to sample does not mean the author has confirmed every entry.
explanation: Chinese source location: lines 3730–3737, ‘16.20.1 Organizing Methods and Sampling Reviews.’ Brief quotation, translated from Chinese: ‘Permission to sample, passing procedural checks, or finding no errors in a sample so far does not mean the author has confirmed every item’ (Chinese source line 3734). The lesson is separate from the source text.

This section addresses usage steps and search entries derived from the source: derivative materials, not the source itself or judgments about reality. It answers how to review those materials, how far the result can be stated, and where an author's experiential judgment belongs if it is to function as theoretical method.

The first paragraph requires stating the population, classification, selection basis, and question before sampling. Samples should cover different mechanisms, objects, and output types, including entries concerning high-impact uses, transitions across scales, or theoretical boundaries. A small convenience sample cannot represent uncovered categories; the review provides no information about a category that never entered the sample.

The second paragraph specifies action after discovering a problem: conceptual omissions, expanded applicability, or confusion between source and derivative content require broader review of the relevant category and tracing methods and conclusions that depend on the entry. Discovery starts an expanded review; fixing only that entry cannot close the matter.

The same paragraph requires reporting separately which entries were actually reviewed and which were not reviewed individually. The basis and scope for adopting the batch require a separate account. These three matters cannot collapse into ‘reviewed.’

The central boundary consists of three nonequivalences: permission to sample is a form of authorization; passing procedural checks shows only that certain process outputs were completed; and finding no errors so far in a sample is a limited observation. None means the author confirmed every entry, and none replaces substantive review of real high-impact judgments. This follows the same line as §16.9's ‘process outputs are not proof of reality’ and §16.20's ‘passing everything yields only publishable, still not authority to act.’

The third paragraph addresses the place of the author's experience. If an experiential judgment is to serve as theoretical method, it should enter the appropriate place in the source, specifying applicable objects, grounds, counterexamples, and stopping conditions. Organizational suggestions not written into the source remain candidates; ancillary method entries cannot establish a separate body of the author's theory.

Entry into the source changes textual status. An experience written into the source becomes part of the framework's text, but the source explicitly says this cannot automatically promote personal experience into a general empirical proposition or proof of effectiveness. Empirical claims still distinguish specific-instance propositions from cross-instance generalization under §16.3, facing proportionate disconfirmation and counterexamples within scope. Effects still require separate evidence.

The strongest objection is that individual confirmation costs too much and sampling is the only feasible method. This section allows sampling, but its result cannot be called ‘confirmed by the author.’ Report coverage honestly without extending sample conclusions to unreviewed categories or real high-impact uses. Proportionality still follows §16.25: compare whether additional records can change judgments and reduce harm with the waiting, exposure, and maintenance costs they impose.
argumentSteps: Premise: steps and entries organized from the source are derivative materials that may omit concepts, expand applicability, or confuse source and derivative content.

Connection: a small convenience sample cannot represent uncovered categories. Before sampling, therefore, specify the population, classification, selection basis, and question, cover distinct mechanisms, objects, and output types, and include entries involving high-impact uses, scale transitions, or theoretical boundaries.

Conclusion: the review report separately lists what was reviewed, what was not individually reviewed, and the basis and scope for adopting the batch. When problems arise, broaden the relevant categories and trace dependencies.

Qualification: permission to sample, passing procedural checks, and finding no errors so far in a sample do not mean the author confirmed every entry, or replace substantive review of real high-impact judgments.

Normative responsibility: an author's experience serving as theoretical method must enter the appropriate source passage with stated conditions. Organizational suggestions outside the source remain candidates.

distinctions.leftText: Authorization to use a review method.
distinctions.rightText: The author has confirmed each entry; sampling cannot produce that status.

distinctions.leftTitle: No errors found so far in the sample
distinctions.leftText: Covers only entries actually reviewed.
distinctions.rightText: Cannot be inferred from a limited sample, especially for unsampled categories.

distinctions.leftText: Shows only completion of the process outputs checked.
distinctions.rightText: Real high-impact judgments have additional requirements.

distinctions.leftText: What changes is textual status.
distinctions.rightTitle: A general empirical proposition or proof of effectiveness
distinctions.rightText: A change in textual status cannot automatically promote personal experience into either.

distinctions.leftTitle: Organizational suggestions not written into the source
distinctions.leftText: Remain candidates.
distinctions.rightText: A separate version cannot be established through ancillary method entries.

boundaries: A sampling report must separately state what was actually reviewed, what was not individually reviewed, and the basis and scope for adopting the batch. It cannot reduce these to ‘reviewed.’
A small convenience sample cannot represent uncovered categories; entries concerning high-impact uses, scale transitions, and theoretical boundaries must enter the sample.
Conceptual omissions, expanded scope, or confusion between source and derivative content require broader review of the relevant categories and tracing dependencies.
Passing a sampling review cannot replace substantive review of real high-impact judgments or confer authority for real-world action.
Writing the author's experience into the source changes only textual status; what remains outside the source remains a candidate.

counterexamples.text: Constructed conditional counterexample: ‘The author allowed sampling. Twenty entries had no problems, so the author has confirmed the whole batch.’
counterexamples.effect: Neither permission to sample nor finding no sample errors means the author confirmed every entry.

counterexamples.text: Constructed conditional counterexample: ‘All samples came from category A and A had no problems, so B and C are usable too.’
counterexamples.effect: The review has no information about unsampled categories; a convenience sample cannot represent them.

counterexamples.text: Constructed conditional counterexample: ‘The author mentioned this experience in a group discussion, so it is already part of the theory.’
counterexamples.effect: Suggestions not written into the source remain candidates. Even inclusion does not automatically make them general empirical propositions.

teachingExamples.title: Formal construction: zero findings do not mean zero errors
teachingExamples.text: Suppose a batch has 200 derived entries in four categories A, B, C, and D, each containing 50. A reviewer randomly samples 20 entries only from A and finds no errors. First, none of the 150 entries in B, C, or D entered the sample; this review has no information about them. Second, even within A, ‘no errors found in twenty entries’ does not exclude errors. Suppose A actually contains five errors and every sampled error would be detected. Under simple random sampling without replacement, the probability that all twenty avoid errors is C(45,20)/C(50,20) ≈ 0.067. If a category instead has 100 entries with five errors, the same twenty-entry sample avoids all errors with probability C(95,20)/C(100,20) ≈ 0.319, about one third. Under these assumptions, ‘twenty sampled with zero findings’ can coexist with ‘five errors remain.’ If the review itself misses errors, the probability of zero findings is even higher.
teachingExamples.assumptions: Totals, categories, error counts, random sampling, and perfect detection of sampled errors are all stipulated, not results of a real review.
teachingExamples.boundary: This only illustrates limits on conclusions from a finite sample. It gives no real entry error rate or recommended sample size; this section specifies no universal sample size.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: writing a review record
teachingExamples.text: Imagine a maintainer organizing forty search entries, with the author's agreement to sampling review. An appropriate record first states: population of forty; three categories by mechanism, with each entry's object and output type marked; the question is whether entries omit concepts, expand applicability, or confuse source and derivative content. Selection randomly takes two from each category and additionally includes all three entries concerning high-impact uses, two concerning scale transitions, and one concerning theoretical boundaries, checking that different mechanisms, objects, and output types are covered. Twelve entries were actually reviewed, with IDs listed; twenty-eight were not individually reviewed. The basis for adopting the batch is ‘the sample revealed no scope violations, and all high-impact, cross-scale, and theoretical-boundary entries were reviewed,’ with adoption limited to search assistance, not real-world judgments. This cannot be written as ‘the author confirmed all forty.’
teachingExamples.assumptions: Entry counts, categories, and record contents are teaching designs, not a real review. The illustrative rationale is not a sufficient condition.
teachingExamples.boundary: This record format is not the source's uniquely prescribed field set, nor does it prove such adoption proportionate in a real situation.

teachingExamples.title: Teaching construction: two statuses of an experiential suggestion
teachingExamples.text: Suppose the author says in discussion: ‘For conflicts in this kind of small team, pausing for a week before talking usually works better.’ If it remains only in organizational notes, it is a candidate suggestion, not citable as a framework method. If the author puts it in the appropriate source passage, the applicable objects, grounds, counterexamples, and stopping conditions must accompany it. Its textual status then changes, but ‘a week's pause works better’ remains an empirical claim requiring separate testing and evidence.
teachingExamples.assumptions: The author's statement and its content are fictional, not the author's actual views.
teachingExamples.boundary: The example neither evaluates a week's pause nor decides which experiences the author should include in the source.

questions: Which three layers must a ‘no errors found in sampling’ report separate at minimum?
Why must entries concerning high-impact uses, scale transitions, and theoretical boundaries enter the sample?
After the author's experience enters the source, which statuses change and which do not?

questionAnswers.question: Which three layers must a ‘no errors found in sampling’ report separate at minimum?
questionAnswers.answer: Which entries were actually reviewed; which were not reviewed individually; and the decision to adopt the batch, with its basis and scope.
questionAnswers.basis: §16.20.1, second paragraph.

questionAnswers.question: Why must entries concerning high-impact uses, scale transitions, and theoretical boundaries enter the sample?
questionAnswers.answer: The source requires including these entries without separately explaining why. A review has no information about categories absent from its sample. One interpretation is that errors in high-impact uses are costly, while scale transitions and theoretical boundaries are prone to exceeding the source's applicability.
questionAnswers.basis: §16.20.1, first paragraph.

questionAnswers.question: After the author's experience enters the source, which statuses change and which do not?
questionAnswers.answer: Textual status changes: it becomes part of the framework's text. Personal experience does not thereby automatically become a general empirical proposition or proof of effectiveness.
questionAnswers.basis: §16.20.1, third paragraph.

openQuestions: This section requires stating the population, classification, selection basis, and question before sampling, but prescribes no universal sample size or coverage rate. This lesson recommends no number.

applicability.reason: This section specifies sampling review and reporting for derivative materials. The lesson uses formal and teaching constructions, reports no real review result, and adds no figure.

16.20.1.summary: Sampling speaks only for the entries examined; passing it cannot be written as ‘confirmed by the author.’

2.4.3.title: 2.4.3 Constitutive and Causal Relations
2.4.3.lead: Whether a right or eligibility is established and whether it is realized are two questions requiring separate answers.
explanation: A constitutive relation asks whether, under applicable rules and valid conditions, this act constitutes appointment, commitment, a right, or a decision. First check the rule's source, the authorized subject, required form, and specific applicability. Recognition of status need not first identify a causal effect changing behavior.

A causal relation then asks whether established status changes actions, resources, or outcomes through a channel. Constitutive evidence can help establish who has which status, but cannot prove actual fulfillment. Effects that have occurred cannot retroactively repair an invalid procedure either.

Keep four columns separate when reading: constitutive conditions, participants' understandings, actual implementation or realization, and normative justification. They can yield different answers. A right may be validly established but not yet realized; an actual arrangement may be effective while lacking legal status or justification.

This is not an ontological claim that all objects arise from convention. It explains the division of evidential responsibilities and should be read alongside §5.5.5: the connection here concerns legal validity, which cannot be absorbed into the question of an institution's factual existence.

keyTerms.text: Explains how a status is established under applicable rules.
Explains how a change affects subsequent outcomes through a channel.

sourceQuotes.text: The two kinds of question are evidenced separately, and neither can pay in place of the other.

argumentSteps: A constitutive relation asks whether, under applicable rules and valid conditions, this act constitutes appointment, commitment, a right, or a decision. First check the rule's source, the authorized subject, required form, and specific applicability. Recognition of status need not first identify a causal effect changing behavior.

A causal relation then asks whether established status changes actions, resources, or outcomes through a channel. Constitutive evidence can help establish who has which status, but cannot prove actual fulfillment. Effects that have occurred cannot retroactively repair an invalid procedure either.

Keep four columns separate when reading: constitutive conditions, participants' understandings, actual implementation or realization, and normative justification. They can yield different answers. A right may be validly established but not yet realized; an actual arrangement may be effective while lacking legal status or justification.

distinctions.leftText: Judged by the rule's source, authority, form, and applicability conditions.
distinctions.rightText: Judged by implementation records, outcomes, and proportionate causal comparisons.

teachingExamples.title: Constructed teaching scenario
teachingExamples.text: Suppose a valid procedure has granted eligibility for a service, but the applicant has not received it. Eligibility can be confirmed while the realization gap is recorded. Nonreceipt does not mean eligibility never existed, and eligibility alone does not prove delivery.
teachingExamples.boundary: Illustrates conditions and counterexamples only; it reports no real event or completed mechanism test.

boundaries: Status, understanding, realization, and justification cannot prove one another.
Actual causal effects cannot manufacture legal authority; lawful status does not guarantee beneficial outcomes.

counterexamples.text: Suppose a valid procedure has granted eligibility for a service, but the applicant has not received it. Eligibility can be confirmed while the realization gap is recorded. Nonreceipt does not mean eligibility never existed, and eligibility alone does not prove delivery.
counterexamples.effect: Status, understanding, realization, and justification cannot prove one another.

questions: If no causal effect of a right is measured, can one say the right was not established?

questionAnswers.question: If no causal effect of a right is measured, can one say the right was not established?
questionAnswers.answer: Not directly. First check constitutive conditions. An unidentified causal effect limits the effect claim; realization, understanding, and justification remain separate judgments.

2.14.title: 2.14 Freezing and Reopening Questions
2.14.lead: Freezing makes the old question evaluable; reopening allows omissions and the framing itself to be challenged.
explanation: Freezing objects, aims, boundaries, and constraints before outcomes preserves reviewable comparisons; it does not permanently give the original questioner control over framing. Affected people, excluded people, and analysts may identify inadequate representation, uncounted losses, omitted members, or constraints mistakenly treated as given.

Whether a reopening request is accepted or rejected, record the request, reasons, and disposition. If accepted, establish a new question and state whether it replaces, sits alongside, or refines the old one. Preserve the old question, results, failures, and costs. Analysts can answer both questions side by side; actual institutional changes still depend on authorized procedures.

An unfavorable answer alone is insufficient reason to change the question. An answer exposing omitted affected people or defective representation can supply a reason. Distinguishing evidenced reflection prompted by results from retrospectively moving the success line depends on whether new reasons, old records, and the decision's grounds remain traceable.

For example, expanding ‘short-term output’ to ‘output and sustained labor burden’ leaves the original output result evaluated under its original aim. The new multi-objective comparison proceeds separately: it cannot erase failure of the original task, and freezing cannot justify refusing to acknowledge labor burdens.

keyTerms.text: Evidenced problems such as inadequate original representation, omitted positions or losses, and contestable constraints.
Whether the new question replaces, accompanies, or refines the old one must be stated publicly.

sourceQuotes.text: Freezing does not give the person who posed the question a monopoly over it.

argumentSteps: Freezing objects, aims, boundaries, and constraints before outcomes preserves reviewable comparisons; it does not permanently give the original questioner control over framing. distinctions.rightText: Registering a new question with reasons and explaining its relationship to the old one.

teachingExamples.title: Constructed teaching scenario
teachingExamples.text: A plan required completion within three months, but the task was unfinished. Moving the deadline to six months cannot make the old plan successful. If necessary care responsibilities were also found missing from the original plan, retain the three-month failure and separately assess a new plan including care conditions.
teachingExamples.boundary: Illustrates conditions and counterexamples only; it reports no real event or completed mechanism test.

boundaries: A new question does not overwrite old failure; freezing does not cancel standing to challenge.
Parallel analytical answers do not confer authority to change institutional objectives.

counterexamples.text: A plan required completion within three months, but the task was unfinished. Moving the deadline to six months cannot make the old plan successful. If necessary care responsibilities were also found missing from the original plan, retain the three-month failure and separately assess a new plan including care conditions.
counterexamples.effect: A new question does not overwrite old failure; freezing does not cancel standing to challenge.

questions: If flawed framing is discovered after results, is revision forever prohibited?

questionAnswers.question: If flawed framing is discovered after results, is revision forever prohibited?
questionAnswers.answer: Reopening with reasons is possible, while retaining the old task and results and recording the new question and decision procedure. Success under a new aim cannot be backfilled into the old one.

6.10.1.title: 6.10.1 Formation, Maintenance, Recovery, and Replication
6.10.1.lead: Initial formation, continued maintenance, recovery after damage, and replication elsewhere may depend on different conditions.
explanation: Formation asks how an arrangement arises; maintenance asks what keeps it operating; recovery asks how specified functional or identity goals are met again after damage; replication asks whether corresponding outcomes can be obtained with a different object, place, or scale. These four can have different answers, and earlier success guarantees no later stage.

Recovery here connects to repair in D1: specify the functional or identity goal, without automatically interpreting recovery as a return to the historical original. Maintenance may rely on different people, resources, and rules from formation. Replication may face different capabilities, authority, external conditions, and scale effects.

Failure of replication or expansion requires comparing at least four possibilities: the scheme itself failed, including that it did not cause the original result; implementation departed from the content specified beforehand; the target lacked enabling conditions specified beforehand; or scale changed the treatment or object. Each explanation needs independently checkable evidence, not selection after failure to protect the original conclusion.

Implementation content and enabling conditions must be stated before outcomes and independently checkable. ‘The conditions were actually wrong,’ introduced only after failure, enters only as a candidate for the next round. Records obtained after outcomes that check previously declared conditions should be evaluated as evidence, not categorically excluded merely because collection was late.

keyTerms.text: Conditions for emergence and for continued operation require separate evidence.
Implementation content and enabling conditions declared before outcomes and independently checkable.

sourceQuotes.text: The four are judged separately, and none can vouch for another. All four are also descriptive judgments and do not mean that the arrangement should be maintained, recovered, or replicated.

argumentSteps: Formation asks how an arrangement arises; maintenance asks what keeps it operating; recovery asks how specified functional or identity goals are met again after damage; replication asks whether corresponding outcomes can be obtained with a different object, place, or scale. These four can have different answers, and earlier success guarantees no later stage.

Recovery here connects to repair in D1: specify the functional or identity goal, without automatically interpreting recovery as a return to the historical original. Maintenance may rely on different people, resources, and rules from formation. Replication may face different capabilities, authority, external conditions, and scale effects.

Failure of replication or expansion requires comparing at least four possibilities: the scheme itself failed, including that it did not cause the original result; implementation departed from the content specified beforehand; the target lacked enabling conditions specified beforehand; or scale changed the treatment or object. Each explanation needs independently checkable evidence, not selection after failure to protect the original conclusion.

distinctions.rightText: Maintenance, recovery, and replication each require renewed checks of conditions and outcomes.

questions: Can failed replication elsewhere directly negate the original success?

questionAnswers.question: Can failed replication elsewhere directly negate the original success?
questionAnswers.answer: No. First distinguish the original arrangement, implementation, enabling conditions, and scale changes, preserving achievements within the original scope. At the same time, newly added post hoc conditions cannot evade the current failure.

7.6.1.title: 7.6.1 Mutual Reinforcement of Allocation and Capability
7.6.1.lead: Task allocation can shape capability, and capability differences can influence the next allocation. The actual connection across two rounds must be observed.
explanation: The candidate chain is: allocation of tasks, training, or opportunities → actual practice → capability change → next-round allocation. It has two aspects: continually giving critical work to one experienced person may create dependence on them; repeatedly excluding others from practice may create a gap then used to justify further exclusion.

Establishing the chain in this case requires at least two allocation rounds, identifiable decisions, a capability genuinely formed through practice, practice obtained mainly through that allocation, later allocation actually changing on the basis of capability, and a gap or concentration greater than initially. Capability formation, retention, and invocation require evidence under §4.5. Hearing ‘because they are highly capable’ does not prove the decision actually operates that way. Formal mechanism support additionally requires evidence under C10's carrier-reproduction route; two rounds of surface correlation cannot replace its conditions.

Competing explanations include prior capability gaps, different pay, missing authority, long training cycles, external certification or legal restrictions, personal choice or exit, general resource scarcity, and capability language concealing discrimination or interests. They may coexist. State what each predicts, rather than merely listing names.

Discriminating observations can ask whether the gap appeared before or after allocation; whether equally capable people receive comparable allocations; and whether the gap falls after training, resources, authority, and handovers meet standards declared beforehand. Units with similarly tight resources but different allocation rules can also be compared, with matched observation windows.

When observations contradict expectations, narrow or withdraw the corresponding link. If training does not reduce the gap, do not invent a new standard of ‘real training.’ Continued exclusion despite equal capability also challenges the link from capability to later allocation and requires examining other exclusion mechanisms. This candidate does not imply malice, irreversibility, or invalidity of prior achievements.

keyTerms.text: The actual distribution of tasks, training, resources, and opportunities across positions.
A connection across rounds in which allocation changes capability and capability changes allocation in turn.

sourceQuotes.text: If any one of these runs contrary to expectation, narrow or withdraw the claim for the corresponding link. It must not be said, only after no decline is seen, that the conditions granted were not genuine.

questions: Is always giving critical tasks to one person enough to prove mutual reinforcement of allocation and capability?

questionAnswers.question: Is always giving critical tasks to one person enough to prove mutual reinforcement of allocation and capability?

14.4.1.title: 14.4.1 Scope and Boundaries of the Responsibility to Identify
14.4.1.lead: First list every position that must be identified, then explain how far more distant effects are traced, why tracing stops, and how unknowns limit adoption.
explanation: Three categories must be listed in full: directly affected positions; low-power positions already known or pointed out by others; and positions the application module requires listing separately. Proportionality standards for shortening the search do not apply to them. High costs of speaking up or difficulty producing statistics cannot justify deletion.

Trace other indirect, second-order, cross-domain, and intergenerational positions along declared channels and the nine axes. The more severe, irreversible, widespread, or cumulative the potential harm, and the lower a position's power, the farther tracing should go. It may stop when further tracing cannot reasonably alter the judgment, comparison of plans, or protective arrangements. Record the boundary, channels checked, positions consulted, and unknowns.

If others identify undeclared channels, include them or explain rejection. Unknowns reasonably capable of revealing failure of the protection floor or changing minimum-harm, proportionality, or distributional comparisons block the affected part of adoption until further evidence, a narrower plan, or independently justified protection is provided. Record other unknowns and set observation and reidentification conditions.

The boundary, direct/indirect classification, and categories of unknowns cannot be decided solely by the party benefiting from a narrower boundary. Grounds must be public beforehand and open to appeal, with independent review for high-impact matters or conflicts of interest. The same responsibility applies to inaction; people already harmed do not disappear because their harm predates the decision.

Positions identified only later receive equal access to appeal, correction, and remedy without first proving the losses were foreseeable. Proportionate identification scope does not weaken protection of identified positions, and inability to exhaust all effects should not delay protection against known harms.

keyTerms.text: Unknowns with reasonable grounds to reveal protection failures or change comparisons of plans.
Inquiry scope adjusts to harm, accumulation, numbers affected, and positions of power.

sourceQuotes.text: Positions identified only after the fact enjoy the same appeal, correction, and remedy and need not first prove that they could have been foreseen.

14.9.1.title: 14.9.1 Bounded Judgment When Every Option Entails Loss
14.9.1.lead: When no option is lossless, a bounded recommendation remains possible while preserving unmet claims, losses, and subsequent responsibilities.
explanation: First include inaction, waiting, and maintaining the status quo in the same comparison. If every feasible option leaves irreversible loss, a pause cannot be portrayed as costless. Within the bounds allowed by evidence and explicit normative premises, a bounded judgment for deliberation should still be offered. Costs of waiting do not automatically generate authority to execute.

A recommendation must state the N-premises and decision rule used; why this option is provisionally selected; who bears which losses; which legitimate claims remain unmet; who retains duties of harm reduction, remedy, explanation, and review; and what conditions would change the choice. A public rule is a normative position undertaken by its proposer and adopter, not proof that the rule qualifies.

If the rule itself is disputed, judgments under different rules can be presented side by side. Show whether disagreement comes from facts, constraints, or values, rather than inventing an aggregate score that makes conflict disappear. The claims of those harmed do not become zero because a recommendation is made.

‘There is no alternative’ also requires review: are the constraints real, who controls them, and did questionable earlier decisions create them? Were options removed because decision-makers were unwilling to bear costs? Was a lack of authority referred to a subject with the necessary authority? This account is appealable and subject to review independent of the decision-maker.

Nonwaivable legal and protective requirements do not lapse because every option involves loss. Claims that even these cannot all be preserved must state which of them conflict and which options have been ruled out and on what grounds, and require a determination by a reviewer independent of the decision-maker. If the claim is not confirmed, return to options that do not breach them. If it is confirmed, the framework still supplies no authorized endorsement, and protections that can still be preserved continue to apply. Subjects with the relevant duties and powers may decide only within the narrowest scope under their own independent statutory or emergency authority, bearing responsibility and setting expiry and retrospective review.

An explicit recommendation bounded by evidence, normative premises, conditions, and authority.

teachingExamples.title: Constructed teaching scenario
teachingExamples.text: Two residents need nighttime assistance simultaneously, but only one carer is available. Under a publicly stated rule of addressing the more imminent danger first, one resident may be recommended for first assistance, while retaining the other's loss and the institution's remedial responsibility and investigating why only one carer was available. Responsibility for resource arrangements cannot simply be placed entirely on the worker on duty.
